name: (1-3)-BETA D GLUCAN LEVEL
interpretation: (1-3)-Beta-D-Glucan (BDG) is a cell wall component of most pathogenic fungi (Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis) but not Mucorales or Cryptococcus. BDG is used as a non-invasive biomarker for invasive fungal diseases (IFD). Elevated BDG supports diagnosis of invasive candidiasis, aspergillosis, and pneumocystis pneumonia. BDG is included in the EORTC/MSGERC diagnostic criteria for IFD as a major criterion. Levels correlate with disease burden and can be used to monitor treatment response. False positives occur with albumin infusion, surgical sponges, certain antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate), and Gram-positive bacteraemia. False negatives: Mucorales infections, cryptococcosis, antifungal prophylaxis. Turnaround: 4 hours. Reference ranges: assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting not required. Preparation: note immunosuppression status, neutropenia, antifungal therapy, recent surgery, albumin/IVIG use. Handling: separate within 30 min. Positive: IFD possible. Negative: does not exclude IFD. False positives: albumin, surgery, antibiotics. False negatives: Mucorales, Cryptococcus, prophylaxis. Reference ranges: assay-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 80 pg/mL (assay-specific). Positive: greater than or equal to 80 pg/mL (suggestive of IFD). Grey zone: 60-79 pg/mL. Sensitivity: approximately 70-80 percent for invasive candidiasis and aspergillosis. Specificity: limited by false positives. Reference ranges: assay-specific.
refs: Sources: EORTC/MSGERC IFD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 17-ALPHA HYDROXY PROGESTERONE (17-OHP)
interpretation: 17-α-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) is the cornerstone biomarker for diagnosing and monitoring 21-hydroxylase deficiency (21-OHD), the most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), accounting for >90% of cases. It is essential in neonatal screening for classic salt-wasting and simple virilizing forms, and in the evaluation of hirsutism, infertility, and menstrual irregularities in adult women (non-classic CAH). ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation testing is the gold standard for detecting heterozygous carriers and mild non-classic cases. Synacthen stimulation (60-minute) values ≥10 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) are diagnostic of 21-OHD, while levels >100 ng/mL indicate classic CAH. Important limitations: (1) 17-OHP levels exhibit significant diurnal variation with morning peaks, and are elevated by stress, illness, and the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle; (2) false positives in neonatal screening are common, particularly in premature and low-birth-weight infants; (3) liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) is strongly preferred over immunoassays for improved specificity, especially at low concentrations; (4) CYP21A2 gene sequencing is recommended for confirmatory diagnosis, as 17-OHP levels alone cannot distinguish between heterozygous carriers, non-classic, and simple virilizing forms.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (preferred) or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Collection: Early morning (08:00) fasting sample is critical due to diurnal variation (peak at ~08:00, nadir at ~22:00). For ACTH stimulation test: draw baseline sample, administer synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin 0.25 mg IV/IM), collect 60-minute sample. Note: In females, ideally collect in early follicular phase (days 3–7) of menstrual cycle to avoid luteal-phase elevation. Transport: within 2 hours; separate serum/plasma. Storage: stable 7 days at 2–8°C, >3 months at -20°C.
ref_ranges: Baseline (adults, 08:00): 0.3–2.0 ng/mL (0.9–6.0 nmol/L). ACTH-stimulated (60 min): <10 ng/mL (<30 nmol/L) excludes 21-OHD; 10–100 ng/mL indicates non-classic CAH; >100 ng/mL (>300 nmol/L) is diagnostic of classic CAH. Neonates (day 3–5): <30 ng/mL (<90 nmol/L); preterm: up to 100 ng/mL (300 nmol/L) may be normal. CAH newborn screening cut-offs are assay- and gestational age-specific; LC-MS/MS significantly reduces false positives.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY 17-KETOSTEROIDS
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary 17-Ketosteroids (17-KS) measures the total urinary excretion of C17-ketosteroid metabolites, which are metabolites of adrenal androgens (DHEA, DHEA-S, androstenedione) and testicular testosterone. In men, approximately 2/3 of 17-KS are derived from adrenal androgens and 1/3 from testicular androgens. In women and children, nearly all 17-KS are adrenal in origin. Elevated 17-KS: adrenal carcinoma (markedly elevated), Cushing syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), ectopic ACTH syndrome, testicular tumours. Low 17-KS: Addison disease, hypopituitarism, hypogonadism, renal failure, liver cirrhosis, malnutrition. 17-KS have been largely replaced by specific serum androgens (DHEA-S, testosterone, androstenedione) and by 17-Ketogenic steroids (17-KGS) which more accurately reflect cortisol production. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet and medications affect results. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age and gender: variable.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note adrenal symptoms, hirsutism, virilisation, medications (barbiturates, spironolactone). Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: adrenal CA, Cushing, CAH. Low: Addison, hypopituitarism. Replaced by: specific androgens. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Men: 8 to 20 mg/24h. Women: 5 to 15 mg/24h. Children: 1 to 8 mg/24h (age-dependent). Elevated: adrenal CA, Cushing, CAH. Low: Addison, hypogonadism. Diet: high-fat affects. Medications: barbiturates elevate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY 17-OH CORTICOSTEROIDS
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary 17-Hydroxycorticosteroids (17-OHCS) measures the urinary excretion of cortisol metabolites. 17-OHCS reflects adrenal cortisol production and is used to assess hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function. Elevated 17-OHCS: Cushing syndrome (ACTH-dependent and independent), ectopic ACTH syndrome, stress, obesity. Low 17-OHCS: Addison disease, hypopituitarism, adrenal suppression (exogenous glucocorticoid use), congenital adrenal hypoplasia. 17-OHCS has been largely replaced by serum cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, and the overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet, medications, and stress affect results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note Cushing features, medications (glucocorticoids, oestrogens), stress. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: Cushing syndrome. Low: Addison, hypopituitarism. Replaced by: UFC, DST. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Men: 3 to 10 mg/24h. Women: 2 to 8 mg/24h. Elevated: Cushing syndrome, stress. Low: Addison, hypopituitarism. Oestrogens: elevate. Glucocorticoids: suppress. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cushing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY 5-HYDROXY INDOLE ACETIC ACID (HIAA)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic Acid (5-HIAA) measures the urinary excretion of 5-HIAA, the main metabolite of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine). Elevated urinary 5-HIAA is the most sensitive and specific biochemical marker for carcinoid tumours (neuroendocrine tumours of the midgut). Carcinoid tumours produce excess serotonin, which is metabolised to 5-HIAA in the liver. Elevated 5-HIAA: carcinoid tumour (sensitivity approximately 70 percent, specificity approximately 90 percent), other serotonin-producing NETs. Normal 5-HIAA: does not exclude carcinoid tumour (some tumours produce little serotonin). False positives: foods rich in serotonin (bananas, walnuts, avocados, pineapples, plums, aubergines), drugs (MAO inhibitors, cough syrups with guaifenesin, methyldopa). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet and medications must be restricted for 48 hours before and during collection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: restrict serotonin-rich foods for 48h. Note carcinoid symptoms (flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze). Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: carcinoid tumour. False positives: serotonin-rich foods, MAO inhibitors. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 2 to 8 mg/24h (method-specific). Elevated: greater than 10 mg/24h (suggestive of carcinoid). Carcinoid: elevated (sensitivity 70%, specificity 90%). Foods: restrict for 48h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY ALDOSTERONE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Aldosterone measures the total urinary excretion of aldosterone and its metabolites. Aldosterone is the principal mineralocorticoid produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. It regulates sodium and potassium balance and blood pressure via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Elevated urinary aldosterone: primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome - aldosterone-producing adenoma, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia), renovascular hypertension, malignant hypertension, heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Low urinary aldosterone: Addison disease, hypopituitarism, ACE inhibitor/ARB use, heparin use, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) is the preferred screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism. Urinary aldosterone is less commonly used than serum aldosterone and plasma renin activity. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Sodium intake affects results (high sodium suppresses, low sodium stimulates). Medications affect results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note hypertension, hypokalaemia, medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone), sodium intake. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: primary hyperaldosteronism. Low: Addison, medications. ARR: preferred screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 5 to 20 ug/24h (on normal sodium diet). Elevated: greater than 20 ug/24h (primary hyperaldosteronism). Low: less than 5 ug/24h. Sodium: high suppresses, low stimulates. ARR: preferred screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY ARSENIC
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Arsenic measures total urinary arsenic excretion, which includes both organic (arsenobetaine, arsenosugars - relatively non-toxic) and inorganic arsenic (arsenite, arsenate - highly toxic) forms. Total urinary arsenic is used as a screening test for arsenic exposure. Inorganic arsenic is a known human carcinogen (skin, lung, bladder cancer) and causes peripheral neuropathy, skin changes (keratosis, melanosis), and cardiovascular disease. Limitations of total urinary arsenic: includes non-toxic organic arsenic from seafood (arsenobetaine), which can cause false-positive elevations. Patients should avoid seafood for 3 to 5 days before collection. Fractionated arsenic (inorganic arsenic, MMA, DMA) is preferred over total arsenic for assessing inorganic arsenic exposure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. CRITICAL: avoid seafood for 3 to 5 days before collection. Preparation: note occupational exposure, water source, seafood intake. Handle: metal-free container. Total arsenic: includes organic forms. Seafood: causes false positive. Fractionated: preferred for inorganic arsenic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 50 ug/L total arsenic (varies with diet). Elevated: arsenic exposure. Seafood: false positive (arsenobetaine). Fractionated: preferred. Inorganic arsenic: most toxic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Arsenic Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CADMIUM
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Cadmium measures cadmium excretion in urine, reflecting cumulative cadmium exposure. Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal that accumulates in the kidneys (half-life 10 to 30 years). Cadmium exposure occurs through smoking, occupational exposure (battery manufacturing, welding, pigments), and contaminated food/water. Cadmium nephrotoxicity: proximal tubular dysfunction (beta-2-microglobulinuria, glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia). Cadmium is classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen (lung cancer). Elevated urinary cadmium: chronic cadmium exposure (occupational, environmental, smoking). Limitations: urinary cadmium reflects cumulative body burden (long half-life). Acute exposure does not elevate urinary cadmium immediately. Smoking increases urinary cadmium by approximately 2-fold. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: increases with age.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note occupational exposure, smoking status, dietary sources. Handle: metal-free container. Elevated: chronic cadmium exposure. Smoking: increases approximately 2-fold. Nephrotoxicity: proximal tubular. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 3 ug/g creatinine (non-smokers). Smokers: up to 2-fold higher. Elevated: chronic exposure. Nephrotoxicity: proximal tubular dysfunction. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Cadmium Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CALCIUM
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Calcium

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- 24-hour urinary calcium excretion reflects net calcium balance: dietary intake, intestinal absorption, skeletal turnover, and renal handling.
- Hypercalciuria: Nephrolithiasis (most common metabolic risk factor in calcium stone formers), primary hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis (↑1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), malignancy (bone metastases), distal RTA, hyperthyroidism, glucocorticoid excess, loop diuretic use.
- Hypocalciuria: Renal failure, hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, thiazide diuretics, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH).
- Stone Risk: Combined with serum Ca, PTH, and 25-OH-vitamin D for complete stone workup.

Limitations
- Incomplete Collection: Most common cause of falsely low results. Verify with 24h creatinine.
- Dietary Impact: High-sodium, high-protein, or high-calcium diets significantly increase excretion.
- Preservative Required: Must have acid (6N HCl) to prevent calcium phosphate precipitation.
- Spot vs. 24h: Spot Ca/Cr ratio useful in children but insufficient for adult stone evaluation.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: 24-hour urine in acid-washed container. Add 10 mL 6N HCl as preservative (pH <2.0) to prevent calcium phosphate precipitation.
- Collection: Discard first morning void, collect all urine for 24 hours including final void.
- Patient Prep: Maintain usual diet; avoid excess calcium supplements. Ensure proper mixing of acid with urine.
- Storage: Stable 7 days at 2-8°C with HCl.
- Record: Total 24h volume, height, weight.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Normal: 100–300 mg/24h (2.5–7.5 mmol/24h) on unrestricted diet.
- Hypercalciuria: >300 mg/24h (>4 mg/kg/24h) or >0.1 mmol/kg/24h.
- FHH: Typically low-normal or frankly low excretion despite ↑Ca²⁺.
- Reference ranges method-dependent and should be lab-verified.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CATECHOLAMINES
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Catecholamines measures total urinary excretion of catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine). Elevated catecholamines are the hallmark of phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Urine metanephrines (normetanephrine and metanephrine) are now preferred over urine catecholamines as the first-line screening test for PPGL due to superior sensitivity (97 to 99 percent versus 85 to 90 percent for catecholamines). Elevated catecholamines: phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal elevation), paraganglioma, neuroblastoma, severe stress, exercise, medications. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives: stress, exercise, certain foods, medications. Less sensitive than metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note paroxysmal hypertension, headache, palpitations, medications. Handle: protect from light. Elevated: PPGL. Less sensitive: than metanephrines. False positives: stress, exercise, medications. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: PPGL, stress, exercise. Less sensitive: than metanephrines (85-90% vs 97-99%). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS PPGL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CHLORIDES
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Chloride

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Aids in evaluation of acid-base and electrolyte disorders, particularly metabolic alkalosis.
- Chloride-Responsive Metabolic Alkalosis (urine Cl <10–20 mEq/L): Vomiting, NG suction, diuretic therapy, post-hypercapnia.
- Chloride-Resistant Metabolic Alkalosis (urine Cl >20 mEq/L): Mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism, Cushing, Liddle syndrome, Bartter/Gitelman).
- Differential Diagnosis of Hyponatremia: Urine Cl mirrors Na in most cases.

Limitations
- Dietary Intake: Highly variable day-to-day; 24h collection more reliable than spot.
- Interpretation: Must be interpreted with serum electrolytes, pH/HCO₃, volume status, and drug history.
- Sample Integrity: No acid preservative; thymol or refrigeration preferred.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: 24-hour urine in preservative-free or thymol container. No acid preservative.
- Collection: Discard first morning void, collect 24 hours. Record total volume.
- Patient Prep: Maintain usual diet. Avoid diuretics before collection if possible.
- Storage: Stable 4 days at 2-8°C or 48h at room temp.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Normal: 110–250 mEq/24h (mmol/24h), varying with dietary salt intake.
- Cl-responsive metabolic alkalosis: urine Cl <10–20 mEq/L.
- Cl-resistant: urine Cl >20 mEq/L.
- Interpret with serum electrolytes and pH.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CHROMIUM
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Chromium measures chromium excretion in urine. Chromium is an essential trace element involved in insulin signalling and glucose metabolism. Chromium deficiency impairs glucose tolerance and may contribute to insulin resistance. Elevated urinary chromium: excessive chromium supplementation, occupational exposure (chromium plating, welding, leather tanning), chromium toxicity (renal tubular damage, liver damage, lung cancer). Low urinary chromium: chromium deficiency (rare in developed countries). Chromium supplementation is sometimes used for diabetes mellitus and weight loss, but evidence for efficacy is limited. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note supplements, occupational exposure, diabetes. Handle: metal-free container. Elevated: supplementation, occupational exposure. Low: deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.05 to 0.5 ug/24h (method-specific). Elevated: supplementation, occupational exposure. Low: deficiency (rare). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Chromium Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CITRATE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Citrate measures citrate excretion in urine. Citrate is an important inhibitor of calcium stone formation in urine. Citrate binds calcium in urine, reducing calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate supersaturation. Hypocitraturia (low urinary citrate) is a major risk factor for calcium-containing kidney stones and is found in approximately 50 percent of stone formers. Hypocitraturia: distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1 RTA - hallmark finding), chronic diarrhoea/malabsorption, metabolic acidosis, thiazide diuretics, high animal protein diet, strenuous exercise. Hypercitratuaria: primary hyperparathyroidism, proximal RTA (type 2), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Potassium citrate supplementation is the treatment of choice for hypocitraturia. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note kidney stone history, diet, medications (thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors). Handle: 2-8C. Low: hypocitraturia (stone risk). High: hyperparathyroidism. Type 1 RTA: hallmark finding. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 320 to 980 mg/24h (method-specific). Low: less than 320 mg/24h (hypocitraturia, stone risk). High: greater than 980 mg/24h. Type 1 RTA: low citrate. Thiazides: lower. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: European Association of Urology Stone Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY COBALT
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Cobalt measures cobalt excretion in urine. Cobalt is a trace element used in industrial applications (alloys, batteries, pigments) and is a component of vitamin B12. Cobalt toxicity causes pulmonary fibrosis (hard metal lung disease), cardiomyopathy, polycythaemia, and dermatitis. Elevated urinary cobalt: occupational exposure (cobalt alloy manufacturing, hard metal grinding), vitamin B12 supplementation, cobalt-containing hip prostheses (metal-on-metal). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note occupational exposure, hip prosthesis, B12 supplements. Handle: metal-free container. Elevated: occupational exposure, hip prosthesis. Cardiomyopathy: toxicity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1.0 ug/24h. Elevated: occupational exposure, B12 supplementation. Cardiomyopathy: toxicity. Metal-free: container required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Cobalt Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY COPPER
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Copper measures copper excretion in urine. Copper is an essential trace element involved in enzymes (ceruloplasmin, superoxide dismutase, cytochrome c oxidase). Elevated urinary copper is the hallmark biochemical finding in Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene. Wilson disease causes hepatic copper accumulation (hepatitis, cirrhosis), neuropsychiatric symptoms (tremor, dysarthria, personality changes), and Kayser-Fleischer corneal rings. Elevated urinary copper: Wilson disease (greater than 100 ug/24h), primary biliary cholangitis, chronic active hepatitis, nephrotic syndrome, copper intoxication. Low urinary copper: copper deficiency (rare, causes sideroblastic anaemia and myelopathy). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. Wilson disease: greater than 100 ug/24h is highly suggestive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms, family history. Handle: metal-free container. Elevated: Wilson disease, PBC, hepatitis. Low: copper deficiency. Wilson: greater than 100 ug/24h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 40 ug/24h. Wilson disease: greater than 100 ug/24h (highly suggestive). Elevated: PBC, hepatitis, nephrotic syndrome. Low: copper deficiency (rare). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AASLD Wilson Disease Guidelines; EASL Wilson Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CORTISOL
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- First-line screening test for Cushing syndrome. Reflects integrated free cortisol secretion over 24h, overcoming serum cortisol's circadian variability.
- Elevated UFC (especially >3× ULN) → high likelihood of Cushing syndrome. Values 1–3× ULN → may need confirmatory testing (dexamethasone suppression, CRH stimulation).
- Potential False Elevations: Stress, depression, alcoholism, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes, ACTH therapy.
- Adrenal Insufficiency: Low UFC but serum cortisol preferred for diagnosis.

Limitations
- Incomplete Collection: Most common cause of falsely low results.
- Drug Interferences: Carbamazepine, fenofibrate, some diuretics cross-react in immunoassays. LC-MS/MS preferred.
- Renal Function: GFR <30 mL/min reduces UFC excretion.
- Assay Variability: Immunoassays vs. LC-MS/MS give different ranges.
- Reference Range: 20–90 µg/24h by LC-MS/MS; immunoassay ranges vary (20–120 µg/24h).
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: 24-hour urine; no preservative needed (cortisol stable).
- Collection: Discard first morning void, collect all urine for 24 hours.
- Patient Prep: Avoid stress, strenuous exercise, and excessive alcohol during collection. Note any medications.
- Storage: Stable 7 days at 2-8°C.
- Record: Total 24h volume, time of collection, cortisol-secreting medications.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Normal: 20–90 µg/24h (55–248 nmol/24h) by LC-MS/MS.
- Immunoassay: 20–120 µg/24h (variable).
- >3× ULN → strong likelihood of Cushing syndrome.
- 1–3× ULN → requires confirmatory testing.
- Always interpret with serum cortisol, ACTH, and clinical context.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CREATININE
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Creatinine

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Primarily serves as validation marker for completeness of timed urine collection. Not a diagnostic test itself.
- Expected Daily Excretion: Males 20–25 mg/kg, Females 15–20 mg/kg. Values decline ~1%/year after age 40.
- Low Excretion: Suggests incomplete collection, muscle wasting, malnutrition, or chronic illness.
- High Excretion: Rare; may indicate excessive meat intake or vigorous exercise.
- Also used in creatinine clearance calculation (CrCl = [U-Cr × V] / S-Cr).

Limitations
- Muscle Mass Dependency: Values differ significantly by age, sex, ethnicity (lower in elderly, women, and Asian populations).
- Dietary Meat Intake: Can increase daily creatinine by 10–30%.
- Falsely Normal: Over-collection and under-collection can coincidentally produce normal results.
- Spectrophotometric Interference: Ketones, cephalosporins, bilirubin interference in Jaffe method.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: 24-hour urine, no preservative needed.
- Collection: Discard first morning void, collect all urine for 24 hours including final void.
- Patient Prep: Avoid excessive meat intake day before/ during collection.
- Storage: Stable 6 days at 2-8°C, 2 months at -20°C.
- Record: Total 24h volume, height, weight, age, sex.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Expected: Males 20–25 mg/kg/day (177–221 µmol/kg/day); Females 15–20 mg/kg/day (133–177 µmol/kg/day).
- Minimum adequate: ~15 mg/kg in adults, ~10 mg/kg in elderly.
- Low values → suspect incomplete collection.
- Expected total volume: 800–1800 mL (M), 600–1600 mL (F).

name: 24 HOURS URINARY CREATININE CLEARANCE
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Creatinine Clearance (CrCl)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Estimates GFR using 24h urinary creatinine excretion + single serum creatinine. Largely supplanted by eGFR, but remains useful when eGFR unreliable (unusual body habitus, extremes of muscle mass, pregnancy, amputees, vegetarian/vegan diets).
- CKD Staging: Stage 1: ≥90, Stage 2: 60–89, Stage 3: 30–59, Stage 4: 15–29, Stage 5: <15 mL/min.
- Tubular Secretion: CrCl overestimates true GFR by ~10–20% (creatinine is partially secreted by proximal tubules).

Limitations
- Incomplete Collection: Single greatest source of error.
- Overestimation: Tubular creatinine secretion proportional to serum creatinine; may overestimate GFR significantly in CKD.
- Diet/Medication: Cimetidine, trimethoprim, and ketones inhibit tubular secretion → reduce CrCl falsely.
- Muscle Mass: Low creatinine production (elderly, malnourished) → spuriously low CrCl.
- Cystatin C: May be preferred when CrCl unreliable.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Samples: 24h urine (no preservative) + serum creatinine drawn during collection (mid-morning day 2).
- Urine Collection: Discard first void, collect 24 hours.
- Patient Prep: Avoid strenuous exercise, cimetidine, and ketogenic diets.
- Storage: Urine stable 6 days at 2-8°C.
- Record: Total 24h volume, height, weight, age, sex for BSA correction.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Normal: 90–130 mL/min/1.73m² (adults <40 y). Declines ~1 mL/min/year after 40.
- CKD Stages: ≥90 (S1), 60–89 (S2), 30–59 (S3), 15–29 (S4), <15 (S5).
- BSA correction: Adjusted CrCl = Measured × (1.73/BSA).
- CrCl overestimates GFR by 10–20% due to tubular secretion.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY DOPAMINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Dopamine measures dopamine excretion in urine. Dopamine is a catecholamine neurotransmitter and precursor of noradrenaline and adrenaline. Urinary dopamine is primarily derived from renal tubular metabolism of L-DOPA. Elevated urinary dopamine: neuroblastoma, phaeochromocytoma (sometimes), L-DOPA therapy, dietary factors. Low urinary dopamine: Parkinson disease (reduced central dopamine but urinary levels may not reflect central levels). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet and medications affect results. Less commonly measured than catecholamines and metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.

Elevated: neuroblastoma, L-DOPA therapy. Low: Parkinson (central, not necessarily urinary). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: neuroblastoma, L-DOPA therapy. Low: Parkinson (central). Less common: than catecholamines/metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY ELECTROLYTES
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Electrolytes (Panel)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Integrated assessment of daily Na, K, Cl (often Ca, Mg, P, uric acid) excretion.
- Dietary Assessment: Objective measure of salt intake (correlates with cardiovascular risk).
- Hypertension Workup: High Na + low K suggests dietary imbalance; aldosterone/renin ratio with electrolytes.
- Nephrolithiasis Workup: Na, Ca, uric acid, citrate, oxalate, Mg all required.
- FENa/FEK: Fractional excretion of Na/K used in AKI differential.

Limitations
- Collection Completeness: Highly dependent on accurate 24h collection. Verify with 24h creatinine.
- Dietary Variation: Single 24h collection may not reflect long-term intake. 2–3 collections preferred.
- Preservative Compatibility: Cannot use acid preservative if multiple analytes (Ca vs. uric acid/citrate require different preservatives). Multiple containers may be needed.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: Multiple 24-hour collections (at least 2 for dietary assessment).
- Containers: May need separate containers for different analytes (acid vs. plain vs. alkali). Check lab requirements.
- Collection: Discard first void, collect 24 hours. Maintain usual diet.
- Patient Prep: Record dietary intake. Note all medications (diuretics, ACEi/ARBs, NSAIDs affect values).
- Storage: Varies by analyte. Generally 4°C refrigeration.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Na: 40–220 mEq/24h (varies with intake; Western 100–250).
- K: 25–125 mEq/24h.
- Cl: 110–250 mEq/24h.
- FENa <1%: prerenal AKI; >2%: intrinsic renal.
- Multiple collections recommended for accurate dietary assessment.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY FREE KAPPA LIGHT CHAINS
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Free Kappa Light Chains measures the excretion of free kappa immunoglobulin light chains in urine. Free light chains (FLC) are produced by plasma cells and are normally filtered by the glomerulus and reabsorbed by the proximal tubule. Elevated urinary kappa FLC: multiple myeloma, light chain amyloidosis, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), Bence Jones proteinuria. The urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) and immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) are used to detect and characterise monoclonal light chains. Free kappa light chain excretion greater than 1 mg/L (or kappa/lambda ratio abnormal) is suggestive of a plasma cell disorder. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Renal function affects results (reduced GFR increases FLC excretion). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note myeloma symptoms (bone pain, anaemia, renal failure), family history. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: myeloma, AL amyloidosis, MGUS. Bence Jones: monoclonal light chains. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1 mg/L. Elevated: myeloma, AL amyloidosis, MGUS. Bence Jones: monoclonal. Renal function: affects. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IMWG Myeloma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY FREE LIGHT CHAINS KAPPA AND LAMBDA
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Free Light Chains Kappa and Lambda measures total urinary excretion of both kappa and lambda immunoglobulin light chains. Simultaneous measurement allows calculation of the kappa/lambda ratio, which is more sensitive than individual light chain measurement for detecting monoclonal gammopathies. The kappa/lambda ratio in urine is normally 0.3 to 3.0. A ratio outside this range suggests clonal expansion of plasma cells producing one light chain type. Elevated kappa/lambda ratio: kappa-restricted myeloma, MGUS, AL amyloidosis. Low kappa/lambda ratio: lambda-restricted myeloma, MGUS, AL amyloidosis. Urine electrophoresis and immunofixation should be performed alongside FLC measurement. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Renal function affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note myeloma symptoms, family history. Handle: 2-8C. Kappa/lambda ratio: 0.3 to 3.0 (normal). Ratio abnormal: clonal expansion. Renal function: affects. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal kappa/lambda ratio: 0.3 to 3.0. Kappa-restricted: ratio greater than 3.0 (kappa myeloma). Lambda-restricted: ratio less than 0.3 (lambda myeloma). Renal function: affects absolute values. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY GLUTAMIC ACID QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Glutamic Acid measures the excretion of glutamic acid (glutamate), the most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Urinary glutamic acid excretion reflects amino acid metabolism and renal handling. Elevated urinary glutamic acid: renal tubular disorders (Fanconi syndrome), aminoacidurias, liver disease, maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). Low urinary glutamic acid: malnutrition, liver failure. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Less commonly measured than specific amino acid screens. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY GLUTAMINE (QUANTITATIVE)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Glutamine measures glutamine excretion in urine. Glutamine is the most abundant free amino acid in plasma and a key nitrogen carrier. It is a non-essential amino acid synthesised in skeletal muscle and brain. Elevated urinary glutamine: renal tubular disorders (Fanconi syndrome), hyperammonaemia (urea cycle disorders), liver cirrhosis, stress states. Low urinary glutamine: malnutrition, impaired renal tubular reabsorption. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY GLYCINE QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Glycine measures glycine excretion in urine. Glycine is the simplest non-essential amino acid and a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. Elevated urinary glycine: hyperglycinemia (non-ketotic and ketotic forms), renal tubular disorders (Fanconi syndrome), primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (glycine is a precursor to glyoxylate which is converted to oxalate). Low urinary glycine: malnutrition, impaired renal tubular reabsorption. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY HCG BETA SUBUNIT
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary hCG Beta Subunit measures the excretion of the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in urine. The beta subunit is unique to hCG and distinguishes it from LH, FSH, and TSH which share alpha subunits. Elevated urinary hCG beta: pregnancy (normal and ectopic), gestational trophoblastic disease (molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma), testicular tumours (seminoma, non-seminomatous GCT), ovarian germ cell tumours, pituitary hCG production (menopausal women). Urine hCG is the basis of standard pregnancy tests. Serial quantitative hCG measurements are used to monitor GTD treatment response and to differentiate normal from abnormal early pregnancy. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives: pituitary hCG in menopausal women, hook effect at very high concentrations. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note pregnancy status, GCT history, menopausal status. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: pregnancy, GTD, GCT. False positives: menopausal pituitary hCG. Hook effect: very high concentrations. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: undetectable (non-pregnant). Elevated: pregnancy, GTD, GCT. Serial: monitor treatment. Hook effect: at very high concentrations. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY HOMOVANILLIC ACID (HVA)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Homovanillic Acid (HVA) measures the urinary excretion of HVA, the final metabolic product of the dopamine pathway. HVA is produced by the metabolism of dopamine via DOPAC and then COMT. Elevated urinary HVA is a biochemical marker for neuroblastoma (in children) and phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma. In neuroblastoma, HVA and VMA are elevated in approximately 90 percent and 75 percent of cases respectively. Combined HVA and VMA measurement increases diagnostic sensitivity. Elevated HVA: neuroblastoma (childhood), phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma, L-DOPA therapy, stress, certain foods. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet and medications affect results. Less specific than metanephrines for PPGL. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note symptoms, medications (L-DOPA), diet. Handle: protect from light. Elevated: neuroblastoma, PPGL. Combined with VMA: increases sensitivity. Less specific: than metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 10 mg/24h (children), less than 15 mg/24h (adults). Elevated: neuroblastoma, PPGL. Combined HVA+VMA: higher sensitivity. Less specific: than metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY IMMUNOFIXATION ELECTROPHORESIS
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Immunofixation Electrophoresis (IFE) detects and identifies monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones protein) in urine. IFE is more sensitive than serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) for detecting free light chains and is the gold standard for confirming monoclonal gammopathies. Positive urine IFE: multiple myeloma (approximately 30 to 50 percent of patients have Bence Jones proteinuria), light chain amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), light chain deposition disease. Urine IFE is essential for staging and monitoring of plasma cell disorders. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives: can occur with concentrated urine. False negatives: may miss low-level light chain excretion. Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative for monoclonal band).
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note myeloma symptoms (bone pain, anaemia, renal failure). Handle: 2-8C. Positive: monoclonal light chains. Bence Jones: myeloma, AL amyloidosis. Qualitative: positive/negative. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative for monoclonal band. Positive: monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones protein). Myeloma: 30-50% have Bence Jones. AL amyloidosis: often positive. MGUS: may be positive. Reference ranges: qualitative.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY IRON
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Iron measures iron excretion in urine. Iron is an essential trace element and a component of haemoglobin, myoglobin, and many enzymes. Iron excretion in urine is normally very low because the body tightly conserves iron. Elevated urinary iron: haemosiderinuria (intravascular haemolysis, PNH), iron overload states, iron supplementation, haemochromatosis. Low urinary iron: iron deficiency (rarely measured in this context). Urine haemosiderin (Prussian blue stain) is a more common test for intravascular haemolysis than quantitative urinary iron. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with no preservative (metal-free container). CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note haemolysis, iron overload, supplements. Handle: metal-free container. Elevated: haemosiderinuria, iron overload. Low: iron deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.1 mg/24h. Elevated: haemosiderinuria, iron overload. Haemosiderin stain: more common. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY MAGNESIUM
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Magnesium

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Assesses renal Mg handling in hypo- and hypermagnesaemia.
- Hypomagnesaemia + UMg <1 mmol/24h (<24 mg/day): Extrarenal losses (poor intake, GI losses, redistribution).
- Hypomagnesaemia + UMg >1 mmol/24h (>24 mg/day): Renal Mg wasting (Gitelman syndrome, Bartter syndrome, diuretic phase of ATN, post-transplant, drugs: loop diuretics, calcineurin inhibitors, amphotericin, cisplatin, EGF receptor inhibitors).
- Hypermagnesaemia + UMg >6 mmol/24h: Renal Mg wasting (rare — osmotic diuresis, nephrocalcinosis).
- Fractional Excretion of Mg (FEMg): (UMg × S-Cr) / (0.7 × S-Mg × U-Cr) × 100. FEMg >2-3% suggests renal Mg wasting.
- Nephrolithiasis: Hypomagnesiuria is a risk factor for calcium oxalate stones.

Limitations & Interferences
- Incomplete Collection: Most common cause of falsely low UMg.
- Diet: Low Mg intake reduces excretion regardless of renal function.
- Preanalytical: Hemolysis falsely elevates serum Mg (RBCs contain Mg). Acid preservative recommended.
- FEMg: Requires paired serum Mg + Cr and urine Cr. FeNa and FEK should also be checked for overlapping tubulopathies.
pre_analytical:
Pre-analytical Requirements
- Sample: 24-hour urine in acid-washed container. 10 mL 6N HCl or boric acid preservative acceptable.
- Collection: Discard first void, collect 24 hours.
- Patient Prep: Maintain usual diet. Avoid Mg-containing antacids/supplements before collection.
- Storage: Stable 7 days at 2-8°C with acid preservative.
- Record: Total 24h volume. Ordered with serum Mg for FEMg calculation.
ref_ranges:
Reference Range Notes
- Normal: 50–150 mg/24h (2.1–6.2 mmol/24h).
- Hypomagnesaemia + UMg <24 mg/day (<1 mmol/24h): suggests extrarenal losses.
- Hypomagnesaemia + UMg >24 mg/day (>1 mmol/24h): renal Mg wasting.
- FEMg >2-3%: suggests renal Mg wasting.
- Reference ranges method-dependent.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY METANEPHRINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Metanephrine measures metanephrine and normetanephrine excretion over 24 hours. Metanephrines are metabolites of catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) produced by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) in catecholamine-producing tissues. Elevated 24H urinary metanephrine: pheochromocytoma (adrenal paraganglioma, 95% sensitivity), paraganglioma (extra-adrenal sympathetic/parasympathetic), neuroblastoma (children), drugs (tricyclics, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics). Pheochromocytoma: elevated metanephrine greater than 2x upper limit of normal is highly suggestive. Metanephrines: more sensitive than catecholamines due to continuous tumour metabolism versus episodic catecholamine secretion. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet: bananas, caffeine, vanilla may affect results. Drugs: tricyclics, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics cause false elevation. Stress: acute illness causes transient elevation. Reference ranges: method-specific.

ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Pheochromocytoma: greater than 2x ULN. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY MICROALBUMIN
interpretation:
Based on the provided context, here is the information regarding 24-hour urinary microalbumin:

Sample Collection & Preanalytical Requirements
*   Definitive method: A 24-hour sample is the definitive means of demonstrating and quantifying proteinuria [Source 6, p.938].
*   Acceptable samples: The 24-hour collection, along with overnight collections and first-morning samples, are considered acceptable for albumin measurement [Source 9, p.1985].
*   Collection protocols: Urine can be collected via various methods, including 24-hour, spot, or timed specimens, with the specific method depending on the downstream analyses [Source 2, p.290].
*   Limitations:
    *   24-hour collections are described as "inconvenient" for patients [Source 5, p.2074].
    *   They can suffer from false-positive results which are not as easily avoided as with plasma measurements [Source 5, p.2074].
*   Normalization: For spot or timed urine specimens (especially in children), creatinine adjustment is crucial for normalization [Source 3, p.2296].

Reference Ranges & Diagnostic Utility
*   Diagnosis of albuminuria: Diagnosis requires demonstration of increased albumin loss (increased ACR or albumin in a timed collection) in at least 2 out of 3 urine samples collected in the absence of infection or acute metabolic crisis [Source 6, p.938].
*   Reference intervals: Gender-specific reference intervals exist for urinary metanephrines to optimize diagnostic sensitivity and specificity [Source 3, p.2296]. Age-appropriate reference intervals are particularly important for urinary measurements in children [Source 3, p.2296].
*   Factors affecting results: Urine samples should not be collected after exertion, during urinary tract infection, acute illness, or after an acute fluid load [Source 9, p.1985].

Interferences & Limitations
*   Interferences: Results can be affected by exercise within 24 hours, posture, diuresis, infection, fever, marked hyperglycemia, and marked hypertension [Source 9, p.1985].
*   Limitations: The context does not provide specific clinical interpretation details or a direct reference range for "microalbumin" under this specific term.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY NICKEL
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Nickel measures nickel excretion in urine. Nickel is a trace element with both essential and toxic properties. Elevated urinary nickel: occupational exposure (nickel mining, plating, alloy manufacturing), environmental contamination, nickel allergy (contact dermatitis), renal tubular damage. Low urinary nickel: nickel deficiency (rare, poorly characterised in humans). Nickel allergy: one of the most common causes of allergic contact dermatitis. Nickel is a Group 1 carcinogen (IARC). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. Occupational history essential for interpretation. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY NOR ADRENALINE (NOR-EPINEPHRINE)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Noradrenaline (Norepinephrine) measures the excretion of noradrenaline, the principal postganglionic sympathetic neurotransmitter. Noradrenaline is produced by decarboxylation of dopamine in sympathetic nerve endings and adrenal medulla. Elevated urinary noradrenaline: phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal elevation), paraganglioma, neuroblastoma, severe stress, exercise, certain medications (tricyclic antidepressants, clonidine withdrawal). Normetanephrine is now preferred over noradrenaline for PPGL screening due to superior sensitivity (97-99% vs 85-90%). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives: stress, exercise, medications. Less sensitive than normetanephrine. Reference ranges: method-specific.

ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: PPGL, stress. Less sensitive: than normetanephrine (85-90% vs 97-99%). Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY NOR-METANEPHRINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Normetanephrine measures the O-methylated metabolite of noradrenaline. Normetanephrine is produced by the enzyme catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) and is the preferred first-line screening test for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Normetanephrine is superior to catecholamines because it is produced continuously (not just during tumour secretion), providing more consistent elevation. Sensitivity: 97 to 99 percent for PPGL detection. Specificity: limited by false positives from medications, stress, and certain foods. Elevated normetanephrine: phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma, neuroblastoma, medications (MAO inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics), renal failure. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives common. Confirmatory: plasma free metanephrines or imaging. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note medications, symptoms. Handle: protect from light. Elevated: PPGL (sensitivity 97-99%). False positives: medications, stress. Confirmatory: plasma metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: PPGL (sensitivity 97-99%). False positives: medications, stress, renal failure. Confirmatory: plasma metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY NTxN TELLOPEPTIDE (COLLAGEN CROSSLINKED)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary NTx (N-Telopeptide of Type I Collagen) measures bone resorption marker. NTx is a cross-linked peptide released during type I collagen degradation, which constitutes approximately 90 percent of bone matrix. Elevated urinary NTx: increased bone resorption - osteoporosis (postmenopausal, glucocorticoid-induced), Paget disease of bone, bone metastases (breast, prostate, lung cancer), hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, immobilisation. Low urinary NTx: decreased bone resorption - bisphosphonate therapy, denosumab therapy. NTx is used to monitor antiresorptive therapy response (decrease of greater than 30 percent suggests adequate response). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Creatinine correction often used. Diurnal variation present. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine with boric acid preservative. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note bone disease, fracture risk, medications (bisphosphonates, denosumab). Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: increased resorption. Low: antiresorptive therapy. Monitor: treatment response. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: increased bone resorption. Low: antiresorptive therapy response. Monitor: greater than 30% decrease indicates response. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY OXALATE (OXALIC ACID)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Oxalate measures oxalate excretion in urine. Oxalate is a metabolic end-product and a major constituent of calcium oxalate kidney stones (the most common stone type). Hyperoxaluria (elevated urinary oxalate) is a significant risk factor for calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis. Primary hyperoxaluria types 1, 2, and 3 are autosomal recessive disorders of hepatic oxalate metabolism (AGXT, GRHPR, HAO1 gene mutations). Type 1 is the most common and severe, causing recurrent stones, nephrocalcinosis, and systemic oxalosis (renal failure, cardiac, bone involvement). Secondary hyperoxaluria: dietary (high oxalate foods - spinach, rhubarb, nuts), enteric (inflammatory bowel disease, short bowel syndrome, fat malabsorption - increased calcium binding in gut leaves oxalate unbound), medications (vitamin C megadosing). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet must be controlled. Metal-free container. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY PHOSPHOROUS
interpretation:
## 24-Hour Urinary Phosphorus

Based on the provided context, here is the information regarding 24-hour urinary phosphorus analysis:

### Preanalytical & Sample Collection Requirements
- Urine should be collected in 6 mol/L HCl (20 to 30 mL for a 24-hour specimen) to avoid precipitation of phosphate complexes. [Source 7, p.2129]
- A non-restricted diet is standard for 24-hour collections. [Source 7, p.2129]

### Reference Ranges (Conventional)
- On a nonrestricted diet: 0.4 to 1.3 g/24 hours (12.9 to 42 mmol/24 hours). [Source 7, p.2129]
- Alternative method: Fasting morning spot or 1- to 2-hour timed collections (with creatinine adjustment) are used for the renal phosphate threshold (TmPO4/GFR). [Source 7, p.2129]
- Note: All tests involving urinary calcium and phosphate excretion require a creatinine clearance ge 40-50 mL/min for valid interpretation. [Source 5, p.84]

### Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Increased urinary phosphate (U up): Hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D-resistant rickets, immobilization after paraplegia or a fracture, vitamin D intoxication, renal tubular damage (e.g., Fanconi's syndrome), familial hypophosphatemia, and nonrenal acidosis. [Source 5, p.84]
- Decreased urinary phosphate (U down): Hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, parathyroidectomy. [Source 5, p.84]
- Significant diurnal variation exists in urinary phosphate excretion, with values in the afternoon being highest [Source 5, p.84] and output varies widely depending on diet [Source 7, p.2129].
- Measurement of phosphaturia is not useful in detecting osteomalacia. [Source 5, p.84]

### Limitations & Interferences
- Very dilute urine (creatinine < 2 mmol/L) is unsuitable for analysis [Source 2, p.1408].
- Refrigerate the 24-hour collection (collected in a dark container with 5 g of Na2CO3) [Source 9, p.84].
- Protect from light - porphyrin/pigment degradation can occur if exposed [Source 2, p.1408].

name: 24 HOURS URINARY POTASSIUM
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Potassium measures potassium excretion over 24 hours. Potassium is the major intracellular cation, critical for cardiac conduction, neuromuscular function, and acid-base balance. Urinary potassium helps differentiate causes of hypokalaemia and hyperkalaemia. Elevated urinary potassium: renal potassium wasting (renal tubular acidosis, Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, diuretic use, hyperaldosteronism), metabolic alkalosis. Low urinary potassium: extrarenal potassium loss (GI losses - vomiting, diarrhoea, laxative abuse), transcellular shift (alkalosis, insulin excess), inadequate dietary intake. Urinary K greater than 20 mmol/day in hypokalaemia: renal potassium wasting (renal cause). Urinary K less than 20 mmol/day in hypokalaemia: extrarenal loss (GI, transcellular). Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Diuretic use affects interpretation. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY PROTEIN
interpretation:
Based on the retrieved context, here is the information on 24-hour urinary protein:

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- A 24-hour urine sample is the "definitive means of demonstrating and quantifying the presence of proteinuria".
- Proteinuria is a "potent risk marker for progressive kidney disease," and "reduction of protein excretion is a therapeutic target".
- Diagnosis of albuminuria requires "increased albumin loss... in at least two out of three urine samples collected in the absence of infection or an acute metabolic crisis" to avoid errors from short-term clinical changes and high variability.

Reference Ranges
- Upper limit: 150 to 300 mg/day depending on laboratory.
- This is a "clinical decision point" defined by expert groups, dependent on age, gender, hypertension, and obesity.
- "Clinical proteinuria" (reagent strip) equates to ~300 mg/L or ~500 mg/day loss.

Sample Collection & Preanalytical Requirements
- 24-hour collection is the definitive method, but spot ACR/PCR is used in practice for convenience.
- Patient must be given clear illustrated instructions.

Limitations & Interferences
- Limitations: Inaccuracies in urinary collection; high within-subject variation.
- Interferences (increase protein): Aminoglycosides, non-visible hematuria, infused modified gelatin solutions (plasma expanders).
- Specificity issues: Most methods react more strongly with albumin than globulin; marked between-method variation for low-molecular-weight proteins.

interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Protein Electrophoresis (UPEP) separates and identifies proteins in urine by electrophoretic mobility. name: 24 HOURS URINARY SODIUM
interpretation:
Based strictly on the provided context, here is the clinical information on 24-hour urinary sodium:

Preanalytical Requirements & Sample Collection
* A 24-hour urine collection is recommended for chemistry analytes. Spot or timed specimens may suffice with creatinine adjustment.
* Documentation of whether the patient intentionally drank excessive amounts of water to aid voiding.

Reference Ranges
* Adults: 40-220 mEq/day (mmol/day).
* Children (6-10 yr): Male 41-115, Female 20-69.
* Children (10-14 yr): Male 63-177, Female 48-168.

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
* Prerenal vs. Renal/Postrenal Oliguria: FENa most reliable.
    * Prerenal: Urinary Na < 20 mmol/L; FENa < 1.
    * Renal/Postrenal: Urinary Na > 40 mmol/L; FENa > 1.
* Diurnal Variation: Nighttime excretion is one-fifth of peak daytime rate.
* Low Values (<15 mmol/L): Prerenal acidosis.
* High Values: Acute tubular necrosis; salt-losing nephritis.

Interferences & Limitations
* Falsely Low: Salt depletion.
* Medications: Caffeine, diltiazem, diuretics, ethanol, lithium (increase output); bacitracin, carbamazepine (decrease output).
* Note: The context does not provide specific details on analytical method limitations (ISE vs. colorimetric) or specific storage temperature requirements for 24-hour urine sodium.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY UREA
interpretation:
Based on the retrieved context, I can provide the following information regarding 24-hour urinary urea:

Preanalytical Requirements & Sample Collection
The context indicates that 24-hour urine is the standard collection method for most urine chemistry tests. General instructions: void first morning urine (not included), collect all subsequent urine for 24 hours including next morning's first void.

Storage & Stability
- Urine samples stable for 4 days at 2-8°C and 2 days at 15-25°C. Process immediately for best results.

Reference Ranges
The provided context does not include specific reference ranges for 24-hour urinary urea.

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
* Measurement of urinary urea in timed samples provides a crude index of overall nitrogen balance. Used to guide protein requirements in critically ill patients and those receiving parenteral nutrition.
* Limitations in GFR Estimation: Due to tubular back-diffusion, urea clearance underestimates GFR. Poor clinical tool for estimating GFR.
* Outdated Practice: Averaging urea clearance and creatinine clearance to estimate GFR is no longer recommended.

Interferences & Limitations
* Endogenous Ammonia: Interference from endogenous ammonia with urease-glutamate dehydrogenase method, particularly in aged samples, some urines, and certain metabolic disorders.
* Analytical Performance: Acceptable within-run CVs <3.0% and between-day imprecision <4.0%.

Preanalytical Requirements
* 24-hour collection recommended for chemistry analytes. Spot/timed specimen may suffice with creatinine adjustment.
* Patient should not intentionally drink excessive water.

Reference Ranges (Serum Urea)
* Healthy Adults: 2.1 to 7.1 mmol/L (6-20 mg/dL as urea nitrogen).
* Adults >60: 2.9 to 8.2 mmol/L (8-23 mg/dL).
* Higher in men than women; increases with age (~50% from 20s to 70s).
* Pregnancy: Associated with lower urea concentrations.
* Pediatric: Low in first year, rises to slightly above adult levels to ~age 10, then falls to young adult values.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY UREA NITROGEN
interpretation:
Urinary urea nitrogen (UUN) is a direct measure of the end-product of protein metabolism excreted by the kidneys.

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Nitrogen Balance Studies: UUN is 85-90% of total urinary nitrogen, critical for calculating nitrogen balance in hospitalized patients (parenteral nutrition, critical illness, burns). Positive balance = anabolism; negative = catabolism.
- Protein Catabolism Assessment: Elevated UUN suggests increased catabolism (surgery, trauma, sepsis, starvation, high-protein diet, Cushing syndrome).
- Renal Function: Low UUN may indicate renal impairment or decreased protein intake/malnutrition.
- Dialysis Adequacy: Used for URR and Kt/V calculations.
- Dietary Protein Intake: Correlates with protein intake in stable patients with normal renal function.

Interferences & Limitations
- Hydration Status: Affected by urine volume; accurate 24-hour collection essential.
- Renal Function: Underestimates total nitrogen excretion in renal impairment.
- Incomplete Collection: Most common error; verify with creatinine excretion.
- Non-Urea Nitrogen: Does not account for stool/skin/fistula losses.

Reference Ranges
- Urine Urea Nitrogen: ~6-17 g/24h (varies with protein intake)
- Nitrogen Balance: N-bal = (Protein intake / 6.25) - (UUN + 4 g/day)

name: 24 HOURS URINARY URIC ACID
interpretation:
24-Hour Urinary Uric Acid

Preanalytical Requirements & Sample Collection
- Sample Type: 24-hour urine collection standard; fasting morning spot/timed collections with creatinine adjustment may be used as alternatives.
- Patient Instructions: Void first morning urine, collect all urine for 24 hours, include next morning's first void. Container may have preservative (Thymol) — do NOT discard.
- Recording: Height, weight, and total 24-hour volume must be recorded.

Reference Ranges
- Conventional Units: 250-750 mg/24h (1.5-4.5 mmol/24h)
- Gender: Higher in males than females; varies with age.

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Increased: Gout, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, tumor lysis syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, chemotherapy, high-purine diet.
- Decreased: Renal failure, hypothyroidism, allopurinol/probenecid therapy.
- Kidney Stone Risk: High uric acid a risk factor for uric acid nephrolithiasis, particularly in acidic urine (pH < 5.5).

Interferences & Limitations
- Diet: High purine intake (red meat, seafood, alcohol) can falsely elevate.
- Drugs: Diuretics, aspirin (low-dose decreases excretion; high-dose increases), uricosuric agents affect results.
- Dilute Urine: Creatinine < 2 mmol/L unsuitable for accurate measurement.
- Storage: Stable 4 days at 2-8°C, 2 days at 15-25°C.

name: 24 HOURS URINARY VANILLYL MANDELIC ACID (VMA)
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Vanillyl Mandelic Acid (VMA) measures the final metabolic product of catecholamine (adrenaline and noradrenaline) metabolism. VMA was historically the primary screening test for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). VMA has been largely replaced by urine metanephrines (normetanephrine and metanephrine) which offer superior sensitivity (97-99% vs 65-77% for VMA). Elevated urinary VMA: phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal elevation), paraganglioma, neuroblastoma, severe stress, certain medications. VMA is still used in some settings, particularly in resource-limited areas and in paediatric neuroblastoma screening. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. False positives: medications (MAO inhibitors, catecholamines), stress, certain foods. Less sensitive than metanephrines. Reference ranges: method-specific.

Elevated urinary zinc: zinc supplementation, Wilson disease treatment (penicillamine increases zinc excretion), acrodermatitis enteropathica (genetic zinc deficiency paradoxically shows increased urinary zinc during treatment), renal tubular disorders. Low urinary zinc: zinc deficiency (dietary, malabsorption), liver cirrhosis, chronic renal failure. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Metal-free container required. interpretation: 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic Acid (5-HIAA) Random Urine measures 5-HIAA concentration in a spot urine sample. 5-HIAA is the main metabolite of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) and is used as a screening marker for carcinoid tumours (neuroendocrine tumours of the midgut). Random urine 5-HIAA is less reliable than 24-hour urine due to variable urine concentration but is useful as a rapid screening test. Elevated random urine 5-HIAA: carcinoid tumour, other serotonin-producing NETs, certain foods (bananas, walnuts, avocados), medications (MAO inhibitors). interpretation: 5-Hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin) Urine measures serotonin excretion in urine. Serotonin is a biogenic amine neurotransmitter produced by enterochromaffin cells in the gut (approximately 90 percent of body serotonin) and by platelets. Elevated urinary serotonin: carcinoid tumour (neuroendocrine tumours of the midgut), mast cell disorders, myeloproliferative neoplasms. Low urinary serotonin: depression (urinary levels do not reliably reflect CNS levels). Urinary 5-HIAA is more commonly measured than urinary serotonin. name: 5-HYDROXYTRYPTAMINE (SEROTONIN)
interpretation: 5-Hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin) Serum measures whole blood serotonin concentration. Limitations: platelet count affects results (high platelets = high serotonin). Less commonly measured than urine 5-HIAA. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: A1C DERIVED AVERAGE GLUCOSE (ADAG)
interpretation: A1C Derived Average Glucose (ADAG) is a calculated estimate of mean plasma glucose over the preceding 2 to 3 months based on the haemoglobin A1C result. The ADAG formula converts A1C percentage to an estimated average glucose (eAG) in mg/dL: eAG (mg/dL) equals 28.7 times A1C minus 46.7. This provides a more intuitive representation of glycaemic control for patients and clinicians. An A1C of 7 percent corresponds to an eAG of approximately 154 mg/dL. ADAG helps patients understand what their A1C means in terms of daily glucose values. Limitations: ADAG is a calculated value, not a direct measurement. The formula is derived from a study population and may not apply equally to all ethnic groups, patients with haemoglobin variants, or those with conditions affecting red blood cell lifespan. Conditions that alter RBC lifespan (haemolytic anaemia, iron deficiency, blood transfusion, pregnancy) affect both A1C and ADAG accuracy. Reference ranges: same as A1C. EAG does not replace A1C for diagnosis or monitoring.
pre_analytical: Sample: Derived from serum A1C result. No additional blood draw required. Preparation: same as A1C. No fasting required. ADAG: eAG equals 28.7 times A1C minus 46.7. A1C of 7 percent equals eAG of 154 mg/dL. Limitations: does not apply to all ethnic groups equally. Haemoglobin variants: affect accuracy. RBC lifespan: affects accuracy. Reference ranges: same as A1C.
ref_ranges: Derived from A1C. A1C of 5 percent equals eAG of 97 mg/dL. A1C of 7 percent equals eAG of 154 mg/dL. A1C of 9 percent equals eAG of 212 mg/dL. A1C of 12 percent equals eAG of 298 mg/dL. Limitations: calculated not measured. Haemoglobin variants: affect. Reference ranges: same as A1C.
refs: Sources: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes; NGSP ADAG Study; manufacturer IFU.

name: ACETAMINOPHEN (PARACETAMOL)
interpretation: Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) measures the concentration of acetaminophen in serum. Acetaminophen is one of the most commonly used analgesics and antipyretics worldwide. Acetaminophen overdose is a leading cause of acute liver failure in many countries. Acetaminophen is primarily metabolised in the liver by glucuronidation and sulphation. A small fraction is metabolised by CYP2E1 to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), a toxic metabolite that is normally detoxified by glutathione. In overdose, glutathione is depleted and NAPQI causes hepatocyte necrosis. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram is used to predict hepatotoxicity risk based on serum acetaminophen concentration and time since ingestion. Treatment: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) replenishes glutathione. Limitations: timing of sample relative to ingestion is critical. Multiple peaks possible with sustained-release formulations. Reference ranges: therapeutic 10 to 30 mcg/mL. Toxic: varies by time post-ingestion.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: note time of ingestion. Preparation: note amount ingested, other substances, liver disease. Handle per standard. Timing: critical for Rumack-Matthew. NAC: antidote. Therapeutic: 10-30 mcg/mL. Toxic: time-dependent.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 10 to 30 mcg/mL. Toxic: time-dependent (Rumack-Matthew nomogram). 4 hours post-ingestion: greater than 150 mcg/mL suggests hepatotoxicity. NAC: antidote. Sustained-release: multiple peaks. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Rumack-Matthew Nomograph; manufacturer IFU.

name: ACETYL CHOLINE RECEPTOR ANTIBODY (ACHR)
interpretation: Acetylcholine Receptor (AChR) Antibody measures autoantibodies directed against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. AChR antibodies are the pathognomonic autoantibodies of myasthenia gravis (MG), present in approximately 85 percent of generalised MG and 50 percent of ocular MG. AChR antibodies can be binding (most common), blocking, or modulating types. Binding antibodies: most sensitive, detected by radioimmunoassay. Blocking antibodies: prevent acetylcholine binding, cause more severe disease. Modulating antibodies: cause receptor degradation. AChR antibody-negative MG: approximately 15 to 20 percent of MG patients are seronegative. In these patients, anti-MuSK (muscle-specific kinase) antibodies should be tested. Seronegative MG: may have low-affinity antibodies detectable only by cell-based assay. Limitations: false positives: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (rarely). False negatives: early disease, ocular-only MG, seronegative MG. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note muscle weakness (fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia), medications (anticholinesterases, immunosuppressants), thymoma history. Handle per standard. Positive: MG (85% generalised). Seronegative: 15-20%. Anti-MuSK: test if AChR negative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: MG (85% generalised, 50% ocular). Seronegative: 15-20%. Anti-MuSK: test if AChR negative. False positives: ALS, LEMS (rare). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MGFA Myasthenia Gravis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ACID PHOSPHATASE (ACP)
interpretation:
Acid Phosphatase

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Primary Clinical Use: Historically used as a tumor marker for prostatic carcinoma, especially for monitoring therapy and detecting metastasis.
- Other Causes of Elevation: Gaucher disease, multiple myeloma, thrombocytopenia, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and bone resorption conditions (Paget disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, hyperparathyroidism).
- Gaucher Disease: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) is specifically elevated and used to monitor disease activity.
- Cellular Origin: Highest concentrations in prostate, spleen, bone marrow, platelets, and erythrocytes.

Limitations
- PSA Replacement: Acid phosphatase has largely been replaced by PSA for prostate cancer screening and diagnosis due to PSA's superior sensitivity and specificity.
- Poor Sensitivity: Limited as a screening tool for early prostate cancer; role is chiefly for advanced/metastatic disease monitoring.
- Hemolysis: In vitro hemolysis falsely elevates results.
- Sample Stability: Highly labile — must be processed rapidly or serum acidified and frozen. Significant activity lost within 2 hours at room temperature unless serum is separated and acidified to pH 5-6.
- Non-Prostatic Sources: Elevations from bone, liver, platelets must be considered, especially in women/children.

Reference Ranges: Method-dependent.
pre_analytical: - Primary Clinical Use: Serum acid phosphatase as a tumor marker for prostatic carcinoma — monitoring therapy and detecting metastasis. - Other Causes of Elevation: Gaucher disease, multiple myeloma, thrombocytopenia, BPH, Paget disease, hyperparathyroidism. - TRAP: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase elevated in Gaucher disease. - Replaced by PSA for screening due to superior sensitivity/specificity.
ref_ranges: - PSA Replacement: Acid phosphatase largely replaced by PSA for prostate cancer screening. - Poor Sensitivity: Chiefly for advanced/metastatic disease monitoring. - Hemolysis: Falsely elevates results. - Labile: Significant activity lost within 2h at RT unless serum acidified to pH 5-6. - Non-Prostatic Sources: Bone, liver, platelet sources must be considered (especially women/children). - Reference Range: Method-dependent.
