name: ACID PHOSPHATE PROSTATIC FRACTION
interpretation: Serum Acid Phosphatase Prostatic Fraction (PAP) measures the prostate-specific isoenzyme of acid phosphatase. PAP is a glycoprotein secreted by prostate epithelial cells. Elevated PAP: metastatic prostate cancer (bone metastases), benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostatic biopsy/instrumentation. PAP: largely superseded by PSA for prostate cancer screening but retains value in monitoring metastatic disease. Limitations: prostatic massage, biopsy, catheterisation cause transient elevation. Assay variability. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note prostate disease, recent procedures. Handle per standard. Elevated: metastatic prostate cancer, BPH. PSA: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 3 ng/mL (method-specific). Elevated: metastatic prostate cancer. PSA: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AUA Prostate Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ACYL CARNITINE-QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Acyl Carnitine Quantitative measures the concentration of individual acylcarnitine species in blood (serum/plasma). Acylcarnitines are intermediates in fatty acid beta-oxidation and are used to screen for inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) affecting fatty acid oxidation. Elevated specific acylcarnitine species indicate specific fatty acid oxidation disorders: C2 (acetylcarnitine): elevated in multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MADD/glutaric aciduria type II), long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (LCHAD). C4 (butyrylcarnitine): elevated in short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (SBCAD). C5 (isovalerylcarnitine): elevated in isovaleric acidemia (IVA). C8 (octanoylcarnitine): elevated in medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD). C14:1: elevated in very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (VLCADD). C16 (palmitoylcarnitine): elevated in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (LCHAD). Neonatal screening: acylcarnitine profile is the basis of newborn screening for IEM. Limitations: fasting state affects results (non-fasting: elevated C2). Medications affect results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dried blood spot (neonatal screening) or serum/plasma. Preparation: note family history of IEM, clinical symptoms (vomiting, lethargy, metabolic acidosis, hepatomegaly). Handle: 2-8C or -20C. Neonatal: dried blood spot. Specific species: indicate specific disorders. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and fasting state). Elevated specific species: indicate specific FAO disorders. MCADD: C8 elevated. VLCADD: C14:1 elevated. Neonatal: screening basis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Newborn Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ACYLCARNITINE QUANTITATIVE NEONATAL
interpretation: Acylcarnitine Quantitative Neonatal is a newborn screening test performed on dried blood spots to detect inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) affecting fatty acid oxidation, amino acid metabolism, and organic acid metabolism. The acylcarnitine profile includes multiple species (C0 through C18) and is analysed by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). The neonatal screen also typically includes amino acid analysis. Elevated specific acylcarnitine species indicate specific disorders: C8: MCADD. C14:1: VLCADD. C5: IVA. C3: methylmalonic acidemia (MMA), propionic acidemia (PA). C0 (free carnitine): carnitine deficiency. Low C0: primary or secondary carnitine deficiency. Limitations: false positives: prematurity, medication effects (valproic acid), parenteral nutrition. False negatives: early collection (before 24h of age), metabolic decompensation not yet occurred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dried blood spot (heel prick). CRITICAL: collect after 24 hours of age and after first feed. Preparation: note prematurity, medications, parenteral nutrition. Handle per standard. MCADD: C8. VLCADD: C14:1. False positives: prematurity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated species: indicate specific IEM. MCADD: C8. VLCADD: C14:1. False positives: prematurity, medications. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Newborn Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA)
interpretation: Serum Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) measures the activity of adenosine deaminase, an enzyme involved in purine metabolism. ADA is elevated in T-lymphocyte activation and is used as a marker of tuberculous effusions. Elevated ADA: tuberculosis (pleural, peritoneal, pericardial effusions), infectious mononucleosis, lymphoproliferative disorders, haemolytic anaemia. ADA in TB: sensitivity 90%, specificity 90% for tuberculous pleural effusion. ADA greater than 40 U/L: strongly suggestive of TB. Limitations: method-specific cut-offs. Lymphocytic predominance may elevate ADA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note TB exposure, lymphoproliferative disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: TB, infectious mononucleosis. TB: ADA greater than 40 U/L. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 40 U/L (method-specific). TB: greater than 40. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BTS Pleural Effusion Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - ASCITIC FLUID
interpretation: Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) in Ascitic/Peritoneal Fluid measures ADA activity in ascitic fluid. ADA in ascitic fluid is used to differentiate tuberculous peritonitis from other causes of ascites (cirrhotic, malignant). Elevated ADA in ascites: tuberculous peritonitis (sensitivity 85-100%, specificity 85-95%). ADA greater than 40 U/L in ascitic fluid: strongly suggestive of TB peritonitis. Limitations: cut-off varies by population. Lymphocytic exudative effusions may elevate ADA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Ascitic fluid (diagnostic paracentesis). Preparation: note TB risk, HIV, immunosuppression. Handle per standard. Elevated: TB peritonitis. ADA greater than 40 U/L. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 40 U/L. TB peritonitis: greater than 40. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AASLD Ascites Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - CSF
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — CSF

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM): CSF-ADA is significantly elevated in TBM.
- Diagnostic Performance: Cut-off ~10 U/L gives sensitivity 80-90%, specificity 85-95% for distinguishing TBM from other meningitides.
- Differential Diagnosis: Not elevated in viral meningitis or partially treated bacterial meningitis — particularly useful for lymphocytic meningitis in TB-prevalent populations.
- Prognostic: Persistently elevated during treatment → poor response or complications.

Limitations
- False Positives: Lymphomatous meningitis, neurobrucellosis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis.
- Cut-off Variability: Optimal cut-off varies by population/lab.
- Preanalytical: CSF must be free of blood (RBCs contain ADA).
- Age: Pediatric reference ranges needed for children.
pre_analytical: - TBM: CSF-ADA significantly elevated. - Performance: ~10 U/L cut-off, sensitivity 80-90%, specificity 85-95% for TBM vs. other meningitides. - Not elevated in viral or partially treated bacterial meningitis. - Useful for lymphocytic meningitis in TB-prevalent populations.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: Lymphomatous meningitis, neurobrucellosis, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis. - Cut-off varies by population. - Blood contamination falsely elevates (RBCs contain ADA). - Pediatric reference ranges needed.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - OTHER FLUIDS
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Other Fluids

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Tuberculous Effusions: Key diagnostic test for tuberculous serositis in pleural, peritoneal, pericardial fluids.
- Pleural Fluid: >40 U/L → sensitivity >90%, specificity >85% for tuberculous pleurisy (lymphocytic predominant).
- Peritoneal Fluid: >30 U/L in ascites → highly suggestive of tuberculous peritonitis.
- Pericardial Fluid: Elevated in tuberculous pericarditis (sensitivity 85-90%).
- Other: Elevated in rheumatoid arthritis (synovial fluid), brucellosis, certain malignancies (e.g., lymphoma).

Limitations
- False Positives: Empyema, rheumatoid effusions, lymphoma, mesothelioma, parapneumonic effusions.
- Cut-off Variability: Optimal cut-offs vary by fluid type (pleural vs. peritoneal vs. pericardial) and population.
- Lymphocyte Predominance: Highest diagnostic value in lymphocyte-predominant effusions. Neutrophil-predominant + elevated ADA → consider empyema.
- Hemolyzed Samples: Blood contamination falsely elevates ADA.
pre_analytical: - Tuberculous Effusions: Key test for tuberculous serositis (pleural, peritoneal, pericardial). - Pleural: >40 U/L, sens >90%, spec >85% for TB pleurisy. - Peritoneal: >30 U/L → TB peritonitis. - Pericardial: Elevated in TB pericarditis. - Also elevated in RA (synovial), brucellosis, lymphoma.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: Empyema, RA effusions, lymphoma, mesothelioma, parapneumonic. - Cut-off varies by fluid type. - Highest value in lymphocyte-predominant effusions. - Blood contamination falsely elevates.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - PERICARDIAL FLUID
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Pericardial Fluid

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Tuberculous Pericarditis: Valuable diagnostic tool, especially in high-prevalence settings.
- Diagnostic Performance: Cut-off ~30-40 U/L → sensitivity 85-90%, specificity 80-85%.
- Combined Testing: With IGRA or PCR for M. tuberculosis, diagnostic accuracy improves significantly.
- Prognostic: Persistently elevated levels despite treatment may indicate complicated course.

Limitations
- False Positives: Rheumatoid pericarditis, uremic pericarditis, lymphomatous involvement, bacterial pericarditis.
- Prevalence-Dependent: PPV depends on local TB prevalence. In low-prevalence settings, positive result likely false positive.
- Nadir Effect: Very early TB pericarditis (<2 weeks) may not show elevated ADA.
- Hemolyzed/Clotted Samples: May yield unreliable results.
pre_analytical: - Tuberculous Pericarditis: Valuable diagnostic tool, cut-off ~30-40 U/L, sensitivity 85-90%, specificity 80-85%. - Combined Testing: With IGRA or PCR improves accuracy. - Prognostic: Persistently elevated → complicated course.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: RA, uremic, lymphomatous, bacterial pericarditis. - Prevalence-Dependent: Low PPV in low-TB settings. - Nadir Effect: <2 weeks may be normal. - Hemolyzed/Clotted: Unreliable.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - PERINEPHRIC FLUID
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Perinephric Fluid

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Used in investigation of suspected perinephric tuberculosis or abscess.
- General principle: ADA rises in body fluids with T-cell mediated immune activation (mycobacterial antigens).
- Limited Data: Specific perinephric fluid ADA data is limited. Cut-offs extrapolated from pleural/pericardial ADA principles.

Limitations
- Limited Evidence Base: Cut-off values for TB diagnosis in perinephric fluid not well-established.
- Blood Contamination: Falsely elevates ADA (RBCs contain enzyme).
- Infection vs. Malignancy: Both TB and lymphoma/metastatic disease can elevate ADA.
pre_analytical: - Perinephric Abscess/TB: ADA used in investigation. - Principle: Rises with T-cell activation to mycobacterial antigens. - Limited Data: Cut-offs not well-established; extrapolate from other body fluids.
ref_ranges: - Limited Evidence: Not as well-studied as pleural/pericardial ADA. - Blood Contamination: Falsely elevates. - Infection vs. Malignancy: Both can elevate ADA.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - PERITONEAL FLUID
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Peritoneal Fluid

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Tuberculous Peritonitis: Highly sensitive/specific marker. Cut-off ~30 U/L → sensitivity 90-95%, specificity 90-98%.
- Differential Diagnosis: Distinguishes TB peritonitis from cirrhotic ascites, SBP, and malignant ascites.
- Lymphocytic Ascites: Highest performance in lymphocyte-predominant ascites (lymphocytes >50% of WBCs).
- Combination Testing: Elevated ADA + SAAG <1.1 g/dL highly suggestive of TB peritonitis.

Limitations
- False Positives: Secondary bacterial peritonitis, pancreatitis-associated ascites, peritoneal carcinomatosis, lymphoma, hepatic hydrothorax.
- Cirrhosis: Decompensated cirrhosis may show mild elevation (20-30 U/L).
- Early Disease: Very recent-onset may have normal ADA; repeat after 1-2 weeks if suspicion remains.
- Hemolyzed Samples: Blood contamination falsely elevates.
pre_analytical: - Tuberculous Peritonitis: Cut-off ~30 U/L, sensitivity 90-95%, specificity 90-98%. - Differential: TB peritonitis vs. cirrhotic ascites, SBP, malignant ascites. - Lymphocytic Ascites: Highest diagnostic performance. - SAAG <1.1 g/dL + elevated ADA → highly suggestive of TB.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: Secondary bacterial peritonitis, pancreatitis, carcinomatosis, lymphoma. - Cirrhosis: Mild elevation (20-30 U/L) in decompensated cirrhosis. - Early Disease: May be normal; repeat in 1-2 weeks. - Blood contamination falsely elevates.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - PLEURAL FLUID
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Pleural Fluid

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Tuberculous Pleurisy: First-line diagnostic test in high-prevalence settings. Cut-off ~40 U/L → meta-analytic sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%.
- ADA2 Isoenzyme: Accounts for majority of ADA elevation in TB pleural effusions.
- Lymphocytic Exudates: Most useful in lymphocyte-predominant exudative effusions (lymphocytes >50%).
- Prognostic: Persistently high levels during treatment → complicated parapneumonic effusion.

Limitations
- False Positives: Parapneumonic effusions/empyema, rheumatoid pleurisy, lymphoma, lung cancer, mesothelioma.
- Neutrophil-Predominant: With elevated ADA → likely bacterial empyema, not TB.
- Cut-off Variation: Optimal cut-off varies (35-50 U/L range depending on region/prevalence).
- HIV Co-infection: Lower pleural ADA due to impaired T-cell response → potential false negatives.
- Early Disease: May be normal in first 2 weeks of TB pleurisy.
pre_analytical: - Tuberculous Pleurisy: First-line test. Cut-off ~40 U/L, sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%. - ADA2 Isoenzyme: Majority of TB elevation. - Lymphocytic Exudates: Highest utility.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: Empyema, RA, lymphoma, lung cancer, mesothelioma. - Neutrophil-Predominant + elevated ADA: Consider bacterial empyema. - HIV: Lower ADA → false negatives. - Early Disease: May be normal in first 2 weeks.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - PUS
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Pus

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Differentiates tuberculous abscesses from pyogenic abscesses.
- Pott disease (spinal TB) and tuberculous psoas abscess — common applications.
- Diagnostic Performance: Cut-off 50-100 U/L → sensitivity 80-90%, specificity 85-95% for TB vs. pyogenic.
- Lymph Node TB: Aspirated pus shows markedly elevated ADA.

Limitations
- False Positives: Any pyogenic infection with high neutrophil/macrophage content can elevate ADA.
- Variable Cut-offs: No universally accepted cut-off; depends on anatomical source.
- Viscosity: May require pre-treatment (hyaluronidase/sonication) before accurate measurement.
- Matrix Effects: Pus may contain substances interfering with enzymatic assay.
- Blood Contamination: Frankly bloody pus → falsely elevated ADA.
pre_analytical: - Differentiates TB abscesses from pyogenic. Used in Pott disease, psoas abscess, lymph node TB. - Cut-off 50-100 U/L, sensitivity 80-90%, specificity 85-95%.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: Any pyogenic infection can elevate. - Variable Cut-offs: No universal; depends on source. - Viscosity: May need pre-treatment. - Blood: Falsely elevates.

name: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - SYNOVIAL FLUID
interpretation:
ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) — Synovial Fluid

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Differentiates tuberculous arthritis from other causes of monoarthritis (RA, crystal-induced, pyogenic).
- Diagnostic Performance: Cut-off 10-15 U/L → sensitivity 85-95%, specificity 80-90%.
- Rheumatoid Arthritis: Also elevated but lower ADA2 proportion — ADA2 isoenzyme fractionation helps distinguish TB (high ADA2) from RA (lower ADA2 proportion).
- Treatment Monitoring: Decreasing levels may indicate response to anti-TB therapy.

Limitations
- False Positives: RA, gouty arthritis, reactive arthritis, septic arthritis (non-TB bacterial).
- Crystal-Induced Arthritis: Acute gout/pseudogout → transient ADA elevation.
- Cut-off Variability: Optimal cut-off varies (higher cut-offs e.g., 20 U/L improve specificity but reduce sensitivity).
- Bloody Tap: Traumatic arthrocentesis → falsely elevated.
pre_analytical: - Differentiates tuberculous arthritis from other monoarthritis. Cut-off 10-15 U/L, sensitivity 85-95%, specificity 80-90%.
ref_ranges: - False Positives: RA, gout, reactive, septic arthritis. - Crystal-Induced: Transient elevation. - ADA2 Fractionation: Helps distinguish TB (high ADA2) from RA. - Bloody Tap: Falsely elevates.

name: ADIPONECTIN
interpretation: Serum Adiponectin measures the concentration of adiponectin, an adipokine (hormone) secreted by adipose tissue. Adiponectin has anti-inflammatory, anti-atherogenic, and insulin-sensitising properties. Low adiponectin levels are associated with obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease. Elevated adiponectin: anorexia nervosa, liver cirrhosis, type 1 diabetes mellitus. Adiponectin is inversely correlated with body mass index (BMI) and visceral adiposity. Adiponectin is also inversely associated with colorectal cancer risk. Adiponectin is not routinely measured in clinical practice but is used in research settings. Limitations: not routinely measured. Affected by obesity, insulin resistance, liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note BMI, metabolic syndrome, liver disease. Handle per standard. Low: obesity, insulin resistance, T2DM. High: anorexia, cirrhosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (sex and method dependent). Low: obesity, T2DM, metabolic syndrome. High: anorexia, cirrhosis. Not routine: research use. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ADRENOCORTICOTROPIC HORMONE (ACTH)
interpretation:
ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Cushing Syndrome Differential: ACTH-Dependent (elevated ACTH → pituitary adenoma vs. ectopic production) vs. ACTH-Independent (suppressed ACTH → adrenal adenoma/carcinoma).
- Adrenal Insufficiency: Primary (Addison) → low cortisol + elevated ACTH. Secondary (pituitary) → low cortisol + low/inappropriately normal ACTH.
- Cosyntropin Stimulation Test: Gold standard for adrenal insufficiency (250 mcg IV/IM, 30/60-min cortisol).

Limitations
- Highly Labile: Must collect in pre-chilled EDTA tube, immediate cold centrifugation, frozen transport. Degraded rapidly by proteases at RT.
- Circadian Rhythm: Peaks 6-8 AM, nadirs midnight. Collection timing critical.
- Stress Response: Acute illness, pain, fever, psychological stress elevate ACTH.
- Drug Effects: Glucocorticoids (including topical/inhaled) suppress ACTH.
- Assay Variability: IRMA vs. CLIA differ in specificity; reference ranges assay-dependent.

Reference Range: Morning (8 AM): 10-60 pg/mL (2.2-13.2 pmol/L) — assay dependent.
pre_analytical: - Cushing: ACTH-Dependent (pituitary/ectopic) vs. ACTH-Independent (adrenal). - Adrenal Insufficiency: Primary = ↑ACTH, Secondary = ↓/inappropriately normal ACTH. - Cosyntropin Test: Gold standard.
ref_ranges: - Highly Labile: Pre-chilled EDTA, immediate cold centrifugation, frozen. - Circadian Rhythm: 6-8 AM peak. - Stress: Acute illness/psychological stress elevates. - Drugs: Glucocorticoids suppress. - Assay Variability: IRMA vs. CLIA.

VDC SOP: Wintrobes Clinical Hematology 13E (2013) (p.12600)

VDC SOP: DHEA (p.18)

name: ALBUMIN
interpretation:
Albumin (Serum)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- Liver Function: Synthesized exclusively by the liver. Decreased albumin → chronic liver disease (cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis).
- Nutritional Status: Marker of protein-energy malnutrition; long half-life (15-20 days) → reflects chronic status.
- Nephrotic Syndrome: Hypoalbuminemia hallmark of nephrotic syndrome.
- Protein-Losing Enteropathy: Crohn disease, other GI protein loss → low albumin.
- Inflammatory States: Negative acute-phase reactant; decreases in inflammation, infection, malignancy, trauma.
- Hyperalbuminemia: Rare; usually dehydration/hemoconcentration.

Limitations
- Long Half-Life: Not useful for acute nutritional status changes.
- Negative Acute-Phase: Inflammatory states lower albumin independently of nutrition/liver function.
- Hemolysis, Icterus, Lipemia: Can interfere with assay.
- Reference Range: Method/lab dependent.
pre_analytical: - Liver Function: ↓ in chronic liver disease. - Nutrition: Marker of chronic PEM. - Nephrotic Syndrome: Hypoalbuminemia hallmark. - Negative Acute-Phase Reactant: ↓ in inflammation/infection. - Hyperalbuminemia: Rare; dehydration.
ref_ranges: - Long Half-Life (15-20d): Not for acute assessment. - Negative Acute-Phase: Inflammation lowers independently. - Interferences: Hemolysis, icterus, lipemia. - Reference Range: Method/lab dependent.
refs:
VDC SOP: Procedure for handling of reagents (p.35)
VDC SOP: Quality Manual - Himayathnagar (p.363)
VDC SOP: Format for routine instrument daily maintenance (p.34)
Ref: Clinical Chemistry-Analytes - KIDNEY FUNCTION TESTS (p.1065)

name: ALBUMIN - FLUID
interpretation:
Albumin — Fluid (SAAG)

Clinical Interpretation & Diagnostic Utility
- SAAG (Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient): Preferred method for classifying ascites. SAAG = Serum Albumin - Ascitic Fluid Albumin.
- SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL → Transudate (portal hypertension: cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd-Chiari).
- SAAG <1.1 g/dL → Exudate (peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome).
- Accuracy: >95% correct classification, outperforms total protein methods.
- Pleural Fluid: Serum-pleural albumin gradient similarly classifies pleural effusions.

Limitations
- Therapeutic Paracentesis: Large-volume removal transiently alters gradient.
- Paired Sample Required: Accuracy depends on simultaneously collected serum albumin.
- Hemodilution/Hemoconcentration: Affects results.
- Chylous Ascites: May produce intermediate gradient.
- Collection Timing: Serum and fluid must be collected within 24 hours.
pre_analytical: - SAAG: Preferred for classifying ascites. ≥1.1 = transudate (portal HTN). <1.1 = exudate. - Accuracy: >95%, outperforms total protein methods.
ref_ranges: - Therapeutic Paracentesis: Transiently alters gradient. - Paired Sample: Simultaneous serum required. - Hemodilution/Hemoconcentration: Affects results. - Chylous Ascites: May give intermediate gradient.
refs: Content synthesized from standard clinical biochemistry references.

name: ALCOHOL QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Alcohol Quantitative Serum measures the concentration of ethanol in serum. Ethanol is absorbed from the GI tract, metabolised primarily by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) in the liver to acetaldehyde, and then by aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) to acetate. Serum ethanol levels correlate with clinical effects: 10-25 mg/dL: mild euphoria. 25-50 mg/dL: intoxication. 50-100 mg/dL: stupor. Greater than 100 mg/dL: coma. Greater than 400 mg/dL: potentially lethal. Ethanol metabolism follows zero-order kinetics (approximately 15-20 mg/dL per hour). Serum ethanol is used for: clinical assessment of intoxication, monitoring alcohol withdrawal, forensic purposes, and as an osmolal gap marker. Limitations: timing relative to last drink is critical. Serum/plasma ethanol is approximately 1.2 times whole blood ethanol. Active metabolites not measured. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fluoride-oxalate preferred to prevent in vitro glycolysis). Preparation: note time of last drink, amount, other substances, liver disease. Handle per standard. Zero-order kinetics: 15-20 mg/dL/h. Serum: ~1.2x whole blood. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0 mg/dL (abstinent). Mild: 10-25 mg/dL. Intoxication: 25-50 mg/dL. Stupor: 50-100 mg/dL. Coma: greater than 100 mg/dL. Lethal: greater than 400 mg/dL. Zero-order: 15-20 mg/dL/h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACEP Ethanol Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALCOHOL QUANTITATIVE - URINE
interpretation: Alcohol Quantitative Urine measures the concentration of ethanol in urine. Urine ethanol reflects serum ethanol concentration with a lag time and is used as a screening test for recent alcohol consumption. Urine ethanol is positive when serum ethanol is greater than approximately 30 to 50 mg/dL. Urine ethanol can remain positive for up to 12 to 24 hours after last drink (depending on dose and renal function). Urine ethanol does not correlate well with serum ethanol concentration or clinical impairment. Urine ethanol is used for: workplace drug testing, forensic purposes, and monitoring alcohol abstinence. Ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) are more sensitive and longer-lasting markers of alcohol exposure (up to 80 hours). Limitations: does not correlate with serum ethanol or impairment. Lag time. False positives: fermentation in urine. EtG/EtS: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note drinking history, time of last drink. Handle per standard. Positive: greater than 30-50 mg/dL serum. Lag time. Up to 12-24h. EtG/EtS: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0 mg/dL (abstinent). Positive: recent drinking. Lag time. Up to 12-24h. EtG/EtS: more sensitive (up to 80h). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALDOLASE
interpretation: Serum Aldolase measures the concentration of aldolase (fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A) in serum. Aldolase is a glycolytic enzyme present in high concentrations in skeletal muscle, heart, liver, and brain. Serum aldolase is a marker of muscle damage and is elevated in: dermatomyositis and polymyositis (more specific than CK for inflammatory myopathies), muscular dystrophy (Duchenne, Becker), muscle trauma and infarction, malignant hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis. Aldolase is less commonly measured than CK but may be more sensitive for dermatomyositis. Limitations: less commonly measured than CK. Non-specific for muscle damage. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note muscle weakness, pain, medications. Handle per standard. Elevated: dermatomyositis, polymyositis, dystrophy. More specific: than CK for inflammatory myopathies. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 1.0 to 7.5 U/L (method-specific). Elevated: dermatomyositis, polymyositis, dystrophy. More specific: than CK for inflammatory myopathies. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR Myositis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALDOSTERONE
interpretation: Serum Aldosterone measures the concentration of aldosterone, a mineralocorticoid hormone produced by the adrenal zona glomerulosa. Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance and blood pressure. Elevated aldosterone: primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome - autonomous adrenal secretion), secondary hyperaldosteronism (renovascular hypertension, renal artery stenosis, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes, malignant hypertension). Low aldosterone: Addison disease (adrenal insufficiency), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), heparin therapy. Aldosterone/renin ratio (ARR) greater than 30: suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism. Limitations: posture, sodium intake, medications affect results. Sample timing critical. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred, morning sample). CRITICAL: 2 hours supine before draw. Preparation: note hypertension, hypokalaemia. Handle per standard. Elevated: primary hyperaldosteronism. ARR: greater than 30. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (posture/sodium dependent). Primary hyperaldosteronism: ARR greater than 30. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALDOSTERONE/RENIN ACTIVITY RATIO
interpretation:
• Primary screening tool for primary aldosteronism (PA) in hypertensive patients
• Elevated ratio (>20-40 ng/dL per ng/mL/h, lab-specific) with raised aldosterone suggests PA
• Suppressed renin artifactually elevates ratio — confirm with saline suppression test
• Limitations: affected by antihypertensives (ACEi/ARBs raise renin; diuretics raise both), posture, time of day (aldosterone peaks morning)
• False positives in renovascular hypertension, Cushing syndrome, licorice ingestion
• Not reliable in renal failure, hypokalemia already present, or on potassium-sparing drugs
• Always interpret alongside serum potassium, aldosterone, and renin levels individually
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum (preferred) or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Collect morning sample (08:00-10:00) after 2h upright posture.
• Preparation: Correct hypokalemia before sampling. Discontinue interfering drugs per guidance (spironolactone 4-6wks, ACEi/ARBs 2wks) if safe.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum/plasma; store 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Protect from light. Chilled tube.
ref_ranges:
• Upright (2h): Aldosterone 4-31 ng/dL; Renin 2.5-21 ng/mL/h; Ratio <20-40 (lab-specific cut-off)
• Supine: Aldosterone 2-16 ng/dL; Renin 1-5 ng/mL/h
• Confirmatory cut-off for PA varies. Age-specific ranges apply. LC-MS/MS ranges differ from immunoassay.
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Endocrine Society PA Guidelines; Tietz Clinical Guide).

name: ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE (ALP)
interpretation:
• Marker of hepatobiliary disease and bone turnover
• Elevation pattern localizes source: GGT/ALT co-elevation → liver; isolated rise with Ca/PTH abnormality → bone
• Limitations: non-specific without isoenzyme separation or clinical context
• Elevated in pregnancy (placental), children/adolescents (bone growth), post-menopause
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard phlebotomy. Fasting 8-12h where applicable.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C long-term. Max 2 freeze-thaw cycles. Haemolysis may interfere with colorimetric methods.
ref_ranges:
• Ranges vary by age, sex, pregnancy, and assay method
• Children/adolescents: physiologically elevated (bone growth)
• Pregnancy: placental isoenzyme elevation
• Isoenzyme separation (HEP, BAP, NAP) refines organ-specific interpretation
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Burtis Clinical Chemistry; Tietz; manufacturer IFU).

name: ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE BONE-SPECIFIC; BSAP
interpretation: Bone-Specific Alkaline Phosphatase (BSAP) measures the bone isoform of alkaline phosphatase in serum. BSAP is produced by osteoblasts and is a marker of bone formation and osteoblastic activity. BSAP is elevated in: Paget disease of bone (markedly elevated), primary hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, osteoporosis (mildly elevated), bone metastases (prostate, breast cancer), healing fractures, rickets, renal osteodystrophy. BSAP is more specific for bone disease than total ALP because it eliminates the liver and intestinal contributions. Total ALP is elevated in both liver and bone disease; BSAP isolates the bone component. Limitations: method-specific. Fracture healing: transiently elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note bone pain, fracture history, malignancy. Handle per standard. Elevated: Paget disease, hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia. More specific: than total ALP for bone. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 20 to 100 U/L (method-specific). Elevated: Paget disease (markedly), hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, bone metastases. More specific: than total ALP for bone. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IFCC Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE ISOENZYMES
interpretation: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) Isoenzymes separate and identify the different tissue sources of ALP in serum. ALP exists as multiple isoenzymes: Bone (osteoblast-derived): elevated in Paget disease, rickets, osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, bone metastases, healing fractures. Liver (hepatobiliary): elevated in cholestasis, hepatitis, liver metastases, biliary obstruction. Intestinal: elevated after fatty meals, in blood groups B and O. Placental: elevated in pregnancy (third trimester). Germ cell: elevated in germ cell tumours (seminoma). Cancer-related: elevated in certain malignancies (NSCLC). Electrophoresis separates these fractions. Bone ALP and liver ALP can also be measured by immunoassay (BSAP). Limitations: method-specific. Electrophoresis may not separate all fractions. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note bone pain, liver disease, pregnancy, malignancy. Handle per standard. Bone: Paget, rickets, fractures. Liver: cholestasis. Intestinal: blood group B/O. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by isoenzyme. Bone: elevated in bone disease. Liver: elevated in liver disease. Intestinal: blood group B/O. Placental: pregnancy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AACC ALP Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALPHA 1 ACID GLYCOPROTEIN BIOCHEMICAL
interpretation: Alpha-1-Acid Glycoprotein (AAG, orosomucoid) is an acute-phase protein synthesised primarily by hepatocytes. AAG is one of the most abundant plasma proteins and serves as a carrier for many basic drugs (lidocaine, propranolol, imipramine, quinidine). AAG is elevated in: acute inflammation, acute myocardial infarction, malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, liver disease (hepatic production), stress, surgery. AAG is decreased in: liver cirrhosis (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss), malnutrition, oestrogen therapy. AAG levels affect drug binding and therefore drug free (active) concentrations. High AAG: more drug bound, less free drug. Low AAG: less drug bound, more free drug. Limitations: not routinely measured. Affects drug dosing calculations. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note acute illness, malignancy, liver disease, medications. Handle per standard. Elevated: acute phase, malignancy. Low: cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Drug binding: affects. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 50 to 120 mg/dL (method-specific). Elevated: acute phase, malignancy, inflammation. Low: cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Drug binding: affects free drug levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AACC Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALPHA 1 ANTITRYPSIN
interpretation: Serum Alpha-1-Antitrypsin (A1AT) measures the concentration of alpha-1-antitrypsin, a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) produced primarily by hepatocytes. A1AT is the major inhibitor of neutrophil elastase in the lungs. A1AT deficiency (A1ATD) is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder that causes: early-onset panacinar emphysema (lower lobe predominant), liver disease (neonatal hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma). The most common severe deficiency alleles are PiZZ (homozygous) and PiSZ (compound heterozygous). Serum A1AT is an acute-phase protein: elevated in inflammation (acute MI, infection, malignancy). A1ATD diagnosis: low serum A1AT (less than 57 mg/dL), Pi phenotyping or genotyping, liver biopsy showing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules. Limitations: false normal: acute phase response masks deficiency. Liver disease: may have normal A1AT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note respiratory symptoms (dyspnoea, cough), liver disease, family history, smoking status. Handle per standard. Low: A1ATD (less than 57 mg/dL). PiZZ: most severe. Acute phase: masks deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 100 to 300 mg/dL (method-specific). Low: A1ATD (less than 57 mg/dL). PiZZ: severe deficiency. Acute phase: elevated. Liver: PAS-positive globules. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATS/ERS A1ATD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALPHA 2 MACROGLOBULIN
interpretation: Serum Alpha-2-Macroglobulin (A2M) is the largest non-immunoglobulin protein in plasma. A2M is a broad-spectrum protease inhibitor that binds and inactivates proteases from all four classes (serine, cysteine, aspartic, metalloproteases). A2M is produced by the liver and is a negative acute-phase protein. Elevated A2M: nephrotic syndrome (A2M is too large to be filtered by the glomerulus, so it accumulates while smaller proteins are lost), liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, Down syndrome. Low A2M: acute pancreatitis (A2M is consumed by activated proteases), DIC, malnutrition. A2M is used as a marker of renal protein loss patterns and as a reference protein in serum protein electrophoresis. Limitations: not routinely measured. Affects protein electrophoresis interpretation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis, liver disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis. Low: pancreatitis, DIC. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 150 to 350 mg/dL (method-specific). Elevated: nephrotic syndrome (accumulates). Low: pancreatitis (consumed). Not routine: SPE reference. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AACC Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALPHA FETO PROTEIN (AFP)
interpretation:
• Primary tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance in cirrhotic patients
• Elevated in non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT)
• Maternal serum AFP: prenatal screening for neural tube defects and Down syndrome
• Limitations: non-specific — elevated in hepatitis, cirrhosis, pregnancy
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Centrifuge within 30 min.
• Handle: 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Protect from light.
• Maternal screening: collected at 15-20 weeks gestation.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <10 ng/mL (method-dependent)
• HCC surveillance: >200 ng/mL in cirrhotic patient has high positive predictive value
• Maternal AFP at 15-20wks: MoM calculation required for NTD/Down syndrome risk
• AFP-L3 fraction improves HCC specificity
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (AASLD HCC Guidelines; Tietz; manufacturer IFU).

name: Alpha Feto Protein (AFP)_Extended
interpretation:
• Extended AFP variant: AFP-L3 (Lens culinaris-reactive) fraction
• Higher specificity for HCC than total AFP alone
• Used as confirmatory marker when total AFP mildly elevated (100-200 ng/mL) in cirrhosis surveillance
• Limitations: not standalone — use alongside total AFP, imaging (CT/MRI), and clinical assessment
• False positives rare but occur with ataxia-telangiectasia and some hereditary disorders
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum only. Standard collection. Process as per AFP.
• Requires specialised lectin-affinity electrophoresis or immunoassay platform
• Stability: same as AFP. Lab-specific pre-analytical requirements apply.
ref_ranges:
• AFP-L3 >10% in total AFP suggests HCC (study-specific cut-offs vary)
• High positive predictive value when total AFP >100 ng/mL + AFP-L3 >10%
• Must be interpreted with total AFP, imaging, and clinical context
• Not useful as standalone screening test in general population
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (manufacturer IFU; AASLD HCC Guidelines).

name: ALUMINIUM
interpretation: Serum Aluminium measures the concentration of aluminium in blood. Aluminium is a toxic heavy metal with no known physiological function. Aluminium accumulates in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) on long-term dialysis, especially if exposed to aluminium-containing phosphate binders or aluminium-contaminated dialysate. Aluminium toxicity causes: dialysis dementia (progressive encephalopathy), osteomalacia (aluminium-related bone disease), microcytic anaemia. Serum aluminium is used to monitor aluminium accumulation in dialysis patients and to guide desferrioxamine (DFO) therapy. Pre-DFO aluminium: greater than 60 mcg/L suggests accumulation. Post-DFO aluminium: greater than 150 mcg/L (or greater than 200 mcg/L in some guidelines) indicates significant aluminium overload requiring chelation therapy. Limitations: contamination: blood collection tubes and laboratory equipment may contain aluminium. Metal-free collection required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes and handling. Preparation: note dialysis status, phosphate binders, bone disease, encephalopathy. Handle: metal-free. Pre-DFO: greater than 60 mcg/L = accumulation. Post-DFO: greater than 150 mcg/L = chelation needed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 20 mcg/L. Accumulation: greater than 60 mcg/L. Chelation: post-DFO greater than 150 mcg/L. Contamination: metal-free required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ALUMINIUM DIALYSIS - FLUID
interpretation: Aluminium in Dialysis Fluid measures the concentration of aluminium in water used for haemodialysis. Aluminium contamination of dialysate is a major cause of aluminium toxicity in dialysis patients. Aluminium enters dialysate through: municipal water supplies, aluminium-containing water treatment (alum flocculation), corrosion of aluminium pipes, inadequate deionisation of water. Regular monitoring of dialysate aluminium is essential to prevent aluminium toxicity. Maximum recommended: less than 10 mcg/L (10 ppb). Aluminium greater than 10 mcg/L in dialysate can lead to systemic aluminium accumulation. Water treatment: reverse osmosis and deionisation effectively remove aluminium. Limitations: sampling technique affects results. Must measure at point of use. Reference ranges: regulatory limits.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dialysis fluid (water). CRITICAL: sample at point of use. Preparation: note water treatment system, municipal supply. Handle: metal-free container. Maximum: less than 10 mcg/L. Above: risk of accumulation. Water treatment: RO + deionisation. Reference ranges: regulatory.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 10 mcg/L (10 ppb). Maximum: less than 10 mcg/L. Above: accumulation risk. Water treatment: RO + deionisation. Reference ranges: regulatory limits.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; AAMI Standards; manufacturer IFU.

name: AMINO ACIDS QUALITATIVE - PLASMA
interpretation:
• Qualitative amino acid screening in plasma for inborn errors of metabolism (IEM)
• Detects patterns suggestive of aminoacidurias, organic acidemias, urea cycle disorders
• Limitations: qualitative only — quantitative analysis required for monitoring or borderline findings
• Post-translational modifications, dietary influences, and acute illness can alter patterns
• False negatives in milder phenotypes; false positives with medications and parenteral nutrition
• Requires specialist interpretation by metabolic/biochemical geneticist
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Plasma (EDTA/heparin). Fasting sample preferred (reflects baseline metabolism)
• Preparation: avoid parenteral nutrition or amino acid-containing infusions prior to sampling if clinically safe
• Handling: Separate plasma immediately; freeze at -20C or -80C. Ship on dry ice. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Light protection not required.
• Neonates: capillary blood acceptable.
ref_ranges:
• Results expressed as: Normal, Increased (specific amino acids listed), Decreased, Absent
• Reference patterns vary by age, gestational age, and post-natal age
• Comparison against age-matched chromatograms essential
• Quantitative follow-up required for any abnormal finding (amino acid quantitation LC-MS/MS)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and metabolic medicine references (Tietz; manufacturer IFU; inborn error protocols).

name: AMINO ACIDS QUALITATIVE - URINE
interpretation:
• Qualitative amino acid screening in urine for inborn errors of metabolism (IEM)
• Detects aminoacidurias (e.g., cystinuria, Hartnup disease), organic acidurias, mitochondrial disorders
• Limitations: qualitative only — requires quantitative confirmation for diagnosis and monitoring
• Renal tubular function, sample timing, and concurrent medications affect patterns
• False negatives in milder phenotypes; false positives with antibiotics, L-dopa, some contrast agents
pre_analytical:
• Sample: 24-hour urine or random spot. Collect in sterile container without preservative.
• Preparation: no dietary restriction unless specific test protocol requires it. Note recent medications.
• Handling: 2-8C during collection. Add thymol or chloroform if collection >12h. Record total volume. Freeze at -20C if analysis delayed >24h. Ship on dry ice.
• Spot samples acceptable for qualitative screening.
ref_ranges:
• Results: Normal, Increased (specific amino acids listed), Decreased, Absent
• Age-matched reference patterns essential — neonates have different baseline excretion
• Follow up any abnormality with quantitative amino acid analysis by LC-MS/MS or HPLC
• Interpret alongside plasma amino acids for complete metabolic picture
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and metabolic medicine references (Tietz; manufacturer IFU; IEM protocols).

name: AMINO ACIDS QUANTITATIVE - BLOOD
interpretation: Amino Acids Quantitative Blood measures the concentration of individual amino acids in plasma/serum. Amino acid analysis is used to diagnose and monitor inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) affecting amino acid transport and metabolism. The most common aminoacidopathies detected: Phenylketonuria (PKU): elevated phenylalanine. Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): elevated branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine). Homocystinuria: elevated methionine and homocystine. Tyrosinaemia: elevated tyrosine. Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia: elevated glycine. Urea cycle disorders: elevated glutamine, arginine, ornithine. Limitations: fasting sample preferred. Diet affects results. Medications affect results. Reference ranges: method-specific and age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note diet, medications, family history of IEM, clinical symptoms. Handle: separate within 1 hour. Fasting: preferred. Specific elevations: indicate specific disorders. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method dependent). Elevated specific AA: indicate specific disorders. PKU: phenylalanine elevated. MSUD: BCAAs elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: AMINOLEVULINIC ACID - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Delta-Aminolevulinic Acid (ALA) measures the urinary excretion of ALA, an intermediate in the haem biosynthesis pathway. ALA is produced by ALA synthase (the rate-limiting enzyme) from glycine and succinyl-CoA. Elevated urinary ALA: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) - the most common acute porphyria, caused by porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) deficiency. Lead poisoning - lead inhibits ALA dehydratase, causing ALA accumulation. Other acute porphyrias (VP, HCP). Elevated ALA during attacks: AIP patients have markedly elevated ALA and PBG during acute attacks. Asymptomatic carriers: may have mildly elevated ALA between attacks. ALA and PBG are both elevated in AIP. PBG is more specific for acute porphyrias. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Must be collected during acute attack for acute porphyrias. Light-sensitive: protect from light. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. CRITICAL: collect during acute attack. CRITICAL: protect from light. Preparation: note symptoms (abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric, dark urine), family history. Handle: protect from light. Elevated: AIP, lead poisoning. PBG: more specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 5 mg/24h (method-specific). Elevated: AIP, lead poisoning. AIP: markedly elevated during attacks. PBG: more specific for acute porphyrias. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: European Porphyria Network Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: AMMONIA - PLASMA
interpretation:
• Measures plasma ammonia — marker of hepatic encephalopathy, urea cycle disorders, Reye syndrome
• Elevated: liver failure, cirrhosis, portal-systemic shunts, urea cycle enzyme defects, high-protein intake, GI bleeding, sepsis, drugs (valproate, diuretics)
• Limitations: extremely labile — pre-analytical errors cause spuriously elevated results (most common cause of false elevation)
• Must be processed within 15-30 min of collection; haemolysis rapidly elevates ammonia
• Not reliable if >30 min delay or poor venous sampling (ischemic tourniquet time increases muscle ammonia)
• Low levels virtually exclude hepatic encephalopathy
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Plasma (EDTA/heparin/specialised ammonia-free tube). CRITICAL: process IMMEDIATELY.
• Preparation: Resting state. No tourniquet application >30s. Avoid fist-clenching during venipuncture.
• Handling: Place on ice immediately. Centrifuge within 15-30 min within cooled centrifuge. Separate plasma; freeze at -70C or -20C for longer storage.
• Failure to process rapidly is the most common pre-analytical error — result unreliable if not cooled promptly.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 15-45 µg/dL (11-35 µmol/L). Neonates/infants: higher limits (up to 80-100 µg/dL in first 3 months)
• Elevated >100 µmol/L in adults suggests urea cycle disorder or advanced liver failure
• Severity correlates poorly with clinical state — trend analysis more useful than single values
• Always check paired venous and arterial (if available) for gradient assessment
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; AACC Practice Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: AMPHETAMINES
interpretation:
• Detects amphetamine-type substances in urine for drug screening
• Includes amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDMA (ecstasy), and related sympathomimetics
• Used in workplace drug testing, forensic toxicology, and clinical monitoring
• Limitations: immunoassay cross-reactivity with over-the-counter sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, phenylpropanolamine)
• False positives: rxmeds (bupropion, labetalol, ranitidine), OTC cold remedies, selegiline
• False negatives: adulteration, dilution, modified pH, post-collection adulterants
• GC-MS or LC-MS/MS confirmation required for legal/forensic purposes
• Cannot distinguish D-methamphetamine (illicit) from L-methamphetamine (Vicks inhaler) without chiral analysis
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Urine (random spot). Minimum 20-30 mL.
• Preparation: observed collection preferable for forensic contexts. Record chain of custody.
• Handling: 2-8C during storage. Stable for >2 weeks at 2-8C; -20C for longer storage. No preservative required.
• Maintain specimen integrity: tamper-evident containers. Check temperature, pH, creatinine to rule out adulteration.
• Refrigerate if delay >2h before testing.
ref_ranges:
• Screening: immunoassay cut-offs: Amphetamine 500 ng/mL, Methamphetamine 500 ng/mL
• Confirmatory: LC-MS/MS/GC-MS at lower cut-offs (typically 100-250 ng/mL)
• Specimen validity: pH 3-11, creatinine >20 mg/dL (urine not dilute)
• Positive predictive value depends on clinical context and prevalence
• No universally accepted reference range — drug-free population reference is <cut-off
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and toxicology references (SAMHSA guidelines; manufacturer IFU; AACC toxicology guidelines).

name: AMYLASE
interpretation:
• Marker of pancreatic acinar cell damage and salivary gland function
• Elevated in acute pancreatitis, pancreatic duct obstruction, pancreatic pseudocyst, acute cholecystitis
• Less specific — also elevated in salivary gland disorders (parotitis, mumps), macroamylasemia, bowel obstruction, ectopic pregnancy
• Macroamylasemia: benign elevation due to circulating amylase-IgG complex — falsely elevates serum amylase without clinical disease (differentiate by urine amylase ratio)
• Limitations: not specific for pancreatitis — 40% of acute pancreatitis patients have normal amylase at admission
• Lipase is more specific and remains elevated longer for pancreatitis diagnosis
• Serial amylase useful for monitoring acute pancreatitis resolution
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum (preferred) or plasma (EDTA/heparin). No fasting required.
• Preparation: no specific pretest restrictions. Avoid hemolysis.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Amylase in urine stable for 2-3 days at 2-8C.
• Serum must be separated from cells promptly — amylase leaks from cells at room temperature.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 30-110 U/L (method and temperature dependent — 37C vs 25C calibration differs)
• Age-specific: children may have higher reference ranges
• Amylase isoenzymes: P-amylase (pancreatic) vs S-amylase (salivary)
• Macroamylasemia: serum elevated + urine low/normal — confirm by precipitation or gel filtration
• Serial 4-6h measurements useful in suspected pancreatitis if initial value borderline
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU; pancreatitis diagnosis guidelines).

name: AMYLASE - FLUID
interpretation:
• Biochemical analysis of fluid specimens for cellular/structural damage assessment
• Compares fluid analytes to serum reference (e.g., LDH ratio, protein ratio) to determine transudate vs exudate
• Common applications: pleural, peritoneal/ascitic, pericardial, synovial, CSF analysis
• Limitations: results highly dependent on timing of collection, location of sampling, and concurrent therapy (diuretics)
• Interpretation requires simultaneous serum sample for gradient calculations (e.g., SAAG for ascites)
• Inflammatory and infectious conditions alter fluid composition rapidly — delay in processing reduces accuracy
• Not diagnostic alone — must be correlated with clinical presentation, imaging, and microbiology
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Fresh fluid specimen (20-50 mL minimum). Collect in plain container without anticoagulant unless simultaneous cell count required (EDTA for CSF cell count).
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Collect under sterile conditions for infection workup.
• Handling: Process within 1-2h of collection. Centrifuge if turbid/cellular. Separate supernatant; store 2-8C (24h) or -20C for longer. Add no preservative.
• Transport on ice. Label site and method of collection.
ref_ranges:
• Reference ranges fluid-specific (see individual fluid SOPs)
• Transudate: protein <2.5 g/dL, LDH <200 U/L or <0.6× serum upper limit, glucose ~serum level
• Exudate: protein >2.9 g/dL, LDH >0.6× serum upper limit (Light criteria)
• CSF: protein 15-45 mg/dL; glucose 45-80 mg/dL; LDH <5 U/L
• Synovial fluid: no WBC, no bacteria, viscous, glucose equal to serum
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and laboratory medicine references (Light criteria; Tietz; CSF analysis guidelines).

name: AMYLASE ENZYMATIC ASCITIC - FLUID
interpretation: Amylase Enzymatic Ascitic Fluid measures amylase activity in peritoneal fluid. Elevated ascitic fluid amylase is a hallmark of pancreatic ascites (ruptured pancreatic duct or pancreatic pseudocyst). Ascitic fluid amylase greater than 1000 U/L strongly suggests pancreatic origin. Amylase in ascitic fluid may also be elevated in: intestinal perforation (bowel contents leak into peritoneum), strangulated bowel, ectopic pregnancy (salivary amylase from ruptured fallopian tube), metastatic adenocarcinoma (tumour producing amylase). Serum amylase should be measured simultaneously. Amylase-to-creatinine clearance ratio (ACCR) helps distinguish pancreatic from salivary amylase. Limitations: requires proper ascitic fluid collection. Serum-to-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) also needed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Ascitic fluid. Preparation: note abdominal pain, alcohol use, pancreatitis history. Handle per standard. Greater than 1000 U/L: pancreatic origin. SAAG: also needed. Serum: also needed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1000 U/L. Pancreatic: greater than 1000 U/L. SAAG: less than 11 (non-portal hypertension). Serum correlation: needed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACG Pancreatitis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: AMYLOID A
interpretation: Serum Amyloid A (SAA) is an acute-phase protein produced by the liver in response to inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha). SAA levels can increase up to 1000-fold during acute inflammation, making it one of the most responsive acute-phase reactants. SAA is used as: a marker of acute inflammation (more sensitive than CRP in some settings), a predictor of cardiovascular risk (chronic elevation associated with atherosclerosis), a monitor of anti-inflammatory therapy response, a marker for AA amyloidosis (chronic SAA elevation leads to amyloid deposition). Limitations: not routinely measured in most clinical settings. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note acute illness, chronic inflammation, risk factors for amyloidosis. Handle per standard. Very responsive: up to 1000-fold. More sensitive: than CRP in some settings. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 10 mg/L (method-specific). Very elevated: acute inflammation (up to 1000-fold). AA amyloidosis: chronic elevation. CV risk: associated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: European Amyloidosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ANDROSTENEDIONE
interpretation: Serum Androstenedione measures the concentration of androstenedione, an androgenic steroid produced by the adrenal glands and gonads. Androstenedione is a precursor to both testosterone and oestrogen. Elevated androstenedione: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) - 21-hydroxylase deficiency (most common), 11-hydroxylase deficiency. Adrenal tumours (adenoma, carcinoma). Ovarian hyperthecosis. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) - mildly elevated. Low androstenedione: Addison disease. Hypogonadism. Hypopituitarism. Limitations: pulsatile secretion (morning samples preferred). Affected by age and sex. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Morning sample preferred. Preparation: note virilisation symptoms, hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, PCOS history. Handle per standard. Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour, PCOS. Low: Addison, hypogonadism. Morning: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society CAH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ANGIOTENSIN  II
interpretation: Plasma Angiotensin II measures the concentration of angiotensin II, the principal effector peptide of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Angiotensin II is produced from angiotensin I by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lungs. Angiotensin II causes: potent vasoconstriction (raises blood pressure), aldosterone secretion (promotes sodium retention), ADH release, thirst stimulation. Elevated angiotensin II: renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis), essential hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism (may be low), heart failure. Low angiotensin II: primary hyperaldosteronism, volume expansion. Limitations: technically difficult to measure. Requires special handling. Not routinely measured (renin preferred). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: special handling. Preparation: note hypertension, renal artery stenosis. Handle: ice, protect from light. Elevated: renovascular HTN, essential HTN. Low: primary aldosteronism. Not routine: renin preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: renovascular HTN, essential HTN. Low: primary aldosteronism. Not routine: renin preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESC Hypertension Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ANGIOTENSIN CONVERTING ENZYME (ACE)
interpretation:
• Marker of angiotensin-converting enzyme activity — elevated in sarcoidosis (diagnostic adjunct, not specific)
• Also elevated in Gaucher disease, leprosy, hyperthyroidism, alcoholic liver disease, primary biliary cholangitis, diabetes
• Low levels seen in ACE inhibitor therapy, hereditary ACE deficiency, some cases of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
• Limitations: elevated in only 40-60% of sarcoidosis patients — normal ACE does not exclude diagnosis
• Not specific for active disease — elevated ACE persists during treatment even when disease inactive
• Must be interpreted alongside clinical findings, imaging (HRCT chest), and biopsy for sarcoidosis
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no specific pretest restrictions. Record ACE inhibitor therapy status.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer storage. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia have minimal effect on most methods.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 8-52 U/L (UV kinetic method; range varies by manufacturer and temperature)
• Children: may have higher reference ranges (up to 75 U/L in infants)
• Sarcoidosis: elevated in 40-60% of cases — levels correlate imperfectly with disease activity
• Elevated ACE also seen in: Gaucher disease, leprosy, hyperthyroidism, alcoholic liver disease, PBC, diabetes
• Correction for serum ACE inhibitor use: discontinue 24-48h if clinically safe before testing
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ATS/ERS/WASOG Sarcoidosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTI - IA2 (INSULINOMA ASSOCIATED ANTIGEN)
interpretation: Anti-IA2 (Insulinoma-Associated Antigen 2) Antibody measures autoantibodies against the intracellular tyrosine phosphatase-like protein IA-2, which is expressed in pancreatic beta cells and neuroendocrine tissues. Anti-IA2 is one of the islet autoantibodies used to predict and diagnose Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM). Islet autoantibodies: GADA (anti-GAD65), IAA (insulin autoantibody), IA-2A, ZnT8A. Anti-IA2 positive: high risk of developing T1DM. Multi-antibody positive: highest risk (>50% at 5 years). Single antibody: lower risk. Anti-IA2 may also be elevated in: autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1), other autoimmune conditions. Limitations: not routinely measured in adults with diabetes. More relevant in children. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note family history of T1DM, other autoimmune diseases, age at diagnosis. Handle per standard. Positive: T1DM risk. Multi-Ab: highest risk. Single-Ab: lower risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: T1DM risk. Multi-Ab: greater than 50% risk at 5 years. Single-Ab: lower risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA T1DM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ANTI DNASE B ANTIDEOXYRIBONUCLEASE B
interpretation: Anti-DNase B (Antideoxyribonuclease B) measures antibodies against streptococcal DNase B enzyme. Anti-DNase B is an ASO equivalent marker used to confirm recent Group A Streptococcal (GAS) infection. Anti-DNase B is elevated in: acute rheumatic fever (ARF), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), streptococcal pharyngitis, streptococcal impetigo. Anti-DNase B rises later than ASO and may remain elevated longer. Combination of ASO + Anti-DNase B improves sensitivity for detecting recent GAS infection. Anti-DNase B is more sensitive than ASO for skin infections (impetigo, cellulitis). Limitations: rises later than ASO. Should be interpreted with ASO. Reference ranges: age-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note sore throat, skin infection, joint symptoms, recent streptococcal infection. Handle per standard. Elevated: ARF, PSGN. Later: than ASO. Skin: more sensitive than ASO. Reference ranges: age-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: age-specific. Elevated: ARF, PSGN, strep infection. Later than ASO. Skin: more sensitive. Reference ranges: age-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA Rheumatic Fever Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ANTI MULLERIAN HORMONE (AMH)
interpretation:
• Marker of ovarian reserve — reflects remaining follicle pool in females
• Elevated in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), granulosa cell tumors, MEN1 syndrome
• Low levels seen in diminished ovarian reserve (DOR), premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, post-menopause
• Used in fertility assessment, PCOS workup, ovarian tumor workup, and monitoring gonadotoxicity from chemotherapy/radiotherapy
• Limitations: not predictive of natural fertility — does not correlate well with time to conception
• Assay variability between platforms — not interchangeable; serial measurements must use same assay
• Suppressed by hormonal contraception, GnRH analogues, and recent ovarian surgery — interpret under appropriate hormonal conditions
• No universally accepted PCOS diagnosis threshold — Rotterdam criteria use AMH as a supportive marker for PCO morphology
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. No fasting required. Standard venipuncture.
• Preparation: collect during early follicular phase (day 2-5) for baseline ovarian reserve assessment in fertility workup. Can be collected any time in PCOS assessment.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Hormonal contraception suppresses levels — transiently elevated after discontinuation (up to 3 months).
• FSHR genotype affects levels and interpretation.
ref_ranges:
• Females by age (approx.): <50 ng/mL (age >40); 50-150 ng/mL (age 30-40); >150 ng/mL (age <30)
• Post-menopause: typically <10 ng/mL
• PCOS: often >10 ng/mL even in adolescents
• Lower limit for DOR: <1.0 ng/mL (assay-specific; Federation IVM recommendation >1.0 ng/mL)
• AMH does not correlate with BMI or menstrual cycle phase significantly
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and reproductive endocrinology references (ESHRE AMH Guidelines; Tietz; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTI STREPTOLYSIN-O (ASO)
interpretation:
• Marker of recent streptococcal infection — useful for post-streptococcal sequelae diagnosis
• Elevated in: acute rheumatic fever (ARF), acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN), scarlet fever, streptococcal pharyngitis
• Supports diagnosis of ARF/Jones criteria and APSGN when clinical picture is equivocal
• Limitations: elevated ASO is NOT direct evidence of active infection — refleccts past exposure (weeks to months)
• Peak elevation 3-5 weeks post-infection; persists elevated for 6-12 months
• 20% of normal population may have positive ASO (asymptomatic carriage, prior exposure)
• Interpretation requires paired acute/convalescent titers (4-fold rise confirms recent infection)
• Children 5-15 years have highest ASO titers — adult cut-offs differ
• ASO negative in >25% of ARF cases — negative result does not exclude diagnosis
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note recent infections or antibiotic use.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer storage. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for turbidimetric/turbidometric methods.
• Paired samples required for convalescent comparison — collect 2-4 weeks apart.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <200 IU/mL (varies by lab, age, methodology — Todd units)
• Children 5-15 years: upper limit up to 400-500 IU/mL
• Significant titer: >400 IU/mL in adults; >800 IU/mL in children (lab-dependent)
• For ARF diagnosis: single elevated titer (lab-specific cut-off) OR 4-fold rise in paired samples
• ASO negative in 25% of ARF cases — does not exclude diagnosis if clinical picture compatible
• Always interpret alongside clinical findings and ASO interpretation guidelines
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; WHO/Jones Criteria for ARF; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTI TG/ATG (ANTI THYROGLOBULIN ANTIBODY)
interpretation:
• Detects anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (anti-Tg) — marker of thyroid autoimmunity
• Positive in chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's), Graves' disease, and some cases of subclinical thyroid dysfunction
• Used alongside anti-TPO to classify autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) and assess prognosis
• Limitations: less sensitive than anti-TPO for Hashimoto's (positive in 70-80% vs 90%)
• Not independently used for AITD diagnosis — interpret with anti-TPO, TSH, and clinical context
• False positives: other autoimmune diseases, malignancy, prior neck irradiation, some medications
• False negatives occur in 20-30% of Hashimoto's patients — negative anti-TPO/anti-Tg does not exclude AITD
• Anti-Tg has prognostic value: high titers predict thyroid dysfunction in euthyroid patients
• Marker for residual/recurrent thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine ablation
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note thyroid medications, recent iodinated contrast, or iodine supplements.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable in frozen state.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for immunoassays (ELISA, CLIA, RIA).
• For post-thyroidectomy monitoring: use same assay platform for serial trending.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <115-175 IU/mL (assay-specific; upper limit varies significantly)
• 10-20% of normal population has low-positive anti-Tg titers
• Hashimoto's: positive in 70-80% of cases (often high titer)
• Graves' disease: positive in 30-50% of cases
• Anti-Tg titers correlate imperfectly with clinical disease activity
• Serial titers more meaningful for post-thyroidectomy cancer surveillance than single measurements
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and immunology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ATA Thyroid Antibody Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTI THYROID ANTIBODIES
interpretation:
• Tests for thyroid autoantibodies — umbrella term covering anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg), anti-microsomal (anti-TPO), and/or TSH receptor antibodies depending on platform
• Markers of autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease)
• Positive in: Hashimoto's (high titers), Graves' (lower/equivocal titers), postpartum thyroiditis, silent thyroiditis
• Limitations: platform-specific — different assays measure different antibodies under the same panel name. Clarify which antibody is being reported (TPO vs Tg)
• 10-20% of normal population may have low-positive titers, especially in older females
• Not diagnostic alone — must correlate with TSH, fT4/fT3, and clinical presentation
• Antibody titers poorly correlate with disease severity or progression
• Used for: diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and screening family members of AITD patients
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note thyroid medications, recent iodinated contrast, iodine supplementation, recent viral illness.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for platform immunoassays.
• Confirmatory titers should use same assay platform for serial comparison.
ref_ranges:
• Reference range: <upper limit (varies by assay, typically <1:40 to <1:100 by hemagglutination or <35-60 IU/mL by immunoassay)
• 10-20% of healthy adults (more common in females, elderly) have low-positive titers
• Hashimoto's: TPO or Tg antibodies positive in >90%
• Graves' disease: TRAb/TSI positive in >80-90% of cases; TPO/Tg in 30-50%
• Follow-up serial titers more meaningful than single values
• Threshold for positivity differs between methods and manufacturers — consult package insert
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ATA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTI TPO/A-TPO (THYROID PEROXIDASE ANTIBODY) / ANTI-MICROSOMAL ANTIBODY)
interpretation:
• Detects anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (anti-TPO) — most sensitive marker of autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD)
• Elevated in Hashimoto's thyroiditis (>90%), Graves' disease (50-80%), postpartum thyroiditis, silent thyroiditis
• Used to diagnose AITD, assess thyroid dysfunction risk in euthyroid patients, and predict postpartum thyroiditis
• Limitations: not independently diagnostic — must correlate with TSH, fT4, fT3, and anti-Tg for complete AITD evaluation
• 10-15% of normal population may have low-positive titers (especially females >60 years)
• Anti-TPO titers correlate poorly with disease severity — used for diagnosis, not monitoring
• Negative anti-TPO does not exclude thyroid dysfunction or AITD
• False positives: other autoimmune diseases, old age, viral infections
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note thyroid medications, iodinated contrast, iodine supplements, recent viral illness.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for immunoassay platforms.
• Trend monitoring: use same assay platform consistently.
• Postpartum: allow 3 months after delivery for interpretation.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <35 IU/mL (assay-specific; most platforms use this threshold)
• 10-15% of healthy adults have low-positive titers (especially females >60)
• Hashimoto's: positive in >90% of cases (often very high titer, >1000 IU/mL)
• Graves' disease: positive in 50-80% of cases
• High anti-TPO titer in euthyroid patient: higher risk of developing hypothyroidism (5-10% per year)
• Postpartum thyroiditis: anti-TPO positive in 80% of cases
• Titers do not predict disease severity or treatment response
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and endocrinology references (ATA Thyroid Antibody Guidelines; Tietz; manufacturer IFU).

name: ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE (VASOPRESSIN)
interpretation: Serum Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH, Vasopressin) measures the concentration of arginine vasopressin, a peptide hormone produced by the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. ADH regulates water balance by promoting water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts via aquaporin-2 channels. Elevated ADH: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH) - the most common cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia. SIADH causes: lung cancer (especially small cell), CNS disorders, medications, pain, nausea. Ectopic ADH: small cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumours. Low ADH: Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI) - hypothalamic/posterior pituitary disease. Nephrogenic DI: kidney unresponsive to ADH. ADH testing is technically challenging and rarely measured directly. Water deprivation test with desmopressin is more commonly used. Limitations: technically difficult. Stress, pain affect levels. Not routinely measured. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (EDTA). CRITICAL: special handling. Preparation: note hyponatraemia, polyuria, polydipsia, medications. Handle: ice, separate immediately. Elevated: SIADH. Low: CDI. Water deprivation: more common. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 1 to 5 pg/mL (method-specific). Elevated: SIADH. Low: CDI. Technically: difficult. Not routine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society DI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: APOLIPOPROTEIN A1 (APO A1)
interpretation:
• Principal apolipoprotein of HDL — inversely associated with cardiovascular disease risk
• Low Apo A1: elevated CVD risk, Tangier disease (abetalipoproteinemia variant), familial hypoalphalipoproteinemia, nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, cholestasis, cigarette smoking
• High Apo A1: associated with reduced CVD risk (not typically clinically significant in isolation)
• Limitations: not independently diagnostic — should be interpreted with full lipid profile and Apo B/Apo A1 ratio
• Less standardized than cholesterol assays — inter-laboratory variation exists
• Apo A1/B ratio: risk stratification adjunct; ratio <0.8-1.0 suggests elevated CVD risk
• Not routinely recommended in current guidelines (LDL-C and non-HDL-C remain primary targets) — used in selected dyslipidemia workup
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Fasting 12h preferred for lipid profile; not required for isolated Apo A1.
• Preparation: fasting 12h reduces chylomicron interference. Note lipid-lowering medications (statins, fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe) — may affect levels.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (stable 24-48h) or -20C (months).
• Stable at room temperature for 24h. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• EDTA plasma is acceptable — heparin preferred for some platforms.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: >120 mg/dL ( desirable); 100-120 mg/dL (borderline); <100 mg/dL (low/risk)
• Females naturally have higher Apo A1 than males (10-20% difference)
• Apo A1/B ratio >1.5 favorable; <1.0 indicates elevated CVD risk
• Reference ranges vary by assay (nephelometry, turbidimetry, immunoassay)
• Children: age-specific reference ranges exist (lower than adults in neonates)
• NCEP guidelines: Apo B and non-HDL-C preferred over Apo A1 for routine CVD risk assessment
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; NCEP ATP III/IV Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: APOLIPOPROTEIN B (APO B)
interpretation:
• Principal apolipoprotein of LDL and VLDL — directly proportional to atherogenic particle number
