• Elevated Apo B: elevated CVD risk, high CVD event rate, familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, hepatic lipidosis
• Low Apo B: rare, seen with abetalipoproteinemia, severe malabsorption, malnutrition, some hypobetalipoproteinemias
• Limitations: not standalone — interpret alongside HDL-C, LDL-C, non-HDL-C, triglycerides, and clinical risk factors
• Apo B more closely reflects LDL particle number than LDL-C — useful in hypertriglyceridemia or metabolic syndrome where LDL-C underestimates atherogenic burden
• Apo B/Apo A1 ratio: stronger risk predictor than LDL-C/HDL-C ratio per emerging data
• Not yet universally adopted in guidelines despite evidence advantage over LDL-C in some contexts
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Fasting 12h preferred.
• Preparation: fasting 12h for optimal lipid profile interpretation. Note lipid-lowering therapy.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C longer-term. Stable at room temperature for 24h.
• EDTA plasma acceptable. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Pre-analytical: catenary sampling, hemolysis, lipemia generally acceptable for nephelometric methods.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <100 mg/dL (desirable); 100-120 mg/dL (moderate risk); >120 mg/dL (high risk)
• Females: slightly lower than males (10-15% difference)
• FH (heterozygous): often >130 mg/dL; (homozygous): >200 mg/dL
• Apo B/Apo A1 ratio <0.8 desirable; >1.0 indicates elevated atherogenic risk
• Reference ranges: assay-specific (nephelometry vs IRMA)
• Non-HDL-C equivalents each Apo B ≈ 1:1 with LDL-C (useful in hypertriglyceridemia)
• Serial monitoring for therapy response more useful than single measurement
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and lipidology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; NCEP ATP III/IV; AHA/ACC Lipid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: ARSENIC
interpretation: Serum Arsenic measures the concentration of total arsenic in blood. Blood arsenic is useful for detecting acute arsenic exposure (within days of ingestion). Blood arsenic is less useful for chronic exposure monitoring (urine preferred). Arsenic is metabolised in the liver and excreted in urine. Blood arsenic: useful for acute exposure (0 to 7 days). Urine arsenic: preferred for chronic exposure. Arsenobetaine (fish arsenic): non-toxic, not metabolised. Inorganic arsenic: most toxic. Fractionated arsenic: preferred for distinguishing sources. Limitations: seafood ingestion causes false positive (arsenobetaine). Blood arsenic peaks 1 to 2 hours after ingestion. Urine: preferred for chronic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (heparin preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seafood intake, occupational exposure, water source. Handle per standard. Acute: blood preferred. Chronic: urine preferred. Seafood: false positive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 10 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: acute arsenic exposure. Seafood: false positive (arsenobetaine). Blood: acute. Urine: chronic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Arsenic Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: ARYL SULFATASE A METACHROMATIC LEUCODYSTROPHY
interpretation: Aryl Sulphatase A (ASA) measures the activity of arylsulphatase A, a lysosomal enzyme that hydrolyses cerebroside-3-sulphate. Deficiency of ASA causes Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (MLD), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder characterised by progressive demyelination of the CNS and peripheral nerves. ASA activity is measured in: leucocytes (preferred), dried blood spots (screening), fibroblasts. MLD clinical features: progressive gait disturbance, spasticity, cognitive decline, peripheral neuropathy, seizures. Three forms: late-infantile (most severe, onset 1-2 years), juvenile (onset 4-12 years), adult (onset after 16 years). Carrier detection: approximately 50% of normal activity. Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Pseudodeficiency alleles: low activity but no disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note developmental regression, gait abnormalities, family history. Handle per standard. Low: MLD. Carrier: 50% normal. Pseudodeficiency: low activity, no disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 10 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: MLD. Carrier: 50% normal. Pseudodeficiency: possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG MLD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ARYL SULPHATASE B MPS VI - BLOOD
interpretation: Aryl Sulphatase B (ASB, N-Acetylgalactosamine-4-Sulphatase) measures the activity of arylsulphatase B, a lysosomal enzyme that hydrolyses N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulphate. Deficiency of ASB causes Mucopolysaccharidosis Type VI (MPS VI, Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. MPS VI is characterised by: skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex), corneal clouding, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac valve disease, normal intelligence. ASB activity is measured in: leucocytes, fibroblasts, dried blood spots. MPS VI severity: severe (progressive), attenuated (milder). Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Enzyme alone may not distinguish from other MPS types. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note skeletal abnormalities, corneal clouding, developmental concerns, family history. Handle per standard. Low: MPS VI. Carrier: variable. Genotyping: recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 5 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: MPS VI. Carrier: variable. Genotyping: recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ASPARAGINE QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Plasma Asparagine Quantitative measures the concentration of asparagine, a non-essential amino acid synthesised from aspartate by asparagine synthetase. Asparagine is important for: protein synthesis, nucleotide synthesis, neurotransmitter metabolism, immune function (lymphocyte proliferation). Asparagine is elevated in: hyperasparaginemia (rare metabolic disorder). Asparagine is decreased in: asparagine synthetase deficiency, malnutrition, liver disease. Asparagine is the substrate for L-asparaginase therapy in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) - the enzyme depletes asparagine, which leukaemic cells cannot synthesise. Limitations: fasting sample preferred. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note leukaemia history, medications (L-asparaginase), diet. Handle: separate within 1 hour. ALL therapy: depletes asparagine. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method dependent). Elevated: hyperasparaginemia (rare). Low: L-asparaginase therapy, malnutrition. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ASPARAGINE QUANTITATIVE - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Asparagine Quantitative measures the excretion of asparagine in urine. Urinary asparagine excretion reflects plasma asparagine levels and renal tubular handling. Elevated urinary asparagine: hyperasparaginemia, renal tubular dysfunction (reduced reabsorption). Low urinary asparagine: malnutrition, liver disease. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note diet, medications, metabolic disease history. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: hyperasparaginemia, tubular dysfunction. Low: malnutrition. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method dependent). Elevated: hyperasparaginemia, tubular dysfunction. Low: malnutrition. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ASPARTIC ACID QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Plasma Aspartic Acid (Aspartate) Quantitative measures the concentration of aspartate, a non-essential amino acid involved in the urea cycle and aspartate-glutamate shuttle. Aspartate is important for: urea cycle (condenses with citrulline to form argininosuccinate), malate-aspartate shuttle (transports NADH equivalents into mitochondria), nucleotide synthesis (purine and pyrimidine rings). Elevated aspartate: aspartylglucosaminuria (AGU, lysosomal storage disease), non-ketotic hyperglycaemia (NKH). Decreased aspartate: aspartate aminotransferase deficiency (rare). Limitations: fasting sample preferred. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note metabolic disease history, diet, medications. Handle: separate within 1 hour. Elevated: AGU, NKH. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method dependent). Elevated: AGU, NKH. Low: AST deficiency (rare). Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ASPARTIC ACID QUANTITATIVE - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Aspartic Acid Quantitative measures the excretion of aspartate in urine. Urinary aspartate excretion reflects plasma aspartate levels and renal tubular handling. Elevated urinary aspartate: aspartylglucosaminuria (AGU), non-ketotic hyperglycaemia (NKH), renal tubular dysfunction. Low urinary aspartate: malnutrition, liver disease. Limitations: requires complete 24-hour urine collection. Diet affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note diet, medications, metabolic disease history. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: AGU, NKH, tubular dysfunction. Low: malnutrition. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method dependent). Elevated: AGU, NKH, tubular dysfunction. Low: malnutrition. Reference ranges: method-specific, age-dependent.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BARBITURATES
interpretation:
• Detects barbiturate-class sedative-hypnotics (phenobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, amobarbital, butabarbital)
• Used in emergency toxicology, workplace drug testing, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), forensic analysis
• Barbiturates have largely been replaced by safer sedative-hypnotics and anticonvulsants — current use primarily limited to seizure disorders, anesthesia induction, and rare insomnia
• Limitations: immunoassay cross-reactivity varies significantly between barbiturates — some platforms detect only phenobarbital
• False positives: rarely with ibuprofen (phenobarbital-specific assays)
• False negatives: partial cross-reactivity — newer barbiturate analogues may not be detected by immunoassays
• Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS-MS required for legal/forensic or equivocal cases
• Chronic phenobarbital therapy induces hepatic enzymes — interpretation requires knowledge of dose, duration, and timing of last dose
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Urine (screening) or Serum/plasma (TDM, confirmation).
• Preparation: observed collection for forensic contexts. Chain of custody documentation.
• Handling: 2-8C storage. Stability: urine >1 week at 2-8C; serum/plasma stable >1 week refrigerated, months at -20C. No preservative required.
• For TDM: Trough (pre-dose) levels preferred. Note dose, time of collection, duration of therapy.
• Refrigerate if delay >2h. Check for adulteration in workplace contexts.
• Chronic phenobarbital therapy: time of last dose critical for interpretation.
ref_ranges:
• Screening: variable cut-offs (typically 200 ng/mL total barbiturates in urine)
• TDM therapeutic: Phenobarbital 15-40 µg/mL (maintenance); toxicity generally >40 µg/mL
• Phenobarbital half-life: 80-120h → steady state reached after 1-2 weeks
• GC-MS/LC-MS confirms individual barbiturates at lower cut-offs
• Chronic use with good control: aim for bottom of therapeutic range (15-25 µg/mL)
• Acute overdose: levels poorly predict clinical severity (individual tolerance varies widely)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and toxicology references (Tietz; AACC Toxicology Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: BENZODIAZEPINES
interpretation:
• Detects benzodiazepine-class sedative-hypnotics/anxiolytics (alprazolam, diazepam, lorazepam, clonazepam, oxazepam, etc.)
• Used in emergency toxicology, workplace drug testing, forensic toxicology, clinical monitoring
• Limitations: major cross-reactivity variability between benzodiazepine immunoassays — short-acting agents (alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam) poorly detected by some platforms (oxylipam-specific antibodies needed)
• False positives: sertraline, oxaprozin (oxaprozin-oxazepam cross-reactivity), trazodone — rare with most platforms
• False negatives: true negatives with low-dose short-acting BZDs, adulteration, dilution, atypical metabolites
• Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS — cannot distinguish active drug from metabolites without chiral analysis
• Extended detection: some BZD metabolites detectable in urine for >1 week after single dose (diazepam: up to 2-4 weeks)
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Urine (screening) or Serum/plasma (TDM, confirmation).
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note patient medication history (dose, timing, duration).
• Handling: 2-8C refrigeration. Urine stable >1 week; serum/plasma stable weeks refrigerated, months at -20C. No preservative required.
• For TDM: collect trough (pre-dose) level at steady state for interpretation
• Check specimen integrity (temperature, creatinine, pH) in workplace/forensic contexts
• Metabolite persistence: long-acting BZDs (diazepam, clonazepam) detectable for extended periods
ref_ranges:
• Screening cut-offs (urine immunoassay): typically 200-300 ng/mL (varies by platform)
• TDM therapeutic ranges (serum): Diazepam 0.1-2.5 µg/mL; Alprazolam 20-40 ng/mL; Clonazepam 20-70 ng/mL (assay-specific)
• No universal reference range — platform-specific cut-offs and standards apply
• Urine drug screen positive does not indicate intoxication — merely presence
• Interpretation without clinical context and drug history is unreliable
• Chronic users: tolerance develops — therapeutic range shifts significantly with chronic use
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and toxicology references (AACC Toxicology Guidelines; SAMHSA; manufacturer IFU).

name: BETA 2 MICROGLOBULIN
interpretation:
• Low-molecular-weight protein marker — elevated in renal tubular dysfunction, lymphoproliferative disorders, inflammatory conditions
• Primary clinical use: assessing renal tubular function (preferred over serum markers for tubular disease), staging/monitoring multiple myeloma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma
• Also elevated in: HIV infection, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, solid tumors
• Low levels seen in severe liver disease, drug-induced nephrotic syndrome, some malignancies
• Limitations: not specific — elevation pattern depends on renal handling (filtered at glomerulus, reabsorbed in proximal tubule)
• Serum β2M preferred for renal function in myeloma — urine β2M assesses tubular damage
• Rapidly cleared by kidney — rises early in renal impairment before creatinine increases
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or 24-hour urine. Random/spot urine acceptable for screening.
• Preparation: no fasting required. No pretest restrictions.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C.
• Urine: collect 24h in preservative-free container or acidify (HCl) if delay >24h.
• Stable: serum >1 week at 2-8C; urine >1 week at 2-8C with HCl.
• Avoid haemolysed or lipaemic samples — can interfere with immunoassay.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <3.0 mg/L (serum); <0.3 mg/L (urine spot, corrected for creatinine)
• 24h urine: <0.3 mg/L or <0.4 mg/24h (varies by assay)
• Renal tubular disease: serum elevated + urine disproportionately elevated (reabsorption failure)
• Glomerular disease: serum elevated + urine normal/low (filtered but reabsorbed until GFR very low)
• Multiple myeloma: serum elevated, correlates with disease burden and prognosis
• Dialysis patients: persistently elevated serum β2M (amyloidosis risk with long-term hemodialysis)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU; nephrology/oncology guidelines).

name: BETA 2 MICROGLOBULIN - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Beta-2-Microglobulin (B2M) measures the concentration of beta-2-microglobulin in CSF. B2M is a light chain of the MHC class I molecule found on all nucleated cells. CSF B2M is elevated in: primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL), CNS lymphoproliferative disorders, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) with CNS involvement. CSF B2M greater than 3 mg/L is suggestive of PCNSL. CSF B2M is used as a diagnostic and prognostic marker in CNS lymphoproliferative disorders. Limitations: less commonly measured than serum B2M. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF. Preparation: note neurological symptoms (headache, focal deficits, cognitive decline). Handle per standard. Greater than 3 mg/L: suggestive of PCNSL. Less common: than serum B2M. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 2.5 mg/L (method-specific). Elevated: PCNSL, CNS lymphoproliferative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: PCNSL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA 2 MICROGLOBULIN - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Beta-2-Microglobulin (B2M) measures B2M concentration in spot urine. B2M is freely filtered by the glomerulus and almost completely reabsorbed by the proximal tubule. Elevated urinary B2M indicates: proximal tubular dysfunction (tubulointerstitial nephritis, Fanconi syndrome), cadmium nephrotoxicity, renal transplant rejection, cisplatin nephrotoxicity. Urinary B2M is more sensitive than serum creatinine for detecting early tubular damage. Limitations: urine pH affects stability (B2M degrades below pH 5.5). Fresh sample needed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note nephrotoxic medications, tubular disease history. Handle per standard. Fresh: needed. pH below 5.5: degradation. Elevated: tubular dysfunction. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 300 mcg/g creatinine. Elevated: proximal tubular dysfunction. Sensitive: more than serum creatinine. pH: affects stability. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO AKI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA 2 TRANSFERRIN - NASAL SECRETIONS
interpretation: Beta-2-Transferrin in Nasal Secretions is a highly specific marker for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhoea (CSF leak through the nose). Beta-2-transferrin is produced exclusively in the CNS by neuraminidase action on transferrin. Its presence in nasal secretions confirms a CSF leak. Beta-2-transferrin is absent from normal nasal secretions, serum, and other body fluids. Beta-2-transferrin is used to: confirm CSF rhinorrhoea, differentiate CSF from mucus/saliva, guide surgical repair of dural defects. Limitations: requires special collection (sterile nasal swab or fluid). False negatives: dilute samples, contaminated with blood. Reference ranges: qualitative (present/absent).
pre_analytical: Sample: Nasal secretion (sterile collection). CRITICAL: sterile collection. Preparation: note head trauma, surgery, recurrent meningitis, clear nasal discharge. Handle per standard. Present: CSF leak. Absent: normal. False negatives: dilute samples. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: CSF leak. Specific: 100%. False negatives: dilute, blood contamination. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: Rhinology Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA CROSSLAPS BETA CTX
interpretation: Serum Beta-Crosslaps (Beta-CTX, C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen) is a bone resorption marker. Beta-CTX is released during osteoclastic degradation of type I collagen (which constitutes approximately 90% of bone matrix). Beta-CTX is used to: monitor antiresorptive therapy (bisphosphonates, denosumab), assess bone resorption rate, predict fracture risk, monitor osteoporosis treatment response. A decrease of greater than 25-30% from baseline indicates adequate response to antiresorptive therapy. Limitations: affected by food (fasting required, especially for serum). Diurnal variation (morning peak). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-12 hours). Morning sample preferred (8-10 AM). Preparation: note osteoporosis, fracture history, antiresorptive therapy. Handle per standard. Fasting: required. Morning: preferred. Response: greater than 25-30% decrease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: increased bone resorption. Decreased: antiresorptive therapy response. Fasting: required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA GALACTOCEREBROSIDASE
interpretation: Beta-Galactocerebrosidase (GALC) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme galactocerebrosidase. GALC deficiency causes Krabbe disease (Globoid Cell Leukodystrophy, GCL), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder characterised by progressive demyelination. GALC hydrolyses galactocerebroside (cerebroside) to ceramide and galactose. Krabbe disease clinical features: infantile form (most common, onset 3-6 months): irritability, feeding difficulty, hypertonia, seizures, optic atrophy, developmental regression. Late-onset forms: peripheral neuropathy, visual loss, cognitive decline. GALC activity is measured in: leucocytes (preferred), dried blood spots (newborn screening), fibroblasts. Newborn screening: GALC is included in some newborn screening panels. Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note developmental regression, irritability, hypertonia, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Krabbe disease. Carrier: variable. Newborn: screening included. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 1.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Krabbe disease. Carrier: variable. Newborn: screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Krabbe Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA GALACTOSIDASE GM 1 / MPS IV B
interpretation: Beta-Galactosidase (GM1 / MPS IV B) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme beta-galactosidase. Beta-galactosidase deficiency causes: GM1 Gangliosidosis (GM1): accumulation of GM1 ganglioside. Three forms: infantile (most severe), juvenile, adult. Mucopolysaccharidosis IV B (Morquio B): accumulation of keratan sulphate. Milder than MPS IVA. GM1 Gangliosidosis clinical features: infantile: progressive neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot on fundoscopy, skeletal abnormalities. MPS IV B: skeletal dysplasia, corneal clouding, normal intelligence. Beta-galactosidase activity is measured in: leucocytes, fibroblasts, dried blood spots. Limitations: enzyme alone may not distinguish GM1 from MPS IVB. Genotyping recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note neurodegeneration, skeletal abnormalities, hepatosplenomegaly, family history. Handle per standard. Low: GM1 or MPS IVB. Genotyping: recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 2.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: GM1 gangliosidosis or MPS IVB. Genotyping: recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA GLUCOSIDASE GAUCHER - BLOOD
interpretation: Beta-Glucosidase (GCase, Acid Beta-Glucosidase) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase. GCase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, the most common lysosomal storage disorder. GCase hydrolyses glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) to ceramide and glucose. Gaucher disease: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic, most common): hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain crises, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, normal intellect. Type 2 (acute neuronopathic): severe neurodegeneration, early death. Type 3 (chronic neuronopathic): slower neurodegeneration. GCase activity is measured in: leucocytes (preferred), dried blood spots (newborn screening). GCase activity less than 15% of normal is diagnostic. Limitations: pseudodeficiency alleles (low activity, no disease). Genotyping recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, anaemia, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Gaucher disease. Carrier: 30-50% normal. Pseudodeficiency: possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 5.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Gaucher disease (less than 15% normal). Carrier: 30-50% normal. Genotyping: recommended. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Gaucher Registry Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA HCG
interpretation:
• Pregnancy-specific hormone — marker of trophoblastic tissue viability
• Primary uses: pregnancy confirmation, monitoring gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD: hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT), surveillance after complete/partial molar pregnancy evacuation
• Also used in: Down syndrome screening (combined with PAPP-A, nuchal translucency), high-risk pregnancy monitoring, non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) adjunct
• Limitations: extremely variable in normal pregnancy — peak at 8-10 weeks, then declines sharply. Serial trends more meaningful than single values.
• Not specific for viable intrauterine pregnancy — elevated in ectopic pregnancy, GTD, and some malignancies
• False elevation: heterophilic antibodies, post-menopausal LH cross-reactivity in some assays (use anti-hCG antibody blocking)
• Declines after delivery with t½ ~24-36h — persistent elevation suggests retained products or choriocarcinoma
• Very low/hCG in early pregnancy: monitor serial doubling every 48h for viable pregnancy confirmation
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or urine. Standard venipuncture for serum; urine random spot acceptable.
• Preparation: no fasting required. Note gestational age, last menstrual period (LMP), any recent pregnancy-related events.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C (months).
• Urine: no preservative. 2-8C. Stable >1 week.
• No special preparation for GTD monitoring — collect per institutional protocol.
• Serial monitoring: same assay platform essential for trend comparison.
ref_ranges:
• Pregnancy reference: complex — varies by gestational age
  - Peak: 25,000-200,000 mIU/mL at 8-10 weeks
  - 12 weeks: 13,300-254,000 mIU/mL
  - 16 weeks: 3,640-117,000 mIU/mL
  - 2nd/3rd trimester: declines to 1,000-30,000 mIU/mL
  - Post-menopause: <7 IU/L
• GTD monitoring: aim for undetectable (<5 IU/L) after evacuation — persistent elevation requires chemotherapy evaluation
• Doubles approximately every 48-72h in early viable pregnancy
• Non-pregnant: <5-10 IU/L (assays differ)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and obstetrics references (Tietz; IFCC hCG Standardization Guidelines; FIGO GTD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: BETA HEXOSAMINIDASE A GM2-1/ SANDHOFF BLOOD
interpretation: Beta-Hexosaminidase A (Hex A) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme hexosaminidase A. Hex A deficiency causes GM2 Gangliosidoses: Tay-Sachs disease (Hex A deficiency only) and Sandhoff disease (Hex A + Hex B deficiency). Hex A hydrolyses GM2 ganglioside to GM3 ganglioside and N-acetylneuraminic acid (sialic acid). Tay-Sachs disease: infantile form (most severe): cherry-red spot on fundoscopy, progressive neurodegeneration, seizures, developmental regression, early death. Late-onset: slower progression, muscle weakness. Sandhoff disease: similar to Tay-Sachs but with hepatosplenomegaly (due to Hex B deficiency). Hex A activity is measured in: leucocytes, dried blood spots (newborn screening). Newborn screening: Hex A is included in most newborn screening panels. Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot, seizures, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Tay-Sachs or Sandhoff. Carrier: variable. Newborn: screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 1.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Tay-Sachs or Sandhoff. Carrier: variable. Newborn: screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Tay-Sachs Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA HEXOSAMINIDASE A GM2-1/ TAYSACHS BLOOD
interpretation: Beta-Hexosaminidase A (Tay-Sachs) specifically measures Hex A activity in the context of Tay-Sachs disease screening. This is the same enzyme as row 342 but is listed separately for Tay-Sachs-specific screening. Tay-Sachs disease is caused by HEXA gene mutations leading to Hex A deficiency. The Ashkenazi Jewish population has the highest carrier frequency (1 in 30). Tay-Sachs screening: carrier testing for at-risk populations, newborn screening, diagnostic testing. Hex A less than 1% of normal: infantile Tay-Sachs. Hex A 1-10%: late-onset Tay-Sachs. Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note ethnicity, family history, neurological symptoms. Handle per standard. Low: Tay-Sachs. Carrier: variable. Ashkenazi: higher carrier rate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 1.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Tay-Sachs (less than 1% = infantile). Carrier: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Tay-Sachs Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA MANNOSIDASE - BLOOD
interpretation: Beta-Mannosidase measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme beta-mannosidase. Beta-mannosidase deficiency causes beta-mannosidosis, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. Beta-mannosidase hydrolyses mannose residues from glycoproteins and glycolipids. Beta-mannosidosis clinical features: Type 1 (severe, infantile): severe neurodegeneration, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal abnormalities, early death. Type 2 (mild, adult): peripheral neuropathy, behavioural changes, hearing loss. Beta-mannosidase activity is measured in: leucocytes, fibroblasts, dried blood spots. Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note neurodegeneration, coarse features, neuropathy, family history. Handle per standard. Low: beta-mannosidosis. Carrier: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 2.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: beta-mannosidosis. Carrier: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG LSD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BETA-TRACE PROTEIN(BTP) - NASAL SECRETIONS
interpretation: Beta-Trace Protein (BTP) in Nasal Secretions is a marker for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhoea, similar to beta-2-transferrin. BTP (prostaglandin D2 synthase) is produced in the CNS and is the second most abundant protein in CSF after albumin. BTP is present in CSF at high concentrations (17-38 mg/dL) and is absent from normal nasal secretions. BTP in nasal secretions: confirms CSF leak. BTP is more stable and more abundant than beta-2-transferrin, making it potentially more sensitive. BTP testing can be performed by nephelometry (more widely available than beta-2-transferrin). Limitations: requires sterile collection. Reference ranges: qualitative (present/absent).
pre_analytical: Sample: Nasal secretion (sterile collection). CRITICAL: sterile collection. Preparation: note head trauma, surgery, recurrent meningitis, clear nasal discharge. Handle per standard. Present: CSF leak. More sensitive: than beta-2-transferrin. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: CSF leak. More sensitive: than beta-2-transferrin. More available: nephelometry. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: Rhinology Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BICARBONATE
interpretation:
• Measures serum bicarbonate (HCO3-) — component of acid-base assessment and electrolyte panel
• Elevated: metabolic alkalosis, compensated respiratory acidosis, diuretic therapy, excessive alkali ingestion, hypokalemia, Cushing syndrome
• Low: metabolic acidosis (anion gap vs non-anion gap), compensated respiratory alkalosis, renal tubular acidosis, sepsis, Ketoacidosis (DKA, starvation), diarrhea (GI HCO3- loss)
• Limitations: measured as calculated (from CO2 electrode or chemistry panel) — reflects total CO2 content (HCO3- + dissolved CO2) not pure bicarbonate
• Interpretation requires simultaneous venous blood gas (pH, pCO2, HCO3-) for complete acid-base assessment
• Single HCO3- value insufficient for acid-base diagnosis — use anion gap, delta gap, Winter's formula for stepwise interpretation
• EDTA contamination (from collection tube) causes falsely low values
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (lithium heparin). Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Avoid haemolysis.
• Handling: Process within 1-2h. Centrifuge; separate serum/plasma; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C.
• Critical for accuracy: blood gas syringes preferred for acid-base assessment. Standard chemistry tubes acceptable for isolated HCO3-.
• Air exposure increases pCO2 → falsely elevates calculated HCO3- — minimize air gap in syringe.
• EDTA contamination artefactually lowers HCO3- — use correct tube.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 22-29 mEq/L or mmol/L (method-specific)
• Neonates: slightly lower (18-25 mEq/L); rises to adult range by 1-2 years
• Elevated >30 mEq/L: metabolic alkalosis — investigate cause (vomiting, diuretics, over-alkalization)
• Low <18 mEq/L: metabolic acidosis — calculate anion gap for classification
• HCO3- does NOT distinguish respiratory from metabolic disturbance — requires pH and pCO2
• Delta gap and Winter's formula assist in acid-base diagnosis
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and blood gas analysis references (Tietz; NPPA Acid-Base Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: BILIRUBIN
interpretation:
• Bilirubin: marker of heme catabolism — assesses hepatic function, biliary patency, and hemolytic activity
• Components: Total (TB), Direct/conjugated (DB), Indirect/unconjugated (IB) = TB - DB
• Unconjugated elevation: hemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, ineffective erythropoiesis
• Conjugated elevation: hepatocellular disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury), biliary obstruction (choledocholithiasis, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic head cancer), Dubin-Johnson syndrome
• Mixed elevation: hepatitis, cirrhosis, sepsis, drug reactions
• Limitations: bilirubin poorly sensitive for early biliary obstruction or mild hepatocellular injury — ALT, AST, ALP more sensitive
• Neonatal jaundice: phototherapy treatment thresholds based on bilirubin level, age, risk factors (Rh incompatibility, prematurity)
• Haemolysis artefactually elevates indirect bilirubin in vitro — same-day processing required if haemolysis suspected
• Gilbert syndrome: benign condition with mild unconjugated elevation (1-5 mg/dL), provoked by fasting
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum only. Standard venipuncture. Light-protected tube (amber or foil-wrapped) preferred — bilirubin photosensitive.
• Preparation: fasting 8-12h reduces postprandial unconjugated rise. No specific pretest restrictions.
• Handling: Process within 1-2h of collection. Minimize light exposure. Separate serum; 2-8C (protected from light, stable 8h) or freeze -20C (light-protected).
• Haemolysis causes spurious elevation — if haemolysis present, note and process immediately.
• Neonates: capillary or venous. Minimize heelstick haemolysis.
• Phototherapy patients: measure after turning off lights for 15-30 min.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: Total 0.2-1.2 mg/dL; Direct 0.0-0.4 mg/dL; Indirect 0.2-0.8 mg/dL
• Neonates (first 24h): <5 mg/dL; (48h): <10 mg/dL; (72h): <12 mg/dL (term) — phototherapy based on age-specific nomograms
• Gilbert syndrome: unconjugated 1-4 mg/dL, normal on repeated testing without fasting
• Crigler-Najjar type I: >20 mg/dL in neonates (fatal without treatment); type II: 6-20 mg/dL
• Conjugated >2 mg/dL with normal ALT/AST: investigate biliary tract (ultrasound first)
• Fulminant liver failure: bilirubin may not accurately reflect severity — INR and encephalopathy are better markers
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD Neonatal Jaundice Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: BIOTINIDASE ACTIVITY (QUANTITATIVE)
interpretation: Serum Biotinidase activity measures the capacity of biotinidase to recycle biotin from biocytin. Biotinidase deficiency is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder that causes impaired biotin recycling, leading to biotin depletion. Biotin is a cofactor for four carboxylases: acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase. Biotinidase deficiency clinical features: seizures, developmental delay, alopecia, dermatitis, hearing loss, optic atrophy, metabolic acidosis. Partial deficiency: milder symptoms, may present later. Newborn screening: biotinidase is included in most newborn screening panels. Treatment: biotin supplementation (effective if started early). Limitations: carrier detection requires combination with genotyping. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (or dried blood spot for newborn screening). Preparation: note seizures, dermatitis, alopecia, developmental delay, family history. Handle per standard. Low: biotinidase deficiency. Carrier: variable. Newborn: screening. Treatment: biotin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/min/mL (method-specific). Low: biotinidase deficiency. Partial: milder symptoms. Carrier: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Biotinidase Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BLOOD UREA NITROGEN (BUN)
interpretation:
• Measures blood urea nitrogen — indirect marker of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal function
• Elevated (azotemia): acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), pre-renal states (dehydration, GI bleed, heart failure), post-renal obstruction, high protein intake/catabolic states
• Low BUN: severe liver disease (impaired urea synthesis), malnutrition, overhydration, SIADH
• Limitations: BUN less reliable than creatinine for GFR estimation — affected by protein intake, catabolism, age, muscle mass, hydration, GI bleeding, corticosteroids
• BUN:creatinine ratio >20:1 suggests pre-renal azotemia; ratio ~10-15:1 suggests ATN; ratio <10:1 suggests low muscle mass, liver disease
• CrCl and eGFR preferred for renal function assessment — BUN used as adjunct
• Asymptomatic BUN elevation in substrate context (high-protein diet, corticosteroids, GI bleeding — recheck after correction)
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions but avoid high-protein meal immediately before collection if evaluating baseline renal function.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (stable 48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for enzymatic (urease) methods.
• EDTA: acceptable for most platforms.
• Delayed separation: urea may be degraded by bacterial urease — keep separated.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 7-20 mg/dL (2.5-7.1 mmol/L) — varies by age, muscle mass, diet, assay
• Elderly/high muscle mass: slightly higher upper limit acceptable
• Children: age-specific lower ranges (up to 5 years: <15-18 mg/dL)
• BUN:Cr ratio >20:1 suggests pre-renal azotemia (dehydration, CHF, GI bleeding); ratio <10:1 suggests low muscle mass/hepatic synthesis
• eGFR (CKD-EPI or MDRD): preferred renal function index — BUN is secondary
• BUN alone does not diagnose renal disease — confirm with creatinine, urinalysis, renal ultrasound
• Asymptomatic elevation: compare diet, medications, recent illness before initiating workup
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: BULLOS PEMPHIGOID 180 VESICULOBULLOUS DISORDER
interpretation: Anti-Bullous Pemphigoid 180 (BP180, BPAG2, Type XVII Collagen) Antibody measures autoantibodies against the BP180 protein, a transmembrane hemidesmosomal protein essential for dermal-epidermal adhesion. BP180 antibodies are pathognomonic for Bullous Pemphigoid (BP), the most common autoimmune blistering disease. BP180 antibody levels correlate with disease activity. BP180 ELISA: sensitivity approximately 90%, specificity approximately 98% for BP. BP180 is more sensitive than BP230. BP180 antibodies: NC16A domain is the primary target. Monitoring: serial BP180 levels can predict relapse. Limitations: lower titres may be seen in remission. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note blistering, pruritus, medications, age. Handle per standard. Positive: BP (sensitivity 90%, specificity 98%). More sensitive: than BP230. NC16A: primary target. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: BP (sensitivity 90%, specificity 98%). More sensitive: than BP230. Monitoring: serial levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: International Pemphigoid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BULLOS PEMPHIGOID 230 VESICULOBULLOUS DISORDER
interpretation: Anti-Bullous Pemphigoid 230 (BP230, BPAG1, Bullous Pemphigoid Antigen 1) Antibody measures autoantibodies against the BP230 protein, an intracellular hemidesmosomal protein. BP230 antibodies are found in Bullous Pemphigoid (BP) and are present in approximately 50-70% of BP patients. BP230 is less sensitive than BP180 for BP diagnosis. BP230 antibodies: intracellular target (hemidesmosomal plaque). Lower sensitivity: than BP180. May be positive: in other autoimmune blistering diseases (mucous membrane pemphigoid, pemphigus vulgaris). Limitations: less sensitive than BP180. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note blistering, pruritus, medications, age. Handle per standard. Positive: BP (sensitivity 50-70%). Less sensitive: than BP180. Intracellular: target. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: BP (sensitivity 50-70%). Less sensitive: than BP180. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: International Pemphigoid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: BUPROPION
interpretation: Serum Bupropion measures the concentration of bupropion and its active metabolites (hydroxybupropion, erythrohydrobupropion, threohydrobupropion). Bupropion is a noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) used as an antidepressant and smoking cessation aid. Therapeutic monitoring: bupropion is not routinely monitored by serum levels. Therapeutic range: approximately 50-100 ng/mL (parent drug). Hydroxybupropion (active metabolite): 600-1500 ng/mL. Toxic levels: parent greater than 1000 ng/mL. Bupropion lowers seizure threshold (dose-dependent risk). Overdose: seizures, hallucinations, tachycardia. Limitations: parent drug level is less important than metabolite. Hydroxybupropion: active, may be more relevant. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note depression, smoking cessation, seizure history, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 50-100 ng/mL (parent). Metabolite: 600-1500 ng/mL. Seizure risk: dose-dependent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 50-100 ng/mL (parent). Metabolite: 600-1500 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 1000 ng/mL (parent). Seizure risk: dose-dependent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Manufacturer IFU; toxicology references.

name: C-PEPTIDE(FASTING)
interpretation: Serum C-Peptide (Fasting) measures fasting C-peptide concentration. C-peptide is co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells (1:1 molar ratio) and reflects endogenous insulin production. Low fasting C-peptide: type 1 diabetes mellitus (beta cell destruction), late-stage type 2 diabetes (beta cell failure), pancreatectomy. Normal/high C-peptide: type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance), insulinoma, factitious hypoglycaemia (exogenous insulin suppresses C-peptide). C-peptide: more reliable marker of endogenous insulin than insulin (not affected by hepatic first-pass metabolism). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting, 8-12 hours). CRITICAL: fasting sample. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note diabetes type, insulin use. Handle per standard. Low: T1DM. Normal/high: T2DM, insulinoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.8 to 3.5 ng/mL (fasting). Low: T1DM. High: T2DM, insulinoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: C-PEPTIDE(POST PRANDIAL/POST STIMULATION)
interpretation: Serum C-Peptide (Post Prandial/Post Stimulation) measures C-peptide after glucose stimulation (meal or OGTT). Post-prandial C-peptide: assesses beta cell reserve and response to glucose challenge. Inadequate rise: beta cell failure (T1DM, late T2DM). Excessive rise: insulinoma, early T2DM (compensatory hyperinsulinaemia). C-peptide stimulation test: glucagon stimulation test or mixed meal tolerance test (MMTT) for beta cell function assessment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (post-prandial, 2 hours after meal/stimulation). Preparation: note diabetes type, insulin use. Handle per standard. Inadequate rise: beta cell failure. Excessive: insulinoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 1.5 ng/mL (post-stimulation). Inadequate: less than 1.5. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: C-PEPTIDE(RANDOM)
interpretation: Serum C-Peptide (Random) measures C-peptide concentration at any time of day without fasting. Random C-peptide is less standardised than fasting C-peptide but can provide information about endogenous insulin production. Useful for: distinguishing T1DM (low C-peptide) from T2DM (normal/high C-peptide), monitoring beta cell function in known diabetics. Limitations: affected by recent meals, glucose levels. Fasting sample preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note diabetes type, insulin use. Handle per standard. Low: T1DM. High: T2DM, insulinoma. Fasting: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (non-fasting). T1DM: low. T2DM: normal/high. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: C-REACTIVE PROTEIN (CRP)
interpretation:
• High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) specific clinical interpretation
• hs-CRP is a highly sensitive, non-specific marker of low-grade systemic inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability
• Primary clinical use: independent CVD risk stratification in adults without known CVD (primary prevention)
• hs-CRP >3 mg/L + LDL-C 130-160 mg/dL: JUPITER trial demonstrated statin benefit — rosuvastatin reduced MACE by 44% in this population
• hs-CRP does NOT distinguish CVD from any other source of inflammation — must rule out acute infection, trauma, surgery, active inflammatory disease before using for CVD risk stratification
• Conventional CRP does NOT substitute for hs-CRP in CVD risk — different assay sensitivity (conventional detects >10 mg/dL; hs-CRP detects <0.3 mg/dL)
• Limitations: diurnal variation (higher in morning); affected by menstrual cycle (higher mid-cycle); affected by OCP/pregnancy; falls with statins, weight loss, exercise — changes in hs-CRP do not equal changes in CVD risk
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Standard venipuncture. Fasting NOT required for hs-CRP.
• Preparation: draw in baseline state — NO acute illness, surgery, trauma, vaccination within 2-4 weeks; NO recent intense exercise within 48h. Note OCP use, pregnancy, smoking status, BMI.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia: acceptable for most hs-CRP assays. EDTA plasma acceptable.
• Conventional CRP method INSUFFICIENT — must use validated hs-CRP assay (immunoturbidimetric or ELISA with <0.3 mg/dL detection limit)
• Simultaneous fasting lipid profile (LDL-C, non-HDL-C, TG) recommended for complete CVD risk context.
• hs-CRP assay: high-sensitivity method required; confirm lab uses assay validated per AHA/CDC 2003 guidelines
ref_ranges:
• Adults (CVD risk stratification): <1.0 mg/L (low risk); 1.0-3.0 mg/L (moderate risk); >3.0 mg/L (high risk)
• Primary prevention statin threshold: hs-CRP ≥2.0 mg/L + LDL 130-160 mg/dL (JUPITER criteria) — consider statin in intermediate ASCVD risk
• Secondary prevention: no hs-CRP threshold — treat all ASCVD patients with statin unless contraindicated
• Acute inflammation: CRP >10 mg/L — hs-CRP not interpretable for CVD risk during acute illness/infection
• Pregnancy: 2-5x normal (physiologic) — use pregnancy-adjusted ranges. Third trimester may reach 5-10 mg/L.
• Obesity (BMI >30): baseline 2-4 mg/L common — associated with adipose cytokine production
• Smoking: 2-3x non-smokers (partially reverses within 1-2 years of cessation)
• Diurnal: slightly higher in morning (6-10 AM) vs evening (4-8 PM) — standardize timing if serial monitoring
• Seasonal: higher in winter — do not compare across seasons without adjustment
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and cardiology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; AHA/CDC hs-CRP Recommendations; JUPITER Trial; manufacturer IFU).

name: C1 ESTERASE INHIBITOR
interpretation: Serum C1 Esterase Inhibitor (C1-INH) measures the concentration and functional activity of C1-INH, a serine protease inhibitor that regulates the classical complement pathway, contact activation (kallikrein-kinin), and fibrinolysis. C1-INH deficiency causes Hereditary Angioedema (HAE), an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of severe subcutaneous/submucosal oedema. HAE Type 1: low C1-INH antigen (approximately 85% of cases). HAE Type 2: normal/high C1-INH antigen but dysfunctional (approximately 15% of cases). C1-INH functional assay: more sensitive than antigen level. Low functional C1-INH: diagnostic of HAE. Acquired C1-INH deficiency: associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, autoimmune diseases. Limitations: functional assay preferred. Antigen alone may miss Type 2. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recurrent angioedema, family history, triggering factors. Handle per standard. Functional: preferred. Low: HAE. Type 1: low antigen. Type 2: dysfunctional. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 70 to 130 percent (functional). Low: HAE (Type 1 or Type 2). Acquired: lymphoproliferative, autoimmune. Functional: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WAO/EAACI HAE Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CA 125
interpretation:
• Ovarian cancer tumor marker — elevated in epithelial ovarian carcinoma, fallopian tube carcinoma, peritoneal carcinoma
• Sensitivity: stage I ~50%, stage III-IV ~80-90% — not suitable for population screening
• Used for: monitoring response to treatment, surveillance for recurrence after cytoreductive surgery + chemotherapy
• Also elevated in: endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), menstruation, pregnancy, liver disease, heart failure, peritonitis, Meigs syndrome, ascites
• Limitations: NOT a screening test for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic women (not sensitive/specific enough for population screening — UKCTOCS trial showed mortality benefit uncertainty)
• CA 125 alone cannot diagnose or exclude ovarian cancer — imaging (transvaginal ultrasound) is essential
• False positives: conditions causing peritoneal irritation elevate CA 125 (PID, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, cirrhosis, ascites of any cause)
• Pre-menopausal CA 125 elevation: limited specificity (endometriosis/PID common causes)
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: collect any time of day. Note menstrual status, reproductive history, current conditions (endometriosis, PID).
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for immunoassay.
• Note: avoid collection during menstruation if possible (may artefactually elevate).
• Serial monitoring: same assay platform, ideally same laboratory (inter-assay variability 10-15%).
ref_ranges:
• Adults (pre-menopausal): <35 U/mL (upper reference limit)
• Post-menopausal: naturally lower — upper limit ~23-30 U/mL
• Stage III-IV ovarian carcinoma: frequently >100-1000 U/mL
• Monitoring: half of cases with elevated CA 125 show levels trending down with successful treatment
• Recurrence: CA 125 rise precedes clinical symptoms by ~3 months in ~75% of cases
• Endometriosis: CA 125 20-100 U/mL (overlap with early-stage malignancy)
• ROMA score: combines CA 125 + HE4 for ovarian vs benign pelvic mass risk stratification
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz; ACOG/ASCO Ovarian Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; UKCTOCS data).

name: CA 15.3
interpretation:
• Marker for staging and monitoring advanced breast carcinoma — limited standalone utility
• Elevated in: metastatic breast cancer (~30-40% of metastatic cases), some ovarian and lung cancers
• Also elevated in: benign breast disease, pregnancy, lactation, liver disease, benign ovarian cysts
• Limitations: low sensitivity for early-stage or localized breast cancer — not suitable for screening or early detection
• Elevated in only 30-40% of metastatic breast cancer — majority of patients have normal CA 15.3 at diagnosis
• Not recommended by ASCO for routine monitoring when imaging is feasible — insufficient data to support serial use
• CA 15.3 elevation poorly correlates with disease burden — large changes (doubling or halving) more significant than borderline changes
• False positives: benign breast conditions, pregnancy, liver disease, other adenocarcinomas
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note clinical context (pregnancy, lactation, benign breast conditions).
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable.
• For monitoring: same assay platform and laboratory — inter-lab coefficient of variation ~5-10%.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <30 U/mL (upper reference limit, assay-specific: IRMA, ELISA, CLIA ranges differ)
• Metastatic breast cancer: elevated in 30-40% of cases (higher with visceral metastases)
• Not elevated in ~60% of metastatic cases — normal CA 15.3 does not exclude active disease
• Rising trend >25% confirms progression in monitoring context (ASCO criteria)
• Falling trend post-treatment: supports response; rising trend suggests recurrence
• Pregnancy/lactation: may be physiologically elevated up to 3-4× upper limit
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz; ASCO Tumor Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CA 19.9
interpretation:
• Gastrointestinal and pancreatic cancer marker — elevated in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer
• Sensitivity: pancreatic adenocarcinoma ~70-80% at diagnosis; lower for early disease
• Used for: monitoring therapy response, surveillance for recurrence after curative resection of pancreatic cancer
• Also elevated in: cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, liver disease, interstitial lung disease, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroiditis, benign biliary strictures
• Limitations: NOT a screening test for pancreatic cancer in asymptomatic population (insufficient PPV)
• Elevated in many benign conditions — positive predictive value for malignancy ~2-5% in asymptomatic population
• CA 19.9 negative in ~10% of population (Lewis antigen negative) — these individuals cannot produce CA 19.9 regardless of disease state
• Serial trends more clinically meaningful than single values (rising suggests progression)
• False positives: pancreatitis, cholangitis, cholecystitis, interstitial lung disease, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note biliary tract symptoms, GI conditions, and medications.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C for longer storage. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable.
• Lewis antigen negative patients: note that CA 19.9 elevation cannot be assessed in this subgroup.
• Serial monitoring: same platform and laboratory essential.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <37 U/mL (upper reference limit, assay-specific)
• Pancreatic adenocarcinoma: frequently >100-1000 U/mL in advanced disease
• Cholangiocarcinoma: elevated in ~70% of cases
• Benign biliary disease: may reach 50-200 U/mL — overlap with malignancy
• Cholangitis/cholecystitis/pancreatitis: acute elevations (100-500 U/mL) that resolve with clinical recovery
• Lewis antigen negative (~10% of population): CA 19.9 cannot be produced — test not interpretable in this subgroup
• Rising trend in monitored patient: suggests recurrence or progression (confirm with imaging)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz; NCCN Pancreatic Cancer Guidelines; ASCO Tumor Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CA 27.29
interpretation: Serum CA 27.29 (Cancer Antigen 27.29) measures a tumour-associated antigen shed from breast cancer cells. CA 27.29 is an epitope of the MUC1 mucin (breast cancer mucin, BCM). CA 27.29 is used as a monitoring marker for metastatic breast cancer, not for screening or diagnosis. Elevated CA 27.29: metastatic breast cancer (sensitivity 57-80%), benign breast disease, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, liver cirrhosis, renal failure. CA 27.29 rises before clinical recurrence (lead time 5-10 months). Rising CA 27.29 despite treatment: indicates disease progression. CA 27.29 is more specific than CA 15-3 for breast cancer. Limitations: false positives: benign breast disease, liver/renal disease, first trimester pregnancy. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note breast cancer history, treatment status, other conditions. Handle per standard. Elevated: metastatic breast cancer. Rising: disease progression. More specific: than CA 15-3. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 38 U/mL. Elevated: metastatic breast cancer (sensitivity 57-80%). Rising: progression. False positives: benign disease, liver/renal. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ASCO Breast Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CA 72.4
interpretation: Serum CA 72.4 (Cancer Antigen 72.4, TAG-72) measures a tumour-associated glycoprotein found on adenocarcinoma cells. CA 72.4 is used as a monitoring marker for gastric cancer and other adenocarcinomas. Elevated CA 72.4: gastric cancer (sensitivity 40-60%), ovarian cancer, colon cancer, pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer. CA 72.4 is often used in combination with CEA for gastric cancer monitoring. Limitations: false positives: benign GI disease, liver disease, pregnancy. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note gastric/ovarian/colon cancer history, treatment status, other conditions. Handle per standard. Elevated: gastric cancer, ovarian cancer. Combination: with CEA. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 6.9 U/mL. Elevated: gastric cancer (sensitivity 40-60%), ovarian, colon. Combination: with CEA. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESMO Gastric Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CADMIUM
interpretation: Serum Cadmium measures cadmium concentration in blood. Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal with a biological half-life of 10 to 30 years, accumulating primarily in the kidneys and liver. Blood cadmium reflects recent exposure (within weeks to months). Blood cadmium is used to assess: occupational exposure (battery manufacturing, welding, smelting), environmental exposure (cigarette smoking, food contamination), nephrotoxicity monitoring. Blood cadmium less than 5 mcg/L: low risk. Blood cadmium 5-20 mcg/L: moderate risk. Blood cadmium greater than 20 mcg/L: high risk. Urine cadmium reflects cumulative exposure (more useful for chronic exposure). Limitations: smoking elevates blood cadmium significantly. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note occupational exposure, smoking status, diet. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Urine: cumulative. Smoking: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 5 mcg/L. Moderate: 5-20 mcg/L. High: greater than 20 mcg/L. Blood: recent. Urine: cumulative. Smoking: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Cadmium Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: CADMIUM - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Cadmium measures cadmium concentration in spot urine. Urine cadmium reflects cumulative cadmium exposure over months to years (long biological half-life). Urine cadmium is the preferred biomarker for chronic cadmium exposure and early nephrotoxicity detection. Elevated urine cadmium: chronic occupational exposure, environmental exposure (food, water), cigarette smoking. Urine cadmium greater than 2 mcg/g creatinine: evidence of renal tubular dysfunction. Urine cadmium greater than 5 mcg/g creatinine: significant accumulation. Beta-2-microglobulin: companion marker for tubular damage. Limitations: smoking elevates urine cadmium. Beta-2-microglobulin: needed for tubular assessment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note occupational exposure, smoking status, diet. Handle per standard. Urine: cumulative. Greater than 2 mcg/g: tubular dysfunction. Greater than 5 mcg/g: significant. Beta-2-M: companion. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 2 mcg/g creatinine. Tubular dysfunction: greater than 2 mcg/g. Significant: greater than 5 mcg/g. Beta-2-M: companion. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Cadmium Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: CALCITONIN
interpretation:
• Marker of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) — both primary and persistent/recurrent disease
• Elevated in: sporadic MTC, MEN2A/2B-associated MTC, familial MTC, C-cell hyperplasia
• Used for: diagnosis of thyroid nodules when FNA cytology nondiagnostic/inconclusive, monitoring for residual/recurrent disease after thyroidectomy, surveillance in MEN2 carriers
• Also elevated (less commonly): small cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumors, VIPomas, renal failure, atrophic gastritis, proton pump inhibitor use (transient)
• Limitations: not suitable for population screening of thyroid nodules — low sensitivity (~50-60%) and specificity in nodules
• CT (calcitonin) stimulation test improves diagnostic yield in equivocal cases — >100 pg/mL basal or stimulated strongly suggests MTC
• Half-life: ~10 min — levels fall rapidly after total thyroidectomy (undetectable expected at 24h post-op)
• Persistent elevation post-op indicates residual disease or lymph node metastases
• False positives: renal failure, PPIs, heterophilic antibodies, cross-reactive peptides
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: collect any time. For stimulation test: basal sample then IV calcium gluconate or pentagastrin (where available), collect at 2-5 min post-stimulus.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 15-30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (stable 24h) or -20C (months). Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Cool promptly.
• Calcitonin is labile — delayed processing may cause falsely low results.
• EDTA plasma acceptable. Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable for RIA/CLIA methods.
• Note: women have naturally higher levels than men. Post-menopausal women: higher still.
• Stimulation test: requires institutional protocol — confirm assay compatibility before test.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: <10 pg/mL (male); <5 pg/mL (female); post-menopausal <30 pg/mL (gender-specific ranges critical)
• MTC: typically >100 pg/mL (sporadic); >1000 pg/mL strongly suggests MTC
• C-cell hyperplasia: 10-100 pg/mL — requires stimulation test for equivocal cases
• Post-thyroidectomy target: undetectable at 24h, <10 pg/mL by 6 months
• Rising trend post-op: residual disease or recurrence until proven otherwise
• Age-specific: neonates/infants physiologically higher (up to 40 pg/mL at birth, normalizes by 3 months)
• Stimulation test: 2-5× basal strongly supports MTC diagnosis
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and endocrinology references (Tietz; ATA MTC Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CALCIUM
interpretation:
• Total calcium measures circulating calcium — critical for bone health, neuromuscular function, coagulation, and cellular signaling
• Ionized calcium (iCa) reflects biologically active fraction — preferred in critically ill, transfusion, and acid-base abnormalities
• Total calcium affected by albumin levels — corrected calcium = measured + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin g/dL) when albumin <4.0 g/dL
• Low: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency/deficiency states, CKD (secondary hyperparathyroidism), hypomagnesemia, acute pancreatitis, osteomalacia, medications (bisphosphonates, denosumab, phenytoin)
• High: primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy (PTHrP-mediated), vitamin D intoxication, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB), immobilization, thiazide diuretics, thyrotoxicosis
• Limitations: albumin correction is approximate — direct iCa measurement preferred when albumin <3 g/dL, pH altered, or critical illness
• Ionized calcium: extremely labile — pH, temperature, and anaerobic collection alter results rapidly
• Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D assessment required for complete calcium disorder workup
• Fasting and posture affect calcium minimally — no strict fasting requirement
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum (total) or heparinized whole blood / plasma (ionized). Standard venipuncture.
• Preparation: no strict fasting required. Avoid haemolysis (cellular calcium released). Minimize tourniquet time.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Total calcium serum: 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Ionized calcium: process IMMEDIATELY, avoid air exposure, anaerobic collection preferred, 2-8C if delay <1h.
• Ionized calcium requires special collection (heparin syringe, avoid air). Unheparinized serum NOT suitable for iCa.
• Keep iCa on ice, measure promptly — pH drift alters iCa values.
• Blood gas syringes suitable for iCa (anaerobic collection).
ref_ranges:
• Adults (total): 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.1-2.6 mmol/L); ionized: 4.5-5.3 mg/dL (1.1-1.3 mmol/L)
• Albumin-corrected calcium applies when albumin <4.0 g/dL; correction unreliable <3.0 g/dL (use iCa)
• Children: slightly higher reference ranges (10.0-11.5 mg/dL in neonates)
• Pregnancy: decreases slightly (up to 0.2-0.4 mg/dL lower in 3rd trimester)
• Hypocalcemia: total <8.5 mg/dL; corrected <8.5 mg/dL
• Primary hyperparathyroidism: high iCa + high PTH (inappropriately elevated)
• PTHrP-mediated malignancy: high iCa + suppressed PTH
• Ionized hypercalcemia: iCa >5.3 mg/dL — correlates with clinical symptoms better than total
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and endocrinology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; ATA Hypoparathyroidism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CALCIUM CREATININE RATIO - RANDOM URINE
interpretation:
• Extended calcium interpretation panel
• Ionized calcium (iCa2+): biologically active fraction — preferred in critical illness, massive transfusion, acid-base abnormalities, and total calcium unreliable
• Corrected calcium: compensates for hypoalbuminemia — when albumin <4.0 g/dL, corrected Ca = measured + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin) [formula varies per lab]
• Limitations: albumin correction is an approximation — directly measured iCa preferred in severe hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), rapid pH changes, critical care
• Ionized calcium collection is technically demanding — requires anaerobic collection, heparin syringe, immediate measurement or refrigeration on ice
• Total calcium alone insufficient: do not miss iCa measurement errors in ICU and perioperative settings
• Seasonal variation: calcium may be 2-4% lower in winter
• Reference ranges differ for ionized vs total, EDTA vs heparin plasma, age groups
pre_analytical:
• Sample: iCa — heparinized whole blood or arterial blood (blood gas syringe). Total calcium — serum or plasma (EDTA/lithium heparin).
• Preparation: no fasting required. Note albumin, pCO2, pH simultaneously when measuring iCa.
• Handling: iCa — process IMMEDIATELY after collection, keep on ice, anaerobic collection essential (pH changes in open sample alter iCa within minutes). Total Ca: 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Blood gas syringes: suitable (pre-charged with balanced heparin) for iCa — measure within 15-30 min.
• EDTA: not suitable for total Ca (chelates calcium).
• Avoid haemolysed samples for iCa — intracellular Ca contamination.
ref_ranges:
• Adults (total Ca): 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.1-2.6 mmol/L); iCa: 4.5-5.3 mg/dL (1.1-1.3 mmol/L)
• Children: slightly higher (10.0-11.5 mg/dL in neonates)
• Pregnancy: up to 0.2-0.4 mg/dL lower in 3rd trimester (dilutional + albumin effect)
• Albumin-corrected Ca formula: corrected = measured + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin g/dL) when albumin <4.0
• iCa <4.5 mg/dL or <1.1 mmol/L: symptomatic hypocalcemia threshold; hypercalcemia threshold: >5.3 mg/dL
• Hypoparathyroidism: low iCa + high PTH (inappropriately elevated)
• PTHrP malignancy: high iCa + suppressed PTH
• Hypercalcemia of granulomatous disease: high iCa + high 1,25(OH)2D
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; ATA Hypoparathyroidism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CANAVAN DISEASE
interpretation: Canavan Disease is a leukodystrophy caused by aspartoacylase (ASPA) deficiency, leading to accumulation of N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA) in the brain. Elevated plasma/urinary NAA is diagnostic. Canavan disease is an autosomal recessive disorder with high carrier frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish, Cajun, and Saudi populations. Clinical features: macrocephaly, hypotonia, developmental delay, seizures, optic atrophy, white matter demyelination. Diagnosis: elevated NAA in plasma/urine (urinary NAA greater than 100 mmol/mol creatinine). Enzyme: aspartoacylase in leucocytes. Genetic: ASPA gene mutations. Limitations: macrocephaly is early sign. NAA: highly elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h) or plasma. Preparation: note macrocephaly, hypotonia, developmental delay, family history, ethnicity. Handle per standard. NAA: highly elevated (greater than 100 mmol/mol creatinine). Enzyme: aspartoacylase. ASPA gene: mutations. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: NAA less than 5 mmol/mol creatinine. Elevated: greater than 100 mmol/mol creatinine (Canavan). Enzyme: aspartoacylase deficient. ASPA gene: mutations. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Canavan Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CANDIDA ALBICANS AB BY INDIRECT HEAMAGGULATION
interpretation: Candida albicans Antibodies by Indirect Haemagglutination (IHA) measures antibodies against Candida albicans. Elevated Candida antibodies may indicate: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), invasive candidiasis (limited sensitivity), recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis. IHA detects agglutinating antibodies against Candida cell wall antigens. Limitations: Candida is a normal commensal, so low titre antibodies are common. High titres may indicate invasive disease. IHA is less sensitive than mannan/anti-mannan or beta-D-glucan. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recurrent candidiasis, immunosuppression, HIV. Handle per standard. High titres: invasive candidiasis. CMC: elevated. IHA: less sensitive than BDG. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: low titre (common in healthy individuals). Elevated: invasive candidiasis, CMC. IHA: less sensitive than BDG. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESCMID Candidiasis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CARBAMAZEPINE (TEGRETOL)
interpretation: Serum Carbamazepine (Tegretol) measures the concentration of carbamazepine, an anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser. Carbamazepine is used to treat epilepsy (partial and generalised seizures), trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder. Therapeutic range: 4 to 12 mcg/mL (20 to 50 mcol/L). Toxic levels: greater than 12 mcg/mL. Carbamazepine induces hepatic enzymes (CYP3A4), causing auto-induction (levels decrease over first 2-4 weeks). Carbamazepine also induces metabolism of many other drugs (oral contraceptives, warfarin, corticosteroids). Active metabolite: carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide (may contribute to toxicity). Toxicity: diplopia, nystagmus, ataxia, drowsiness, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (HLA-B*1502). Limitations: auto-induction (levels change over time). Active metabolite may contribute. HLA-B*1502: SJS risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: trough timing (just before next dose). Preparation: note seizure control, side effects, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 4-12 mcg/mL. Auto-induction: levels decrease. HLA-B*1502: SJS risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 4 to 12 mcg/mL (20 to 50 mcol/L). Toxic: greater than 12 mcg/mL. Auto-induction: levels decrease. Active metabolite: epoxide. HLA-B*1502: SJS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CARCINO EMBRYONIC ANTIGEN (CEA)
interpretation:
• Anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer — used for epilepsy (grand mal, focal, mixed), trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar disorder (mood stabilizer)
• Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) required due to narrow therapeutic window, autoinduction, and dose-dependent toxicity
• Toxicity: nystagmus, diplopia, ataxia, drowsiness, confusion, hyponatremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity, cardiac arrhythmias
• Autoinduction: carbamazepine induces its own metabolism → dose escalation required in first weeks (t½ decreases from 30-40h → 12-17h at steady state)
• Limitations: TDM targets are for TOTAL carbamazepine. Active metabolite carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide (CBZ-E) responsible for ~30% of clinical activity — metabolite measurement is complex and not routine
• No clear therapeutic range in all patients — clinical response controls dosing more than absolute level
• Toxicity risk increased by: interacting drugs (erythromycin, azoles, calcium channel blockers, Diltiazem — inhibit metabolism), hepatic impairment, elderly, dehydration
• Valproate co-administration inhibits CBZ-E metabolism → metabolite accumulation risk
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum (preferred) or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Trough (pre-dose) level preferred for monitoring. Peak/serum level 8-12h post-dose if requested.
• Preparation: collect trough level (just before next dose) for routine TDM. Note timing of last dose and current dose.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (stable 1 week) or -20C (months). Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable at room temperature for 24h.
• For metabolite assay (CBZ-E): collect simultaneously with parent drug; note metabolite requirement to laboratory.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia: acceptable for most immunoassay.
• Autoinduction: monitor prominently in early treatment phase.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 4-12 µg/mL (therapeutic); 8-20 µg/mL (some psychiatrists use higher range for refractory bipolar)
• Toxicity generally >12-20 µg/mL (varies by individual tolerance, age, hepatic function)
• Neonates infants (for seizures): 4-12 µg/mL
• Peak target: 8-12h post-dose 6-12 µg/mL — trough levels ~2-4 µg/mL lower
• Autoinduction: t½ 30-40h (initial) → 12-17h (steady state) — dose may double or triple over first 4-8 weeks
• CBZ-E (metabolite): contributes ~30% activity — not measured routinely but relevant in toxicity
• Maintenance dosing: colony 400-1600 mg/day in divided doses (target TDM guides maximum)
• Note: metabolic ratio (CBZ-E/CBZ) may indicate abnormal metabolism
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ILAE Epilepsy Treatment Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CARNITINE
interpretation: Serum Carnitine (free and total) measures the concentration of carnitine, a molecule essential for mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Free carnitine: unbound, biologically active form. Total carnitine: free + acylcarnitine esters. Acylcarnitine/free carnitine ratio: important for diagnosing carnitine disorders. Primary carnitine deficiency: SLC22A5 gene mutation, renal tubular reabsorption defect. Secondary carnitine deficiency: organic acidemias, fatty acid oxidation disorders, renal tubular disorders, cirrhosis, valproic acid therapy, hemodialysis. Carnitine supplementation: effective in primary deficiency and some secondary deficiencies. Limitations: fasting affects levels. Medications affect levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
