pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note metabolic disease, medications (valproic acid), dialysis, liver disease. Handle per standard. Free: biologically active. Total: free + acyl. Ratio: important. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 25 to 70 mcmol/L (free). Total: 40 to 100 mcmol/L. Ratio: variable. Low: primary/secondary deficiency. Supplementation: effective. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Carnitine Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CAROTENE
interpretation: Serum Beta-Carotene measures the concentration of beta-carotene, a provitamin A carotenoid. Beta-carotene is converted to retinol (vitamin A) in the intestine and is also an antioxidant. Low serum beta-carotene: indicates poor dietary intake of carotenoid-rich vegetables and fruits. Elevated serum beta-carotene: hypothyroidism (decreased conversion to retinol), diabetes mellitus, liver disease, carotenoderma (yellow skin discoloration from excessive intake). Beta-carotene supplementation has been associated with increased lung cancer risk in smokers. Limitations: fasting preferred. Diet affects levels. Smoking decreases levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred. Preparation: note diet, thyroid status, medications. Handle per standard. Low: poor intake, smoking. High: hypothyroidism, diabetes, liver. Smokers: avoid supplementation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 10 to 85 mcg/dL (method-specific). Low: poor intake, smoking. High: hypothyroidism, diabetes, liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Vitamin A Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CATECHOLAMINES - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Catecholamines (Adrenaline, Noradrenaline, Dopamine) measures the concentration of circulating catecholamines. Catecholamines are produced by the adrenal medulla and sympathetic nervous system. Plasma catecholamines are used to evaluate phaeochromocytoma (tumour of chromaffin cells). Fasting plasma sample preferred (supine). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma (sensitivity 80-90%). Noradrenaline: most commonly elevated in phaeochromocytoma. Adrenaline: elevated in paraganglioma. Dopamine: less commonly elevated. Limitations: supine fasting sample required. Medications affect levels (tricyclics, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics). Stress affects levels. Metanephrines are preferred (more sensitive 97-99%). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: supine fasting sample (30 minutes rest). Preparation: note paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, sweating, headache, medications. Handle per standard. Fasting supine: required. Metanephrines: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma (sensitivity 80-90%). Supine fasting: required. Metanephrines: preferred (sensitivity 97-99%). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS PPGL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CERULOPLASMIN
interpretation:
• Measures carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) — indicator of carbon monoxide (CO) exposure/poisoning
• Elevated in: acute CO poisoning (accidental, intentional), smoke inhalation, chronic low-level exposure (home/automobile exhaust, fires), haemolytic anaemia (falsely elevated in lab due to cell lysis)
• Clinical signs correlate poorly with COHb levels — depends on age, comorbidities, exertion, duration of exposure
• COHb half-life: ~5h breathing room air; ~1.5h with 100% O2; ~20 min with hyperbaric O2 (HBOT)
• Limitations: COHb does NOT reliably distinguish CO source — elevated in non-smokers near heavy traffic, smokers (2-10% at baseline), dwelling fires
• Smoking history essential: heavy smokers have baseline 5-10% COHb. Baseline >15% suggests significant exposure or smoker status
• Elevated in anaerobic specimen storage — CO produced by bacterial activity → spuriously elevated COHb if delayed processing >24h
• Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) binds CO with higher affinity — infants and neonates more susceptible to CO poisoning
• Direct spectrophotometric oximetry (CO-Oximetry) preferred over calculated COHb — may underestimate due to dyshemoglobinins (metHb, sulfhemoglobin) interference
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Arterial or venous whole blood. Heparinized syringe preferred. Anaerobic collection critical.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions in acute poisoning (draw immediately on presentation). Note exposure history (smoking, fires, automobile exhaust, suicidal ideation).
• Handling: IMMEDIATE processing. Place on ice. Separate or analyse within 30 min if refrigeration on ice. Centrifuge if plasma COHb needed.
• Critical: anaerobic collection (air-free syringe). Oxygen exposure displaces CO from Hb → falsely LOW COHb.
• If delay unavoidable: keep anaerobic, on ice, analyse within 2-4h of collection.
• Bacterial production of CO: results unreliable if sample >24h old or not cooled.
• CO-Oximetry required: pulse CO-oximetry unreliable.
ref_ranges:
• Non-smokers: <2-3% COHb
• Smokers: 3-10% (average ~4-6% in chronic smokers); up to 15% in heavy smokers
• Light smokers: 2-5%
• CO poisoning — mild: 10-20% (headache, nausea, dyspnea on exertion); moderate: 20-30% (severe headache, confusion, syncope); severe: >30-40% (coma, cardiovascular instability, death risk >50%)
• Infants/neonates: physiologically higher (up to 5% at birth declining to adult levels in first weeks)
• Symptoms correlate poorly with COHb — assess with clinical context
• HBOT consideration: COHb >25% with neurological symptoms; >15% in pregnancy; any level with loss of consciousness
• Chronic low-level: 5-15% (home exposure, traffic); effects on cognitive/behavioral function emerge at lower levels than assumed
• COHb in smokers: falls to baseline within 6-12h of last cigarette — recheck if recent dosing unknown
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and toxicology references (Tietz; AACC Toxicology Guidelines; WHO CO Poisoning Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CH-50 (COMPLEMENT TOTAL)
interpretation: Total Haemolytic Complement Activity (CH50) measures the functional capacity of the classical complement pathway to lyse antibody-sensitised sheep red blood cells. CH50 reflects the combined activity of all nine classical pathway components (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8, C9). CH50 is zero if any single component is completely absent. CH50 is a screening test for complement deficiencies. Low CH50: hereditary complement deficiency, consumptive process (SLE vasculitis, acute MPGN), decreased synthesis (liver disease). Elevated CH50: acute phase response, inflammation, autoimmune disease (active SLE). CH50 cannot differentiate between classical and terminal pathway defects. Limitations: specimen handling affects results (complement is heat-labile). Not for monitoring therapy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (separate within 2 hours). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: process quickly (complement is heat-labile). Preparation: note autoimmune disease, recurrent infections, family history. Handle: separate rapidly, store -70C. Low: deficiency or consumption. Zero: complete absence. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 60 to 144 U/mL (method-specific). Low: deficiency, consumption (SLE). Zero: any component absent. Elevated: inflammation, acute phase. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR SLE Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHITOTRIOSIDASE - PLASMA
interpretation: Serum Chitotriosidase measures the activity of chitotriosidase (chitinase-1), a glycosyl hydrolase produced by activated macrophages. Chitotriosidase is a biomarker for Gaucher disease (elevated in untreated Gaucher disease) and other lysosomal storage disorders. Chitotriosidase is also elevated in: inflammatory bowel disease, liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, visceral leishmaniasis, fungal infections. Approximately 6% of the population are chitotriosidase-deficient (homozygous for the null allele), making this marker uninterpretable in this population. Chitotriosidase was historically used as a biomarker for Gaucher disease before enzyme assays became available. Limitations: 6% of population are deficient (uninterpretable). Not specific for Gaucher disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note Gaucher disease symptoms, IBD, liver disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: Gaucher, IBD, liver fibrosis. Deficient: 6% of population. Not specific: for Gaucher. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: Gaucher disease, IBD, liver fibrosis. Deficient: 6% of population (uninterpretable). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Gaucher Registry Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHLORIDES
interpretation: Serum Cholinesterase (Pseudocholinesterase, Butyrylcholinesterase, BChE) measures the activity of butyrylcholinesterase, an enzyme produced by the liver. Cholinesterase hydrolyses succinylcholine and ester-type local anaesthetics. Low cholinesterase: liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis - reduced hepatic synthesis), organophosphate poisoning (irreversible inhibition), succinylcholine sensitivity (genetic deficiency - homozygous atypical variants), malnutrition, chronic infection. Cholinesterase and liver function: low cholinesterase reflects synthetic liver function (like albumin). Succinylcholine apnoea: homozygous atypical BChE causes prolonged paralysis after succinylcholine. Limitations: pregnancy lowers cholinesterase. Medications (echothiophate, corticosteroids) inhibit BChE. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver disease, anaesthetic history. Handle per standard. Low: liver disease, succinylcholine sensitivity. Organophosphate: poisoning. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 4,000 to 12,000 U/L (method-specific). Low: liver disease. Succinylcholine: apnoea risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AASLD Liver Function Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHLORIDES - FLUID
interpretation: Serum Chromogranin A (CgA) measures the concentration of chromogranin A, a protein co-stored and co-released with catecholamines from neuroendocrine cells. CgA is the most widely used tumour marker for neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). Elevated CgA: carcinoid tumour (midgut NETs), pancreatic NETs (gastrinoma, insulinoma, VIPoma), phaeochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, neuroblastoma, small cell lung carcinoma. CgA and NETs: sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 70-90%. CgA monitoring: useful for disease recurrence and treatment response. CgA and PPIs: proton pump inhibitors cause false CgA elevation (2-3x). Limitations: PPI use causes false elevation. Renal failure elevates CgA. Assay variability (different methods give different results). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note NET symptoms, diarrhoea, flushing. Handle per standard. Elevated: NETs, carcinoid. PPIs: interfere. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 ng/mL (method-specific). NETs: elevated. PPIs: interfere. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHLORIDES URINE SPOT
interpretation:
• Fluoride-preserved tube used for glucose determination when glycolysis is likely to continue post-collection
• Sodium fluoride (NaF) inhibits enolase → halts glycolysis for ~24h — allows delayed processing for glucose measurement in glucose tolerance tests, hospitalization, or field collections
• Plain red-top tubes (no fluoride) are unsuitable for delayed glucose measurement — glycolysis by viable RBCs and WBCs leads to progressive glucose loss (~5-7% per hour at room temperature)
• Fluoride tubes do NOT reliably preserve lactate — whole blood lactate must be processed immediately on ice
• Limitations: fluoride is NOT an absolute glycolysis inhibitor — early glycolysis in first 1-2h before full enzyme inhibition may cause 10-15% loss even in fluoride tube
• For accurate glucose: fluoride tube + immediate refrigeration OR plasma separator tube (PST) is optimal
• Fluoride overdose can alter some enzyme assays — does not interfere with most routine chemistry but lipase may be underestimated
• Fluoride inhibits some immunoassays — check assay compatibility before using fluoride plasma for purposes other than glucose
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Blood in sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate (grey-top) tube for glucose. NOT for routine chemistry unless glucose-specific requirement.
• Preparation: collect in correct order of draw. Fill tube completely (correct NaF:blood ratio). Underfilled tubes reduce glycolysis inhibition.
• Handling: Separate plasma within 30 min. Plasma stable at 2-8C for 24h in fluoride tube; -20C for longer storage.
• Oxalate anticoagulant (potassium oxalate in grey-top) allows plasma separation.
• Do NOT use fluoride tubes for calcium, LDH, or amylase assays (oxalate anticoagulant affects these).
• For glucose tolerance tests: fluoride tubes at each collection time point minimize glycolysis error.
• Blood gas syringes for lactate: heparinised, on ice, process within 15 min — NOT suitable for fluoride tube.
ref_ranges:
• Sodium fluoride inhibits glycolysis — glucose stable for 24h in properly filled tube at 2-8C
• Underfilled tubes: glycolysis inhibition compromised — 5-7% loss per hour at room temp may occur
• Recommended colour-coded tubes: GREY-TOP (NaF/K-oxalate)
• Post-collection refrigeration immediately after filling is essential for maximum stability
• Fluoride tube: suitable for glucose, lactate (limited), some enzyme assays
• NOT suitable for: calcium (oxalate precipitation), amylase (oxalate inhibition), LDH (RBC penetration)
• Reference ranges: same as non-fluoride glucose (fasting <100 mg/dL, <5.6 mmol/L for IFG)
• For lactate: fluoride tube NOT reliable — process whole blood on ice within 15 min
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; CLSI Glucose/Sodium Fluoride Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHOLESTEROL - FLUID
interpretation:
• Free light chains (FLC, kappa and lambda) — produced by clonal plasma cells in myeloma and related disorders
• Elevated FLC ratio: diagnostic cornerstone for AL amyloidosis, light-chain multiple myeloma (LCMM), and myeloma with non-diagnostic bone marrow
• Absolute elevation: plasma cell dyscrasia staging (MGUS → smoldering myeloma → active myeloma). FLC ratio key for AL amyloidosis risk stratification (Mayo 2012: involved:uninvolved >100 = high risk)
• Normal ratio: 0.26-1.65 (depends on assay; Freelite, N Latex, SPIRA reference ranges differ)
• Limitations: FLC assay NOT universally standardized — assays differ in calibrators, antisera, reference ranges limits (inter-assay CV ~15-20%)
• Acute kidney injury (AKI) transiently elevates FLC (reduced renal clearance) — new FLC elevation in AKI needs recheck after recovery to distinguish from true clonal process
• In renal failure: reference ranges change (FLC both elevated, ratio may drift) — use renal-adjusted ranges or percentiles
• FLC do NOT substitute for serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) or immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) — combine all three for complete plasma cell dyscrasia assessment
• Polymeric FLC (rheumatoid factor, anti-idiotype antibodies) interfere with nephelometric/turbidimetric assays
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum (preferred) or plasma (EDTA/heparin/heparinised PST).
• Preparation: no fasting required. No pretest restrictions. Note renal function (eGFR/Cr) simultaneously — renal impairment affects interpretation independently of clonal disease.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum/plasma; 2-8C (24-48h) or -20C (months). Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for nephelometric/turbidometric methods.
• Paired samples: kappa + lambda MUST be measured simultaneously in same assay.
• Serial monitoring: same platform consistently (inter-assay variation significant).
• AKI patients: recheck FLC ratio once renal function recovers to confirm persistent clonal process vs. renal clearance artefact.
ref_ranges:
• Free light chain reference (healthy adults): Kappa 3.3-19.4 mg/L; Lambda 5.7-26.3 mg/L; Ratio (K/L) 0.26-1.65
• Renal impairment: both kappa and lambda elevated — ratio still informative but ranges broaden
• AL amyloidosis risk: ratio >100 (involved:uninvolved) associated with 80% 4-year mortality without therapy
• Light chain MM: involved FLC >100 mg/L with abnormal ratio
• MGUS-lite chain: involved FLC >10 mg/L + abnormal ratio + bone marrow clonal plasma cells <10%
• 2014 IMWG diagnostic criteria: FLC-difference <100 + involved >100 + abnormal ratio = MM diagnosis (with CRAB criteria)
• Accurate FLC ratio interpretation requires: same assay, same laboratory, paired kappa+lambda results
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and haematology references (Tietz; IMWG Myeloma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHOLESTEROL HDL
interpretation:
• Cholesterol type marker — currently less used for routine CVD risk assessment (LDL-C and non-HDL-C preferred)
• Free cholesterol represents cholesterol not esterified in lipoproteins
• Measurement context: rarely ordered alone — used in specialised lipid research, lipoprotein subfraction analysis, or monitoring lipid-lowering therapy effects on cholesterol esterification
• Limitations: rarely used clinically as standalone marker — LDL-C/HDL-C/non-HDL-C/apo B provide superior risk stratification
• Reference ranges poorly standardized across laboratories — inter-method and inter-laboratory variation is significant
• Free cholesterol content of lipoproteins varies with diet and drug therapy (statins increase esterification fraction)
• Total cholesterol ≈ free cholesterol + cholesterol esters — fractionation by analytical ultracentrifugation or NMR gives additional clinical insight in selected cases (not routine)
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA/heparin). Fasting 12h preferred.
• Preparation: fasting 12h reduces chylomicron interference. Note lipid-lowering therapy (statins, fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe) — affects esterification fraction.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (stable 24-48h) or -20C for longer-term storage. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Stable at room temperature for 24h. EDTA plasma acceptable for most methods.
• Haemolysis and severe lipaemia acceptable for enzymatic/spectrophotometric cholesterol methods.
• Free cholesterol assay format: cholesterol oxidase/peroxidase enzymatic colorimetric or LC-MS/MS.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: varies by assay and method (enzymatic colorimetric vs LC-MS/MS)
• Total cholesterol fraction: free cholesterol ~20-30% of total; cholesterol esters ~70-80%
• Reference ranges poorly standardized — ranges must be interpreted in context of complete lipid profile
• LDL-C (Friedewald calculation): preferred calculated marker for CVD risk; Non-HDL-C = TC - HDL-C
• Free cholesterol not independently used for risk assessment in current guidelines (AHA/ACC, ESC)
• Elevated free cholesterol fraction: associated with dietary hyperlipidemia and some rare metabolic conditions
• Esterification fraction increase with statin therapy — free cholesterol decreases relative to total
• Colour-coded reference: Free cholesterol test names may appear as 'CHOLESTEROL FREE', 'UNESTERIFIED CHOLESTEROL'
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and lipidology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; AHA/ACC Lipid Guidelines; NCEP; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHOLESTEROL LDL DIRECT
interpretation:
• Gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT, gamma-GT) — highly sensitive marker of hepatobiliary disease and alcohol consumption
• Elevated in: cholestasis (extrahepatic and intrahepatic), alcoholic liver disease (alcohol consumption marker — rises before AST/ALT in alcoholic liver disease), drug-induced liver injury, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), pancreatic disease
• Also elevated: myocardial infarction (minor), pancreatitis, renal failure, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, non-liver conditions (cardiac failure, obesity, non-liver malignancy)
• AST:GGT ratio in alcoholic vs viral hepatitis: GGT rises disproportionately in alcohol use disorder with AST <300 U/L + GGT >3× ULN
• Limitations: NOT specific for alcohol — elevated in almost any hepatobiliary disease
• GGT best use: detecting cholestasis and monitoring alcohol consumption — not for etiologic diagnosis
• Biliary obstruction: GGT elevates in parallel with ALP — if GGT normal with elevated ALP, source is likely bone, not liver
• False positives: enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin), obesity, diabetes, mild elevations in otherwise healthy individuals
• Mild GGT elevation (1-2× ULN): common incidental finding in primary care — correlates with alcohol intake, NAFLD, medication use, and metabolic syndrome
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: note alcohol consumption history (units/week) — GGT falls with 4-8 weeks abstinence and rises rapidly with resumption (useful monitoring tool)
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for most methods.
• Antiepileptic enzyme-inducing drugs: phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin, rifabutin elevate GGT — interpret with medication knowledge.
• Serial monitoring for alcohol abstinence: baseline GGT before intervention essential.
• GGT not affected by age or sex significantly — useful as alcohol marker across demographics.
• EDTA/heparin: acceptable for spectrophotometric methods.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 9-48 U/L (men); 5-27 U/L (women) — ranges differ by sex and method (kinetic colorimetric 37C most common)
• Men have naturally higher GGT than women (biological sex difference 1.5-2×)
• Alcohol-associated elevation: GGT >3× ULN + AST <300 U/L strongly suggests alcohol hepatitis
• Cholestasis: GGT rises early and disproportionately (earlier than ALP in biliary obstruction) — GGT ALP confirmation
• ALP rises with bone origin: check ALP isoenzyme or co-check GGT — elevated ALP + NORMAL GGT → bone source
• GGT monitoring alcohol: falls to normal over 4-8 weeks with sustained abstinence
• Drug-associated: enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, rifampicin) consistently elevate GGT 2-3×
• Mild elevations (1-2× ULN): common incidental findings — monitor and correlate with other markers for cause (NAFLD, alcohol, drugs)
• Pregnancy: slight elevation in third trimester (placental contribution)
• NAFLD: GGT 2-5× ULN — often the only abnormal LFT in early NAFLD
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD/AACC Liver Test Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHOLESTEROL TOTAL
interpretation:
• Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) screening enzyme assay — detects G6PD deficiency (X-linked enzymopathy)
• Deficiency manifestations: acute hemolytic anemia (AHA) triggered by infections, certain drugs (primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin — see CDC FDA warning), fava beans, metabolic stress
• Neonatal jaundice (unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) in G6PD-deficient neonates
• Chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia (CNSHA) in severe variants (Mediterranean variant: severe <10% residual enzyme activity)
• Limitations: acute hemolytic phase misconception — during AHA enzyme levels may appear NORMAL due to reticulocytosis (young RBCs have normal G6PD) → falsely NORMAL result in active hemolysis
• Best testing time: at least 2-3 months after hemolytic episode for accurate diagnosis
• False negatives during hemolytic episodes AND due to X-inactivation (Lyonization) in heterozygous females — heterozygous females may be falsely NORMAL on qualitative tests
• Quantitative assay preferred for diagnosis — qualitative screening tests (fluorescent spot test) acceptable for population screening
• Heterozygous females: quantitative assay essential — may have intermediate enzyme levels (10-60%) that are missed by qualitative screening
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Whole blood in EDTA (preferred) or heparin. ABSOLUTELY NO fluoride tubes (NaF inhibits G6PD activity — invalidates test).
• Preparation: no fasting required. No pretest restrictions. Note recent hemolytic episode, transfusion, or prior testing results.
• Handling: process within 24-48h of collection if refrigerated. 2-8C for transport and short-term storage. Avoid freezing whole blood.
• CRITICAL: do NOT use fluoride/oxalate grey-top tube — fluoride irreversibly inhibits G6PD enzyme.
• Observe stability — enzyme activity decreases with sample age: optimal within 24h; acceptable within 5 days if refrigerated.
• Transfusion: donor RBCs have normal G6PD → may mask deficiency — wait 3 months after transfusion for testing.
• Testing females: quantitative assay essential due to Lyonization — single qualitative test insufficient.
ref_ranges:
• Normal activity (varies by method, age, assay): >70-80% of normal reference (quantitative) or positive on fluorescent spot
• G6PD deficiency (WHO classes):
  - Class I: <10% activity (chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia — Mediterranean variant)
  - Class II: <10% activity (severe, intermittent hemolysis AHA)
  - Class III: 10-60% activity (moderate, AHA episodes with triggers)
  - Class IV: >60% (variant/enzyme normal)
• Acute hemolytic anemia trigger: hemolysis 24-48h after exposure to trigger (infection, drugs, fava beans, stress)
• Heterozygous females: 10-60% activity due to Lyonization — rules of X-inactivation mean reticulocyte elevation may mimic normal
• Neonatal: G6PD deficiency may present with unconjugated jaundice (first week of life) — screen if at-risk population
• WHO class I (Mediterranean): severe phenotype with chronic ongoing hemolysis and AHA episodes
• Male hemizygotes: activity <10% or absent = full deficiency (no variable expressivity like in females)
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and haematology references (Tietz; WHO G6PD Working Group; AABB Standards; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHOLINESTERASE
interpretation:
• Glucose measurement — primary diagnostic marker for diabetes mellitus, impaired fasting glucose (IFG), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), hypoglycemia assessment
• Also monitors glucose control in known diabetic patients (HbA1c preferred for long-term; fasting glucose for short-term)
• Elevated FPG >126 mg/dL (≥7.0 mmol/L) on two occasions: diagnostic of diabetes mellitus (WHO/ADA criteria)
• Limitations: highly variable — affected by food intake, exercise, stress, medications, diurnal rhythm (dawn phenomenon), rate of glycolysis in vitro
• False elevation: haemolysis (if glycolysis rapid), recent meal, stress hyperglycemia in acute illness (not diagnostic for diabetes in acute setting)
• False low: fasting >12h, intense exercise, insulinoma, insulin overdose, alcohol ingestion
• Stress hyperglycemia in acute illness: transient elevation not diagnostic of diabetes — recheck after recovery
• Gestational diabetes: OGTT required — fasting glucose alone may miss late-onset GDM
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum or plasma (fluoride/heparin grey-top preferred for delayed processing). Standard venipuncture.
• Preparation: fasting 8-12h for fasting glucose; OGTT requires 3-day carbohydrate loading then 8-12h overnight fast; random glucose: no fasting.
• Handling: Separate serum within 30 min if NOT in fluoride tube. Fluoride tube stable 24h at 2-8C (inhibits glycolysis). Non-fluoride tube: process immediately — glucose drops 5-7% per hour.
• Avoid haemolysis (RBC glycolysis). Keep refrigerated if delay.
• EDTA/lithium heparin acceptable. Fluoride/oxalate grey-top preferred for delayed analysis.
• For oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT): collect timed fasting + 2h post-75g glucose load samples in fluoride tubes.
ref_ranges:
• Adults (fasting): 70-100 mg/dL (3.9-5.5 mmol/L); pre-diabetes IFG: 100-125 mg/dL (5.6-6.9 mmol/L)
• Adults (2h post-load OGTT): <140 mg/dL (<7.8 mmol/L); IGT: 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L); diabetes: ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L)
• Random glucose: <140 mg/dL (non-fasting); diabetes suspicion if ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms
• HbA1c ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) diagnostic for diabetes; 5.7-6.4% = pre-diabetes
• Gestational diabetes (IADPSG/WHO): fasting ≥92 mg/dL OR 1h ≥180 mg/dL OR 2h ≥153 mg/dL after 75g load
• Hypoglycemia: plasma glucose <55 mg/dL (symptomatic threshold); <40 mg/dL (Whipple's triad)
• Neonates: 40-60 mg/dL (first 3h) rising to 70-100 mg/dL (24h+)
• Dawn phenomenon: early morning (4-8 AM) glucose 10-20 mg/dL higher than bedtime (normal physiology)
• Somogyi rebound: nocturnal hypoglycemia → rebound hyperglycemia (dawn); assess overnight profile in unexplained morning hyperglycemia
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA/WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHROMIUM - BLOOD
interpretation: Serum Chromium measures chromium concentration in blood. Chromium is an essential trace element involved in insulin signalling (potentiating insulin action). Chromium deficiency: impaired glucose tolerance, peripheral neuropathy, weight loss. Elevated: occupational exposure (chrome plating, leather tanning), dialysis patients (chromium accumulation from stainless steel dialysis equipment). Blood chromium: reflects recent exposure. Urine chromium: reflects cumulative exposure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note diabetes, dialysis, occupational exposure. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Urine: cumulative. Dialysis: accumulates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.5 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: occupational, dialysis. Deficiency: glucose intolerance. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Chromium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHROMIUM - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Chromium measures chromium concentration in spot urine. Urine chromium reflects cumulative chromium exposure and is used to assess occupational exposure and chromium-related nephrotoxicity. Elevated urine chromium: occupational exposure (chrome plating, leather tanning, welding), environmental contamination, stainless steel dialysis equipment. Urine chromium greater than 10 mcg/g creatinine: significant occupational exposure. Blood chromium: reflects recent exposure. Urine chromium: reflects cumulative exposure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note occupational exposure, dialysis, diet. Handle per standard. Urine: cumulative. Greater than 10 mcg/g: significant exposure. Blood: recent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 2 mcg/g creatinine. Elevated: occupational exposure. Greater than 10 mcg/g: significant. Blood: recent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Chromium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CHROMOGRANIN-A
interpretation:
• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) — gonadotropin regulating ovarian folliculogenesis and spermatogenesis
• Elevated FSH: primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), menopause, primary hypogonadism in males (Klinefelter syndrome), ovarian dysgenesis, gonadal failure after chemotherapy/radiotherapy
• Low FSH: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome, pituitary failure), anorexia nervosa, excessive exercise, stress, hypothalamic suppression
• Used in: menstrual disorder workup (oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea), infertility assessment, menopause confirmation, male hypogonadism evaluation, assisted reproduction cycle monitoring, precocious/delayed puberty assessment
• FSH:LH ratio: LH>FSH in PCOS (2-3:1 ratio), FSH>LH in premature ovarian failure, both elevated in menopause
• Limitations: pulsatile secretion — single measurement may be misleading; pooled samples or timed collection improves reliability
• Pre-menopausal cyclic variation: FSH peaks mid-cycle (day 12-14); LH>FSH in follicular phase; menopausal surge 5-10× baseline
• Assay standardized to IS 98/690 — inter-assay variation minimal but not absent
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: note menstrual phase (day of cycle), menopausal status, presenting symptoms, medications (clomiphene, GnRH analogues affect results).
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia generally acceptable.
• For fertility workup: collect day 2-5 of menstrual cycle (early follicular phase). For amenorrhea: any time (if no menses >6 weeks, treat as early follicular).
• Serial monitoring in assisted reproduction: measured daily or every 2 days during stimulation (follicular phase timing critical).
• Note: clomiphene citrate raises FSH/LH (anti-estrogen effect) — avoid during stimulation for baseline assessment.
ref_ranges:
• Females (pre-menopausal, early follicular phase day 2-5): 3.5-12.5 mIU/mL (assay-specific ranges vary)
• Mid-cycle (day 12-14): FSH 4.7-21.5 mIU/mL (surge)
• Post-menopausal: 25-138 mIU/mL (markedly elevated after ovarian failure)
• Males (adult): 1.4-18.1 mIU/mL (slightly higher in elderly)
• Children (prepubertal): 0.3-5.0 mIU/mL (low); puberty surge at Tanner stages
• Primary ovarian insufficiency/POI: FSH >40 mIU/mL (often >80-100 mIU/mL); amenorrhea + low estradiol
• PCOS: FSH low-normal 3-7 mIU/mL, LH elevated 10-20 mIU/mL (LH:FSH >2:1)
• Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: both FSH and LH low/normal despite gonadal failure
• Pulsatility: single measurement 8-10 AM preferred (circadian peak), pooled/sequential sampling for borderline cases
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and reproductive endocrinology references (Tietz; WHO/ICMART Reproductive Medicine Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: CHYLOMICRON (QUALITATIVE) - URINE
interpretation: Qualitative Urine Chylomicron Test detects the presence of chylomicrons in urine. Chylomicrons are large lipoprotein particles that transport dietary triglycerides from the intestine to peripheral tissues. Chylomicronuria (chylomicrons in urine) indicates lymphatic dysfunction or disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier. Causes: nephrotic syndrome (severe proteinuria), lymphatic obstruction, chyluria (parasitic filariasis, filariasis), constrictive pericarditis, mesenteric lymphoma. Chyluria: milky urine that clears with ether treatment. Chylomicrons are normally absent from urine. Reference ranges: qualitative (present/absent).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note nephrotic syndrome, lymphatic disease, filariasis. Handle per standard. Present: lymphatic dysfunction, nephrotic syndrome. Chyluria: milky urine. Ether: clears. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: nephrotic syndrome, lymphatic dysfunction, filariasis. Chyluria: milky urine. Ether: clears. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Nephrotic Syndrome Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CK-MB (MASS)
interpretation:
• Free triiodothyronine (fT3) — small fraction of total T3 not bound to transport proteins (TBG, transthyretin, albumin)
• Reflects biologically active thyroid hormone — elevated in hyperthyroidism (T3 toxicosis), thyroid hormone resistance syndrome, amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (type 1)
• Low fT3: hypothyroidism, euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome — non-thyroidal illness), severe acute/chronic illness, starvation, post-operative state, medications (dopamine, corticosteroids, amiodarone, propranolol)
• Limitations: fT3 is the last hormone to fall and first to recover in thyroid dysfunction — most sensitive early marker of hyperthyroidism recurrence
• Assay interference: free thyroid hormone immunoassays are notoriously unreliable in critical illness, pregnancy, TBG abnormalities, and on T4/T3 therapy — equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration LC-MS/MS preferred in these contexts
• fT3 not routinely required for primary hypothyroidism monitoring — fT4 + TSH sufficient in most cases
• T3 toxicosis: fT3 elevated with normal fT4 in early or mild hyperthyroidism — TSH receptor antibody/tracer uptake scan differentiates Graves' from thyroiditis
• TBG abnormalities: estrogen (pregnancy, OCP, HRT) ↑ TBG → affects total T3/T4 (fT3/fT4 less affected but immunoassays can still be affected)
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: no pretest restrictions. Note thyroid medication, amiodarone, iodine exposure, recent pregnancy/OCP change, severe illness state.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C for longer. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for most immunoassays.
• Equilibrium dialysis/extended incubation methods: more reliable in critical illness, pregnancy, TBG abnormalities — request if clinical picture doesn't match routine assay.
• LC-MS/MS preferred in complex cases.
• For thyroid monitoring: fT4 + TSH sufficient — fT3 rarely needed for hypothyroidism monitoring.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 2.3-4.2 pg/mL (0.7-1.1 ng/dL) — by immunoassay or LC-MS/MS (ranges vary)
• Neonates: physiologically elevated (first week up to 400-750 pg/mL, then declines)
• Children: gradually declines to adult range by 6-12 months
• Hyperthyroidism (T3 toxicosis): fT3 elevated with low/normal fT4; TSH suppressed <0.1 mIU/L
• Euthyroid sick syndrome: fT3 low, fT4 low-normal, TSH normal — NOT hypothyroidism (thyroid gland normal, illness suppresses)
• T3 toxicosis from thyroiditis: self-limiting — fT3 falls as T4 rises; TRAbs/RAIU scan distinguishes from Graves'
• T4 replacement therapy: fT3 usually low-normal or low on T4 monotherapy — not a treatment target
• Pregnancy: total T3 rises (TBG effect), fT3 relatively unchanged on equilibrium dialysis — immunoassay discrepancies in pregnancy
• Neonatal screening: T4 + TSH used for congenital hypothyroidism — fT3 not used in neonatal screening programs
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and endocrinology references (Tietz; ATA Thyroid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; Endocrine Society).

name: CLONAZEPAM
interpretation: Serum Clonazepam measures the concentration of clonazepam, a benzodiazepine used to treat epilepsy (absence seizures, myoclonic seizures), panic disorder, and anxiety. Therapeutic range: 20 to 80 ng/mL (65 to 260 nM). Active metabolite: 7-aminoclonazepam (may contribute to effects). Clonazepam has a long half-life (18 to 50 hours). Toxicity: excessive sedation, respiratory depression, ataxia. Dependence: significant with chronic use. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, side effects, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 20-80 ng/mL. Active metabolite: 7-aminoclonazepam. Long half-life: 18-50h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 20 to 80 ng/mL (65 to 260 nM). Active metabolite: 7-aminoclonazepam. Toxicity: sedation, respiratory depression. Long half-life: 18-50h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CLOZAPINE
interpretation: Serum Clozapine measures the concentration of clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Therapeutic range: 350 to 600 ng/mL (1000 to 1700 nM). Active metabolite: norclozapine. Clozapine requires mandatory blood monitoring due to agranulocytosis risk. Clozapine levels greater than 1000 ng/mL: increased seizure risk. Smoking (CYP1A2 induction): decreases clozapine levels. Caffeine (CYP1A2 inhibition): increases clozapine levels. Limitations: agranulocytosis risk requires monitoring. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: trough timing. Preparation: note seizure risk, smoking, medications, ANC monitoring. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 350-600 ng/mL. Agranulocytosis: monitoring required. Smoking: decreases. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 350 to 600 ng/mL (1000 to 1700 nM). Toxic: greater than 1000 ng/mL (seizures). Agranulocytosis: monitoring. Smoking: decreases. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: APA Schizophrenia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: COBALT
interpretation: Serum Cobalt measures cobalt concentration in blood. Cobalt is a component of vitamin B12 (cobalamin). Blood cobalt is used to assess: occupational exposure (grinding, hard metal production), metal-on-metal hip prosthesis failure, cardiomyopathy from cobalt exposure. Elevated blood cobalt: cobalt poisoning (cardiomyopathy, thyroid dysfunction, polycythaemia). Cobalt from metal-on-metal hip prostheses can cause local and systemic toxicity. Blood cobalt greater than 7 mcg/L: elevated (metal-on-metal hips). Blood cobalt greater than 100 mcg/L: toxic. Urine cobalt: reflects cumulative exposure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note hip prosthesis, occupational exposure, vitamin B12 use. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent. Urine: cumulative. Metal-on-metal hips: monitor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1 mcg/L. Elevated: metal-on-metal hips (greater than 7 mcg/L). Toxic: greater than 100 mcg/L. Blood: recent. Urine: cumulative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MHRA Metal-on-Metal Guidelines; WHO Cobalt Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: COBALT - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Cobalt measures cobalt concentration in spot urine. Urine cobalt reflects cumulative cobalt exposure over weeks to months and is used alongside blood cobalt for occupational exposure assessment and metal-on-metal hip prosthesis monitoring. Elevated urine cobalt: occupational exposure, metal-on-metal hip prosthesis failure. Urine cobalt greater than 10 mcg/g creatinine: significant exposure. Blood cobalt: reflects recent exposure. Urine cobalt: reflects cumulative exposure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note hip prosthesis, occupational exposure. Handle per standard. Urine: cumulative. Greater than 10 mcg/g: significant. Blood: recent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 3 mcg/g creatinine. Elevated: occupational, metal-on-metal hips. Greater than 10 mcg/g: significant. Blood: recent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MHRA Metal-on-Metal Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: COCAINE
interpretation:
• Free thyroxine (fT4) — small fraction of total T4 not bound to thyroid hormone-binding proteins (TBG primarily)
• Elevated fT4: primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma), T4 toxicosis, amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, exogenous thyroid hormone excess, thyroid hormone resistance syndrome
• Low fT4: primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's, after radioiodine/thyroidectomy, iatrogenic), central/secondary hypothyroidism (TSH not elevated), euthyroid sick syndrome (low T4 syndrome)
• Limitations: free thyroid hormone immunoassays notoriously unreliable in critical illness, pregnancy, TBG abnormalities, on thyroxine replacement (especially when adjusting doses near euthyroid state)
• Equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration LC-MS/MS preferred in pregnancy, severe illness, TBG abnormalities, or when immunoassay result contradicts clinical picture
• fT4 does NOT predict Graves' ophthalmopathy activity — TSH receptor antibodies, imaging, and clinical assessment needed
• TSH + fT4 combination: sufficient for most thyroid function monitoring — fT3 rarely needed in routine hypothyroidism workup
• On T4 replacement: fT4 often elevated in first 1-2h post-dose — draw before morning dose for monitoring
• TSH response delayed (4-6 weeks) in hypothyroidism treatment initiation — expect TSH to lag behind fT4 normalization
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required.
• Preparation: collect before morning dose of exogenous T4 if monitoring replacement therapy. Note pregnancy status, severe illness, amiodarone, iodine exposure.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for most platforms.
• Equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration preferred in: pregnancy, severe illness (ICU), TBG abnormalities (liver disease, OCP), discordant TSH/fT4 results.
• LC-MS/MS: most reliable method in complex clinical contexts — preferred over equilibrium dialysis for accuracy.
• For hypothyroidism monitoring: draw before morning T4 dose at steady state (after dose changes, wait 6 weeks for TSH to equilibrate).
• Serial comparison: same assay platform essential.
ref_ranges:
• Adults: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL (10-23 pmol/L) — assay-specific ranges vary
• Neonates: physiologically elevated at birth (first week up to 2.5-3.0 ng/dL); declines to adult range by 6-12 weeks
• Children: gradually declining to adult range by 1-2 years
• Hyperthyroidism: fT4 elevated + TSH suppressed <0.1 mIU/L
• Hypothyroidism: fT4 low + TSH elevated (>10 mIU/L in overt; 4-10 mIU/L subclinical)
• Central/secondary hypothyroidism: fT4 low + TSH low/normal (failure of TSH response)
• T4 replacement: fT4 rises within hours of dose (peaks 4-6h post-dose); draw BEFORE morning dose for steady-state monitoring
• Pregnancy: total T4 rises 2-3× (TBG effect) but fT4 relatively stable on equilibrium dialysis — immunoassay discrepancy in pregnancy
• TSH normalization lags fT4 by 4-6 weeks after initiating/adjusting levothyroxine
• Euthyroid sick syndrome: fT4 low-normal + TSH normal + fT3 low — not hypothyroidism
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and endocrinology references (Tietz; ATA Thyroid Guidelines; Endocrine Society; manufacturer IFU).

name: COCCIDIOIDES ANTIBODY
interpretation: Coccidioides Antibody measures antibodies against Coccidioides immitis/posadasii, the fungi that cause Valley Fever (Coccidioidomycosis). Coccidioidomycosis is an endemic mycosis found in the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Central/South America. IgM antibodies: appear early (1-3 weeks), indicate acute/recent infection. IgG antibodies: appear later (4-8 weeks), indicate past or chronic infection. Complement fixation (CF): titres correlate with disease severity. CF titres greater than 1:16: disseminated disease likely. CF titres greater than 1:128: meningeal involvement likely. Limitations: immunocompromised patients may not seroconvert. Cross-reactivity with other fungi possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note travel to endemic areas, respiratory symptoms, immunosuppression. Handle per standard. IgM: acute. IgG: chronic/past. CF: correlates with severity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. IgM: acute infection (1-3 weeks). IgG: chronic/past (4-8 weeks). CF greater than 1:16: disseminated. CF greater than 1:128: meningeal. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IDSA Coccidioidomycosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: COMPLEMENT C3
interpretation:
• Gastrin — peptide hormone produced by G-cells in gastric antrum and duodenum
• Elevated gastrin: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES, gastrinoma), atrophic gastritis (type A/B), pernicious anemia, proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy, H. pylori infection, renal failure, gastric outlet obstruction, antral G-cell hyperplasia
• Low gastrin: achlorhydria/atrophic gastritis (feedback), VIPoma, some medications
• Limitations: highly affected by PPI therapy (omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole) — levels rise 2-4× normal after 2-4 weeks of PPI; H2-blockers cause milder elevation
• Diagnosis of ZES: basal gastrin >10× upper limit of normal OR >1000 pg/mL with gastric pH <5 — secretin stimulation test (SST) confirms diagnosis (paradoxical gastrin rise >120 pg/mL after IV secretin)
• Atrophic gastritis/pernicious anemia: elevated gastrin (G-cell hyperplasia due to achlorhydria) with gastric pH >7 — differentiate from ZES by pH measurement
• False elevations: PPI (most common), renal failure, H. pylori, gastric outlet obstruction, antrectomy, elderly
• Fasting and gastric pH measurement essential for accurate interpretation — hold PPIs 7 days before testing if clinically safe
pre_analytical:
• Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required but FAVOURED for interpretation.
• Preparation: FASTING 8-12h preferred. ABSOLUTELY HOLD PPIs for 7 days and H2-blockers 48h before testing if clinically safe — PPI effect is the most common cause of falsely elevated gastrin.
• Handling: Centrifuge within 30 min. Separate serum; 2-8C (48h) or -20C. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Stable frozen for weeks.
• Haemolysis and lipaemia acceptable for immunoassay/RIA.
• For secretin stimulation test (SST): basal gastrin sample → IV secretin → repeat at 2, 5, 10 min. Use SST-tested kits.
• Simultaneous gastric pH measurement critical for ZES diagnosis (pH >5 distinguishes atrophic gastritis from gastrinoma).
• Medication history essential: note all GI drugs before testing.
ref_ranges:
• Adults (fasting): <100-150 pg/mL (assay-specific). Occasionally up to 200 pg/mL in elderly.
• PPI users: fasting gastrin 200-2000 pg/mL — NOT diagnostic of ZES — hold PPIs and recheck
• H. pylori-positive: mildly elevated gastrin (100-300 pg/mL)
• ZES (gastrinoma): basal gastrin >10× ULN typically >1000 pg/mL with gastric pH <5
• Secretin stimulation test (SST): normal = no rise or falls; ZES = rise >120 pg/mL from basal at 5-10 min post-secretin
• Atrophic gastritis/pernicious anemia: fasting gastrin elevated >200 pg/mL with GASTRIC pH >7 (achlorhydria)
• Renal failure: moderately elevated gastrin 200-500 pg/mL (reduced clearance)
• Elderly healthy: mildly elevated fasting gastrin (up to 200 pg/mL) — not pathological
• Fasting vs postprandial: fasted sample preferred — postprandial normally rises 2-3×; ZES shows minimal postprandial decrease
refs: Sources synthesised from standard clinical biochemistry and gastroenterology references (Tietz Clinical Guide; ZES/GASTROINOMA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU).

name: COMPLEMENT C4
interpretation: Serum Complement C4 measures the concentration of complement component C4, a protein in the classical complement pathway. C4 is consumed in immune complex-mediated diseases. Low C4: SLE (complement consumption), hereditary angioedema (C1 inhibitor deficiency), immune complex vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia, post-streptococcal GN. Low C4 with normal C3: hereditary angioedema, early SLE. Low C4 with low C3: active SLE, post-streptococcal GN, MPGN. Normal C4 does NOT exclude complement consumption (genetic deficiency). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note autoimmune disease, recurrent angioedema. Handle per standard. Low: SLE, hereditary angioedema. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 10 to 40 mg/dL (method-specific). Low: complement consumption. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR SLE Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: COPPER
interpretation: Serum Copper measures copper concentration. Copper is an essential trace element and cofactor for caeruloplasmin, superoxide dismutase, and cytochrome c oxidase. Elevated copper: Wilson disease (hepatic copper accumulation), acute copper poisoning, primary biliary cholangitis, acute leukaemia. Low copper: Menkes disease (copper transport defect), malnutrition, malabsorption, nephrotic syndrome (urinary copper loss). Wilson disease: low caeruloplasmin, elevated 24H urinary copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings. Caeruloplasmin: carrier protein (90% of serum copper). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). CRITICAL: metal-free tube. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note liver disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings, neuropsychiatric symptoms. Handle: metal-free. Elevated: Wilson disease. Low: Menkes disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 70 to 155 mcg/dL (method-specific). Wilson disease: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AASLD Wilson Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CORTICOSTERONE
interpretation: Serum Corticosterone measures the concentration of corticosterone, a glucocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex. Corticosterone is a precursor to aldosterone and is a less potent glucocorticoid than cortisol. Corticosterone is more prominent in rodents than in humans. In humans, corticosterone is a minor adrenal steroid. Elevated: congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), adrenal tumours. Low: Addison disease, adrenal suppression. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (morning sample preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note adrenal disease, medications (steroids), stress. Handle per standard. Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison. Minor: steroid in humans. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison, adrenal suppression. Minor: in humans. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society CAH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CORTISOL (EVENING)
interpretation: Serum Cortisol (Evening) measures cortisol concentration in the late afternoon/evening. Cortisol follows a diurnal pattern: peaks at 08:00, nadir at midnight. Evening cortisol: used to assess diurnal rhythm. Loss of diurnal rhythm: Cushing syndrome (cortisol remains elevated in evening). Evening cortisol greater than 50% of morning value: suggests Cushing syndrome. Late-night salivary cortisol: more practical than serum for Cushing screening. Limitations: stress, illness, shift work, pregnancy affect cortisol. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (evening sample, 16:00-20:00). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note Cushing symptoms, weight gain, striae. Handle per standard. Elevated: Cushing syndrome. Diurnal rhythm: loss. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 50% of morning value. Cushing syndrome: elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CORTISOL (MORNING)
interpretation: Serum Cortisol (Morning) measures cortisol concentration in the early morning (08:00-09:00). Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone produced by the adrenal zona fasciculata. Morning cortisol: peak of diurnal rhythm. Morning cortisol less than 3 mcg/dL: strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). Morning cortisol greater than 15 mcg/dL: adrenal insufficiency unlikely. Morning cortisol 3-15 mcg/dL: equivocal, requires ACTH stimulation test. Limitations: stress, illness, pregnancy affect cortisol. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (morning sample, 08:00-09:00). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation. Handle per standard. Low: adrenal insufficiency. ACTH stim: gold standard. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 5 to 25 mcg/dL (morning). Low: less than 3 (adrenal insufficiency). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CORTISOL (RANDOM)
interpretation: Serum Cortisol (Random) measures cortisol concentration at any time of day. Random cortisol is less useful than timed samples due to diurnal variation. Random cortisol greater than 30 mcg/dL: may suggest Cushing syndrome (but stress/illness must be excluded). Random cortisol less than 3 mcg/dL: may suggest adrenal insufficiency (but morning sample preferred). Limitations: diurnal variation, stress, illness, medications affect cortisol. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note Cushing or Addison symptoms. Handle per standard. Elevated: Cushing syndrome (stress excluded). Low: adrenal insufficiency (morning preferred). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (time of day dependent). Cushing: greater than 30. Addison: less than 3. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cortisol Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CORTISOL SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Spot Urine Cortisol measures cortisol concentration in a random urine sample. Urine cortisol reflects free cortisol excretion over the collection period. Elevated spot urine cortisol: Cushing syndrome, physical/emotional stress, depression, alcoholism. Spot urine cortisol: screening test; 24-hour urine free cortisol (UFC) is gold standard. Limitations: spot urine less reliable than 24-hour collection. Creatinine correction improves accuracy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine. Preparation: note Cushing symptoms, weight gain. Handle per standard. Elevated: Cushing syndrome, stress. 24H UFC: gold standard. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Cushing: elevated. 24H UFC: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cushing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CPK ISOENZYMES
interpretation: Serum Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK) Isoenzymes separate and identify the tissue sources of CK in serum. CK exists as three isoenzymes: CK-MM (skeletal muscle, approximately 95-100% of total CK in muscle disease). CK-MB (cardiac muscle, approximately 15-25% of total CK in myocardial infarction). CK-BB (brain, smooth muscle, rarely elevated). CK-MB relative index (CK-MB/total CK) greater than 2.5-3%: suggests cardiac source. CK-MB mass is more sensitive than CK-MB activity. Limitations: CK-MB is less specific than troponin for MI. Muscle trauma can elevate CK-MB. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain, muscle injury, recent surgery. Handle per standard. CK-MM: skeletal muscle. CK-MB: cardiac. CK-BB: brain. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by isoenzyme. CK-MM: skeletal muscle. CK-MB greater than 2.5%: cardiac. CK-BB: brain. Less specific: than troponin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA MI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CREATINE KINASE (CPK)
interpretation: Serum Creatine Kinase (CK, CPK) measures the concentration of creatine kinase, an enzyme found in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and brain. CK is the most sensitive marker of muscle injury. Elevated CK: rhabdomyolysis (markedly elevated, greater than 10x ULN), myocardial infarction (CK-MB fraction), skeletal muscle injury (trauma, surgery, seizures), hypothyroidism, statin-induced myopathy, malignant hyperthermia, muscular dystrophy. CK-MB: cardiac-specific fraction (largely superseded by troponin). Limitations: exercise, intramuscular injections cause transient elevation. Haemolysis falsely elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note muscle pain, weakness, statin use. Handle per standard. Elevated: rhabdomyolysis, MI. CK-MB: cardiac fraction. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 22 to 198 U/L (method-specific). Rhabdomyolysis: greater than 10x ULN. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA MI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CREATININE
interpretation: Serum Creatinine measures the concentration of creatinine, a waste product of muscle metabolism excreted by the kidneys. Creatinine is the most commonly used marker of renal function. Elevated creatinine: acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), dehydration, high muscle mass, rhabdomyolysis, drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors). Low creatinine: muscle wasting, malnutrition, advanced liver disease, pregnancy. eGFR: estimated from creatinine using CKD-EPI equation (preferred over MDRD). Limitations: affected by muscle mass, diet (cooked meat), drugs. Creatinine lags behind acute changes in GFR. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note renal disease, muscle mass. Handle per standard. Elevated: AKI, CKD. eGFR: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL (method-specific). CKD: staged by eGFR. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CREATININE (RADIOLOGY)
interpretation: Serum Creatinine (Radiology) measures creatinine for assessment of renal function prior to contrast-enhanced imaging procedures. Pre-contrast creatinine: used to calculate eGFR and assess risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN). eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2: high risk for CIN; consider alternative imaging or prophylactic hydration. eGFR less than 45: relative contraindication for IV contrast. Limitations: creatinine may lag behind acute changes in GFR. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note contrast exposure history. Handle per standard. eGFR: used for CIN risk. Less than 30: high risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL. eGFR less than 30: CIN risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR Contrast Media Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CREATININE SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Spot Urine Creatinine measures creatinine concentration in a random urine sample. Spot urine creatinine: used for creatinine clearance estimation (Cockcroft-Gault), protein/creatinine ratio (PCR), and albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR). PCR greater than 30 mg/mmol: significant proteinuria. ACR greater than 3 mg/mmol: microalbuminuria (diabetic nephropathy screening). Limitations: spot urine creatinine affected by hydration, muscle mass, diet. 24-hour collection more accurate for clearance. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine. Preparation: note renal disease, diabetes. Handle per standard. PCR: protein/creatinine ratio. ACR: albumin/creatinine ratio. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). PCR greater than 30: proteinuria. ACR greater than 3: microalbuminuria. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CRYOGLOBULINS(QUALITATIVE)
interpretation: Serum Cryoglobulins (Qualitative) detects the presence of cryoglobulins — immunoglobulins that precipitate at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius and redissolve upon rewarming. Cryoglobulinaemia is classified into three types: Type I (monoclonal Ig, usually IgM or IgG): associated with haematological malignancies (myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia). Type II (mixed, monoclonal IgM + polyclonal IgG): associated with HCV infection (approximately 90%). Type III (mixed, polyclonal IgM + polyclonal IgG): associated with autoimmune diseases (Sjogren, SLE). Clinical manifestations: palpable purpura, arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy, glomerulonephritis. HCV: major cause (approximately 80-90% of mixed cryoglobulinaemia). Limitations: sample must be kept warm (37C) until clot formation. False negatives: if sample cools before processing. Reference ranges: qualitative (present/absent).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (kept warm at 37C). CRITICAL: sample must be kept at 37C from venipuncture to clot formation. Preparation: note purpura, arthralgia, HCV, autoimmune disease. Handle: 37C until clot. HCV: major cause. False negatives: cooling. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: cryoglobulinaemia. HCV: major cause (80-90%). Type I: monoclonal. Type II/III: mixed. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: AASLD HCV Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CSF INDEX - (CSF AND SERUM)
interpretation: CSF Index (CSF and Serum) calculates the ratio of IgG (or total protein) in CSF to serum, corrected for the blood-CSF barrier integrity (albumin ratio). The CSF Index helps differentiate between: Blood-CSF barrier dysfunction (elevated albumin ratio): meningitis, MS, neurological diseases. Intrathecal IgG synthesis (elevated CSF Index with normal or mildly elevated albumin ratio): multiple sclerosis, neurosyphilis, CNS infections. CSF Index greater than 0.7: suggestive of intrathecal Ig synthesis. CSF Index corrected = (CSF IgG/Serum IgG) / (CSF Albumin/Serum Albumin). Oligoclonal bands: complementary test. Limitations: serum and CSF must be collected within 24 hours of each other. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF and serum (collected within 24 hours). Preparation: note neurological symptoms, MS suspicion, infections. Handle per standard. Elevated: intrathecal Ig synthesis. Albumin ratio: barrier integrity. OCB: complementary. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.7. Elevated: intrathecal Ig synthesis (MS, neurosyphilis). Albumin ratio: barrier dysfunction. OCB: complementary. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MS Diagnostic Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: CYCLOSPORIN A
interpretation: Whole Blood Cyclosporin A measures the concentration of cyclosporin A, a calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant. Cyclosporin A is used to prevent organ transplant rejection, and to treat autoimmune diseases (psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis). Trough levels are monitored. Therapeutic range: 100 to 400 ng/mL (trough, depends on transplant type and time post-transplant). New formulation (Neoral/microemulsion): better absorption. Cyclosporin has significant inter- and intra-patient variability. Drug interactions: many (CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors increase levels). Monitoring: trough levels before next dose. Limitations: variable absorption. Drug interactions. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). CRITICAL: trough level (just before next dose). Preparation: note transplant type, time post-transplant, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 100-400 ng/mL. Variable: absorption. Drug interactions: CYP3A4. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 100 to 400 ng/mL (trough). Variable: absorption. Drug interactions: CYP3A4/P-gp. Neoral: better absorption. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Transplant Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CYFRA 21-1 LUNG CANCER MARKER
interpretation: Serum CYFRA 21-1 (Cytokeratin 19 Fragment) is a tumour marker for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly squamous cell carcinoma. CYFRA 21-1 measures a fragment of cytokeratin 19 released from tumour cells. Elevated CYFRA 21-1: NSCLC (sensitivity 60-80%), squamous cell carcinoma (highest sensitivity), bladder cancer, head and neck cancers. CYFRA 21-1 is more sensitive than CEA for NSCLC. CYFRA 21-1 correlates with tumour stage and prognosis. Monitoring: serial levels can track treatment response. Limitations: false positives: renal failure, liver cirrhosis, pulmonary fibrosis. Not for screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note lung cancer history, treatment status, other conditions. Handle per standard. Elevated: NSCLC (sensitivity 60-80%). Squamous: highest. More sensitive: than CEA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 3.3 ng/mL. Elevated: NSCLC (sensitivity 60-80%). Squamous: highest. Monitoring: serial levels. False positives: renal/liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESMO Lung Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CYSTATIN C
interpretation: Serum Cystatin C is a low-molecular-weight protein produced at a constant rate by all nucleated cells and freely filtered by the glomerulus. Cystatin C is used as a marker of kidney function (GFR estimation). Cystatin C is not affected by: muscle mass (unlike creatinine), diet, or hydration status. Cystatin C-based eGFR (CKD-EPI Cystatin C equation): more accurate than creatinine-based eGFR, especially in extremes of muscle mass, elderly, obese, or malnourished patients. Cystatin C is recommended as a confirmatory test when creatinine-based eGFR is discordant with clinical assessment. Elevated: decreased GFR (kidney disease). Not affected by: muscle mass, diet, age. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note kidney disease, muscle mass concerns. Handle per standard. GFR marker: more accurate than creatinine. Not affected: muscle mass, diet. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: decreased GFR. CKD-EPI Cystatin C: more accurate. Not affected: muscle mass, diet. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CYSTIC FIBROSIS NEWBORN SCREEN
interpretation: Cystic Fibrosis Newborn Screen measures immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) and/or CFTR mutations from a heel-prick dried blood spot. Elevated IRT: suggests CF (trypsinogen leaks from inflamed pancreas). IRT greater than 60 ng/mL: further CF testing (sweat chloride, CFTR genotyping) required. CFTR mutation analysis: identifies specific mutations (F508del most common). Sweat chloride: gold standard for CF diagnosis (greater than 60 mmol/L diagnostic). Limitations: false positives (IRT elevated in prematurity, birth stress). False negatives: rare CF mutations not detected by panels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dried blood spot (heel prick). CRITICAL: collected after 48 hours of life. Preparation: note family history, consanguinity. Handle per standard. Elevated IRT: CF risk. Sweat chloride: gold standard. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: IRT less than 60 ng/mL. CF: IRT elevated, sweat chloride greater than 60. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG CF Newborn Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: CYSTINE SPOT URINE
interpretation: Spot Urine Cystine measures cystine concentration in urine. Cystine is an amino acid formed by the oxidation of two cysteine molecules. Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of renal tubular transport of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA). Elevated urinary cystine: cystinuria, cystine kidney stones (the most common hereditary stone disease). Cystine stones are radiolucent (not visible on plain X-ray). Cystine solubility is pH-dependent (more soluble at pH above 7.5). Treatment: high fluid intake, alkalinisation of urine (pH above 7.5), tiopronin/d-penicillamine (chelating agents). Limitations: crystalluria may occur if urine is acidic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). Preparation: note kidney stone history, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: cystinuria. Stones: radiolucent. pH-dependent: solubility. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 250 mg/g creatinine. Elevated: cystinuria. Stones: radiolucent. pH-dependent: solubility. Treatment: alkalinisation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AUA Nephrolithiasis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DCP DECARBOXY PROTHROMBIN PIVKA II
interpretation: Serum Des-gamma-carboxy Prothrombin (DCP, PIVKA-II) is a tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). PIVKA-II (Protein Induced by Vitamin K Absence or Antagonist-II) is an abnormal prothrombin produced by hepatocellular carcinoma cells due to defective carboxylation. Elevated PIVKA-II: HCC (sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 80-95%). PIVKA-II correlates with tumour size and vascular invasion. PIVKA-II is used alongside AFP for HCC surveillance and diagnosis. PIVKA-II rises before AFP in many HCC cases. Limitations: vitamin K deficiency can cause false positives. Warfarin therapy can cause false positives. Not for screening (HCC surveillance: ultrasound + AFP). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver disease, HCC risk factors, vitamin K status, warfarin use. Handle per standard. Elevated: HCC (sensitivity 60-80%). AFP: complementary. False positives: vit K deficiency, warfarin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 40 mAU/mL. Elevated: HCC (sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 80-95%). AFP: complementary. False positives: vit K deficiency, warfarin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: EASL HCC Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DEHYDROEPIANDROSTERONE (DHEA)
interpretation: Serum Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) measures the concentration of DHEA, an adrenal androgen precursor. DHEA is the most abundant circulating adrenal androgen. Elevated DHEA: congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH - 21-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency), adrenal tumours, PCOS. Low DHEA: adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), hypopituitarism, ageing (DHEA declines with age), anabolic steroid use (suppresses DHEA). DHEA and ageing: DHEA peaks at age 25, declines 2-3% per year thereafter. DHEA supplementation: controversial, limited evidence. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note adrenal symptoms, PCOS. Handle per standard. Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age/sex-specific). CAH: elevated. Addison: low. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society CAH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DEOXYCORTICOSTERONE
interpretation: Serum Deoxycorticosterone (DOC) measures the concentration of deoxycorticosterone, a mineralocorticoid precursor produced by the adrenal cortex. DOC is converted to corticosterone by 11-beta-hydroxylase. DOC contributes to sodium and potassium homeostasis. Elevated DOC: congenital adrenal hyperplasia (11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency), adrenal tumours. Low DOC: Addison disease, adrenal suppression. DOC is not routinely measured (cortisol and aldosterone are preferred). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (morning sample preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note adrenal disease, hypertension, medications. Handle per standard. Elevated: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency. Low: Addison. Not routine: cortisol/aldosterone preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison. Not routine: cortisol/aldosterone preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society CAH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DEXAMETHASONE HIGH DOSE SUPPRESION TEST FOR CORTISOL
interpretation: Serum Cortisol after Dexamethasone High Dose Suppression Test measures cortisol following administration of 8 mg dexamethasone overnight. High-dose dexamethasone test: differentiates pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH syndrome. Cortisol suppressed (less than 50% of baseline): pituitary Cushing disease (adenoma responds to negative feedback). Cortisol NOT suppressed: ectopic ACTH syndrome (autonomous ACTH secretion, no feedback sensitivity). Sensitivity 80-100% for pituitary Cushing. Limitations: false positive in some ectopic ACTH (bronchial carcinoid may suppress). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (morning, 8:00-9:00, after overnight 8 mg dexa). Preparation: note Cushing symptoms, ACTH levels. Handle per standard. Suppressed: pituitary Cushing. Not suppressed: ectopic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: suppressed (less than 50% baseline). Pituitary: suppressed. Ectopic: not suppressed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cushing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DEXAMETHASONE LOW DOSE SUPPRESION TEST FOR CORTISOL
interpretation: Serum Cortisol after Dexamethasone Low Dose Suppression Test measures cortisol following administration of 1 mg dexamethasone overnight (1 mg DST) or 2 mg/day for 48 hours. Low-dose DST: screening test for Cushing syndrome. Cortisol suppressed (less than 1.8 mcg/dL): Cushing syndrome unlikely. Cortisol NOT suppressed (greater than 1.8 mcg/dL): Cushing syndrome suspected, proceed to confirmatory testing. 1 mg DST sensitivity 95%, specificity 80% for Cushing. False positives: depression, alcoholism, stress, medications. Limitations: many false positives. False negatives: cyclic Cushing. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (morning, 8:00-9:00, after overnight 1 mg dexa). Preparation: note Cushing symptoms. Handle per standard. Not suppressed (greater than 1.8): Cushing suspected. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: suppressed (less than 1.8 mcg/dL). Cushing: not suppressed (greater than 1.8). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Cushing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DHEA-S
interpretation: Serum Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulphate (DHEA-S) measures the sulphated form of DHEA, the most abundant circulating adrenal androgen. DHEA-S has a longer half-life than DHEA and is less affected by diurnal variation. Elevated DHEA-S: congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), adrenal tumours (carcinoma more than adenoma), PCOS. Low DHEA-S: adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism, ageing, chronic disease, anabolic steroid use. DHEA-S and PCOS: elevated DHEA-S in 20-30% of PCOS. DHEA-S greater than 700 mcg/dL: adrenal tumour until proven otherwise. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note adrenal symptoms, PCOS, hirsutism. Handle per standard. Elevated: CAH, adrenal tumour. Low: Addison, ageing. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age/sex-specific). CAH: elevated. Adrenal tumour: greater than 700. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society PCOS Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DIGOXIN
interpretation: Serum Digoxin measures the concentration of digoxin, a cardiac glycoside used to treat heart failure and atrial fibrillation/flutter. Therapeutic range: 0.5 to 2.0 ng/mL. Toxic levels: greater than 2.0 ng/mL. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index. Toxicity: nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos), bradycardia, heart block, ventricular arrhythmias. Hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity. Renal impairment: increases digoxin levels (digoxin is renally cleared). Timing: trough level (8-24 hours post-dose). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). CRITICAL: 8-24 hours post-dose. Preparation: note renal function, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+), other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 0.5-2.0 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 2.0 ng/mL. Hypokalaemia: potentiates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 0.5 to 2.0 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 2.0 ng/mL. Narrow index: toxicity risk. Hypokalaemia: potentiates. Renal: clears. Reference ranges: method-specific.
