refs: Sources: AHA Heart Failure Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DIHYDROTESTOSTERONE (DHT)
interpretation: Serum Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) measures the concentration of DHT, the most potent androgen. DHT is converted from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues (prostate, skin, hair follicles). Elevated DHT: benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostate cancer, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (paradoxically low DHT), hirsutism, PCOS. Low DHT: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (ambiguous genitalia in 46,XY males), hypogonadism, ageing. DHT and BPH: DHT drives prostate growth; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) shrink prostate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note prostate disease, hirsutism. Handle per standard. Elevated: BPH, hirsutism. 5-AR deficiency: low. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 30 to 85 ng/dL (method-specific). BPH: elevated. 5-AR deficiency: low. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AUA BPH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DOPAMINE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Dopamine measures the concentration of dopamine, a catecholamine neurotransmitter and hormone. Dopamine is a precursor to noradrenaline and adrenaline. Plasma dopamine is used to evaluate: phaeochromocytoma (less commonly elevated), neuroblastoma (elevated in some cases), autonomic dysfunction. Elevated plasma dopamine: phaeochromocytoma, neuroblastoma, drugs (levodopa). Limitations: supine fasting sample required. Medications affect levels. Metanephrines are preferred for phaeochromocytoma screening. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: supine fasting sample (30 minutes rest). Preparation: note paroxysmal symptoms, medications. Handle per standard. Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, neuroblastoma. Metanephrines: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, neuroblastoma. Supine fasting: required. Metanephrines: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS PPGL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DOUBLE MARKER SCREENING TEST-AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Double Marker Screening Test (Auto DELFIA) measures pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and free beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (free beta-hCG) in first-trimester maternal serum. Used for aneuploidy screening (trisomy 21, trisomy 18) at 11-13 weeks gestation combined with nuchal translucency (NT) ultrasound. Trisomy 21: low PAPP-A, high free beta-hCG. Trisomy 18: low PAPP-A, low free beta-hCG. Detection rate 85-90% for trisomy 21 with 5% false positive rate. Limitations: NT measurement operator-dependent. IVF pregnancies may need adjustment. Multiple pregnancy affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (first trimester, 11-13 weeks). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note gestational age, IVF. Handle per standard. Trisomy 21: low PAPP-A, high hCG. NT: required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: risk assessment (combined with NT). Trisomy 21: low PAPP-A, high hCG. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Fetal Medicine Foundation First Trimester Screening; manufacturer IFU.

name: DPDDEOXYPYRIDINOLINE (PYRILINKS D) - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Deoxypyridinoline (DPD, Pyrilinks D) is a bone resorption marker. DPD is a pyridinium cross-link of type I collagen, released during bone degradation. DPD is more bone-specific than hydroxyproline. DPD is used to monitor: osteoporosis treatment (bisphosphonates, denosumab), Paget disease, bone metastases, osteolytic disease. Elevated: increased bone resorption (osteoporosis, Paget, metastases). Decreased: antiresorptive therapy response. DPD is more bone-specific than urinary hydroxyproline. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note bone disease, fracture risk, medications. Handle: 2-8C. DPD: more bone-specific than hydroxyproline. Elevated: bone resorption. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: osteoporosis, Paget, metastases. Decreased: antiresorptive therapy. More specific: than hydroxyproline. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DPYD (DEOXYPYRIDINOLINE) - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urinary Deoxypyridinoline (DPYD) measures the excretion of deoxypyridinoline, a bone resorption marker. DPYD is a pyridinium cross-link of type I collagen, similar to DPD. DPYD is used to monitor: osteoporosis treatment, Paget disease, bone metastases. Elevated: increased bone resorption. Decreased: antiresorptive therapy response. DPYD is highly correlated with DPD (DPD and DPYD are often measured together). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note bone disease, fracture risk, medications. Handle: 2-8C. DPYD: correlated with DPD. Elevated: bone resorption. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and sex dependent). Elevated: osteoporosis, Paget, metastases. Decreased: antiresorptive therapy. Correlated: with DPD. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DRUG OF ABUSE 10 DRUG PANEL
interpretation: Drug of Abuse 10 Drug Panel screens for 10 common drug classes in urine: amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids (THC), cocaine, opiates, phencyclidine (PCP), methadone, propoxyphene, and tricyclic antidepressants. Positive result: indicates recent drug use (window varies by drug). Confirmatory testing (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS) required for legal/forensic purposes. Limitations: immunoassay screening has cross-reactivity. False positives: medications, foods (poppy seeds for opiates). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). CRITICAL: sample integrity (chain of custody for forensic). Preparation: note medications, consent. Handle: chain of custody if forensic. Positive: recent use. Confirmatory: GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative (all panels). Positive: confirm with GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DRUG OF ABUSE 5 DRUG PANEL
interpretation: Drug of Abuse 5 Drug Panel screens for 5 common drug classes in urine: amphetamines, cannabinoids (THC), cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine (PCP). These represent the most commonly abused drug classes. Positive result indicates recent drug use. Confirmatory testing (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS) required for confirmation. Limitations: immunoassay cross-reactivity. False positives possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). CRITICAL: sample integrity. Preparation: note medications. Handle: chain of custody if forensic. Positive: recent use. Confirmatory: GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: confirm with GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DRUG OF ABUSE 6 DRUG PANEL
interpretation: Drug of Abuse 6 Drug Panel screens for 6 common drug classes in urine: amphetamines, barbiturates, cannabinoids (THC), cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine (PCP). Adds barbiturates to the standard 5-panel screen. Positive result indicates recent drug use. Confirmatory testing required. Limitations: immunoassay cross-reactivity. False positives possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). CRITICAL: sample integrity. Preparation: note medications. Handle: chain of custody if forensic. Positive: recent use. Confirmatory: GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: confirm with GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: DRUG OF ABUSE 9 DRUG PANEL
interpretation: Drug of Abuse 9 Drug Panel screens for 9 common drug classes in urine: amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids (THC), cocaine, methadone, opiates, phencyclidine (PCP), and tricyclic antidepressants. Broader coverage than 5-panel. Positive result indicates recent drug use. Confirmatory testing required. Limitations: immunoassay cross-reactivity. False positives possible. Reference ranges: method-specific.

ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: confirm with GC-MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: E-GFR
interpretation: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) is calculated from serum creatinine using the CKD-EPI equation (2021 race-free). eGFR estimates kidney function and stages chronic kidney disease (CKD). eGFR greater than 90: normal kidney function (CKD stage 1 if other markers present). eGFR 60-89: mild decrease (CKD stage 2). eGFR 30-59: moderate decrease (CKD stage 3). eGFR 15-29: severe decrease (CKD stage 4). eGFR less than 15: kidney failure (CKD stage 5, dialysis considered). Limitations: eGFR affected by muscle mass, diet, medications. Not accurate in extremes of body size. Cystatin C may improve accuracy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note renal disease, medications. Handle per standard. eGFR: CKD staging. Less than 15: dialysis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2. CKD: staged by eGFR. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ELECTROLYTES
interpretation: Serum Electrolytes (Panel) measures sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), chloride (Cl-), and bicarbonate (HCO3-). These are the major serum electrolytes critical for fluid balance, acid-base homeostasis, cardiac conduction, and neuromuscular function. Abnormalities: hyponatraemia (Na less than 135), hyperkalaemia (K greater than 5.5 - medical emergency), metabolic acidosis (low HCO3-), metabolic alkalosis (high HCO3-). Limitations: haemolysis falsely elevates K+. Lipaemia/pseudohyponatraemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (arterial or venous). Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note dehydration, vomiting, diuretics, renal disease. Handle per standard. Emergency: K greater than 6.5. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: Na 136-145, K 3.5-5.0, Cl 98-106, HCO3 22-29 mmol/L. Emergency: K greater than 6.5. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Electrolyte Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ELECTROLYTES SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Spot Urine Electrolytes measures sodium, potassium, chloride, and creatinine in a random urine sample. Used to evaluate renal handling of electrolytes and differentiate causes of acute kidney injury and hyponatraemia. Urine Na less than 20 mmol/L: prerenal AKI (kidney retaining sodium). Urine Na greater than 40 mmol/L: intrinsic AKI (ATN). Urine K less than 20 mmol/day: extrarenal K loss. Urine K greater than 20 mmol/day: renal K wasting. Limitations: affected by recent diet, diuretics, hydration. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine. Preparation: note AKI, hyponatraemia, diuretic use. Handle per standard. Urine Na: differentiates AKI type. Urine K: differentiates K loss. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (diet/hydration dependent). Urine Na: less than 20 (prerenal), greater than 40 (intrinsic). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO AKI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: EPINEPHRINE (ADRENALINE) - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Epinephrine (Adrenaline) measures the concentration of epinephrine, a catecholamine produced by the adrenal medulla and extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue. Plasma epinephrine is used to evaluate: phaeochromocytoma (elevated in approximately 50% of cases), paraganglioma (elevated), stress response. Fasting supine sample required. Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma, stress, drugs. Limitations: supine fasting sample required. Medications affect levels. Metanephrines are preferred (more sensitive). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: supine fasting sample (30 minutes rest). Preparation: note paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, sweating, medications. Handle per standard. Supine fasting: required. Metanephrines: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma. Supine fasting: required. Metanephrines: preferred (sensitivity 97-99%). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS PPGL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ERYTHROPOIETIN
interpretation: Serum Erythropoietin (EPO) measures the concentration of erythropoietin, a glycoprotein hormone produced by the kidney. EPO stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. Elevated EPO: polycythaemia vera (PV - EPO suppressed, distinguishing from secondary polycythaemia), chronic hypoxia (COPD, high altitude, sleep apnoea), renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma. Low EPO: polycythaemia vera (EPO suppressed - diagnostic clue), chronic kidney disease (reduced renal EPO production). EPO and PV: EPO suppressed in PV (JAK2 mutation drives erythropoiesis independently). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note polycythaemia, altitude, lung disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: secondary polycythaemia. Low: PV, CKD. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 4 to 26 mIU/mL (method-specific). PV: suppressed. Secondary: elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BSH Polycythaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ESTRADIOL (E2)
interpretation: Serum Estradiol (E2) measures the concentration of estradiol, the most potent oestrogen. In females: primarily produced by ovarian follicles. In males: produced by testes (Sertoli cells) and peripheral aromatisation. Elevated E2: feminisation in males (gynaecomastia), ovarian tumours, granulosa cell tumour, liver cirrhosis (impaired metabolism), pregnancy. Low E2: ovarian failure (menopause), hypogonadism, anorexia nervosa, hypothalamic/pituitary disease. E2 in IVF: monitoring follicular response. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note menstrual cycle day, pregnancy, HRT. Handle per standard. Elevated: ovarian tumour, feminisation. Low: menopause, ovarian failure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (cycle-specific). Menopause: less than 20 pg/mL. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESHRE IVF Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ETHOSUXIMIDE
interpretation: Serum Ethosuximide measures the concentration of ethosuximide, an anticonvulsant used primarily to treat absence seizures (petit mal epilepsy). Therapeutic range: 40 to 100 mcg/mL. Ethosuximide has a relatively wide therapeutic index compared to other anticonvulsants. Toxicity: nausea, vomiting, lethargy, headache. Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment for absence seizures. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure type (absence seizures), other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 40-100 mcg/mL. First-line: absence seizures. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 40 to 100 mcg/mL. First-line: absence seizures. Wide index: less toxicity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: EVEROLIMUS
interpretation: Whole Blood Everolimus measures the concentration of everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor immunosuppressant and targeted anticancer agent. Everolimus is used for: organ transplant rejection prevention, renal cell carcinoma, breast cancer, neuroendocrine tumours. Therapeutic range: 3 to 8 ng/mL (transplant). Cancer: varies by indication. Everolimus has many drug interactions (CYP3A4/P-gp). Monitoring: trough levels. Limitations: variable absorption. Drug interactions: many. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). CRITICAL: trough level (just before next dose). Preparation: note transplant type, cancer type, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 3-8 ng/mL (transplant). Drug interactions: CYP3A4/P-gp. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 3 to 8 ng/mL (transplant). Cancer: variable. Drug interactions: CYP3A4/P-gp. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Transplant Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FABRY DISEASE QUANTITATIVE - BLOOD
interpretation: Fabry Disease Quantitative (Alpha-Galactosidase A Activity) measures the activity of alpha-galactosidase A, a lysosomal enzyme. Alpha-Gal A deficiency causes Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder. Fabry disease: X-linked dominant. Males: severe (childhood onset: acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis; adult: renal failure, cardiomyopathy, stroke). Females: variable (may be severely affected due to X-inactivation skewing). Alpha-Gal A activity: less than 1% of normal in affected males. Females: may have residual activity (carrier detection requires both enzyme activity and mutation analysis). Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT): agalsidase beta, agalsidase alfa. Newer: oral chaperone (migalastat). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dried blood spot or leucocytes. Preparation: note acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, renal failure, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Fabry disease. Males: less than 1%. Females: variable (X-inactivation). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Fabry disease. Males: less than 1%. Females: variable. ERT: agalsidase. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Fabry Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FASTING PLASMA GLUCOSE
interpretation: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) measures blood glucose concentration after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours. FPG is one of the primary diagnostic tests for diabetes mellitus and prediabetes. FPG reflects hepatic glucose output and peripheral insulin sensitivity during the fasting state. Diagnosis: less than 100 mg/dL normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes), greater than or equal to 126 mg/dL on two separate occasions diagnostic of diabetes mellitus. FPG is also used for monitoring glycaemic control in known diabetic patients. Limitations: FPG is influenced by recent dietary intake (must be truly fasting), acute illness, stress, medications (corticosteroids, thiazides, beta-blockers), and sample handling (delayed separation causes glycolysis and falsely low glucose). Glucose degrades in whole blood at approximately 5 to 7 percent per hour at room temperature if separation is delayed. Haemolysis falsely elevates glucose (red blood cells contain glycolytic enzymes). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: FPG may increase with age. Gender: may vary.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fluoride-oxalate tube preferred). CRITICAL: fasting sample (at least 8 hours). Preparation: note diabetes medications, diet, acute illness, recent surgery, pregnancy. Handle: separate within 30 minutes to prevent glycolysis. Normal: less than 100 mg/dL. IFG: 100 to 125 mg/dL. Diabetes: greater than or equal to 126 mg/dL (two separate occasions). Haemolysis: falsely elevates. Delayed separation: falsely lowers. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 mg/dL. Impaired fasting glucose: 100 to 125 mg/dL. Diabetes: greater than or equal to 126 mg/dL (two separate occasions). Haemolysis: falsely elevated. Delayed separation: falsely low. Fasting: at least 8 hours. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Guidelines; WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FATTY ACIDS WITH VERY LONG CHAINS C22 TO C26 - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Very Long Chain Fatty Acids (VLCFA) C22 to C26 measures the concentration of VLCFAs (behenic acid C22:0, lignoceric acid C24:0, hexacosanoic acid C26:0) and their ratios. VLCFA analysis is used to diagnose X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD), a peroxisomal beta-oxidation disorder caused by ABCD1 gene mutations. X-ALD: X-linked, affects males primarily. Childhood cerebral ALD: demyelination, behavioural changes, adrenal insufficiency. Adrenomyeloneuropathy: spastic paraparesis, adrenal insufficiency. Elevated VLCFA: X-ALD (C24:0/C22:0 and C26:0/C22:0 ratios elevated). Female carriers: may have mildly elevated VLCFA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note demyelination, adrenal insufficiency, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: X-ALD. Ratios: C24:0/C22:0, C26:0/C22:0. Females: mildly elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: X-ALD (C24:0/C22:0, C26:0/C22:0 ratios). Females: mildly elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ALD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FERRITIN
interpretation: Serum Ferritin measures the concentration of ferritin, the intracellular iron storage protein. Ferritin reflects total body iron stores. Elevated ferritin: iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion haemosiderosis), inflammation (acute phase reactant), liver disease, malignancy (lymphoma, leukaemia), metabolic syndrome. Low ferritin: iron deficiency anaemia (most specific marker - ferritin less than 15 virtually diagnostic). Ferritin and anaemia: ferritin less than 15 confirms iron deficiency. Ferritin 15-30: may still be iron deficient in inflammation. Ferritin greater than 300 in males/greater than 200 in females: investigate iron overload. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note anaemia, inflammation, liver disease. Handle per standard. Low: iron deficiency (less than 15). High: overload, inflammation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 30 to 300 ng/mL (males), 15 to 150 ng/mL (females). Less than 15: iron deficiency. Greater than 300: overload. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BSH Iron Deficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FIBROBLAST GROWTH FACTOR 23
interpretation: Serum Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23) is a hormone produced by osteocytes that regulates phosphate and vitamin D metabolism. FGF23 promotes renal phosphate excretion and suppresses 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis. Elevated FGF23: tumour-induced osteomalacia (TIO), X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH), autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (ADHR), chronic kidney disease. FGF23 is the earliest marker of phosphate wasting in XLH and TIO. FGF23 levels guide treatment with burosumab (anti-FGF23 antibody) in XLH and TIO. Limitations: C-terminal FGF23 assay: more stable. Intact FGF23: more variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note hypophosphataemia, osteomalacia, rickets, kidney disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: XLH, TIO, CKD. Intact FGF23: variable. C-terminal: stable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: TIO, XLH, CKD. C-terminal: more stable. Burosumab: treatment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FIBROBLAST GROWTH FACTOR FGF2
interpretation: Serum Fibroblast Growth Factor 2 (FGF2, basic FGF) is a potent angiogenic factor that promotes cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration. FGF2 is elevated in various cancers (bladder, breast, lung, liver) and in wound healing, inflammation, and angiogenic conditions. Elevated FGF2: bladder cancer (urine FGF2), hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, wound healing, diabetic retinopathy. Not a specific tumour marker. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note cancer history, angiogenic conditions. Handle per standard. Elevated: various cancers, angiogenesis. Not specific: tumour marker. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: various cancers, angiogenesis. Not specific: tumour marker. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Manufacturer IFU.

name: FIBROMAX FIBROSIS ACTIVITY STEATO ASH AND NASH OF LIVER
interpretation: FibroMax is a panel of serum biomarkers used to non-invasively assess liver fibrosis, steatosis, activity, and NASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis). FibroMax includes: FibroTest (fibrosis), ActiTest (activity/NASH), SteatoTest (steatosis), NashTest (NASH), AshTest (ASH). FibroMax panels are used to: stage liver fibrosis without biopsy, monitor treatment response, screen for NASH. Limitations: results are proprietary and require specific interpretation. Biopsy may still be needed for definitive diagnosis. Reference ranges: proprietary.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver disease risk factors, NAFLD, hepatitis. Handle per standard. Proprietary: panel interpretation. Non-invasive: alternative to biopsy. Reference ranges: proprietary.
ref_ranges: Normal: proprietary ranges. Fibrosis: F0-F4. Steatosis: S0-S3. Activity: A0-A3. NASH: binary. Reference ranges: proprietary.
refs: Sources: EASL NAFLD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - ASCITIC/PERITONEAL FLUID
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of Ascitic/Peritoneal Fluid evaluates ascitic fluid for diagnostic and monitoring purposes. Key parameters: protein, glucose, LDH, cell count, SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient). SAAG greater than or equal to 11 g/L (1.1 g/dL): portal hypertension (cirrhosis, cardiac ascites). SAAG less than 11 g/L: non-portal hypertension (malignancy, TB, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis). Protein: less than 25 g/L (transudate), greater than 25 g/L (exudate). Glucose: low in TB, bacterial peritonitis. Cell count: greater than 250/mm3 PMNs = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Ascitic fluid (diagnostic paracentesis). CRITICAL: aseptic technique. Preparation: note cirrhosis, ascites. Handle: aseptic. SAAG: most important parameter. SBP: PMN greater than 250. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: SAAG greater than 11 (portal HTN). SBP: PMN greater than 250. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AASLD Ascites Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - CSF FLUID
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of CSF (Cerebrospinal Fluid) evaluates CSF for neurological disease. Key parameters: protein, glucose, lactate, cell count, oligoclonal bands (OCB), IgG index. Elevated CSF protein: meningitis (bacterial greater than viral), MS (OCBs), Guillain-Barre syndrome (albumino-cytological dissociation). Low CSF glucose: bacterial meningitis (CSF:serum glucose ratio less than 0.4), TB meningitis. Elevated CSF lactate: bacterial meningitis, mitochondrial disease. OCBs: MS (present in CSF, absent in serum). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF (lumbar puncture). CRITICAL: aseptic technique. Preparation: note headache, meningism, neurological symptoms. Handle: aseptic, light-protected. Bacterial: protein high, glucose low, lactate high. OCBs: MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: protein 15-45 mg/dL, glucose 50-80 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio greater than 0.6). Bacterial: protein high, glucose low. OCBs: MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN MS Diagnostic Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - OTHERS
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of Other Body Fluids (miscellaneous) covers biochemical testing on various body fluids not included in standard panels. Examples: synovial fluid, amniotic fluid, vitreous humour, saliva, stool. Synovial fluid: glucose, protein, crystal analysis (urate, calcium pyrophosphate). Amniotic fluid: AFP, acetylcholinesterase (neural tube defects). Vitreous humour: glucose, electrolytes (post-mortem). Stool: calprotectin (IBD screening), elastase (pancreatic exocrine function). Reference ranges: fluid-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Fluid-specific collection. Preparation: note fluid type, clinical context. Handle: fluid-specific. Glucose: synovial fluid. AFP: amniotic fluid. Calprotectin: stool. Reference ranges: fluid-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: fluid-specific. Synovial: glucose less than 60% serum. Stool calprotectin less than 50. Reference ranges: fluid-specific.
refs: Sources: Fluid-specific guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - PERICARDIAL FLUID
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of Pericardial Fluid evaluates pericardial effusion fluid. Key parameters: protein, glucose, LDH, cell count, Gram stain, culture. Exudate (protein greater than 30 g/L): infection (bacterial, TB), malignancy, autoimmune. Transudate (protein less than 30 g/L): heart failure, hypothyroidism, uraemia. Low glucose: bacterial pericarditis, rheumatoid arthritis. Cell count: greater than 1000/mm3 PMNs = bacterial pericarditis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Pericardial fluid (pericardiocentesis). CRITICAL: aseptic technique. Preparation: note cardiac symptoms, pericardial rub. Handle: aseptic. Exudate: infection, malignancy. Transudate: heart failure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: transudate (protein less than 30). Exudate: infection, malignancy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESC Pericardial Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - PLEURAL FLUID
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of Pleural Fluid evaluates pleural effusion. Key parameters: protein, glucose, LDH, pH, cell count, SAAG, Light criteria. Light criteria: exudate if any of (pleural:serum protein ratio greater than 0.5, pleural:serum LDH ratio greater than 0.6, pleural LDH greater than 2/3 upper normal serum LDH). Exudate: infection, malignancy, PE, RA. Transudate: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. pH less than 7.2: empyema, rheumatoid pleurisy, TB. Glucose less than 60 mg/dL: complicated parapneumonic effusion. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Pleural fluid (thoracentesis). CRITICAL: aseptic technique. Preparation: note dyspnoea, chest pain. Handle: aseptic. Light criteria: exudate vs transudate. pH less than 7.2: complicated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: transudate (Light criteria negative). Exudate: Light criteria positive. pH less than 7.2: complicated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BTS Pleural Effusion Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUID FOR BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS - SYNOVIAL FLUID
interpretation: Biochemical Analysis of Synovial Fluid evaluates joint fluid for inflammatory and crystalline arthropathies. Key parameters: glucose, protein, cell count, crystal analysis (polarised microscopy), Gram stain, culture. Gout: monosodium urate crystals (negatively birefringent, needle-shaped). Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals (weakly positive birefringent, rhomboid). Septic arthritis: greater than 50,000/mm3 WBC, positive Gram stain/culture. Effusion: glucose less than 50% of serum in inflammatory conditions. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Synovial fluid (arthrocentesis). CRITICAL: sterile technique, minimal heparin. Preparation: note joint pain, swelling, redness. Handle: sterile, minimal heparin. Gout: MSU crystals. Pseudogout: CPPD. Septic: greater than 50,000 WBC. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: glucose 70-100 mg/dL (less than 50% serum = inflammatory). Gout: MSU crystals. Septic: greater than 50,000 WBC. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: EULAR Gout Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FLUOXETINE
interpretation: Serum Fluoxetine (Prozac) measures the concentration of fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant. Therapeutic range: 50 to 500 ng/mL (total). Active metabolite: norfluoxetine (half-life 7-15 days). Toxicity: serotonin syndrome, QT prolongation, seizures. Drug interactions: many (CYP2D6 inhibitor). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note depression, anxiety, other medications, seizure history. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 50-500 ng/mL. Active metabolite: norfluoxetine (long half-life). Toxicity: serotonin syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 50 to 500 ng/mL (total). Active metabolite: norfluoxetine. Long half-life: 7-15 days. Toxicity: serotonin syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: APA Depression Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FREE ANDROGEN INDEX (FAI)
interpretation: Free Androgen Index (FAI) - calculated ratio of total testosterone to SHBG multiplied by 100. Estimates biologically active free testosterone. Elevated FAI: PCOS (most common cause in women), CAH, Cushing syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis, adrenal/testicular tumours, obesity (reduced SHBG), insulin resistance. Low FAI: male hypogonadism, hypopituitarism, liver cirrhosis, oral estrogen therapy (raises SHBG), Klinefelter syndrome. Clinical use: screening marker for androgen excess in women. Limitations: calculated value depends on accurate T and SHBG measurements. Assay-dependent variability. FAI does not directly measure free testosterone - equilibrium dialysis more accurate. Misclassifies with abnormal SHBG binding. SHBG fluctuates with time of day, food, weight, medication. Reference ranges method-specific, not interchangeable.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, fasting preferred. Note menstrual cycle phase, OCP use (raises SHBG - reduces FAI), obesity, medications affecting SHBG. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Simultaneous T + SHBG + albumin = complete androgen assessment. FAI = (Total T / SHBG) x 100. PCOS workup: FAI + T + SHBG + DHEA-S + 17-OHP + prolactin + LH/FSH. Women on OCP: SHBG elevated 2-3x - FAI artificially low. Males: FAI less useful than direct free T measurement.
ref_ranges: Women: FAI 0.7-3.6% (method-specific). PCOS: FAI >5.0% suggestive. Males: FAI 30-100%. Low FAI women <0.7%; males <30%. Free T by dialysis: Women 0.3-1.9 ng/dL; Males 5-21 ng/dL. SHBG: Women 18-144 nmol/L; Males 10-57 nmol/L. FAI cutoff for PCOS controversial - 3.8-5.0% in various studies. Normal FAI does not exclude PCOS. Assay-specific ranges not interchangeable. Ethnic variation and obesity affect results.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESHRE/ASRM PCOS Guidelines; Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FREE BETA HCG - AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Free Beta HCG (auto DELFIA) - measurement of free beta-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin. Used in prenatal screening (Down syndrome, trisomy 18) and tumour marker (gestational trophoblastic disease, germ cell tumours). Prenatal: elevated free b-hCG in Down syndrome (trisomy 21); reduced in trisomy 18. Combined with PAPP-A and nuchal translucency (11-13+6 weeks). GTD: elevated in molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma. Half-life ~36h - useful for monitoring treatment response. Germ cell tumours: elevated in seminoma (30-40%) and NSGCT (50-80%). Limitations: NOT specific for pregnancy - also elevated in ectopic pregnancy, threatened abortion, multiple pregnancy. Non-pregnancy causes: pituitary hCG (menopause), UTI, bladder cancer, GI cancers. False positives in screening: maternal weight, smoking, IVF, twins. Interlaboratory variability in free b-hCG assays. DELFIA platform highly specific for b-hCG subunit.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, no fasting required. Note LMP, gestational age (critical for screening), prior hCG values, GTD risk factors. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Prenatal: 11-13+6 weeks, combine with PAPP-A and NT ultrasound. Expressed as MoM adjusted for gestational age, weight, ethnicity, smoking, IVF. GTD monitoring: serial b-hCG at 1-2 week intervals. Normal post-molar: decline to <5 IU/L within 6-12 months. Rising/plateauing = persistent GTD. Ectopic: b-hCG rising <53% in 48h or falling <21% in 48h. Discriminatory zone >1500-2000 IU/L with no IUP on TVS.
ref_ranges: Prenatal (11-13+6 weeks): 0.5-2.0 MoM normal; >2.0 MoM Down syndrome risk; <0.5 MoM trisomy 18. Non-pregnant: <5.0 IU/L normal; >25 IU/L positive; 5-25 repeat in 48h. Men: <5.0 IU/L. GTD: declining to <5 IU/L = remission. Germ cell tumours: beta-hCG + AFP for staging. Molar pregnancy: beta-hCG often >100,000 IU/L. Method-specific ranges.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; FIGO GTD Guidelines; ACOG Early Pregnancy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FREE LIGHT CHAINS (KAPPA AND LAMBDA) RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Free Light Chains (Kappa and Lambda) measures the concentration of free kappa and lambda immunoglobulin light chains in urine. Urine FLC reflects plasma FLC levels and renal tubular handling. Elevated urine FLC: multiple myeloma, light chain deposition disease, amyloidosis, Bence Jones proteinuria. Urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) and immunofixation (IFE) are complementary. Limitations: urine FLC is less sensitive than serum FLC. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note myeloma, amyloidosis, kidney disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: myeloma, amyloidosis. Bence Jones: light chains. Serum FLC: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: myeloma, amyloidosis. Serum FLC: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IMWG Myeloma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FREE LIGHT CHAINS KAPPA - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Free Light Chain Kappa measures the concentration of free kappa immunoglobulin light chains in urine. Free kappa light chains are produced by plasma cells and normally filtered by the glomerulus and reabsorbed by the proximal tubule. Elevated urine kappa: monoclonal gammopathies (myeloma, MGUS), tubular dysfunction, renal light chain deposition. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note myeloma history, renal disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: monoclonal gammopathies, renal tubular dysfunction. Combined with lambda: kappa/lambda ratio. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: monoclonal gammopathies, tubular dysfunction. Serum FLC: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IMWG Myeloma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FREE T3 (FT3)
interpretation: Free T3 (FT3) - biologically active thyroid hormone; unbound fraction of triiodothyronine. Most sensitive early marker of thyroid dysfunction. Elevated FT3: hyperthyroidism (Graves - FT3 elevated before FT4), T3 thyrotoxicosis (5% of hyperthyroid cases), amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, factitious T3 ingestion, toxic adenoma/MNG. Low FT3: hypothyroidism (may be low before FT4 falls), non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid - FT3 earliest marker; FT4 normal), starvation, drug effects (amiodarone, propylthiouracil, corticosteroids), elderly (reduced T4 to T3 conversion), renal failure. FT3 in critical illness: low FT3 in sick euthyroid - reflects reduced peripheral conversion via decreased type 1 deiodinase. Low FT3 in ICU correlates with severity and prognosis. Limitations: FT3 assays vary between platforms. Analogue immunoassays affected by albumin binding, drugs, interfering antibodies. Equilibrium dialysis gold standard but not widely available. Always interpret with FT4 and TSH.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, no fasting required. Note thyroid medications (levothyroxine, liothyronine, carbimazole), amiodarone, iodinated contrast, pregnancy, acute illness. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Always interpret FT3 with FT4 and TSH. Amiodarone monitoring: FT3/FT4/TSH every 3-6 months. Critical illness: FT3 low, FT4 variable, TSH low-normal = NTI. Do not treat with thyroid hormones in NTI. Pregnancy: trimester-specific ranges. Elderly: FT3 may be low-normal.
ref_ranges: Adults: 3.1-6.8 pmol/L (2.0-4.4 pg/mL) - method/assay specific. Neonates: 1.0-4.2 pmol/L at birth. Hyperthyroidism: FT3 >6.8 pmol/L. T3 thyrotoxicosis: FT3 elevated, FT4 normal, TSH suppressed. Non-thyroidal illness: FT3 <3.1 pmol/L, FT4 normal/elevated, TSH low-normal. FT3/FT4 ratio: >0.07 hyperthyroidism; <0.04 hypothyroidism or NTI. Assay-specific ranges not comparable between dialysis and analogue immunoassay.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ATA Thyroid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; Endocrine Society.

name: FREE T4 (FT4)
interpretation: Free T4 (FT4) - biologically active thyroid hormone; unbound fraction of thyroxine. Most reliable single test for thyroid function when combined with TSH. Elevated FT4: overt hyperthyroidism (Graves, toxic adenoma, toxic MNG), subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH suppressed, FT4 normal), amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, thyroiditis, TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Low FT4: overt hypothyroidism (primary - TSH elevated; central - TSH low/inappropriately normal), non-thyroidal illness, drug effects (amiodarone, lithium, interferon-alpha, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors), iodine deficiency, post-thyroidectomy. FT4 in pregnancy: peaks first trimester (hCG stimulates TSH receptor). Must use trimester-specific reference ranges. Limitations: FT4 assays vary between platforms. Analogue immunoassay affected by binding protein abnormalities (TBG changes, albumin variants). Equilibrium dialysis gold standard. In non-thyroidal illness FT4 may be normal despite low FT3. Always interpret with TSH.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, no fasting required. Note thyroid medications, amiodarone, pregnancy, acute illness, iodinated contrast. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Always interpret with FT3 and TSH. Levothyroxine monitoring: FT4 and TSH at 6-8 weeks after dose change. Pregnancy: trimester-specific ranges - FT4 peaks first trimester. Critical illness: FT4 low-normal, FT3 low, TSH low-normal = NTI. Neonatal screening: cord blood FT4 + TSH.
ref_ranges: Adults: 12-22 pmol/L (0.93-1.7 ng/dL) - method/assay specific. Neonates: 11-22 pmol/L at birth. Hyperthyroidism: FT4 >22 pmol/L with suppressed TSH. Subclinical: FT4 normal, TSH suppressed. Hypothyroidism: FT4 <12 pmol/L with elevated TSH. Central hypothyroidism: FT4 low, TSH low/normal. Non-thyroidal illness: FT4 normal/low-normal. Pregnancy: FT4 peaks first trimester. Levothyroxine target: FT4 upper half of range, TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L. Assay-specific ranges.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ATA Thyroid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; Endocrine Society.

name: FREE TESTOSTERONE
interpretation: Free Testosterone - biologically active fraction not bound to SHBG or albumin. Most accurate marker of androgen status in women and conditions where SHBG is altered. Elevated: PCOS (most common in women), CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency), Cushing syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis, adrenal/testicular tumours, obesity, insulin resistance, exogenous testosterone/anabolic steroid use, idiopathic hirsutism. Low: male hypogonadism (primary/secondary), Klinefelter syndrome, liver cirrhosis, ageing (SHBG rises), opioid therapy, HIV/AIDS, chronic illness, oral oestrogen therapy. Clinical use: free testosterone MOST ACCURATE marker of androgen excess in women. Gold standard: equilibrium dialysis. Calculated free T (Vermeulen) using total T + SHBG + albumin acceptable. Limitations: equilibrium dialysis technically demanding, not widely available. Analogue immunoassays unreliable in women. Calculated free T assumes fixed albumin binding - inaccurate in liver disease. SHBG fluctuates with menstrual cycle, OCP, obesity, age. Assay-dependent variability.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, fasting preferred. Note menstrual cycle phase, OCP use (raises SHBG - lowers free T), obesity, medications, testosterone replacement. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. PCOS workup: free T + total T + SHBG + DHEA-S + 17-OHP + LH/FSH + prolactin. Equilibrium dialysis gold standard. Calculated free T (Vermeulen) acceptable. Males: free T more accurate than total T in obesity, liver disease, ageing. Women on OCP: SHBG elevated 2-3x - free T artificially low.
ref_ranges: Women: Free T 0.3-1.9 ng/dL (equilibrium dialysis). Calculated (Vermeulen): 0.06-0.68 ng/dL. Males: 5-21 ng/dL (dialysis). PCOS: free T >1.5 ng/dL (dialysis) or >0.8 ng/dL (Vermeulen). Hypogonadism (males): <5.0 ng/dL. Prepubertal: very low (<0.1 ng/dL). Assay comparison: dialysis most accurate; analogue unreliable in women; calculated acceptable. Method-specific ranges not interchangeable. Ethnic variation: African Americans higher free T. Age: free T decreases ~1-2% per year after 30 in men.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FRUCTOSAMINE
interpretation: Serum Fructosamine measures the concentration of glycated serum proteins (predominantly glycated albumin). Fructosamine reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2 to 3 weeks (unlike HbA1c which reflects 2 to 3 months). Fructosamine is useful when HbA1c is unreliable: haemoglobinopathies, haemolytic anaemia, iron deficiency, pregnancy. Elevated: poor glycaemic control. Decreased: improved glycaemic control. Limitations: affected by serum protein levels (nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, liver disease). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note diabetes, HbA1c unreliability. Handle per standard. 2-3 week average: glucose. Useful: HbA1c unreliable. Affected: protein levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 285 mcmol/L (method-specific). Elevated: poor glycaemic control. Useful: HbA1c unreliable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: FSH LH AND PROLACTIN
interpretation: FSH, LH and Prolactin - reproductive hormone panel assessing hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis function. FSH: follicle-stimulating hormone drives follicular development in women and spermatogenesis in men. LH: luteinising hormone triggers ovulation (mid-cycle surge) and stimulates testosterone production in men. Prolactin: pituitary hormone regulating lactation; elevated in prolactinoma, hypothyroidism, drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), stalk effect, physiological (pregnancy, lactation, nipple stimulation). Clinical use: female infertility workup (anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency, PCOS - LH:FSH ratio >2:1), male infertility (low FSH/LH with low testosterone = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), amenorrhoea workup, prolactinoma screening, menopausal status confirmation (elevated FSH >25 IU/L). Limitations: FSH/LH pulsatile secretion (GnRH-driven) - single values may not reflect average. LH surge detection requires timed testing for ovulation. Prolactin: stress, exercise, nipple stimulation, sleep, meals elevate prolactin - draw fasting morning sample. Macroprolactin (PRL-IgG complex) causes falsely elevated prolactin - PEG precipitation needed to confirm. Drugs causing hyperprolactinaemia: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, SSRIs, verapamil. Hypothyroidism elevates prolactin (TRH stimulates PRL) - check TSH first.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture. Fasting morning sample preferred (pulsatile secretion). No exercise before test. Note menstrual cycle day (critical for FSH/LH interpretation), menopausal status, oral contraceptive use, HRT, fertility treatment, pregnancy/lactation status, medications affecting prolactin. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Menstrual cycle timing: FSH/LH on day 2-5 for baseline assessment. Mid-cycle LH surge (day 12-14) for ovulation detection. Prolactin: draw fasting, morning, no exercise, no breast stimulation 24h before. Macroprolactin: if prolactin elevated without clinical symptoms, request PEG precipitation to exclude macroprolactin. Hypothyroidism: check TSH if prolactin elevated - elevated prolactin may be secondary to hypothyroidism.
ref_ranges: Women (follicular): FSH 3-10 IU/L; LH 2-8 IU/L; Prolactin 4-25 ng/mL. Mid-cycle surge: LH 20-100 IU/L; FSH 8-25 IU/L. Luteal: FSH 2-8 IU/L; LH 1-6 IU/L. Postmenopausal: FSH >25 IU/L (often >40); LH >15 IU/L. Men: FSH 1.5-12 IU/L; LH 1.5-9 IU/L; Prolactin 4-15 ng/mL. Prolactin >25 ng/mL (women) or >20 ng/mL (men): hyperprolactinaemia. Prolactin >200 ng/mL: almost always macroprolactinoma. Prolactin 50-200: microprolactinoma, drugs, hypothyroidism. PCOS: LH:FSH ratio >2:1 suggestive but not diagnostic. Premature ovarian insufficiency: FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions 4-6 weeks apart in women <40. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: low FSH/LH + low testosterone/oestrogen = pituitary/hypothalamic cause.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESHRE PCOS Guidelines; Endocrine Society Prolactin Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GAD-65
interpretation: GAD-65 antibodies - glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies targeting the 65 kDa isoform of GAD enzyme (synthesises GABA in pancreatic beta cells and CNS). Diagnostic marker for autoimmune diabetes: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) - present in 70-80% of new-onset T1DM, LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) - present in 80-90% of LADA cases. Also associated with: stiff person syndrome (SPS) - present in 60-80% of SPS, cerebellar ataxia, other autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes. Clinical use: distinguishing T1DM from T2DM (GAD-positive suggests autoimmune aetiology), predicting progression to insulin-dependent diabetes in LADA, identifying at-risk individuals (alongside IA-2, ZnT8, ICA antibodies). Limitations: GAD-65 positive does not guarantee progression to T1DM - may remain stable for years (especially in LADA). Low-titre GAD antibodies (especially in T2DM) may be non-specific. Assay variability between platforms (radioligand binding assay vs ELISA vs electrochemiluminescence). GAD-65 antibodies can be positive in non-diabetic autoimmune conditions (SPS, thyroiditis, coeliac disease). Single antibody testing insufficient for T1DM prediction - combined panel (GAD + IA-2 + ZnT8 + ICA) more informative. Age-related: GAD-65 more common in adults with LADA than children with T1DM (children more likely IA-2/ZnT8 positive).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum, standard venipuncture, no fasting required. Note diabetes type, age at onset, family history of autoimmune disease, personal/family history of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome, coeliac disease, thyroid disease, vitiligo, Addison disease. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. No special handling required. Combined autoantibody panel: GAD-65 + IA-2 + ZnT8 + ICA provides highest sensitivity for T1DM prediction. LADA: GAD-65 positive T2DM patients - consider early insulin therapy as beta-cell decline progresses. Stiff person syndrome: GAD-65 positive - check for concurrent diabetes and autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome. Serial testing: not routinely needed - single positive result clinically significant. Neonatal screening: GAD-65 not used in neonatal screening (used in research/clinical prediction of T1DM in at-risk children).
ref_ranges: Negative: <5 IU/mL (method-specific cutoffs). Low positive: 5-10 IU/mL - may be non-specific, especially in elderly or T2DM. Moderate positive: 10-50 IU/mL - clinically significant, suggest autoimmune diabetes. High positive: >50 IU/mL - strongly suggestive of T1DM or LADA. LADA: GAD-65 positive (>5 IU/mL) in T2DM patients not initially insulin-requiring - diagnosis requires GAD positivity + age >30 + no insulin requirement for at least 6 months after diagnosis. T1DM: 70-80% GAD-65 positive at diagnosis (adults). Children: GAD-65 less common than IA-2/ZnT8 in paediatric T1DM. SPS: 60-80% GAD-65 positive. Reference ranges: assay-specific (radioligand binding assay most sensitive). Method comparison: radioligand binding assay detects conformational epitopes better than ELISA.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines; Immunology of Diabetes Society; manufacturer IFU.

name: GALACTOSE 6 SULPHATE SULPHATE - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Galactose 6 Sulphate Sulphatase (GALNS) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine 6-sulphate sulphatase. GALNS deficiency causes Mucopolysaccharidosis IV A (Morquio A syndrome), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. Morquio A: skeletal dysplasia (short stature, kyphoscoliosis), corneal clouding, cardiac valve disease, normal intelligence. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note skeletal dysplasia, corneal clouding, cardiac disease, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Morquio A. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 4.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Morquio A. Carrier: variable. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GALACTOSE SCREENING - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Galactose Screening measures galactose concentration in blood. Galactose is a monosaccharide metabolised by the Leloir pathway (galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase [GALT], UDP-galactose-4-epimerase). Galactosaemia: autosomal recessive. Classic galactosaemia (GALT deficiency): neonatal presentation (poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, E. coli sepsis). Galactokinase deficiency: cataracts, no systemic features. Newborn screening: detects GALT deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Blood (dried blood spot for newborn screening). Preparation: note neonatal symptoms, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: galactosaemia. GALT: classic. Galactokinase: cataracts. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: galactosaemia. GALT deficiency: classic. Newborn screening: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Galactosaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GAMMA GLUTAMYL TRANSFERASE (GGT)
interpretation: Gamma Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) - membrane-bound enzyme catalysing transfer of gamma-glutamyl groups. Sensitive marker of hepatobiliary disease and alcohol-induced liver injury. Elevated GGT: alcohol use (most sensitive marker - elevated in 50-70% of heavy drinkers even before AST/ALT elevation), biliary obstruction (intra/extrahepatic cholestasis), cholestatic liver disease, hepatocellular damage (hepatitis, cirrhosis), drug-induced liver injury (phenytoin, warfarin, barbiturates, NSAIDs), heart failure (hepatic congestion), pancreatitis, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism, nephrotic syndrome. GGT induction: GGT is a microsomal enzyme induced by ethanol, barbiturates, and other CYP450 inducers - elevated GGT does NOT always mean liver disease (may reflect enzyme induction). GGT normalisation: GGT falls faster than ALP after biliary obstruction relief - useful for monitoring response to treatment. Clinical use: sensitive marker for alcohol use (but not specific); combined with AST/ALT for liver disease workup; monitoring cholestasis; detecting biliary obstruction. Limitations: GGT elevated in many non-hepatic conditions (pancreatitis, heart failure, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome). GGT is NOT liver-specific - found in kidney, pancreas, intestine. GGT may be normal in early biliary obstruction. GGT less specific than ALP for hepatobiliary disease. GGT does not differentiate cholestasis from hepatocellular damage. GGT may be falsely low in vitamin B6 deficiency (cofactor for GGT). GGT affected by fasting status (slightly lower fasting).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred (reduces postprandial variation). Note alcohol use, medications (phenytoin, warfarin, barbiturates, NSAIDs, statins), liver disease history, biliary obstruction risk, diabetes, heart failure. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Stable frozen. Haemolysis acceptable. GGT and ALP: always measure both for hepatobiliary assessment - GGT more sensitive for alcohol-related injury; ALP more specific for cholestasis. GGT normalisation after biliary obstruction relief: monitor every 2-4 weeks. Alcohol monitoring: GGT falls with abstinence (half-life ~26-30 days). Drug monitoring: GGT baseline before starting hepatotoxic drugs.
ref_ranges: Men: 8-61 U/L (method-specific). Women: 5-36 U/L (method-specific). Mild elevation (1-3x ULN): non-specific, may be alcohol, drugs, fatty liver, early cholestasis. Moderate elevation (3-10x ULN): alcoholic liver disease, cholestatic liver disease, hepatitis. Severe elevation (>10x ULN): biliary obstruction, severe hepatocellular damage, alcoholic hepatitis. GGT >100 U/L: strong predictor of alcoholic liver disease in heavy drinkers. GGT/ALT ratio: >2 suggests alcoholic liver disease (vs viral hepatitis where ALT > AST). GGT and alcohol: elevated in 50-70% of heavy drinkers before AST/ALT elevation. GGT does NOT reliably detect recent alcohol use (takes 2-3 weeks to normalise after cessation). Reference ranges: assay-specific. Age and sex affect ranges (men higher than women). Ethnic variation: minimal.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD/AACC Liver Test Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GASTRIN
interpretation: Serum Gastrin measures the concentration of gastrin, a hormone produced by G cells in the gastric antrum. Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion. Elevated gastrin: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES, gastrinoma), pernicious anaemia, atrophic gastritis, proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use, renal failure. Fasting gastrin: required. Stimulated gastrin (secretin test): for equivocal cases. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-12 hours). Preparation: note peptic ulcer disease, diarrhoea, PPI use, MEN1. Handle per standard. Fasting: required. ZES: greater than 1000 pg/mL. PPI: elevates. Secretin test: stimulated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 pg/mL (fasting). ZES: greater than 1000 pg/mL. PPI: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS Gastrinoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GCT-100 GMS (GLUCOSE CHALLENGE TEST)
interpretation: Glucose Challenge Test (GCT) with 100g glucose load is a screening test for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The patient drinks a 100g glucose solution and blood glucose is measured at 1 hour post-load. A single elevated value (greater than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour) indicates need for further testing with a full 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). The 100g GCT is used in some protocols as an alternative to the 50g GCT. The 100g GCT has higher sensitivity than the 50g GCT but lower specificity. Limitations: screening test only. False positives: recent meal, stress, illness, medications. False negatives: not fasting. Reference ranges: method-specific. Follow-up: 3-hour OGTT if elevated.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. No fasting required for screening. Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors (obesity, family history, previous GDM), medications. Handle per standard. 100g load: alternative to 50g. 1 hour: greater than 140 mg/dL screen positive. Follow-up: 3-hour OGTT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour. Screen positive: greater than 140 mg/dL. Follow-up: 3-hour OGTT. False positives: stress, medications. False negatives: not fasting. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GCT-50 GMS (GLUCOSE CHALLENGE TEST)
interpretation: Glucose Challenge Test (GCT) with 50g glucose load is the most common screening test for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The patient drinks a 50g glucose solution (non-fasting) and blood glucose is measured at 1 hour post-load. A value greater than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour is considered screen-positive and requires confirmatory testing with a 100g or 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). The 50g GCT is typically performed between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation. Sensitivity approximately 79 to 90 percent, specificity approximately 77 to 84 percent depending on cutoff used. A cutoff of 130 mg/dL increases sensitivity to approximately 90 to 100 percent but reduces specificity. Limitations: screening test only. False positives common (stress, recent meal, illness). False negatives: not possible as it is a one-time test. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. No fasting required. Preparation: note gestational age (24-28 weeks preferred), risk factors, recent meal. Handle per standard. 50g load: most common screening. 1 hour: greater than 140 mg/dL positive. 130 mg/dL: higher sensitivity cutoff. Follow-up: 100g or 75g OGTT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour. Screen positive: greater than 140 mg/dL. High sensitivity cutoff: greater than 130 mg/dL. Follow-up: 100g or 75g OGTT. False positives: stress, meals. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GCT-75 GMS (GLUCOSE CHALLENGE TEST)
interpretation: Glucose Challenge Test (GCT) with 75g glucose load is a screening test for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The patient drinks a 75g glucose solution and blood glucose is measured at 1 hour post-load. The 75g GCT is less commonly used than the 50g or 100g GCT in some protocols. A single elevated value (greater than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour) indicates need for further testing with a full OGTT. The 75g GCT has intermediate sensitivity between the 50g and 100g tests. Limitations: screening test only. False positives: stress, recent meal, illness. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. No fasting required for screening. Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, recent meal. Handle per standard. 75g load: intermediate sensitivity. 1 hour: greater than 140 mg/dL screen positive. Follow-up: OGTT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL at 1 hour. Screen positive: greater than 140 mg/dL. Follow-up: OGTT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLOBULIN
interpretation: Globulin - group of proteins (albumin excluded) measured as total protein minus albumin. Includes alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, and gamma globulins (immunoglobulins). Elevated globulin: chronic inflammation/infection (gamma globulins - polyclonal gammopathy), autoimmune disease (SLE, RA, Sjogren), multiple myeloma (monoclonal gammopathy - M protein spike), Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, chronic liver disease (cirrhosis - elevated gamma globulins, reduced albumin), dehydration (relative elevation), sarcoidosis, chronic infections (TB, HIV, hepatitis). Low globulin: immunodeficiency (common variable immunodeficiency - CVID), nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria preferentially loses gamma globulins), protein-losing enteropathy, severe burns, malnutrition, corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy, congenital agammaglobulinemia. Clinical use: A/G ratio (albumin:globulin) more useful than globulin alone - A/G ratio <1 suggests chronic liver disease, chronic infection, or myeloma. Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for monoclonal gammopathy (myeloma, MGUS, Waldenstrom). Limitations: globulin is a calculated value (total protein minus albumin) - measurement error propagates. Globulin elevation non-specific - requires SPEP or immunofixation for monoclonal gammopathy. Polyclonal vs monoclonal gammopathy: SPEP required to distinguish (polyclonal = broad-based elevation in gamma region = chronic inflammation; monoclonal = sharp spike = myeloma/MGUS). Globulin affected by hydration status (dehydration causes relative elevation). Age-related: gamma globulins increase with age (immunosenescence).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Note chronic disease status, autoimmune history, myeloma risk factors, proteinuria, malnutrition, immunosuppressive therapy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Total protein + albumin: calculate globulin (total protein minus albumin). SPEP: if globulin elevated, request SPEP for monoclonal gammopathy screening. Myeloma workup: SPEP + serum free light chains + urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) + urine Bence Jones protein. Immunodeficiency: if low globulin + recurrent infections, request quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM). A/G ratio: <1 suggests chronic liver disease, chronic infection, or myeloma. Dehydration: globulin elevated relative to albumin - rehydrate then recheck.
ref_ranges: Adults: 2.0-3.5 g/dL (20-35 g/L). Globulin = total protein minus albumin. A/G ratio: 1.0-2.5 (albumin:globulin). A/G ratio <1: abnormal - suggests chronic liver disease, chronic infection, myeloma, or autoimmune disease. Polyclonal gammopathy: broad-based gamma globulin elevation on SPEP = chronic inflammation (hepatitis, HIV, autoimmune). Monoclonal gammopathy: sharp spike on SPEP = myeloma, MGUS, Waldenstrom - requires immunofixation confirmation. Multiple myeloma: monoclonal protein usually >1.5 g/dL on SPEP. MGUS: monoclonal protein <1.5 g/dL, no end-organ damage, normal calcium, renal function, haemoglobin, bone marrow plasma cells <10%. Age: gamma globulins increase with age. Children: lower gamma globulins (immature immune system). Reference ranges: method-specific. SPEP interpretation requires experienced laboratory scientist.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IMWG Myeloma Consensus Guidelines; AABB Standards; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCAGON
interpretation: Serum Glucagon measures the concentration of glucagon, a hormone produced by alpha cells of the pancreatic islets. Glucagon promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (raises blood glucose). Elevated glucagon: glucagonoma (pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour), stress, diabetic ketoacidosis, chronic kidney disease. Glucagonoma: necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss, DVT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-12 hours). Preparation: note diabetes, skin rash, weight loss, DVT. Handle per standard. Fasting: required. Glucagonoma: greater than 500 pg/mL. Necrolytic erythema: classic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 80 pg/mL (fasting). Glucagonoma: greater than 500 pg/mL. Stress: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS NET Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSAMINE N ACETY TRANSFERASE - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Glucosamine N-Acetyltransferase measures the activity of the enzyme glucosamine N-acetyltransferase. This enzyme is involved in the biosynthesis of hyaluronic acid and other glycosaminoglycans. Deficiency: rare metabolic disorder. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood). Preparation: note suspected metabolic disorder, skeletal abnormalities. Handle per standard. Deficiency: rare. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Deficiency: rare metabolic disorder. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG LSD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE - OTHER FLUID
interpretation: Glucose - Other Fluid - measurement of glucose concentration in non-serum/plasma body fluids (CSF, synovial fluid, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, vitreous humour, seminal fluid). Used for diagnostic and monitoring purposes in specific clinical contexts. CSF glucose: bacterial meningitis (low - CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4), viral meningitis (normal or mildly low), tuberculous meningitis (low), fungal meningitis (low), subarachnoid haemorrhage (may be low), cerebral malaria. Synovial fluid glucose: septic arthritis (low - <50% of serum glucose), gout/pseudogout (normal or mildly low), inflammatory arthritis (mildly low), osteoarthritis (normal). Pleural fluid glucose: parapneumonic effusion/empyema (low - <60 mg/dL suggests complex/empyema), rheumatoid pleurisy (low), malignancy (variable), TB (low). Peritoneal fluid glucose: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (low - ascitic fluid glucose <50 mg/dL or serum-ascites gradient >20 mg/dL). Limitations: glucose in body fluids degrades rapidly at room temperature - MUST be analysed immediately or preserved with sodium fluoride. Cell metabolism in vitro consumes glucose - delay in processing falsely lowers glucose. Reference ranges vary by fluid type and collection method. CSF glucose must be interpreted alongside simultaneous serum glucose (CSF:serum ratio more useful than absolute value). Synovial fluid glucose: interpretation requires simultaneous serum glucose. Anticoagulants may affect glucose (use fluoride tubes for stability). Contamination with blood affects results (bloody tap in LP - CSF glucose may be falsely normal/high if significant blood contamination).
pre_analytical: Sample: Specific fluid (CSF via lumbar puncture, synovial fluid via arthrocentesis, pleural/peritoneal fluid via paracentesis, vitreous via vitrectomy). CRITICAL: process immediately or preserve with sodium fluoride (grey-top tube for glucose stability). Handling: analyse within 30 min of collection if no preservative. Sodium fluoride preservative extends stability to 2-4h at room temperature. Do NOT transport on ice without fluoride (cell metabolism continues). CSF: send to lab immediately - glucose degrades rapidly in CSF. Synovial fluid: send in fluoride tube if not analysing within 30 min. Simultaneous serum glucose: always pair body fluid glucose with serum glucose for ratio interpretation. CSF:serum glucose ratio = CSF glucose / serum glucose. Septic arthritis: synovial fluid glucose <50% of serum glucose. Bacterial meningitis: CSF:serum ratio <0.4 (40%). Pseudo-hypoglycaemia: contamination with IV fluid during collection may dilute specimen.
ref_ranges: CSF glucose: 50-80 mg/dL (2.8-4.4 mmol/L) - must be >60% of simultaneous serum glucose. CSF:serum ratio: >0.6 normal; 0.4-0.6 borderline; <0.4 suggests bacterial meningitis. Synovial fluid glucose: 70-120 mg/dL (normal). Septic arthritis: <50% of serum glucose (<60 mg/dL). Gout/pseudogout: normal or mildly low. Pleural fluid glucose: >60 mg/dL normal. <60 mg/dL suggests complex parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Peritoneal fluid (ascites): >50 mg/dL normal. <50 mg/dL or serum-ascites gradient >20 mg/dL suggests spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Reference ranges: fluid-type specific. Simultaneous serum glucose essential for interpretation. Age and metabolic status affect absolute values.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IDSA Bacterial Meningitis Guidelines; BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines; AASLD SBP Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE 6 PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (G6PD)
interpretation: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) - enzyme in pentose phosphate pathway essential for maintaining reduced glutathione and protecting RBCs from oxidative damage. G6PD deficiency: X-linked recessive disorder - most common enzyme deficiency worldwide (400 million affected). Protective against malaria (P. falciparum) - endemic in Africa, Mediterranean, Middle East, Southeast Asia. Clinical presentation: episodic haemolytic anaemia triggered by oxidative stress (fava beans/broad beans [favism], infections, drugs [primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamones, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase], neonatal jaundice, diabetic ketoacidosis). G6PD variants: >400 variants - Class I (severe, chronic haemolytic anaemia), Class II (severe, episodic haemolysis - G6PD Mediterranean), Class III (moderate, episodic - G6PD A- most common in African Americans), Class IV (mild/normal), Class V (enzyme overproduction). Limitations: G6PD levels may appear NORMAL during acute haemolytic episode (reticulocytes and young RBCs have higher G6PD activity - mask deficiency). MUST retest 2-3 months after acute episode. G6PD assays affected by recent blood transfusion (donor RBCs mask deficiency). Quantitative assay preferred over qualitative (screening) - qualitative tests may miss heterozygous females. Heterozygous females: mosaic RBC population (some normal, some deficient) - may have normal G6PD on quantitative assay due to X-inactivation. Neonatal G6PD screening: standard in some countries - but levels may be falsely normal in neonates. G6PD and antimalarials: primaquine/tafenoquine contraindicated in G6PD deficiency - pre-treatment testing mandatory.
pre_analytical: Sample: EDTA whole blood (for quantitative assay) or capillary blood (for qualitative screening). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: do NOT test during acute haemolytic episode - retest 2-3 months after resolution. Preparation: note ethnicity (high-risk populations: Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, Southeast Asian), drug exposure (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamones, nitrofurantoin), fava bean exposure, recent infections. Handling: EDTA whole blood stable 2-8C up to 7 days. Quantitative assay: spectrophotometric method measuring NADPH generation. Qualitative screening: fluorescent spot test (most common) or methemoglobin reduction test. Blood transfusion: do NOT test during or shortly after transfusion - donor RBCs mask deficiency. Neonatal screening: heel-prick blood on filter paper; G6PD levels may be falsely normal in neonates due to high reticulocyte count. Retesting: if acute episode suspected, retest 2-3 months after resolution. Males: hemizygous males fully affected - no carrier state. Females: heterozygous females may have variable expression (X-inactivation mosaicism).
ref_ranges: Normal: >7.0 U/g Hb (quantitative assay, method-specific). G6PD deficiency: <30% of normal activity (<2.1 U/g Hb). G6PD intermediate: 30-70% of normal (heterozygous females, Class IV/V variants). Qualitative screening: normal = fluorescent spot positive (NADPH present); deficient = no fluorescence. Class I (severe): <10% activity, chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Class II (severe, Mediterranean): <10% activity, episodic severe haemolysis. Class III (moderate, A-): 10-30% activity, episodic moderate haemolysis. Class IV (mild/normal): 60-150% activity. Reference ranges: method and population-specific. Quantitative assay preferred for definitive diagnosis. Neonatal levels: may be falsely normal - retest at 3-6 months if suspected. Ethnic variation: G6PD Mediterranean (Class II) - severe; G6PD A- (Class III) - moderate; both common in endemic malaria regions.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; WHO G6PD Working Group; AABB Standards; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST (GTT) 100 GMS - 3 SAMPLES
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 100g with 3 samples is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 100g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. Diagnosis of GDM requires two or more abnormal values. The 100g OGTT uses Carpenter-Coustan criteria (or older NDDG criteria). Limitations: requires 8 to 14 hour fast. Inconvenient for patients. Stress, illness, and medications affect results. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan criteria.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, medications. Handle per standard. 100g load: 4 samples (fasting, 1h, 2h, 3h). 2 or more abnormal: GDM. Carpenter-Coustan: fasting 95, 1h 180, 2h 155, 3h 140 mg/dL. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
ref_ranges: Normal: all values below cutoffs. GDM: 2 or more abnormal values. Fasting: less than 95 mg/dL. 1 hour: less than 180 mg/dL. 2 hours: less than 155 mg/dL. 3 hours: less than 140 mg/dL. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST (GTT) 75 GMS - 3 SAMPLES
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 75g with 3 samples is the WHO-recommended diagnostic test for diabetes mellitus and impaired glucose tolerance in non-pregnant adults. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 75g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 1 hour, and 2 hours post-load. The WHO 2019 criteria define: normal fasting less than 100 mg/dL, impaired fasting glucose (IFG) 100 to 125 mg/dL, normal 2-hour less than 140 mg/dL, impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) 140 to 199 mg/dL at 2 hours, diabetes greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL at 2 hours or fasting greater than or equal to 126 mg/dL. IGT is a prediabetic state with increased risk of progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The 75g 3-sample OGTT is preferred over the 100g 4-sample OGTT for non-pregnant adults. Limitations: requires overnight fast. Inconvenient for patients. Reproducibility is poor (coefficient of variation up to 16 percent). Stress, illness, and medications affect results. Reference ranges: WHO 2019 criteria.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note diabetes risk factors, medications, recent illness. Handle per standard. 75g load: 3 samples (fasting, 1h, 2h). WHO criteria: fasting less than 100, 2h less than 140. IGT: 2h 140 to 199. Diabetes: fasting greater than 126 or 2h greater than 200. Reference ranges: WHO.
ref_ranges: Normal: fasting less than 100, 2h less than 140 mg/dL. IFG: fasting 100 to 125. IGT: 2h 140 to 199. Diabetes: fasting greater than or equal to 126 or 2h greater than or equal to 200. Reproducibility: up to 16 percent variation. Reference ranges: WHO 2019.
refs: Sources: WHO 2019 Diabetes Guidelines; EASD/ADA Consensus; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST (GTT) 75 GMS - 5 SAMPLES
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 75g with 5 samples provides a more detailed assessment of glucose metabolism including early and late postprandial phases. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 75g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. The 5-sample protocol allows assessment of first-phase insulin response (30-minute sample) and more accurate detection of early glucose excursion. The 30-minute sample is useful for detecting impaired early insulin secretion, which is an early defect in type 2 diabetes. The 3-hour sample detects delayed glucose peaks that may be missed with 2 or 3-sample protocols. Limitations: requires overnight fast. More blood draws than 3-sample protocol. Same reproducibility concerns as other OGTT protocols. Reference ranges: WHO criteria apply to fasting and 2-hour values.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note diabetes risk factors, medications, family history.
