Handle per standard. 75g load: 5 samples (fasting, 30min, 1h, 2h, 3h). 30min: first-phase insulin response. 3h: delayed peak. WHO criteria: fasting and 2h. Reference ranges: WHO.
ref_ranges: Same as 3-sample OGTT. Additional: 30-minute sample for first-phase insulin response. 3-hour sample for delayed peaks. WHO criteria apply. Reference ranges: WHO 2019.
refs: Sources: WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST (GTT) 75 GMS - 6 SAMPLES
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 75g with 6 samples provides the most comprehensive assessment of glucose metabolism using the 75g glucose load. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 75g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 1.5 hours, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. This protocol is used in research settings and for detailed metabolic phenotyping. The 6-sample protocol captures the full glucose curve including the nadir (typically at 90 to 120 minutes) and any late reactive hypoglycaemia. Limitations: requires overnight fast. Maximum blood draws. Same reproducibility concerns as other OGTT protocols. Reference ranges: WHO criteria apply to fasting and 2-hour values.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note diabetes risk factors, medications, family history. Handle per standard. 75g load: 6 samples (fasting, 30min, 1h, 1.5h, 2h, 3h). Most comprehensive: 75g protocol. Captures nadir and late hypoglycaemia. WHO criteria: fasting and 2h. Reference ranges: WHO.
ref_ranges: Same as 5-sample OGTT. Additional: 1.5-hour sample for nadir detection. WHO criteria apply. Reference ranges: WHO 2019.
refs: Sources: WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST-(GTT)100 GMS-5 SAMPLES
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) 100g with 5 samples is used in some protocols for diagnosing diabetes mellitus and for research purposes. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 100g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. The 100g load with 5 samples provides detailed glucose kinetics and is sometimes used when the standard 75g OGTT is inconclusive or when detailed metabolic assessment is required. The 100g load produces higher glucose excursions than the 75g load, which may increase sensitivity for detecting mild glucose intolerance. Limitations: requires overnight fast. Larger glucose load may cause more GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting). Same reproducibility concerns as other OGTT protocols. Reference ranges: WHO criteria for fasting and 2-hour values.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note diabetes risk factors, medications. Handle per standard. 100g load: 5 samples (fasting, 30min, 1h, 2h, 3h). Higher load: more GI symptoms. More sensitive: mild intolerance. WHO criteria: fasting and 2h. Reference ranges: WHO.
ref_ranges: Same as 75g OGTT criteria. 100g load: higher excursions. More GI symptoms. WHO criteria apply. Reference ranges: WHO 2019.
refs: Sources: WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST-PREGNANT WOMEN (GDM-100GMS)
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) for gestational diabetes (GDM) with 100g glucose load is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus in pregnant women. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 100g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. Diagnosis of GDM requires two or more abnormal values using Carpenter-Coustan criteria: fasting greater than or equal to 95 mg/dL, 1 hour greater than or equal to 180 mg/dL, 2 hours greater than or equal to 155 mg/dL, 3 hours greater than or equal to 140 mg/dL. The 100g GDM OGTT is the traditional US approach. Limitations: requires overnight fast (8-14 hours). Inconvenient for patients. Stress, illness, and medications affect results. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors (obesity, previous GDM, family history), medications. Handle per standard. 100g load: 4 samples. 2 or more abnormal: GDM. Carpenter-Coustan: fasting 95, 1h 180, 2h 155, 3h 140 mg/dL. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
ref_ranges: Normal: all values below cutoffs. GDM: 2 or more abnormal values. Fasting: less than 95 mg/dL. 1 hour: less than 180 mg/dL. 2 hours: less than 155 mg/dL. 3 hours: less than 140 mg/dL. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST-PREGNANT WOMEN (GDM-75 GMS)
interpretation: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) for gestational diabetes (GDM) with 75g glucose load is the international (WHO/IADPSG) recommended diagnostic test for GDM. The patient fasts overnight, drinks a 75g glucose solution, and blood glucose is measured at fasting, 1 hour, and 2 hours post-load. Diagnosis of GDM requires one or more abnormal values using IADPSG criteria: fasting greater than or equal to 92 mg/dL, 1 hour greater than or equal to 180 mg/dL, 2 hours greater than or equal to 153 mg/dL. The IADPSG criteria are more sensitive than Carpenter-Coustan criteria and diagnose more GDM. The 75g GDM OGTT is simpler (3 samples versus 4) and is recommended by WHO and IADPSG. Limitations: requires overnight fast (8-14 hours). One abnormal value suffices for diagnosis (more sensitive). Reference ranges: IADPSG.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, medications. Handle per standard. 75g load: 3 samples. 1 or more abnormal: GDM. IADPSG: fasting 92, 1h 180, 2h 153 mg/dL. More sensitive: than Carpenter-Coustan. Reference ranges: IADPSG.
ref_ranges: Normal: all values below cutoffs. GDM: 1 or more abnormal values. Fasting: less than 92 mg/dL. 1 hour: less than 180 mg/dL. 2 hours: less than 153 mg/dL. More sensitive: than 100g/CC criteria. Reference ranges: IADPSG.
refs: Sources: IADPSG GDM Consensus; WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLUTAMINE QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Plasma Glutamine Quantitative measures the concentration of glutamine, a non-essential amino acid. Glutamine is the most abundant amino acid in plasma and plays roles in nitrogen transport, immune function, and intestinal health. Elevated: liver disease, Reye syndrome, drugs (valproic acid). Low: sickle cell disease, post-surgery, critical illness. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note metabolic disease, medications. Handle per standard. Elevated: liver disease, Reye syndrome. Low: critical illness, sickle cell. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: liver disease, Reye syndrome. Low: critical illness, sickle cell. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLYCATED HEMOGLOBIN (HbA1c)
interpretation: Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) measures the percentage of haemoglobin that is glycated (glucose-bound). HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2 to 3 months (the lifespan of a red blood cell). HbA1c is the gold standard for long-term glycaemic monitoring in diabetes mellitus. Diagnosis: less than 5.7 percent normal, 5.7 to 6.4 percent prediabetes (increased risk of diabetes), greater than or equal to 6.5 percent diagnostic of diabetes on two separate occasions. Monitoring targets: less than 7 percent for most adults (ADA), less than 6.5 percent for selected patients, less than 8 percent for elderly or comorbid patients. Every 1 percent reduction in HbA1c corresponds to approximately 35 mg/dL reduction in mean glucose and 21 percent reduction in microvascular complications. Limitations: HbA1c is affected by conditions that alter RBC lifespan: falsely low in haemolytic anaemia, iron deficiency anaemia, chronic blood loss, pregnancy (third trimester), splenomegaly. Falsely high in iron deficiency anaemia (untreated), splenectomy, chronic kidney disease. Haemoglobin variants (HbS, HbC, HbF, HbE) may interfere depending on the assay method. NGSP-certified methods are preferred. Biotin supplementation may interfere on some immunoassay platforms. Reference ranges: NGSP-certified. Assay: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: EDTA whole blood (same tube as FBC). No fasting required. Preparation: note diabetes medications, Hb variants, anaemia, pregnancy, renal function, recent transfusions. Handle per standard. HbA1c: reflects 2 to 3 month average. 5.7 to 6.4 percent: prediabetes. Greater than or equal to 6.5 percent: diabetes. NGSP-certified: preferred. Assay: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 5.7 percent. Prediabetes: 5.7 to 6.4 percent. Diabetes: greater than or equal to 6.5 percent. Target: less than 7 percent (most adults). Elderly/comorbid: less than 8 percent. 1 percent HbA1c reduction: 35 mg/dL glucose reduction. Falsely low: haemolysis, blood loss. Falsely high: iron deficiency, CKD. Reference ranges: NGSP-certified.
refs: Sources: ADA Standards of Medical Care; NGSP; IFCC; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLYCINE (QUANTITATIVE) - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Glycine Quantitative measures glycine concentration in CSF. Elevated CSF glycine: nonketotic hyperglycaemia (NKH, glycine encephalopathy), an autosomal defect in glycine cleavage system. NKH: severe neonatal encephalopathy, intractable seizures, apnoea, death. CSF glycine greater than 100 mcmol/L (normal less than 15). Ratio CSF/plasma glycine greater than 0.08. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF. Preparation: note neonatal seizures, encephalopathy, apnoea. Handle per standard. Elevated: NKH. Greater than 100 mcmol/L: diagnostic. Ratio: CSF/plasma greater than 0.08. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 15 mcmol/L. NKH: greater than 100 mcmol/L. Ratio: CSF/plasma greater than 0.08. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG NKH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLYCINE QUANTITATIVE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Glycine Quantitative measures the concentration of glycine, the simplest amino acid. Elevated plasma glycine: nonketotic hyperglycaemia (NKH), hyperglycinemia (transient or persistent), SIDS. Low plasma glycine: malnutrition, non-specific. Plasma glycine is less specific than CSF glycine for NKH diagnosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizures, encephalopathy, metabolic history. Handle per standard. Elevated: NKH, hyperglycinemia. CSF: more specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: NKH, hyperglycinemia. CSF: more specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GLYCOSAMINOGLYCAN - URINE
interpretation: Urine Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) measures the excretion of glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides) in urine. GAGs are long polysaccharide chains found in connective tissue. Elevated urine GAGs: mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS I-Hurler, MPS II-Hunter, MPS III-Sanfilippo, MPS IV-Morquio, MPS VI-Maroteaux-Lamy, MPS VII-Sly). Screening test: cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) turbidity test or dimethylmethylene blue (DMB) assay. Quantitative GAGs with pattern analysis: more specific. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot) or 24-hour urine. Preparation: note skeletal dysplasia, corneal clouding, developmental delay, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: MPS. Screening: CTAB, DMB. Quantitative: more specific. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: age-dependent. Elevated: MPS I-VII. Screening: CTAB/DMB. Quantitative: more specific. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: GROWTH HORMONE (GH)
interpretation: Growth Hormone (GH) - anterior pituitary hormone regulating linear growth, body composition, metabolism, and glucose homeostasis. GH acts directly and indirectly via IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1, produced by liver). Elevated GH: acromegaly (pituitary adenoma - most common cause in adults), gigantism (pituitary adenoma in children), ectopic GH/GHRH secretion (rare - hypothalamic tumours, carcinoid, small cell lung cancer), physiological (exercise, sleep, stress, hypoglycaemia). Low GH: GH deficiency (congenital or acquired - pituitary surgery/radiation, tumour, trauma, infiltrative disease, idiopathic), hypopituitarism, obesity (GH suppressed by hyperinsulinaemia), aging, hypothyroidism. Clinical use: acromegaly diagnosis (elevated GH with elevated IGF-1), GH deficiency diagnosis (GH stimulation testing - insulin tolerance test, GHRH-arginine test, glucagon stimulation test), monitoring treatment of acromegaly. Limitations: GH is pulsatile (secreted in bursts every 2-3h, primarily during deep sleep) - random GH levels are almost useless for diagnosis. GH stimulation testing: insulin tolerance test (ITT) gold standard - GH peak <3-5 ug/L after insulin-induced hypoglycaemia = GH deficiency. GH suppression testing: oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) - GH fails to suppress to <1 ug/L (<0.4 for ultrasensitive assays) after 75g glucose = acromegaly. IGF-1 more reliable than random GH for acromegaly diagnosis (IGF-1 reflects integrated GH secretion over 24h). GH assay: variability between platforms - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. Stress, exercise, sleep, fasting all elevate GH - draw samples in controlled conditions.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Timing critical: draw fasting morning sample (GH peaks during sleep - fasting morning reflects basal GH). For acromegaly screening: random GH unreliable - use IGF-1 first. For GH deficiency: GH stimulation testing required (ITT, GHRH-arginine, glucagon). Preparation: note medications (oestrogen raises GH; GH replacement therapy), fasting status, recent exercise, sleep pattern, pituitary surgery/radiation history, pregnancy status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. ITT (insulin tolerance test): gold standard for GH deficiency - insulin 0.1-0.15 U/kg IV, check GH, glucose, cortisol at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 min. GH peak <3 ug/L = deficiency. Contraindications: epilepsy, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, age >60. GHRH-arginine test: alternative to ITT - less stressful, safer. Glucagon stimulation test: alternative - longer duration (4h), suitable for outpatient. For acromegaly: OGTT GH suppression - 75g glucose load, GH at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min. GH fails to suppress <1 ug/L = acromegaly.
ref_ranges: Random GH (adults): 0-5 ug/L (almost useless for diagnosis due to pulsatility). IGF-1 (acromegaly screening): age/sex-specific normal range. Acromegaly: IGF-1 elevated (>2x ULN highly suggestive). GH deficiency (after stimulation): peak GH <3 ug/L (ITT) = deficiency; 3-5 ug/L borderline; >5 ug/L normal. Acromegaly (OGTT suppression): GH fails to suppress <1 ug/L after 75g glucose = acromegaly. Ultrasensitive GH assay: suppression to <0.4 ug/L = normal. Children: GH higher than adults (2-20 ug/L depending on age/puberty). Neonates: GH very high (10-40 ug/L). Pregnancy: GH suppressed (placental lactogen dominant). Obesity: GH suppressed (0-2 ug/L). Reference ranges: assay-specific and age/sex-dependent. Stimulated GH: thresholds vary by assay and stimulation protocol.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Acromegaly/GHD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HAEMOGLOBIN - FREE BIOCHEMICAL - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Free Haemoglobin measures the concentration of haemoglobin free in plasma (not inside red blood cells). Free Hb indicates intravascular haemolysis. Elevated: intravascular haemolysis (transfusion reactions, mechanical heart valves, paroxysmal nocturnal haemogloburia, DIC, severe malaria). Free Hb is scavenged by haptoglobin (decreased serum haptoglobin). Direct Coombs test: negative in intravascular haemolysis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (free of haemolysis). CRITICAL: avoid haemolysis during collection. Preparation: note haemolysis signs (anaemia, jaundice, dark urine). Handle per standard. Elevated: intravascular haemolysis. Haptoglobin: decreased. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 5 mg/dL. Elevated: intravascular haemolysis. Haptoglobin: decreased. Direct Coombs: negative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ASH Haemolysis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HALOPERIDOL
interpretation: Serum Haloperidol measures the concentration of haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic (butyrophenone). Haloperidol is used to treat schizophrenia, acute psychosis, and nausea/vomiting. Therapeutic range: 1 to 20 ng/mL (total). Toxicity: extrapyramidal side effects (EPS), neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), QT prolongation. Active metabolite: reduced haloperidol. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note psychiatric symptoms, EPS history, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 1-20 ng/mL. Active metabolite: reduced haloperidol. Toxicity: EPS, NMS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 1 to 20 ng/mL (total). Active metabolite: reduced haloperidol. Toxicity: EPS, NMS, QT prolongation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: APA Schizophrenia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HAPTOGLOBIN
interpretation: Haptoglobin - acute-phase glycoprotein that binds free haemoglobin released from intravascular haemolysis, preventing oxidative damage and renal iron loss. Decreased/absent haptoglobin: intravascular haemolysis (most important clinical finding - haptoglobin consumed binding free Hb), haemolytic anaemias (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia [MAHA], G6PD deficiency, sickle cell crisis, spherocytosis), massive haemorrhage (consumption), liver disease (reduced synthesis), megaloblastic anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis), oestrogen/oral contraceptive therapy (mild reduction), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Increased haptoglobin: acute-phase response (infection, inflammation, malignancy, tissue necrosis, myocardial infarction, burns) - haptoglobin is a positive acute-phase protein. Clinical use: most sensitive marker for intravascular haemolysis (haptoglobin low/absent + elevated LDH + low/absent reticulocyte count + elevated bilirubin = intravascular haemolysis pattern). Combined with LDH and reticulocyte count for haemolysis workup. Limitations: haptoglobin is an acute-phase protein - elevated in inflammation/infection, which may mask haemolysis (normal haptoglobin does NOT exclude haemolysis if concurrent inflammation). Haptoglobin elevated in pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, and with advancing age. Haptoglobin is a negative acute-phase protein - decreases in severe liver disease (reduced synthesis may mimic haemolysis). Genetic haptoglobin variants (Hp 2-1, Hp 2-2) affect assay - some immunoassays may underestimate haptoglobin in Hp 2-2 individuals. Neonates have low haptoglobin (synthesis matures by 6 months). Haptoglobin unreliable in neonates for haemolysis diagnosis. Haptoglobin normal does NOT exclude extravascular haemolysis (extravascular haemolysis in spleen does not release enough free Hb to consume haptoglobin).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Note haemolysis risk factors, recent transfusions, liver disease, inflammation/infection, pregnancy, oestrogen/OCP use. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Haemolysis workup: haptoglobin + LDH + reticulocyte count + direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs) + bilirubin. Haemolysis pattern: low/absent haptoglobin + elevated LDH + elevated reticulocytes + elevated unconjugated bilirubin +/- positive DAT. Intravascular vs extravascular: intravascular = very low haptoglobin + haemoglobinuria + elevated LDH; extravascular = mildly low haptoglobin + splenomegaly + spherocytes on film. Neonates: haptoglobin immature until 6 months - use LDH and reticulocyte count for haemolysis assessment. Acute-phase: if inflammation present, haptoglobin may be normal despite haemolysis - use LDH and reticulocyte count as alternative markers.
ref_ranges: Adults: 30-200 mg/dL (0.3-2.0 g/L) - method-specific. Neonates: very low (<10 mg/dL) until 6 months. Children: lower than adults until puberty. Absent haptoglobin (<10 mg/dL): strongly suggests intravascular haemolysis. Low haptoglobin (10-30 mg/dL): possible haemolysis or liver disease. Elevated haptoglobin (>200 mg/dL): acute-phase response (infection, inflammation, malignancy). Haemolytic anaemia: haptoglobin often undetectable (<10 mg/dL). Chronic haemolysis: haptoglobin may be low-normal (body compensates). Sickle cell disease: haptoglobin often absent during steady state. Intravascular haemolysis (MAHA, TTP/HUS): haptoglobin undetectable. Pregnancy: haptoglobin elevated. OCP: haptoglobin mildly reduced. Reference ranges: method-specific. Genetic variants (Hp 2-2): may affect assay accuracy.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; WHO Haemoglobinopathy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HCG BETA SUBUNIT - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) hCG Beta Subunit measures the concentration of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) beta subunit in CSF. Elevated CSF hCG: intracranial germinoma (highly sensitive and specific), CNS choriocarcinoma, CNS metastases (testicular, ovarian, gastric). CSF hCG is used for diagnosis and monitoring of CNS germ cell tumours. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF. Preparation: note headache, visual changes, hormonal symptoms. Handle per standard. Elevated: CNS germinoma, choriocarcinoma. Diagnostic: highly sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.5 IU/L (method-specific). Elevated: CNS germinoma, choriocarcinoma. Highly sensitive: CNS GCT. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESMO CNS GCT Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HCG BETA SUBUNIT - URINE SPOT
interpretation: Random Urine hCG Beta Subunit measures the concentration of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) beta subunit in urine. Urine hCG is used for: pregnancy testing (qualitative), gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD, quantitative), monitoring hCG-secreting tumours. Elevated urine hCG: pregnancy, GTD (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma), germ cell tumours. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Random urine (spot). Preparation: note menstrual history, pregnancy, GTD. Handle per standard. Elevated: pregnancy, GTD. Qualitative: pregnancy. Quantitative: GTD monitoring. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative (pregnancy test). Positive: pregnancy, GTD. Quantitative: varies. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: FIGO GTD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HEAVY AND TRACE METALS PROFILE
interpretation: Blood Heavy and Trace Metals Profile measures concentrations of multiple heavy metals and trace elements simultaneously. Profile includes: lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium, chromium, cobalt, copper, zinc, selenium, aluminium. Used for: occupational exposure assessment, environmental toxicology, nutritional status evaluation. Elevated metals: occupational exposure, environmental contamination. Low metals: nutritional deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or whole blood (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note occupational exposure, environmental exposure, diet. Handle: metal-free. Multiple metals: simultaneous assessment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by metal (method-specific). Elevated: occupational, environmental. Low: nutritional deficiency. Multiple metals: simultaneous. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Metal Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profiles; manufacturer IFU.

name: HEAVY METAL SCREEN
interpretation: Blood Heavy Metal Screen is a screening panel for commonly encountered toxic metals. Panel typically includes: lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium. Used for: occupational exposure assessment, environmental toxicology screening, suspected poisoning. Elevated metals: occupational exposure, environmental contamination, poisoning. Limitations: blood levels reflect recent exposure (not cumulative). Urine: better for cumulative assessment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note occupational exposure, environmental exposure, symptoms of toxicity. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Urine: cumulative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by metal (method-specific). Elevated: exposure/toxicity. Blood: recent. Urine: cumulative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Metal Guidelines; ATSDR Toxicological Profiles; manufacturer IFU.

name: HEPARAN SULPHATE  SULPHAMIDASE SANFILLIPO / MPS III A
interpretation: Blood Heparan Sulphate Sulphatase measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme heparan sulphate N-sulphatase (sulphamidase). Sulphamidase deficiency causes Sanfilippo syndrome type A (MPS IIIA), an autosomal recessive mucopolysaccharidosis. MPS IIIA: severe CNS degeneration, behavioural disturbance, developmental regression, death in adolescence. MPS IIIA is the most common and severe form of Sanfilippo syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note developmental regression, behavioural disturbance, skeletal abnormalities, family history. Handle per standard. Low: MPS IIIA. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: MPS IIIA. Carrier: variable. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HEPCIDIN
interpretation: Serum Hepcidin measures the concentration of hepcidin, a peptide hormone produced by the liver that is the master regulator of iron metabolism. Hepcidin inhibits ferroportin (the iron exporter), reducing intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release. Elevated hepcidin: iron overload, inflammation, infection, malignancy. Low hepcidin: iron deficiency anaemia, hereditary haemochromatosis, ineffective erythropoiesis (thalassaemia, sideroblastic anaemia). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred. Preparation: note iron status, inflammation, anaemia. Handle per standard. Elevated: iron overload, inflammation. Low: iron deficiency, haemochromatosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: iron overload, inflammation. Low: iron deficiency, haemochromatosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESH Iron Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HIGH SENSITIVE C-REACTIVE PROTEIN (hs-CRP)
interpretation: High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP) - quantitative measurement of CRP using high-sensitivity immunoassay detecting low-grade inflammation. CRP is an acute-phase protein produced by hepatocytes in response to IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IL-1beta. Cardiovascular risk assessment: hs-CRP >3.0 mg/L = high cardiovascular risk; 1.0-3.0 mg/L = moderate risk; <1.0 mg/L = low risk. JUPITER trial: rosuvastatin reduced CV events in patients with hs-CRP >2.0 mg/L despite normal LDL-C. AHA/CDC recommendation: hs-CRP for CV risk stratification in intermediate-risk patients (10-year Framingham risk 10-20%). Inflammation detection: hs-CRP detects subclinical inflammation missed by standard CRP (which detects >5-10 mg/L). Elevated hs-CRP: cardiovascular disease (atherosclerosis - vascular inflammation), metabolic syndrome/insulin resistance, obesity (visceral adipose tissue produces IL-6), diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease (RA, SLE), chronic infections, malignancy, periodontal disease, obstructive sleep apnoea. Limitations: hs-CRP is NON-SPECIFIC for any particular disease. Acute infection/inflammation (>10 mg/L) overrides CV risk interpretation - repeat hs-CRP 6-8 weeks after acute illness. hs-CRP affected by: obesity (elevated), smoking (elevated), hormone replacement therapy (variable), renal impairment (reduced clearance). Inter-individual variation: hs-CRP varies ~40% within individuals over time. Biological variation makes single measurement unreliable - consider two measurements 2 weeks apart. Assay variability: different hs-CRP assays may give slightly different results - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. CRP vs hs-CRP: hs-CRP is NOT different from CRP - it is the same protein measured with a more sensitive assay. Standard CRP (measured >5 mg/L) is used for infection/inflammation monitoring; hs-CRP (measured 0.1-10 mg/L) is used for CV risk stratification.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma (EDTA, heparin). Standard venipuncture. Fasting not required for hs-CRP but standard lipid panel fasting may be concurrent. Preparation: note acute illness/infection (hs-CRP unreliable during acute illness - repeat 6-8 weeks later), obesity status, smoking, HRT use, autoimmune disease, renal function. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. CV risk stratification: hs-CRP measured with standard lipid panel for intermediate-risk patients (10-year Framingham 10-20%). hs-CRP >10 mg/L: consider acute illness - repeat in 6-8 weeks before CV risk interpretation. Serial hs-CRP: not routinely recommended - single measurement for risk stratification. Biological variation: ~40% intra-individual - consider two measurements if borderline. hs-CRP and obesity: elevated by obesity - interpret alongside BMI and waist circumference. hs-CRP and smoking: elevated - smoking cessation reduces hs-CRP over time.
ref_ranges: Low risk: <1.0 mg/L. Moderate risk: 1.0-3.0 mg/L. High risk: >3.0 mg/L. Very high: >10 mg/L (suggests acute illness - repeat in 6-8 weeks). JUPITER trial threshold: hs-CRP >2.0 mg/L with LDL-C <130 mg/dL = statin benefit. hs-CRP and metabolic syndrome: elevated (3-10 mg/L typical). hs-CRP and obesity: correlates with BMI. hs-CRP and CKD: elevated with declining eGFR. hs-CRP and diabetes: elevated - independent CV risk marker. Reference ranges: method-specific. Inter-individual variation ~40% - single measurement may not reflect usual level. Age: hs-CRP increases with age. Ethnic variation: African Americans have higher baseline hs-CRP than Caucasians. Sex: women have slightly higher hs-CRP than men (effect of oestrogen).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AHA/CDC hs-CRP Recommendations; JUPITER Trial; manufacturer IFU.

name: HISTAMINE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Histamine measures the concentration of histamine, a biogenic amine involved in immune responses, gastric acid secretion, and neurotransmission. Elevated plasma histamine: systemic mastocytosis, mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), allergic reactions, carcinoid syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: process quickly (histamine is unstable). Preparation: note urticaria, flushing, diarrhoea, anaphylaxis. Handle per standard. Elevated: mastocytosis, MCAS, carcinoid. Unstable: process quickly. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: mastocytosis, MCAS, carcinoid. Unstable: process quickly. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Mastocytosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HISTIDINE (QUANTITATIVE)
interpretation: Plasma Histidine Quantitative measures the concentration of histidine, an essential amino acid. Histidine is a precursor to histamine and is important for gastric acid secretion, immune function, and haemoglobin synthesis. Elevated: histidinaemia (rare autosomal recessive), liver disease, renal failure. Low: histidinuria (renal tubular defect), malnutrition, rheumatoid arthritis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note metabolic disease, liver disease, rheumatoid arthritis. Handle per standard. Elevated: histidinaemia, liver/renal disease. Low: histidinuria, RA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: histidinaemia. Low: histidinuria, RA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HOMA INDEX (HOMA IR)
interpretation: HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance) - calculated index quantifying insulin resistance from fasting glucose and insulin. Formula: HOMA-IR = (Fasting Insulin [uIU/mL] x Fasting Glucose [mmol/L]) / 22.5. Clinical use: screening tool for insulin resistance in metabolic syndrome, PCOS, type 2 diabetes risk assessment, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), cardiovascular risk assessment. Elevated HOMA-IR: insulin resistance (metabolic syndrome, PCOS, obesity, NAFLD/NASH, type 2 diabetes, acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, lipodystrophy). Low HOMA-IR: insulin sensitivity (normal metabolic status, lean individuals). Limitations: HOMA-IR is a CALCULATED VALUE - accuracy depends on accurate fasting glucose AND fasting insulin measurements. Fasting requirements strict: 8-12h overnight fast required. Insulin assays vary significantly between platforms (immunoassay vs chemiluminescence vs ELISA) - HOMA-IR values NOT comparable between different insulin assays. HOMA-IR does NOT replace oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) for diagnosing diabetes or prediabetes. HOMA-IR is a SCREENING tool - not diagnostic. HOMA-IR affected by: acute illness, recent exercise, medications (insulin, metformin, thiazolidinediones), renal impairment (reduced insulin clearance). Reference ranges vary by population, ethnicity, and assay method. Cut-off values for insulin resistance: >2.0 or >2.5 commonly used but not universally standardised. HOMA-IR more useful for population studies than individual diagnosis.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting sample CRITICAL). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast required. Both fasting glucose AND fasting insulin needed simultaneously. Preparation: ensure 8-12h overnight fast. No caloric intake. Water permitted. Note medications affecting glucose/insulin (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, TZDs), recent illness, pregnancy, acute stress. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting glucose AND fasting insulin must be drawn from same fasting sample. HOMA-IR calculation: (Fasting Insulin uIU/mL x Fasting Glucose mmol/L) / 22.5. Alternative formula for HOMA-%B (beta-cell function): (20 x Fasting Insulin) / (Fasting Glucose - 3.5). OGTT: if HOMA-IR elevated, confirm with OGTT for diabetes/prediabetes diagnosis. PCOS workup: HOMA-IR + testosterone + SHBG + LH/FSH + fasting lipid profile.
ref_ranges: HOMA-IR <2.0: normal insulin sensitivity. HOMA-IR 2.0-2.5: borderline/early insulin resistance. HOMA-IR >2.5: insulin resistance likely. HOMA-IR >3.0: significant insulin resistance - strong metabolic syndrome association. HOMA-IR >4.0: severe insulin resistance - high type 2 diabetes and NAFLD risk. PCOS: HOMA-IR >2.5 suggestive of insulin resistance - consider metformin or insulin sensitizer. Obesity: HOMA-IR correlates with BMI and waist circumference. Type 2 diabetes: HOMA-IR often >3.0 at diagnosis. NAFLD/NASH: HOMA-IR >2.5 associated with hepatic steatosis. Reference ranges: population-specific and assay-specific. Ethnic variation: South Asians have higher HOMA-IR at lower BMI than Caucasians. Age: HOMA-IR increases with age. Pregnancy: HOMA-IR increases physiologically (insulin resistance of pregnancy). Cut-off values: not universally standardised - use laboratory/population-specific ranges.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; Endocrine Society Metabolic Syndrome Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HOMOCYSTEINE
interpretation: Homocysteine - sulphur-containing amino acid (intermediate in methionine metabolism). Elevated homocysteine (hyperhomocysteinaemia): independent cardiovascular risk factor (endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, thrombosis), folate deficiency (most common nutritional cause), vitamin B12 deficiency, vitamin B6 deficiency, chronic kidney disease (reduced renal clearance), hypothyroidism, medications (methotrexate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, nitrous oxide), genetic causes (MTHFR C677T polymorphism - most common; MTR/MTRR defects; cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency [homocystinuria - severe]), smoking, alcohol excess, advanced age, female sex (post-menopausal), physical inactivity. Clinical use: cardiovascular risk assessment (emerging marker alongside cholesterol, CRP), thrombophilia workup (recurrent DVT/PE, especially in young patients without other risk factors), folate/B12 deficiency screening (especially in elderly, malabsorption, vegetarian/vegan), monitoring methotrexate therapy (methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase - raises homocysteine), homocystinuria screening (newborn screening in some countries). Limitations: homocysteine elevated in many non-cardiovascular conditions (CKD, hypothyroidism, psoriasis) - exclude secondary causes before attributing to cardiovascular risk. Fasting vs non-fasting: homocysteine NOT significantly affected by food intake - non-fasting sample acceptable. Assay variability: different methods (immunoassay vs HPLC vs mass spectrometry) give different results - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. MTHFR C677T: common polymorphism (homozygous TT ~10% Caucasians) causes mildly elevated homocysteine - does NOT require treatment unless elevated homocysteine documented. Homocysteine and vitamin therapy: folic acid + B12 + B6 supplementation lowers homocysteine by 25-50% but evidence for CV event reduction is limited (HOPE-2, VISP trials showed no significant benefit).
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA) preferred. Serum also acceptable but EDTA recommended. Standard venipuncture. Fasting not required (homocysteine NOT affected by food). Preparation: note folate/B12/vitamin status, renal function, thyroid function, medications (methotrexate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, nitrous oxide), smoking, MTHFR status if known. Handling: EDTA plasma stable 2-8C up to 7 days or -20C long-term. Centrifuge within 1h. Haemolysis acceptable. Fasting not required - draw at any time. Renal function: homocysteine elevated in CKD - interpret alongside eGFR. Thyroid function: hypothyroidism elevates homocysteine - check TSH if elevated. Medication effects: methotrexate raises homocysteine (monitor in RA/psoriasis patients on methotrexate). Nitrous oxide: inactivates B12 - single exposure raises homocysteine. Vitamin supplementation: if elevated, check folate, B12, B6 - supplement if deficient.
ref_ranges: Adults: 5-15 umol/L (method-specific). Optimal for CV risk: <10 umol/L. Mild elevation: 15-30 umol/L (associated with increased CV risk). Moderate elevation: 30-100 umol/L (significant CV and thrombotic risk). Severe elevation: >100 umol/L (homocystinuria - genetic causes). Homocystinuria: >100 umol/L (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency - thromboembolism, lens dislocation, intellectual disability). MTHFR C677T homozygous: homocysteine typically 15-20 umol/L (mild elevation). CKD: homocysteine elevated proportionally to creatinine. Hypothyroidism: homocysteine elevated - normalises with thyroid hormone replacement. Age: homocysteine increases with age (men > women until menopause). Sex: men higher than pre-menopausal women; equal after menopause. Reference ranges: method-specific. Ethnic variation: minimal. Pregnancy: homocysteine decreases in pregnancy (plasma volume expansion). Folic acid fortification: populations with folic acid fortification have lower homocysteine levels.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AHA/ACC Cardiovascular Risk Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; HOPE-2 Trial data.

name: HOMOCYSTEINE - PLASMA
interpretation: Homocysteine - Plasma - same analyte as serum homocysteine but measured in EDTA plasma. EDTA plasma is preferred specimen for homocysteine measurement (more stable than serum). Plasma homocysteine does NOT require fasting (unlike glucose/insulin). Clinical interpretation identical to serum homocysteine: elevated homocysteine (>15 umol/L) associated with cardiovascular disease, thrombosis, stroke, cognitive decline, neural tube defects. This test (plasma) and the serum homocysteine test provide equivalent clinical information - the distinction is specimen type preference. Plasma preferred over serum because EDTA chelates calcium, preventing coagulation-related shifts in homocysteine binding proteins. Limitations: same as serum homocysteine - elevated in CKD, hypothyroidism, folate/B12/B6 deficiency, medications, smoking. Assay method variability applies. MTHFR C677T polymorphism causes mild elevation. Not a substitute for comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment.
pre_analytical: Sample: EDTA plasma (preferred). Standard venipuncture. Fasting NOT required. Preparation: note folate/B12/B6 status, renal function, thyroid function, medications (methotrexate, phenytoin, carbamazepine), smoking, MTHFR status. Handling: EDTA plasma stable 2-8C up to 7 days or -20C long-term. Centrifuge within 1h. Haemolysis acceptable. Preferred over serum due to better stability.
ref_ranges: Adults: 5-15 umol/L (method-specific). Optimal for CV risk: <10 umol/L. Mild elevation: 15-30 umol/L. Moderate: 30-100 umol/L. Severe (>100): homocystinuria. Same interpretation as serum homocysteine.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AHA/ACC Cardiovascular Risk Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HOMOGENTISIC ACID (ALKAPTONURIA) QUALITATIVE
interpretation: Urine Homogentisic Acid (HGA) Qualitative detects the presence of homogentisic acid in urine. HGA accumulates in alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency), an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. HGA turns dark (brown/black) upon standing or alkalinisation (classic diagnostic feature). Alkaptonuria: ochronosis (dark pigmentation of connective tissue), arthritis, cardiovascular disease. Reference ranges: qualitative.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note joint pain, darkening urine, ochronosis, family history. Handle per standard. Positive: alkaptonuria. Darkening: upon standing. Qualitative: yes/no. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: alkaptonuria. Darkening: upon standing/alkalinisation. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HOMOGENTISIC ACID (ALKAPTONURIA) QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Urine Homogentisic Acid (HGA) Quantitative measures the concentration of homogentisic acid in urine. HGA accumulates in alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency). Quantitative HGA: more specific than qualitative (turning dark). HGA greater than 4000 mmol/mol creatinine: alkaptonuria. HGA is also a marker of phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). Preparation: note joint pain, ochronosis, family history. Handle per standard. Quantitative: more specific than qualitative. Greater than 4000 mmol/mol: alkaptonuria. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 30 mmol/mol creatinine. Alkaptonuria: greater than 4000 mmol/mol. Quantitative: more specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HOMOVANILLIC ACID - URINE
interpretation: 24-Hour Urine Homovanillic Acid (HVA) is a dopamine metabolite used as a tumour marker for neuroblastoma and phaeochromocytoma. HVA is produced by the metabolism of dopamine via catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) and monoamine oxidase (MAO). Elevated HVA: neuroblastoma (sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%), phaeochromocytoma, drugs (levodopa). Normalised to creatinine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: 24-hour urine. CRITICAL: complete 24-hour collection. Preparation: note neuroblastoma suspicion, phaeochromocytoma. Handle: 2-8C. Elevated: neuroblastoma (90% sensitivity). Normalised: creatinine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: neuroblastoma, phaeochromocytoma. More sensitive: than VMA for neuroblastoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: SIOP Neuroblastoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HUMAN EPITHELIAL OVARIAN CANCER -EOC MARKER (HE4)
interpretation: Serum Human Epididymis Protein 4 (HE4, WFDC2) is a tumour marker for ovarian cancer. HE4 is a glycoprotein expressed in normal reproductive tissues and overexpressed in ovarian and endometrial cancers. HE4 is more specific than CA-125 (fewer false positives in premenopausal women). HE4 and CA-125 are combined in the ROMA (Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm) score. Elevated HE4: ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer, lung cancer. Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note ovarian cancer risk, menopausal status, other cancers. Handle per standard. Elevated: ovarian/endometrial cancer. ROMA: with CA-125. More specific: than CA-125. Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (menopause-dependent). ROMA score: combined. Elevated: ovarian cancer. More specific: than CA-125. Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
refs: Sources: NCCN Ovarian Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: HYDROXYPROLINE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Hydroxyproline measures the concentration of hydroxyproline, an amino acid found almost exclusively in collagen. Plasma hydroxyproline reflects collagen metabolism and is used as a marker for: bone resorption, collagen turnover, and connective tissue disorders. Elevated: Paget disease, hyperparathyroidism, bone metastases, Marfan syndrome. Low: hypothyroidism, scurvy. Limitations: affected by gelatin intake (dietary). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note bone disease, connective tissue disorders, diet (gelatin). Handle per standard. Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism, bone mets. Low: hypothyroidism, scurvy. Diet: gelatin affects. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism, bone metastases. Low: hypothyroidism, scurvy. Diet: gelatin affects. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IDURONATE 2 SULPHATE SULPHATASE UNTER/ MPS II - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Iduronate-2-Sulphatase (IDS) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulphatase. IDS deficiency causes Mucopolysaccharidosis II (Hunter syndrome), an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder. Hunter syndrome: X-linked, affects males. Features: skeletal dysplasia, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac disease, developmental regression. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note skeletal dysplasia, coarse features, developmental delay, family history. Handle per standard. Low: MPS II (Hunter). X-linked: males. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: MPS II (Hunter). X-linked: males only. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IGG4 SUBCLASS
interpretation: Serum IgG4 Subclass measures the concentration of immunoglobulin G4, the least abundant IgG subclass. Elevated IgG4: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD), a systemic fibroinflammatory condition. IgG4-RD: autoimmune pancreatitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, sclerosing cholangitis, Mikulicz disease, Riedel thyroiditis. IgG4 greater than 135 mg/dL: suggestive of IgG4-RD. IgG4/IgG ratio greater than 10%: supportive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note autoimmune symptoms, pancreatitis, fibrosis. Handle per standard. Elevated: IgG4-RD. Greater than 135 mg/dL: suggestive. Ratio: greater than 10%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 135 mg/dL (method-specific). Elevated: IgG4-RD. Ratio: IgG4/IgG greater than 10%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR/EULAR IgG4-RD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOFIXATION ELECTROPHORESIS (IMMUNOTYPING) QUALITATIVE
interpretation: Immunofixation Electrophoresis (IFE) Qualitative - laboratory technique identifying and typing monoclonal immunoglobulins (M-proteins) in serum or urine. Detects and characterises M-protein bands missed by serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP). Clinical use: multiple myeloma diagnosis and typing (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE heavy chain; kappa/lambda light chain), Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (IgM M-protein), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) diagnosis, light chain myeloma (Bence Jones protein in urine), amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis - free light chains), lymphoproliferative disorders. IFE vs SPEP: SPEP detects abnormal protein pattern; IFE IDENTIFIES the type (heavy chain and light chain) of the M-protein. IFE is the confirmatory test after SPEP shows a suspicious spike. Limitations: IFE is QUALITATIVE (identifies presence and type) - does not quantify M-protein (quantify by SPEP densitometry or serum free light chain assay). IFE sensitivity: can detect M-protein >0.2-0.5 g/dL (some platforms more sensitive). Below this threshold = MGUS or early myeloma may be missed. IFE cannot distinguish MGUS from early myeloma without clinical correlation (CRAB criteria: calcium elevation, renal insufficiency, anaemia, bone lesions). IFE requires experienced laboratory scientist for interpretation - band morphology can be subtle. IFE false positives: oligoclonal bands (post-infection, autoimmune), fibrinogen (if serum not properly separated), rheumatoid factor (IgM can mimic M-protein). IFE negative does NOT exclude light chain myeloma - urine IFE or serum free light chain assay needed. Quantification: M-protein quantified by SPEP densitometry (not IFE). M-protein typing: IFE identifies IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE + kappa/lambda light chains. Serial IFE: monitors treatment response in myeloma (IFE should become negative = complete response).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (most common) or urine (24h urine for light chain detection). Standard venipuncture. Fasting not required. Preparation: note myeloma symptoms (bone pain, fatigue, renal failure, anaemia), monoclonal gammopathy history, family history of myeloma/MGUS. Handling: serum separation within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. SPEP first: if SPEP shows suspicious spike, proceed to IFE for typing. Urine IFE: for suspected light chain myeloma (Bence Jones proteinuria) - 24h urine collection. Serum free light chains: alternative to urine IFE - more sensitive for light chain myeloma. IFE typing: identifies heavy chain (G, A, M, D, E) and light chain (kappa, lambda) type of M-protein. Quantification: SPEP densitometry for M-protein quantification (not IFE). Monitoring: serial IFE in myeloma - IFE negativity = complete response. Amyloidosis: IFE + serum free light chain assay for AL amyloidosis screening.
ref_ranges: Normal: no M-protein detected (no monoclonal band on IFE). MGUS: M-protein present but <1.5 g/dL, no end-organ damage, normal calcium/renal function/haemoglobin, bone marrow plasma cells <10%. Multiple myeloma: M-protein usually >1.5 g/dL on SPEP, CRAB criteria present (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions). Waldenstrom: IgM M-protein, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma on bone marrow biopsy. Light chain myeloma: urine IFE positive for kappa or lambda light chains, serum IFE may be negative (no intact immunoglobulin). AL amyloidosis: M-protein present + amyloid deposits on tissue biopsy. Sensitivity: IFE detects M-protein >0.2-0.5 g/dL. Below this: MGUS or early myeloma may be missed. Oligoclonal bands: multiple faint bands (post-infection, autoimmune) - not monoclonal. Reference ranges: laboratory-specific interpretation required.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IMWG Myeloma Consensus Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN A (IgA)
interpretation: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) - antibody isotype primarily mediating mucosal immunity (secretory IgA protects respiratory, GI, and urogenital surfaces). Elevated IgA: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease - most common glomerulonephritis worldwide - mesangial IgA deposition), multiple myeloma (IgA myeloma - 15-20% of myeloma cases), cirrhosis/alcoholic liver disease (polyclonal IgA elevation - hepatic clearance reduced), autoimmune disease (coeliac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, RA, SLE), chronic infections (TB, HIV, leprosy), IgA vasculopathy (Henoch-Schonlein purpura). Low/absent IgA: selective IgA deficiency (most common primary immunodeficiency - 1:500 Caucasians), common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), protein-losing conditions (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), severe burns, medications (immunosuppressive therapy), congenital agammaglobulinaemia. Clinical use: selective IgA deficiency screening (recurrent sinopulmonary infections, diarrhoea, autoimmunity), IgA nephropathy marker (serum IgA elevated in 50% of cases), coeliac disease association (IgA anti-tTG antibodies), myeloma typing (IgA myeloma). Limitations: IgA nephropathy diagnosis requires RENAL BIOPSY (not serum IgA measurement). Serum IgA elevated in 50% of IgA nephropathy - normal IgA does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Selective IgA deficiency: IgA may be low but some patients produce anti-IgA antibodies (risk of anaphylaxis with blood products containing IgA). IgA myeloma: IgA level correlates with disease burden but is not used alone for treatment monitoring (serum free light chains more sensitive). Assay variability: nephelometry/turbidimetry most common. Polyclonal IgA elevation (inflammation, infection, liver disease) vs monoclonal IgA elevation (IgA myeloma) - SPEP/IFE needed to distinguish.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recurrent infections, autoimmune history, liver disease, proteinuria, coeliac disease risk, family history of immunodeficiency. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Selective IgA deficiency: if suspected, check IgA level first. If low/absent, check IgG and IgM (selective = isolated IgA deficiency; CVID = low IgG + low IgA +/- low IgM). Anti-IgA antibodies: check before blood transfusion in IgA-deficient patients (risk of anaphylaxis if recipient has anti-IgA antibodies and donor blood contains IgA). IgA nephropathy: serum IgA measurement alone insufficient - renal biopsy with immunofluorescence (mesangial IgA deposits) required for diagnosis. Myeloma typing: IgA + IgG + IgM + serum free light chains + SPEP/IFE for monoclonal gammopathy workup.
ref_ranges: Adults: 70-400 mg/dL (0.7-4.0 g/L) - method-specific. Neonates: very low (reflects maternal IgA - crosses placenta poorly compared to IgG). Children: rises to adult range by 10-12 years. Selective IgA deficiency: IgA <7 mg/dL (<0.07 g/L) with normal IgG and IgM. CVID: low IgG (<700 mg/dL) + low IgA (+/- low IgM) + absent antibody response to vaccines. IgA nephropathy: serum IgA elevated in ~50% of cases (100-600 mg/dL typical). IgA myeloma: IgA markedly elevated (>3000 mg/dL). IgA nephropathy diagnosis: RENAL BIOPSY required - mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence. Liver disease: polyclonal IgA elevated (reduced hepatic clearance). Coeliac disease: IgA anti-tTG elevated (selective IgA deficiency causes false-negative IgA-based coeliac tests). Reference ranges: method-specific. Ethnic variation: African Americans have slightly higher IgA than Caucasians.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESID Primary Immunodeficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN E (IgE) - TOTAL
interpretation: Immunoglobulin E (IgE) Total - antibody isotype mediating type I hypersensitivity (allergic) reactions and anti-parasitic immunity. Total IgE reflects overall IgE production (polyclonal) - not allergen-specific. Elevated total IgE: atopic conditions (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, food allergy - but total IgE does NOT diagnose allergy), parasitic infections (helminths - strongyloides, toxocara, ascaris - potent IgE stimulants), hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome - autosomal dominant, very high IgE >2000 IU/mL, recurrent staphylococcal infections, pneumatoceles), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA - IgE typically >1000 IU/mL), allergic fungal sinusitis, drug reactions (DRESS syndrome, drug-induced IgE elevation), IgE myeloma (rare - <1% of myeloma), Hodgkin lymphoma, Kimura disease, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Low/absent IgE: selective IgA deficiency (may have low IgE), Bruton agammaglobulinaemia, cytotoxic chemotherapy, immunosuppressive therapy, ataxia-telangiectasia. Clinical use: hyper-IgE syndrome screening (total IgE >2000 IU/mL), ABPA diagnosis (total IgE >1000 IU/mL + Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG + eosinophilia), parasitic infection screening (total IgE elevated in helminth infections), allergy assessment (total IgE contributes to atopic risk stratification). Limitations: total IgE does NOT diagnose allergy - allergen-specific IgE (RAST/ImmunoCAP) needed for specific allergy diagnosis. Total IgE has LOW sensitivity and specificity for allergy diagnosis. Many allergic patients have normal total IgE. Total IgE elevated in many non-allergic conditions (parasitic infection, hyper-IgE syndrome, ABPA, IgE myeloma, DRESS). Age variation: total IgE high in children, declines with age. Reference ranges: age-specific cutoffs required. Assay variability: different immunoassay platforms give different results. Total IgE used alongside clinical history, physical examination, and allergen-specific IgE for allergy workup.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note atopic history (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, food allergy), parasitic infection risk (travel, endemic exposure), recurrent infections, drug reactions (DRESS), family history of atopy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Hyper-IgE syndrome: if total IgE >2000 IU/mL + recurrent staphylococcal infections + pneumatoceles, suspect Job syndrome - genetic testing (STAT3 mutation). ABPA: total IgE >1000 IU/mL + Aspergillus-specific IgE + peripheral eosinophilia + bronchiectasis. Parasitic infection: total IgE elevated in helminth infections - concurrent stool microscopy + eosinophilia assessment. Allergy workup: total IgE + allergen-specific IgE (ImmunoCAP) + skin prick testing + clinical history. Total IgE alone insufficient for allergy diagnosis. Age: total IgE high in children, declines with age - use age-specific cutoffs. Serial total IgE: monitors ABPA treatment response (IgE falls with steroid therapy).
ref_ranges: Adults: <100 IU/mL (0-100 IU/mL) - method-specific. Children: higher (neonates 0-2 IU/mL; peaks at 10-15 years; normalises by adulthood). Atopic conditions: total IgE 100-1000 IU/mL (variable - does NOT confirm allergy). ABPA: total IgE >1000 IU/mL (often >2000). Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job): total IgE >2000 IU/mL (often >5000). Parasitic infection: total IgE often 500-5000 IU/mL in helminth infections. IgE myeloma: total IgE markedly elevated (>10000 IU/mL). Allergic rhinitis: total IgE may be normal or elevated. Atopic dermatitis: total IgE often >200 IU/mL. Reference ranges: age-specific cutoffs essential. Ethnic variation: IgE higher in tropical/subtropical populations (parasitic exposure, genetic factors). Method comparison: different immunoassay platforms give different results - use laboratory-specific ranges.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AAAAI/ACAAI Allergy/Immunology Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN G (IgG)
interpretation: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) - most abundant immunoglobulin in serum (75-80% of total IgG); mediates opsonisation, complement activation, ADCC, and crosses placenta (passive neonatal immunity). Elevated IgG: multiple myeloma (IgG myeloma - most common type, 50-60% of myeloma), chronic infections (TB, HIV, hepatitis, leprosy), autoimmune disease (SLE, RA, Sjogren), sarcoidosis, cirrhosis, chronic liver disease, IgG4-related disease (IgG4 elevated >135 mg/dL + tissue infiltration). Low IgG: common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton), selective IgA deficiency (IgG may be normal), nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria loses IgG), severe burns, protein-losing enteropathy, immunosuppressive therapy, congenital agammaglobulinaemia. Clinical use: immunodeficiency screening (CVID diagnosis: low IgG + low IgA + absent antibody response to vaccines), myeloma typing (IgG myeloma), IgG4-related disease screening (IgG4 subclass elevated), monitoring IVIG therapy, vaccine response assessment. Limitations: IgG has 4 subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4) - total IgG may be normal while a specific subclass is deficient (e.g., IgG2 deficiency - impaired response to polysaccharide antigens). IgG elevation is NON-SPECIFIC (infection, inflammation, myeloma). SPEP/IFE needed to distinguish monoclonal (myeloma) from polyclonal (infection/inflammation) IgG elevation. Neonatal IgG reflects MATERNAL IgG (crosses placenta) - not infant's own production until 6 months. IgG levels affected by IVIG therapy (infused IgG elevates levels). Assay variability: nephelometry/turbidimetry most common.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recurrent infections, autoimmune history, myeloma symptoms, family history of immunodeficiency, IVIG therapy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Immunodeficiency workup: IgG + IgA + IgM + vaccine antibody response (pneumococcal, tetanus). CVID diagnosis: low IgG + low IgA +/- low IgM + absent antibody response to vaccines. IVIG monitoring: IgG level pre- and post-infusion. Myeloma: IgG + IgG subclasses + SPEP/IFE + serum free light chains. IgG4-related disease: IgG subclass measurement (IgG4 >135 mg/dL suggestive). Neonates: IgG reflects maternal - own production begins at 2-3 months, matures by 6-12 months.
ref_ranges: Adults: 700-1600 mg/dL (7-16 g/L) - method-specific. Neonates: high (600-1400 mg/dL - maternal IgG crossing placenta). Children: low at 3-6 months (maternal IgG lost, own production immature); rises to adult range by 8-10 years. IgG subclasses: IgG1 350-1000 mg/dL; IgG2 150-600 mg/dL; IgG3 25-150 mg/dL; IgG4 5-100 mg/dL. IgG myeloma: IgG markedly elevated (>3000 mg/dL). CVID: IgG <700 mg/dL + low IgA + absent vaccine response. Selective IgG subclass deficiency: total IgG normal, specific subclass low (e.g., IgG2 <50 mg/dL). IgG4-related disease: IgG4 >135 mg/dL. IVIG: IgG elevated post-infusion (3000-10000 mg/dL depending on dose). Reference ranges: method-specific. Ethnic variation: African Americans have slightly higher IgG than Caucasians.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESID Primary Immunodeficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN IgA, IgM & IgG
interpretation: Immunoglobulin Panel (IgA, IgM and IgG) - combined measurement of three major immunoglobulin isotypes for comprehensive immunodeficiency and immunoproliferative disease assessment. Panel provides simultaneous quantification: IgG (most abundant - opsonisation, complement), IgA (mucosal immunity), IgM (primary antibody response - first antibody produced). Clinical use: immunodeficiency screening (primary immunodeficiency: CVID, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgM syndrome, common variable immunodeficiency), myeloma screening (SPEP spike + immunoglobulin levels for typing), monitoring chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis, TB), autoimmune disease assessment, chronic liver disease evaluation. Pattern recognition: IgG low + IgA low + IgM low = severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) or advanced HIV, CVID. IgA low + IgG/IgM normal = selective IgA deficiency. IgM elevated + IgG low = hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L deficiency, AID deficiency). IgG/IgA elevated + IgM normal = chronic antigenic stimulation (infection, autoimmune). Monoclonal gammopathy: one Ig elevated disproportionately (SPEP/IFE confirms). Limitations: immunoglobulin levels are SCREENING tests - not diagnostic alone. Polyclonal elevation (infection/inflammation) vs monoclonal elevation (myeloma) requires SPEP/IFE distinction. Total IgG may mask subclass deficiency (IgG1-4 subclasses). IgA low does not diagnose selective IgA deficiency without checking IgG/IgM. Age-specific ranges required (children have different patterns). Neonatal immunoglobulins reflect maternal IgG (not infant's own). Vaccination status affects Ig levels (post-vaccination IgM may be elevated).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recurrent infections, autoimmune history, family history of immunodeficiency, chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis), liver disease, proteinuria, myeloma symptoms. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Screening panel: IgG + IgA + IgM simultaneously. If abnormal: SPEP/IFE for monoclonal gammopathy, IgG subclasses, vaccine antibody response. CVID: IgG <700 mg/dL + IgA low + absent vaccine response. Selective IgA deficiency: IgA <7 mg/dL + normal IgG/IgM. Hyper-IgM: IgM elevated + IgG low (requires genetic testing). Myeloma: one Ig elevated + SPEP spike + serum free light chains. HIV: IgG elevated (polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia). Liver disease: IgA elevated (especially alcoholic cirrhosis).
ref_ranges: Adults: IgG 700-1600 mg/dL; IgA 70-400 mg/dL; IgM 40-230 mg/dL. Neonates: IgG high (maternal), IgA/IgM very low. Children: IgG reaches adult range by 8-10 years; IgA by 10-12 years; IgM by 5-7 years. CVID: IgG <700 + IgA low + impaired vaccine response. Selective IgA deficiency: IgA <7 mg/dL + normal IgG/IgM. Hyper-IgM syndrome: IgM elevated + IgG low. Monoclonal gammopathy: one Ig markedly elevated disproportionate to others. Polyclonal: all Igs mildly elevated (chronic infection). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age-specific cutoffs essential for paediatric patients.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESID Primary Immunodeficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN IgD SERUM IgD HEAVY CHAIN (SURFACE)
interpretation: Serum IgD (Immunoglobulin D Heavy Chain) measures the concentration of IgD, the least abundant serum immunoglobulin. IgD is primarily found on B cell surfaces and plays a role in B cell activation. Elevated IgD: IgD myeloma (rare), hyper-IgD syndrome (HIDS), chronic infections. Low IgD: selective IgD deficiency (usually asymptomatic). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note myeloma, recurrent fever, infections. Handle per standard. Elevated: IgD myeloma, HIDS. Low: selective deficiency (usually asymptomatic). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 14 mg/dL (method-specific). Elevated: IgD myeloma, HIDS. Low: selective deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IMWG Myeloma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IMMUNOGLOBULIN M (IgM)
interpretation: Immunoglobulin M (IgM) - first antibody produced in primary immune response; exists as pentamer in serum (highest molecular weight immunoglobulin). Elevated IgM: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (IgM monoclonal gammopathy + lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma), hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L deficiency, AID deficiency - IgM elevated + IgG/IgA low), primary biliary cholangitis (PBC - IgM characteristically elevated), chronic infections (hepatitis C, malaria, trypanosomiasis), acute hepatitis (transient IgM elevation), cirrhosis (polyclonal), cryoglobulinaemia (IgM cryoglobulins). Low IgM: CVID (IgM low alongside IgG and IgA), selective IgA deficiency (IgM may be normal), agammaglobulinaemia, immunosuppressive therapy, protein-losing conditions. Clinical use: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia screening (IgM monoclonal protein), hyper-IgM syndrome diagnosis (IgM elevated + IgG low), PBC marker (IgM elevated in 70-80% of PBC), acute hepatitis marker (IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HBc - but total IgM also elevated). Limitations: IgM elevation is NON-SPECIFIC (infection, inflammation, autoimmunity). Monoclonal IgM (Waldenstrom) vs polyclonal IgM (infection) requires SPEP/IFE distinction. IgM is a pentamer - does NOT cross placenta (unlike IgG) - neonatal IgM reflects infant's own immune response (infection in utero if elevated). Hyper-IgM syndrome: genetic testing required (CD40L, AID, UNG genes). PBC: IgM elevated but not diagnostic - anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) more specific. Cryoglobulinaemia: IgM cryoglobulins cause vasculitis - cold agglutinin disease. Assay variability: nephelometry/turbidimetry. Turbidimetry may underestimate IgM at very high levels (pentamer interference).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note autoimmune history (PBC, cryoglobulinaemia), chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis C), Waldenstrom symptoms (fatigue, bleeding, hyperviscosity), recurrent infections, family history of immunodeficiency. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Cryoglobulinaemia: draw blood into pre-warmed tubes at 37C (IgM cryoglobulins precipitate at room temperature - false low IgM). Waldenstrom: IgM + SPEP/IFE + serum viscosity + serum free light chains. PBC: IgM + AMA + liver function tests. Hyper-IgM: IgM elevated + IgG/IgA low - genetic testing (CD40L, AID). Neonatal IgM: elevated = intrauterine infection (TORCH) - infant's own immune response. Cold agglutinin disease: IgM autoantibodies against RBC surface antigens - agglutination at cold temperatures.
ref_ranges: Adults: 40-230 mg/dL (0.4-2.3 g/L) - method-specific. Neonates: very low (IgM does not cross placenta). Children: rises to adult range by 5-7 years. Waldenstrom: IgM markedly elevated (>3000 mg/dL). Hyper-IgM syndrome: IgM elevated + IgG low (<200 mg/dL). PBC: IgM elevated (often 200-500 mg/dL). Acute hepatitis: IgM transiently elevated. Cryoglobulinaemia: IgM elevated (type II mixed cryoglobulinaemia - IgM + IgG). Reference ranges: method-specific. Turbidimetry may underestimate very high IgM levels. Ethnic variation: minimal.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESID Primary Immunodeficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INFLIXIMAB ANTI-TNF BLOCKER
interpretation: Serum Infliximab measures the concentration of infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody against tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha). Infliximab is used to treat: inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis), rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis. Therapeutic drug monitoring: trough levels guide dosing. Low trough: loss of response, dose adjustment needed. Anti-drug antibodies: reduce efficacy, increase infusion reactions. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: trough level (just before next dose). Preparation: note IBD activity, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: greater than 3-7 mcg/mL (trough). Anti-drug antibodies: reduce efficacy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: greater than 3 to 7 mcg/mL (trough). Low: loss of response. Anti-drug antibodies: reduce efficacy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AGA IBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INHIBIN-A
interpretation: Inhibin-A - dimeric glycoprotein (alpha-beta A subunit) produced by granulosa cells of ovarian follicles. Marker of granulosa cell function and tumour marker for granulosa cell tumours of the ovary. Elevated Inhibin-A: pregnancy (placental production - rises from first trimester, peaks in second trimester), ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS - elevated Inhibin-A), granulosa cell tumour of ovary (adult and juvenile types - elevated Inhibin-A + Inhibin-B), mucinous ovarian tumours (some produce Inhibin-A), dysgerminoma (some elevate Inhibin-A), polycystic ovary syndrome (mildly elevated). Low/absent Inhibin-A: menopause (granulosa cell function ceases), premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), Turner syndrome (gonadal dysgenesis), ovarian failure, chemotherapy/radiation-induced gonadal toxicity. Clinical use: Down syndrome screening (second trimester quad screen: Inhibin-A + AFP + hCG + uE3 - elevated Inhibin-A in Down syndrome), ovarian tumour marker (granulosa cell tumour monitoring), ovarian reserve assessment (combined with AMH and FSH). Limitations: Inhibin-A elevated in pregnancy - cannot be used as ovarian tumour marker during pregnancy. Inhibin-A assay variability - method-specific reference ranges. Inhibin-A alone insufficient for ovarian tumour diagnosis - requires imaging (transvaginal USS) and other tumour markers (CA-125, HE4). Inhibin-A and AMH: both reflect ovarian reserve but AMH more reliable (not cyclical). Inhibin-A in quad screen: part of second-trimester maternal serum screening for Down syndrome - not used alone. Assay specificity: some Inhibin-A assays may cross-react with Inhibin-B or pro-alpha-C fragments.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note pregnancy status (Inhibin-A elevated in pregnancy), menstrual cycle day (if not pregnant), ovarian tumour history, fertility treatment, menopausal status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Down syndrome screening: second trimester quad screen (15-20 weeks) - Inhibin-A + AFP + hCG + uE3 combined risk calculation. Ovarian tumour: Inhibin-A + CA-125 + HE4 + transvaginal USS. Granulosa cell tumour: serial Inhibin-A monitoring for treatment response and recurrence. Ovarian reserve: Inhibin-A + AMH + antral follicle count + FSH for comprehensive assessment. Menopause: Inhibin-A low/absent - reflects cessation of granulosa cell function. Fertility treatment: Inhibin-A monitoring during controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) - peak Inhibin-A correlates with follicle development.
ref_ranges: Pre-menopausal women: 0-180 pg/mL (follicular phase low, rises in luteal phase; peaks mid-cycle). Pregnancy: rises from first trimester (20-50 pg/mL), peaks second trimester (200-500 pg/mL), declines third trimester. Down syndrome screening: elevated MoM in Down syndrome. Menopause: <5 pg/mL (low/absent). Granulosa cell tumour: Inhibin-A elevated (>200 pg/mL in many cases). OHSS: Inhibin-A markedly elevated. POI: Inhibin-A low/absent. Children: very low until puberty. Reference ranges: method-specific. Cyclical variation in pre-menopausal women - interpret alongside menstrual cycle day.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; FIGO Ovarian Tumour Markers Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INHIBIN-B
interpretation: Inhibin-B - dimeric glycoprotein (alpha-beta B subunit) produced by Sertoli cells in males and granulosa cells in females. Marker of gonadal function in both sexes. Males: Sertoli cell function marker (prepubertal boys - Inhibin-B reflects Sertoli cell maturation; adult men - correlates with spermatogenesis). Females: granulosa cell function marker (reflects follicular development and ovarian reserve). Elevated Inhibin-B: granulosa cell tumour of ovary (adult and juvenile types), Sertoli cell tumour of testis (some cases), pregnancy (placental production), ovarian hyperstimulation (OHSS), polycystic ovary syndrome (mildly elevated in some studies). Low/absent Inhibin-B: male infertility (impaired spermatogenesis - azoospermia, severe oligozoospermia), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY - absent spermatogenesis), premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), menopause (granulosa cell function ceases), Turner syndrome, chemotherapy/radiation-induced gonadal toxicity, cryptorchidism (impaired Sertoli cell function). Clinical use: male infertility workup (Inhibin-B + FSH + AMH + testosterone for spermatogenesis assessment), Sertoli cell tumour marker, ovarian reserve assessment in females (combined with AMH), cryptorchidism outcome prediction in boys. Limitations: Inhibin-B is cyclical in women (follicular phase elevated, luteal phase low) - interpret alongside menstrual cycle day. Inhibin-B in men: correlates with sperm concentration but does NOT replace semen analysis. Inhibin-B assay variability: different platforms give different results - method-specific reference ranges. Inhibin-B alone insufficient for infertility diagnosis - requires comprehensive hormone panel. Inhibin-B and AMH: both reflect gonadal function but AMH more reliable in women (not cyclical). Inhibin-B in boys: prepubertal levels very low - difficult to interpret without age-matched reference ranges.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note fertility status, menstrual cycle day (women), sperm analysis results (men), Klinefelter risk, chemotherapy/radiation history, ovarian tumour history. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Male infertility: Inhibin-B + FSH + LH + testosterone + semen analysis + AMH. Low Inhibin-B + high FSH = impaired spermatogenesis (primary testicular failure). Low Inhibin-B + low FSH = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Female ovarian reserve: Inhibin-B + AMH + FSH + antral follicle count. Granulosa cell tumour: serial Inhibin-B monitoring for treatment response and recurrence. Sertoli cell tumour: Inhibin-B elevated in some cases - monitor post-surgery. Children: Inhibin-B very low prepubertally - rises at puberty in boys (Sertoli cell maturation).
ref_ranges: Adult men: 20-350 pg/mL (method-specific). Pre-pubertal boys: <10 pg/mL. Pubertal boys: rises with Tanner stage. Women (follicular): 30-120 pg/mL. Women (luteal): 10-50 pg/mL. Post-menopausal: <5 pg/mL. Granulosa cell tumour: Inhibin-B elevated (>200 pg/mL in many cases). Sertoli cell tumour: Inhibin-B elevated in some cases. Male infertility: Inhibin-B <20 pg/mL associated with azoospermia/severe oligozoospermia. Klinefelter: Inhibin-B very low/absent. Reference ranges: method-specific. Cyclical variation in pre-menopausal women.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESHRE Male Infertility Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN (3 SAMPLES WITH GLUCOSE)
interpretation: Insulin (3 Samples with Glucose) - measurement of serum insulin alongside glucose at three time points (typically fasting, 1-hour, and 2-hour post-glucose load) for assessment of insulin secretion and insulin resistance. Used in oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) context. Clinical use: insulinoma diagnosis (Whipple triad: hypoglycaemia + inappropriately elevated insulin + symptoms relieved by glucose), reactive hypoglycaemia (insulin elevated at 1-2h post-glucose in reactive hypoglycaemia), gestational diabetes assessment (insulin response pattern during OGTT), beta-cell function assessment (early phase insulin secretion), insulin resistance quantification (HOMA-IR from fasting sample), type 1 vs type 2 diabetes differentiation (type 1: absent/low insulin response; type 2: delayed/elevated insulin response with insulin resistance). Limitations: insulin assays vary significantly between platforms (immunoassay, chemiluminescence, ELISA) - values NOT comparable between methods.
