Insulin measured in fasting, 1h, 2h post-75g glucose load. Fasting insulin: reflects basal insulin secretion (used for HOMA-IR calculation). Post-glucose insulin: reflects stimulated insulin secretion (early peak at 30-60min in normal; delayed peak in type 2 diabetes). Insulinoma: fasting insulin elevated (>3 uIU/mL) with concurrent hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL) - Whipple triad. Proinsulin and C-peptide may be measured alongside insulin for additional information. Assay cross-reactivity: some insulin assays cross-react with proinsulin and insulin analogues - specify if on insulin therapy. Insulin levels NOT used to diagnose diabetes (glucose-based criteria used).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (multiple time points). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast for fasting sample. Then 75g glucose load (OGTT) with samples at 1h and 2h post-glucose. Preparation: ensure 8-12h overnight fast. No caloric intake. Water permitted. Note diabetes medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), recent illness, pregnancy status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Three time points: fasting (0h), 1h post-75g glucose, 2h post-75g glucose. Insulin + glucose measured at each time point. Fasting insulin: for HOMA-IR calculation. Post-glucose insulin: for insulin secretion pattern. Insulinoma: fasting insulin + fasting glucose + fasting C-peptide simultaneously. Reactive hypoglycaemia: 5h OGTT with insulin and glucose at 0, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300 min. Gestational diabetes: insulin response during OGTT at 24-28 weeks. Proinsulin: may be measured alongside insulin for insulinoma workup.
ref_ranges: Fasting insulin: 2-25 uIU/mL (method-specific). 1h post-glucose: typically 30-120 uIU/mL (normal first-phase response). 2h post-glucose: typically <80 uIU/mL (normal second-phase response). Insulinoma: fasting insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL). Type 1 diabetes: fasting insulin very low/absent; minimal response to glucose. Type 2 diabetes: fasting insulin elevated; delayed peak at 2h (insulin resistance). Reactive hypoglycaemia: insulin elevated at 1h post-glucose (>50 uIU/mL) with subsequent hypoglycaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific. Insulin levels NOT used for diabetes diagnosis - glucose-based criteria used. Proinsulin: fasting proinsulin <25 pmol/L normal; elevated in insulinoma and early type 2 diabetes.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; Endocrine Society Insulinoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN (5 SAMPLES WITH GLUCOSE)
interpretation: Insulin (5 Samples with Glucose) - measurement of serum insulin alongside glucose at five time points during an extended oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) or prolonged fasting protocol. Provides detailed insulin secretion profile and dynamics. Clinical use: insulinoma diagnosis (Whipple triad: hypoglycaemia + inappropriately elevated insulin + symptoms relieved by glucose), reactive hypoglycaemia characterisation (insulin peak timing and magnitude), insulin secretion dynamics (early vs late phase insulin response), beta-cell function assessment, dumping syndrome (early dumping: elevated insulin at 30-60min with rapid glucose drop), autonomic dysfunction (reactive hypoglycaemia after meals), gestational diabetes monitoring. Five time points typically: fasting (0h), 30min, 1h, 2h, and 3h post-75g glucose load. Some protocols extend to 4-5h for hypoglycaemia workup. Limitations: insulin assays vary significantly between platforms - values NOT comparable between methods. Extended OGTT (5h) needed for reactive hypoglycaemia and insulinoma screening. Insulinoma: fasting insulin elevated with hypoglycaemia, but may require prolonged (72h) supervised fast for diagnosis. Reactive hypoglycaemia: insulin peak at 30-60min post-glucose with subsequent glucose nadir <55 mg/dL. Dumping syndrome: early dumping shows rapid glucose rise then rapid fall with elevated insulin. Late dumping: hypoglycaemia at 2-3h post-meal. Assay cross-reactivity: some assays cross-react with proinsulin and insulin analogues. C-peptide measured alongside for confirmation of endogenous insulin production.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (multiple time points). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast for fasting sample. Then 75g glucose load (OGTT) with samples at 30min, 1h, 2h, and 3h post-glucose. Extended protocol: may extend to 4-5h for hypoglycaemia workup. Preparation: ensure 8-12h overnight fast. No caloric intake. Water permitted. Note diabetes medications, recent illness, pregnancy status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Five time points: fasting (0h), 30min, 1h, 2h, 3h post-75g glucose. Insulin + glucose measured at each time point. Insulinoma: if suspected, supervised 72h fast with insulin, glucose, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate at hypoglycaemic episodes. Reactive hypoglycaemia: 5h OGTT with insulin and glucose at 0, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300 min. Dumping syndrome: 5h OGTT post-gastric surgery - rapid glucose rise then fall with elevated insulin. Proinsulin + C-peptide: measured alongside insulin for additional diagnostic information.
ref_ranges: Fasting insulin: 2-25 uIU/mL (method-specific). 30min: typically 20-80 uIU/mL. 1h: typically 30-120 uIU/mL. 2h: typically 20-80 uIU/mL. 3h: typically returns to near-baseline. Insulinoma: fasting insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL). Reactive hypoglycaemia: insulin peak >50 uIU/mL at 30-60min with glucose nadir <55 mg/dL. Dumping syndrome: rapid insulin spike at 30-60min with rapid glucose fall. Type 1 diabetes: very low/absent insulin at all time points. Type 2 diabetes: elevated fasting insulin, delayed peak at 1-2h. Reference ranges: method-specific. Proinsulin: fasting <25 pmol/L normal; elevated in insulinoma. C-peptide: fasting 0.8-3.5 ng/mL normal; low in type 1, elevated in type 2.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; Endocrine Society Insulinoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN (FASTING)
interpretation: Insulin (Fasting) - measurement of serum insulin concentration after an 8-12h overnight fast. Reflects basal (fasting) insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells. Used to calculate HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance) and assess insulin resistance and beta-cell function. Clinical use: HOMA-IR calculation (fasting insulin + fasting glucose), insulin resistance screening (metabolic syndrome, PCOS, NAFLD, type 2 diabetes risk), insulinoma screening (elevated fasting insulin with hypoglycaemia), type 1 vs type 2 diabetes differentiation (type 1: low/absent fasting insulin; type 2: elevated fasting insulin), monitoring insulin therapy (endogenous insulin production assessment). Limitations: insulin assays vary significantly between platforms (immunoassay, chemiluminescence, ELISA) - values NOT comparable between methods. Fasting requirements strict: 8-12h overnight fast required. Fasting insulin alone insufficient for diabetes diagnosis (glucose-based criteria used). HOMA-IR = (Fasting Insulin uIU/mL x Fasting Glucose mmol/L) / 22.5. Fasting insulin affected by: recent meal (non-fasting), medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), acute illness, renal impairment (reduced clearance), obesity (elevated due to insulin resistance), pregnancy (physiological insulin resistance). Insulinoma: fasting insulin >3 uIU/mL with concurrent hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL) = Whipple triad. Assay cross-reactivity: some assays cross-react with proinsulin and insulin analogues. Fasting insulin NOT used alone for insulin resistance diagnosis - HOMA-IR more validated.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast required. Preparation: ensure 8-12h overnight fast. No caloric intake. Water permitted. Note diabetes medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, TZDs), recent illness, pregnancy status, obesity. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. HOMA-IR: fasting insulin + fasting glucose from same fasting sample. HOMA-IR = (Fasting Insulin uIU/mL x Fasting Glucose mmol/L) / 22.5. Insulinoma: fasting insulin + fasting glucose + fasting C-peptide simultaneously. If fasting glucose <55 mg/dL and fasting insulin >3 uIU/mL = Whipple triad. Type 1 diabetes: fasting insulin very low/absent + C-peptide low + glucose elevated. Type 2 diabetes: fasting insulin elevated (insulin resistance) + C-peptide normal/elevated + glucose elevated. Proinsulin: fasting proinsulin alongside insulin for insulinoma workup. C-peptide: measured alongside insulin to confirm endogenous insulin production (C-peptide not present in exogenous insulin).
ref_ranges: Fasting insulin: 2-25 uIU/mL (method-specific). HOMA-IR <2.0: normal insulin sensitivity. HOMA-IR >2.5: insulin resistance likely. HOMA-IR >4.0: severe insulin resistance. Insulinoma: fasting insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL). Type 1 diabetes: fasting insulin <2 uIU/mL (often undetectable). Type 2 diabetes: fasting insulin elevated (>25 uIU/mL) with insulin resistance. Obesity: fasting insulin elevated (reflecting insulin resistance). PCOS: fasting insulin elevated in many cases. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: fasting insulin increases with age. Pregnancy: fasting insulin elevated (physiological insulin resistance). Ethnic variation: South Asians have higher fasting insulin at lower BMI than Caucasians.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; Endocrine Society Insulinoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN (POST PRANDIAL)
interpretation: Insulin (Post Prandial) - measurement of serum insulin concentration 2 hours after a meal (typically a mixed meal containing carbohydrates, protein, and fat). Reflects post-prandial insulin secretion and glucose disposal. Used alongside post-prandial glucose for diabetes monitoring. Clinical use: post-prandial glucose management assessment, insulin resistance evaluation (elevated post-prandial insulin with hyperglycaemia = insulin resistance), gestational diabetes monitoring (post-prandial insulin response), dumping syndrome assessment (rapid insulin spike after meals), reactive hypoglycaemia screening. Limitations: insulin assays vary significantly between platforms - values NOT comparable between methods. Post-prandial timing: 2 hours post-meal is standard (may vary between laboratories). Mixed meal composition affects insulin response - standardised test meals preferred for comparison. Post-prandial insulin alone insufficient for diabetes diagnosis - glucose-based criteria used. Post-prandial insulin affected by: meal composition (carbohydrate content most important), portion size, medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), physical activity, obesity, pregnancy. Insulin resistance pattern: elevated post-prandial insulin with elevated post-prandial glucose. Insulinoma: may show elevated post-prandial insulin with hypoglycaemia. Dumping syndrome: rapid insulin spike at 30-60min post-meal with rapid glucose fall. Assay cross-reactivity: some assays cross-react with proinsulin and insulin analogues.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. 2 hours after a standard meal (mixed meal containing carbohydrates, protein, and fat). Preparation: standard meal (typically 600-1000 kcal, 45-60% carbohydrate). Note diabetes medications, recent illness, pregnancy status, physical activity. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Post-prandial: 2 hours post-meal (standard timing). Mixed meal: contains carbohydrates, protein, and fat (reflects real-world post-prandial response). Gestational diabetes: post-prandial glucose monitoring at 24-28 weeks - post-prandial insulin alongside glucose. Dumping syndrome: post-prandial insulin shows rapid spike at 30-60min with rapid glucose fall. Reactive hypoglycaemia: post-prandial insulin elevated with subsequent glucose nadir <55 mg/dL. Post-prandial insulin: assess glucose disposal - elevated insulin with normal glucose = early insulin resistance. Proinsulin + C-peptide: measured alongside insulin for additional diagnostic information.
ref_ranges: Post-prandial insulin (2h post-meal): typically 30-80 uIU/mL (method-specific). Post-prandial glucose (2h post-meal): <140 mg/dL normal; 140-199 mg/dL impaired glucose tolerance; >=200 mg/dL diabetes. Insulinoma: post-prandial insulin elevated with hypoglycaemia. Type 2 diabetes: post-prandial insulin elevated with hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance). Type 1 diabetes: post-prandial insulin low/absent with hyperglycaemia. Dumping syndrome: rapid insulin spike at 30-60min with rapid glucose fall. Reference ranges: method-specific. Post-prandial insulin not used for diabetes diagnosis - glucose-based criteria used. Ethnic variation: South Asians have higher post-prandial insulin at lower BMI than Caucasians.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN (RANDOM)
interpretation: Insulin (Random) - measurement of serum insulin concentration at an unspecified time relative to meals. Reflects circulating insulin levels at the time of sampling. Used in emergency settings or when fasting status is unknown. Clinical use: insulinoma screening (random insulin elevated with hypoglycaemia - suspicious for insulinoma), hypoglycaemia workup (random insulin with random glucose), gestational diabetes screening (random glucose with insulin), monitoring insulin therapy (if on insulin, random insulin reflects exogenous + endogenous), emergency department hypoglycaemia evaluation. Limitations: insulin assays vary significantly between platforms - values NOT comparable between methods. Random insulin is LEAST USEFUL of all insulin measurements due to lack of standardised timing relative to meals. Random insulin affected by: recent meal (variable timing), physical activity, stress, medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), obesity, pregnancy, circadian rhythm. Insulinoma: random insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL) - suspicious for insulinoma. Whipple triad required: hypoglycaemia + inappropriately elevated insulin + symptoms relieved by glucose. Exogenous insulin: random insulin may be elevated if on insulin therapy - C-peptide low (exogenous insulin suppresses endogenous insulin production). Assay cross-reactivity: some assays cross-react with proinsulin and insulin analogues. For hypoglycaemia workup: fasting insulin + fasting glucose more informative than random. For emergency hypoglycaemia: random insulin + random glucose + C-peptide + beta-hydroxybutyrate + cortisol.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required (random sample). Preparation: note recent meal timing (if known), diabetes medications (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas), recent illness, pregnancy status, physical activity. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Random sample: no fasting required. Note time since last meal if known. Hypoglycaemia workup: random insulin + random glucose + C-peptide + beta-hydroxybutyrate + cortisol. Insulinoma screening: random insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL) - confirm with fasting insulin + supervised 72h fast. Exogenous insulin: random insulin elevated + C-peptide low = exogenous insulin administration (Munchausen syndrome, factitious hypoglycaemia). Emergency hypoglycaemia: random insulin + glucose + C-peptide + beta-hydroxybutyrate + cortisol + medications screen. Proinsulin: random proinsulin alongside insulin for insulinoma workup. Post-prandial: if recent meal known, interpret as post-prandial insulin.
ref_ranges: Random insulin: 2-25 uIU/mL (method-specific) - fasting reference ranges used but interpretation limited without fasting status. Insulinoma: random insulin >3 uIU/mL with hypoglycaemia (<55 mg/dL) - suspicious for insulinoma. Hypoglycaemia: random insulin >3 uIU/mL with glucose <55 mg/dL - Whipple triad if symptoms relieved by glucose. Exogenous insulin: random insulin elevated + C-peptide low (<0.1 ng/mL) = exogenous insulin. Type 2 diabetes: random insulin may be elevated (insulin resistance). Type 1 diabetes: random insulin low/absent. Reference ranges: method-specific. Random insulin LEAST USEFUL without fasting status. Fasting insulin preferred for clinical decision-making. Ethnic variation: South Asians have higher random insulin at lower BMI than Caucasians.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; Endocrine Society Insulinoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN ANTIBODIES
interpretation: Serum Insulin Autoantibodies (IAA) measure autoantibodies against insulin. IAA are one of the islet autoantibodies used in the prediction and diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus. IAA are present in approximately 50% of new-onset type 1 diabetes patients. IAA are more common in children. IAA combined with other islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) increases predictive value. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note diabetes, family history, other autoimmune diseases. Handle per standard. Positive: type 1 diabetes risk. Combined: with other autoantibodies. Children: more common. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: type 1 diabetes risk (sensitivity 50%). Combined: increases predictive value. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN LIKE GROWTH FACTOR -1 (IGF-1)
interpretation: Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) - hormone structurally similar to insulin that mediates many effects of growth hormone (GH). Produced primarily by the liver under GH stimulation. IGF-1 reflects integrated GH secretion over 24h (unlike pulsatile GH). Elevated IGF-1: acromegaly (pituitary adenoma - IGF-1 elevated in >95% of acromegaly cases, more reliable than random GH), gigantism (pituitary adenoma in children - excessive GH before epiphyseal closure), ectopic GH/GHRH secretion (rare), pregnancy (placental production), obesity (mild elevation), hyperthyroidism, liver disease (reduced clearance). Low IGF-1: GH deficiency (congenital or acquired - pituitary surgery/radiation, tumour, trauma), hypopituitarism, malnutrition/starvation, chronic kidney disease, liver failure, hypothyroidism, aging (physiological decline), medications (oestrogen therapy reduces IGF-1, somatostatin analogues). Clinical use: acromegaly diagnosis (IGF-1 elevated + elevated GH after OGTT = acromegaly), GH deficiency screening (low IGF-1 suggests GH deficiency - confirm with GH stimulation testing), monitoring treatment of acromegaly (IGF-1 normalisation = biochemical control), monitoring GH replacement therapy (IGF-1 target mid-normal range). Limitations: IGF-1 is AGE-DEPENDENT (high in puberty, declines with age) - age-matched reference ranges essential. IGF-1 and GH: IGF-1 reflects integrated GH secretion but does NOT distinguish between physiological GH elevation (exercise, sleep) and pathological (acromegaly). IGF-1 assay variability: different immunoassay platforms give different results - method-specific reference ranges. IGF-1 and binding proteins: 99% of circulating IGF-1 bound to IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit (ALS) - free IGF-1 may be more physiologically relevant but not routinely measured. Pregnancy: IGF-1 elevated (placental production) - cannot interpret for acromegaly during pregnancy. Obesity: IGF-1 mildly elevated - do not diagnose acromegaly on IGF-1 alone in obese patients. Somatostatin analogue therapy: lowers IGF-1 (used in acromegaly treatment) - monitor IGF-1 levels.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note acromegaly symptoms (coarsened features, enlarged hands/feet, headache, sweating, sleep apnoea), GH deficiency risk factors (pituitary surgery/radiation, tumour, trauma), pregnancy status, thyroid function, liver/kidney function, medications (somatostatin analogues, GH replacement). Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Acromegaly screening: IGF-1 first (if elevated, confirm with GH suppression testing - OGTT GH failure to suppress <1 ug/L). GH deficiency: IGF-1 low (suggests GH deficiency) - confirm with GH stimulation testing (ITT, GHRH-arginine, glucagon). Monitoring acromegaly: serial IGF-1 levels (target: age-midnormal range). Monitoring GH replacement: IGF-1 target mid-normal range (avoid overshoot). IGF-1 and age: high in puberty, declines with age - use age-matched reference ranges. IGF-1 and pregnancy: elevated (placental) - cannot interpret for acromegaly. IGF-1 and thyroid: hypothyroidism lowers IGF-1 - correct thyroid function first.
ref_ranges: Adults: 100-300 ng/mL (method-specific, age/sex-dependent). Children: higher (50-500 ng/mL depending on age/puberty). Puberty: IGF-1 peaks at Tanner stage 4-5 (400-800 ng/mL). Acromegaly: IGF-1 elevated (>2x ULN highly suggestive). GH deficiency: IGF-1 low (<100 ng/mL). Age-related decline: IGF-1 decreases ~2-3% per decade after age 30. Reference ranges: method-specific and age/sex-specific. IGF-1 normal in some mild acromegaly cases. IGF-1 may be normal during pregnancy (placental production). Obesity: IGF-1 mildly elevated. Reference ranges essential: laboratory-specific, age-matched.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Acromegaly Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INSULIN LIKE GROWTH FACTOR BINDING PROTEIN (IGF BP)-3
interpretation: Serum Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3 (IGFBP-3) is the main carrier protein for IGF-1 in blood. IGFBP-3 modulates IGF-1 bioavailability and has IGF-independent growth effects. IGFBP-3 is used as a screening marker for growth hormone deficiency (GHD) and for evaluating IGF axis disorders. Low IGFBP-3: GHD, nutritional deficiency, liver disease. Elevated IGFBP-3: rarely pathological. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note growth failure, short stature, GH therapy. Handle per standard. Low: GHD, nutritional deficiency. Age-dependent: ranges. Combined: with IGF-1. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
ref_ranges: Normal: age-dependent. Low: GHD. Combined: with IGF-1. Age-dependent: ranges. Reference ranges: age-dependent.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society GHD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: INTERLEUKIN (IL) - 6
interpretation: Serum Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in the acute phase response, immune regulation, and haematopoiesis. IL-6 is elevated in: infections, autoimmune diseases (RA, Castleman disease), malignancies (multiple myeloma, lymphoma), and cytokine release syndrome. IL-6 is used as a biomarker for disease activity and treatment response. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy. Handle per standard. Elevated: infection, RA, myeloma. CRP: correlated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: infection, RA, myeloma. CRP: correlated. Treatment monitoring: serial levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR RA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IONIZED CALCIUM
interpretation: Ionised Calcium (iCa) - measurement of physiologically active free calcium in serum/plasma (approximately 50% of total calcium). Most accurate indicator of calcium homeostasis - not affected by albumin changes. Elevated ionised calcium: primary hyperparathyroidism (most common cause of hypercalcaemia in outpatients), malignancy (PTHrP-secreting tumours - most common cause of hypercalcaemia in inpatients; osteolytic metastases), familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH - autosomal dominant, CaSR mutation - benign), granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB - 1,25(OH)2D production by macrophages), vitamin D intoxication, lithium therapy, thiazide diuretics, immobilisation, milk-alkali syndrome, thyrotoxicosis. Low ionised calcium: hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical - most common cause; autoimmune; DiGeorge syndrome), vitamin D deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia), chronic kidney disease (reduced 1,25(OH)2D production), hypomagnesaemia (impairs PTH secretion/action), acute pancreatitis (saponification of fat), sepsis, massive transfusion (citrate chelates calcium), malabsorption (coeliac disease, bariatric surgery), hypoalbuminaemia (total calcium low but iCa normal - this is why iCa is superior). Clinical use: most accurate assessment of calcium status (superior to total calcium), emergency hypercalcaemia/hypocalcaemia evaluation, post-surgical hypoparathyroidism monitoring, critical care calcium management. Limitations: iCa is pH-dependent - alkalosis increases protein binding (reduces iCa even with normal total calcium); acidosis reduces protein binding (increases iCa). Blood gas analyser required for iCa - cannot be measured on standard chemistry analyser. iCa specimen handling: anaerobic collection required (exposure to air causes CO2 loss, pH rise, falsely low iCa). iCa not routinely measured - total calcium (corrected for albumin) more commonly used. FHH: iCa elevated but calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 - genetic testing confirms (CaSR mutation). Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism: iCa monitored intra-operatively and post-operatively for parathyroidectomy. Critical care: iCa more reliable than total calcium (acid-base changes affect protein binding).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or heparinised plasma (anaerobic collection required). Standard venipuncture or arterial/venous blood gas sample. CRITICAL: anaerobic collection - exposure to air causes CO2 loss, pH rise, falsely low iCa. Preparation: note parathyroid surgery history, malignancy, granulomatous disease, vitamin D status, magnesium level, medications (lithium, thiazides, bisphosphonates). Handling: anaerobic collection - do NOT expose to air. Process immediately or store anaerobically. iCa measured on blood gas analyser (not standard chemistry). pH effect: alkalosis lowers iCa (increased protein binding); acidosis raises iCa (decreased protein binding). Total calcium: measured on standard chemistry analyser - corrected for albumin (total Ca + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin g/dL)). iCa vs total Ca: iCa superior in hypoalbuminaemia, critical care, acid-base disturbances. Magnesium: hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion/action - check magnesium. FHH: CaSR genetic testing if suspected (iCa elevated, urine calcium low).
ref_ranges: Adults: 4.5-5.6 mg/dL (1.12-1.40 mmol/L) - method-specific. Neonates: 4.0-5.6 mg/dL (1.00-1.40 mmol/L). Hypercalcaemia: iCa >5.6 mg/dL (>1.40 mmol/L). Hypocalcaemia: iCa <4.5 mg/dL (<1.12 mmol/L). Critical care: iCa <4.0 mg/dL (<1.00 mmol/L) requires treatment (IV calcium). Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism: iCa maintained >4.0 mg/dL. FHH: iCa elevated, urine calcium low (<100 mg/day). Primary hyperparathyroidism: iCa elevated + PTH elevated. Malignancy: iCa elevated + PTH suppressed (<10 pg/mL). Reference ranges: method-specific. pH-dependent: always interpret alongside blood gas pH.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Calcium/PTH Guidelines; BTF Critical Care Calcium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: IRON
interpretation: Iron - measurement of serum iron concentration (total iron in serum, bound to transferrin). Component of iron studies panel (iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, ferritin). Clinical use: iron deficiency assessment (low serum iron), iron overload assessment (high serum iron), monitoring iron replacement therapy, haemochromatosis screening. Elevated serum iron: haemochromatosis (hereditary - HFE C282Y homozygosity most common), transfusional iron overload (thalassaemia major, myelodysplastic syndrome), iron pill ingestion, lead poisoning (inhibits iron utilisation), hepatitis, aplastic anaemia, sideroblastic anaemia, acute liver disease. Low serum iron: iron deficiency anaemia (most common cause), chronic disease (anaemia of chronic disease - iron sequestered in macrophages), chronic kidney disease, malabsorption, recent blood loss, pregnancy, lead poisoning (impairs iron use). Limitations: serum iron is HIGHLY VARIABLE (fluctuates 30% within a day - circadian variation peaks morning, nadir evening). Serum iron alone insufficient for iron status assessment - must interpret as part of iron studies panel (iron + TIBC + transferrin saturation + ferritin). Serum iron affected by: fasting status (fasting higher), time of day (morning higher), recent iron intake (meal raises iron), inflammation (lowers iron in chronic disease), oral contraceptives (raise iron-binding). Serum iron is NOT specific for iron deficiency - low in chronic disease, infection, malignancy (iron redistribution). Serum iron is NOT specific for iron overload - high in liver disease, haemolytic anaemia. Transferrin saturation (serum iron / TIBC x 100) more clinically useful than serum iron alone.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast recommended (post-prandial iron variably absorbed). Preparation: note recent iron supplementation, transfusion history, chronic disease, infections, inflammatory conditions, pregnancy, liver disease, menstrual status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Iron studies: serum iron + TIBC + transferrin saturation + ferritin. Transferrin saturation = (serum iron / TIBC) x 100. Haemochromatosis screening: transferrin saturation >45% (fasting) - confirm with HFE genotyping. Iron deficiency: serum iron low + TIBC elevated + transferrin saturation low + ferritin low. Anaemia of chronic disease: serum iron low + TIBC low/normal + ferritin elevated. Chronic disease: iron redistribution to macrophages - serum iron low despite adequate stores. Serum iron variability: 30% circadian variation - draw fasting morning sample for consistency. Recent iron intake: meal raises serum iron - fast 8-12h for accurate result.
ref_ranges: Men: 65-175 ug/dL (12-31 umol/L). Women: 50-170 ug/dL (9-30 umol/L). Iron deficiency: serum iron <50 ug/dL (<9 umol/L). Haemochromatosis: serum iron >170 ug/dL (>30 umol/L) with transferrin saturation >45%. Anaemia of chronic disease: serum iron low with elevated ferritin. Transferrin saturation: 20-50% (20-45% in women, 20-55% in men). Transferrin saturation >45%: suggestive of haemochromatosis (confirm with HFE testing). Transferrin saturation <16%: iron deficiency likely. Reference ranges: method-specific. Circadian variation: serum iron varies 30% within a day. Fasting: serum iron 20-30% higher fasting than post-prandial. Age: serum iron stable across age groups. Pregnancy: serum iron may be low in third trimester (physiological iron deficiency).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD Iron Overload Guidelines; BCSH Iron Deficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ISLET CELL ANTIBODY (ICA-512)
interpretation: Serum Islet Cell Antibody (ICA-512/IA-2A) measures autoantibodies against islet antigen-2 (IA-2), a tyrosine phosphatase-like protein on pancreatic beta cells. ICA-512/IA-2A are highly specific markers for type 1 diabetes mellitus. ICA-512/IA-2A are present in approximately 60-75% of new-onset type 1 diabetes. ICA-512/IA-2A combined with other islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IAA, ZnT8) increases predictive value. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note diabetes, family history, other autoimmune diseases. Handle per standard. Positive: type 1 diabetes risk (high specificity). Combined: with GAD65, IAA, ZnT8. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: type 1 diabetes risk (60-75% sensitivity, high specificity). Combined: increases predictive value. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ISOLEUCINE (QUANTITATIVE)
interpretation: Plasma Isoleucine Quantitative measures the concentration of isoleucine, an essential branched-chain amino acid (BCAA). Isoleucine is elevated in maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), an autosomal recessive disorder of BCAA metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency). MSUD: sweet maple syrup odour in urine, encephalopathy, seizures, death if untreated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note neonatal screening, encephalopathy, metabolic history. Handle per standard. Elevated: MSUD. Sweet odour: urine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: MSUD (BCAA metabolism defect). Sweet odour: urine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG MSUD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: KAPPA LAMBDA FREE LIGHT CHAIN
interpretation: Serum Free Light Chains (Kappa and Lambda) - measurement of unbound immunoglobulin light chains (kappa and lambda) in serum. Used to assess plasma cell disorders (monoclonal gammopathies). Free light chains are produced by plasma cells and normally bound to heavy chains to form intact immunoglobulins. Excess free light chains are produced in clonal plasma cell disorders. Elevated kappa free light chains: multiple myeloma (kappa-restricted plasma cell clone), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS - kappa monoclonal), light chain myeloma (no intact immunoglobulin - only free light chains), AL amyloidosis (kappa or lambda free light chains with amyloid deposits), Castleman disease, chronic kidney disease (reduced renal clearance - kappa elevated > lambda). Elevated lambda free light chains: multiple myeloma (lambda-restricted plasma cell clone), MGUS (lambda monoclonal), AL amyloidosis, Castleman disease, chronic kidney disease. Abnormal kappa/lambda ratio: >1.65 or <0.26 = abnormal ratio suggesting monoclonal light chain restriction. Clinical use: light chain myeloma diagnosis (serum free light chains elevated with abnormal kappa/lambda ratio), MGUS monitoring (serial free light chains for clonal progression), AL amyloidosis diagnosis (elevated free light chains + amyloid deposits on tissue biopsy), multiple myeloma staging (International Staging System includes free light chains), monitoring treatment response (free light chains decline with effective therapy). Limitations: free light chains elevated in chronic kidney disease (reduced renal clearance) - must interpret alongside eGFR. Kappa/lambda ratio more useful than absolute values (ratio corrects for renal function in mild-moderate CKD). Free light chains have short half-life (~2-6 hours) - useful for monitoring treatment response but fluctuate. Free light chains are non-specific for haematological disease - elevated in many non-haematological conditions (autoimmune disease, chronic infection, liver disease, obesity). Assay variability: different immunoassay platforms (Freelite, N Latex FLC) give different results - method-specific reference ranges. Free light chains do NOT replace SPEP/IFE for monoclonal gammopathy workup - they complement SPEP/IFE. Normal free light chains do NOT exclude MGUS or early myeloma - SPEP/IFE still required.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note myeloma symptoms (bone pain, fatigue, renal failure, anaemia), monoclonal gammopathy history, renal function, family history of myeloma/MGUS. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Myeloma workup: SPEP + IFE + serum free light chains + serum immunoglobulins + calcium + renal function. Light chain myeloma: serum free light chains elevated with abnormal kappa/lambda ratio, SPEP/IFE may be negative (no intact immunoglobulin). AL amyloidosis: serum free light chains elevated + tissue biopsy showing amyloid deposits + mass spectrometry for amyloid typing. MGUS monitoring: serial free light chains every 6-12 months (kappa/lambda ratio trend). Treatment monitoring: serial free light chains (free light chain response criteria). Renal function: interpret alongside eGFR (free light chains elevated in CKD). CKD: kappa/lambda ratio corrects for renal function in mild-moderate CKD (ratio remains <1.65 in polyclonal elevation).
ref_ranges: Kappa free light chains: 3.3-19.4 mg/L (method-specific). Lambda free light chains: 5.7-26.3 mg/L (method-specific). Kappa/lambda ratio: 0.26-1.65 (normal). Abnormal ratio: >1.65 = kappa restriction (myeloma, kappa MGUS, kappa AL amyloidosis). Abnormal ratio: <0.26 = lambda restriction (myeloma, lambda MGUS, lambda AL amyloidosis). Light chain myeloma: free light chains elevated with abnormal ratio. MGUS: free light chains may be normal or mildly elevated. AL amyloidosis: free light chains elevated with abnormal ratio. CKD: free light chains elevated (polyclonal) - kappa/lambda ratio may be abnormal if CKD severe (eGFR <30). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: free light chains increase with age. Reference ranges essential: laboratory-specific, method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IMWG Myeloma Consensus Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: KETONE BODY - BETAHYDROXYBUTYRATE
interpretation: Serum Beta-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is the predominant ketone body in blood and is used to monitor diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). BHB is a more accurate marker of ketosis than urine ketones (acetoacetate). BHB greater than 0.6 mmol/L: ketosis. BHB greater than 3 mmol/L: DKA likely. BHB less than 0.6 mmol/L: resolution of DKA. BHB monitoring guides treatment and confirms resolution of DKA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note diabetes, DKA symptoms, vomiting. Handle per standard. BHB greater than 3 mmol/L: DKA. More accurate: than urine ketones. Resolution: less than 0.6 mmol/L. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.6 mmol/L. Ketosis: greater than 0.6 mmol/L. DKA: greater than 3 mmol/L. Resolution: less than 0.6 mmol/L. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ADA DKA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LACTATE (LACTIC ACID)
interpretation: Lactate (Lactic Acid) - measurement of serum/plasma lactate concentration. Lactate is the end product of anaerobic glycolysis, produced when oxygen supply is insufficient for aerobic metabolism. Elevated lactate (hyperlactataemia): sepsis (most common cause in critical care - tissue hypoperfusion), shock (cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, septic), severe hypoxia (respiratory failure, pulmonary embolism), massive PE, severe heart failure, liver failure (lactate clearance impaired), metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA - metformin + renal impairment + hypoxia), severe exercise (physiological), seizures, thiamine deficiency (impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase), propofol infusion syndrome, large bowel ischaemia (mesenteric ischaemia), carbon monoxide poisoning, drugs (metformin, linezolid, propofol, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors). Lactic acidosis: lactate >4.0 mmol/L with metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35). Type A: tissue hypoxia (shock, sepsis, hypoxia). Type B: metabolic (metformin, liver failure, thiamine deficiency, malignancy). Clinical use: sepsis marker (lactate >2.0 mmol/L = sepsis; >4.0 mmol/L = severe sepsis/septic shock), shock assessment (lactate clearance monitoring), tissue perfusion assessment, prognostic marker (high lactate = poor prognosis in critical care), mesenteric ischaemia screening, metformin toxicity monitoring. Limitations: lactate affected by: tourniquet use (stagnant blood raises lactate), delayed sample processing (glycolysis continues - falsely elevated), fist clenching (exercise raises lactate), venous stasis, haemolysis (RBC glycolysis raises lactate). Lactate clearance: serial lactate measurements (declining lactate = improving perfusion; rising lactate = worsening). Lactate >2.0 mmol/L in sepsis: associated with increased mortality - requires aggressive fluid resuscitation and source control. Lactate >4.0 mmol/L: severe sepsis/septic shock - high mortality risk. Lactate may be normal in early sepsis - repeat if clinical suspicion high. Lactate elevated in non-critical conditions (exercise, anxiety, venipuncture artefact) - interpret clinically. Arterial vs venous lactate: arterial more accurate for tissue perfusion assessment; venous acceptable for screening (venous lactate ~0.5 mmol/L higher than arterial).
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (heparin) preferred. Serum also acceptable. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: process within 15 minutes (glycolysis continues in separated blood - falsely elevated). Preparation: note sepsis symptoms, shock, metformin use, liver disease, thiamine status, recent exercise, seizure history. Handling: CRITICAL - process within 15 minutes of collection. Centrifuge immediately. Do NOT leave whole blood at room temperature (glycolysis continues - falsely elevated). Arterial blood gas (ABG) lactate: most accurate for tissue perfusion assessment. Venous lactate: acceptable for screening (venous ~0.5 mmol/L higher than arterial). Tourniquet: minimal tourniquet time (<60 seconds) to avoid stagnant blood artefact. Sepsis protocol: lactate + blood cultures + procalcitonin + CRP. Lactate clearance: serial lactates (e.g., 0h, 2h, 6h) - declining = improving perfusion. Metformin toxicity: lactate + renal function + clinical assessment. Mesenteric ischaemia: lactate elevated + abdominal pain + metabolic acidosis. Thiamine: if thiamine deficiency suspected, give thiamine before glucose (to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy).
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.5-1.6 mmol/L (method-specific). Lactate >2.0 mmol/L: elevated - associated with sepsis, tissue hypoperfusion. Lactate >4.0 mmol/L: severe - lactic acidosis (Type A: tissue hypoxia; Type B: metabolic). Sepsis: lactate >2.0 mmol/L = sepsis; >4.0 mmol/L = severe sepsis/septic shock. Shock: lactate >4.0 mmol/L = poor prognosis. Metformin lactic acidosis: lactate >5.0 mmol/L with metabolic acidosis + renal impairment + metformin use. Mesenteric ischaemia: lactate elevated (>4.0 mmol/L). Exercise: lactate may rise to 10-20 mmol/L (physiological). Reference ranges: method-specific. Arterial vs venous: venous ~0.5 mmol/L higher. Age: lactate increases with age. Pregnancy: lactate mildly elevated.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LACTATE - CSF
interpretation: Lactate - CSF - measurement of lactate concentration in cerebrospinal fluid. Elevated CSF lactate: bacterial meningitis (most important finding - CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L strongly suggests bacterial meningitis; >4.2 mmol/L virtually diagnostic), tuberculous meningitis (CSF lactate elevated), cerebral abscess, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (elevated CSF lactate reflects brain tissue hypoxia), mitochondrial encephalopathies (MELAS - mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes), subarachnoid haemorrhage (blood in CSF causes elevated lactate), status epilepticus (seizure activity increases CSF lactate), cerebral malaria, CNS lymphoma. Normal CSF lactate: <3.5 mmol/L. Low CSF lactate: not clinically significant. Clinical use: differentiating bacterial from viral meningitis (CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L suggests bacterial; <3.5 suggests viral), monitoring bacterial meningitis treatment (CSF lactate declining = responding to treatment), diagnosing mitochondrial encephalopathies (CSF lactate elevated, serum lactate normal), evaluating hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury. Limitations: CSF lactate elevated in BOTH bacterial AND tuberculous meningitis - cannot distinguish between them. CSF lactate may be mildly elevated in partially treated bacterial meningitis (antibiotics started before LP). CSF lactate elevated in subarachnoid haemorrhage (blood in CSF) - not necessarily meningitis. CSF lactate normal does NOT exclude bacterial meningitis (early presentation, partially treated). CSF lactate must be interpreted alongside other CSF parameters (glucose, protein, cell count, Gram stain, culture). CSF lactate sampling: anaerobic collection required (exposure to air causes CO2 loss, falsely low lactate). Paired CSF and serum lactate: for mitochondrial encephalopathies (CSF lactate elevated, serum lactate normal). CSF lactate not routinely measured - only in specific clinical scenarios (meningitis evaluation, mitochondrial disease).
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) via lumbar puncture. Anaerobic collection required. CRITICAL: anaerobic collection - exposure to air causes CO2 loss, falsely low lactate. Preparation: note antibiotic use (partial treatment may affect results), seizure history, recent neurological events, mitochondrial disease history. Handling: process immediately - anaerobic collection, do NOT expose to air. CSF lactate measured on blood gas analyser or enzymatic method. Paired CSF and serum lactate: for mitochondrial encephalopathies (CSF lactate elevated, serum lactate normal). Bacterial meningitis: CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L + CSF glucose <40 mg/dL + CSF protein >100 mg/dL + CSF WBC >1000/uL (neutrophil predominant) + Gram stain positive. Viral meningitis: CSF lactate <3.5 mmol/L + CSF glucose normal + CSF protein mildly elevated + CSF WBC 10-500/uL (lymphocyte predominant). TB meningitis: CSF lactate elevated + CSF glucose very low + CSF protein very elevated + CSF lymphocyte predominant. Mitochondrial: CSF lactate elevated + serum lactate normal + clinical features (stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis). Subarachnoid: CSF lactate elevated + xanthochromia + RBCs in CSF.
ref_ranges: Normal CSF lactate: <3.5 mmol/L (<31.5 mg/dL). Bacterial meningitis: CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L (>31.5 mg/dL). Tuberculous meningitis: CSF lactate >4.2 mmol/L (>37.8 mg/dL). Cerebral abscess: CSF lactate elevated. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy: CSF lactate markedly elevated. Mitochondrial encephalopathies: CSF lactate elevated (>4.0 mmol/L) with normal serum lactate. Subarachnoid haemorrhage: CSF lactate elevated (blood contamination). Status epilepticus: CSF lactate mildly elevated. Paired CSF/serum lactate ratio: >1.0 suggests CNS lactate production (mitochondrial disease). Reference ranges: method-specific. Anaerobic collection: essential for accurate results.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IDSA Bacterial Meningitis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LACTATE DEHYROGENASE (LDH)
interpretation: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) - cytoplasmic enzyme found in virtually all tissues; catalyses interconversion of pyruvate and lactate. Non-specific marker of tissue damage/injury. Elevated LDH: myocardial infarction (LDH-1 elevated - historically used but now superseded by troponin), haemolytic anaemia (LDH elevated - released from lysed RBCs), liver disease (LDH elevated in hepatitis, cirrhosis), malignancy (LDH elevated in lymphoma, leukaemia - tumour marker), pulmonary embolism (LDH elevated), pneumonia, pancreatitis, skeletal muscle injury, renal disease, megaloblastic anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis), meningitis (CSF LDH elevated), HIV/AIDS (LDH elevated). LDH isoenzymes: LDH-1 (heart, RBCs), LDH-2 (RBCs, serum), LDH-3 (lung, brain), LDH-4 (kidney, pancreas), LDH-5 (liver, skeletal muscle). Elevated LDH-1/LDH-2 ratio (>1.0) = myocardial infarction (historically). LDH-5 elevated = liver disease. Clinical use: tissue damage marker (non-specific), haemolysis marker (LDH elevated with low haptoglobin), lymphoma/tumour marker (LDH elevated = high tumour burden), prognosis marker (LDH elevated in many cancers = poor prognosis), CSF LDH (bacterial meningitis elevated). Limitations: LDH is HIGHLY NON-SPECIFIC - elevated in many conditions. LDH alone has limited clinical utility - must interpret in clinical context. LDH isoenzyme pattern more useful than total LDH (LDH-1 for heart/RBC, LDH-5 for liver/muscle). LDH affected by: haemolysis (even in vitro - falsely elevated), vigorous exercise (skeletal muscle LDH released), sample handling (LDH unstable at room temperature - process promptly). LDH and haptoglobin: combined for haemolysis workup (LDH elevated + haptoglobin low = intravascular haemolysis). LDH and tumour marker: elevated LDH in lymphoma = high tumour burden, poor prognosis (International Prognostic Index). LDH and CSF: CSF LDH elevated in bacterial meningitis (>2x serum LDH normal). Assay variability: different methods (UV kinetic vs colourimetric) give different results - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. LDH declining: suggests resolution of tissue damage (monitoring marker).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note recent strenuous exercise (raises LDH), haemolysis risk factors, liver disease, malignancy, cardiac symptoms. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. LDH unstable at room temperature - process promptly. Haemolysis: even mild haemolysis falsely elevates LDH - check for haemolysis visually. LDH isoenzymes: LDH-1 (heart/RBC), LDH-5 (liver/muscle). LDH-1/LDH-2 ratio: >1.0 historically suggested MI (superseded by troponin). Haemolysis workup: LDH + haptoglobin + reticulocyte count + bilirubin + DAT. Lymphoma: LDH elevated = high tumour burden = poor prognosis (IPI score). CSF LDH: elevated in bacterial meningitis (>2x serum LDH normal). Liver: LDH-5 elevated. Heart: LDH-1 elevated. Exercise: LDH elevated - avoid pre-analytical exercise artefact.
ref_ranges: Adults: 140-280 U/L (method-specific). Neonates: higher (200-600 U/L). Children: higher than adults. Haemolytic anaemia: LDH elevated (>400 U/L). Liver disease: LDH elevated (>300 U/L). Myocardial infarction: LDH-1 elevated, LDH-1/LDH-2 ratio >1.0 (historical). Lymphoma: LDH elevated (>300 U/L) = high tumour burden. Malignancy: LDH elevated in many cancers. Exercise: LDH transiently elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Haemolysis: even in vitro haemolysis falsely elevates LDH. Ethnic variation: minimal. Age: LDH higher in children and neonates.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IFCC LDH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LAMOTRIGINE LEVELS - PLASMA
interpretation: Serum Lamotrigine measures the concentration of lamotrigine, an anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser. Lamotrigine is used to treat epilepsy (focal and generalised seizures) and bipolar disorder. Therapeutic range: 2.5 to 15 mcg/mL. Toxicity: serious rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis), particularly if dose escalation is too rapid. Active metabolite: 2,3-diaminoxlamotrigine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, rash history, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 2.5-15 mcg/mL. Rash risk: SJS, TEN. Dose escalation: slow. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 2.5 to 15 mcg/mL. Toxicity: SJS, TEN (dose-dependent). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LDH - FLUID
interpretation: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) - Fluid - measurement of LDH in body fluids (pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, CSF, synovial fluid, pericardial fluid). LDH in body fluids reflects local tissue damage/inflammation. Clinical use: Light's criteria for pleural effusion (pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio >0.6 = exudate; <0.6 = transudate), peritonitis diagnosis (peritoneal fluid LDH elevated), meningitis evaluation (CSF LDH elevated in bacterial meningitis), synovial fluid analysis (LDH elevated in inflammatory arthritis), pericardial effusion characterisation. Light's criteria (pleural effusion): exudate = pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5 OR pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6 OR pleural fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of serum LDH. Limitations: LDH in body fluids is NON-SPECIFIC - elevated in many conditions (infection, malignancy, inflammation, trauma). Light's criteria: pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio >0.6 = exudate (infection, malignancy, PE, RA); <0.6 = transudate (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). Light's criteria false positives: diuretic use (concentrates pleural fluid), thoracentesis on day 2+ (LDH rises over time). CSF LDH: elevated in bacterial meningitis (>2x serum LDH normal). Peritoneal fluid LDH: elevated in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) - >250 U/L suggestive. Synovial fluid LDH: elevated in inflammatory arthritis (RA, gout). Paired fluid and serum LDH: ratio interpretation required (absolute values less useful than ratios). Assay variability: different methods give different results. Pre-analytical: process promptly - LDH unstable at room temperature.
pre_analytical: Sample: Body fluid (pleural, peritoneal, CSF, synovial, pericardial). Standard collection for each fluid type. Paired serum sample required for Light's criteria ratio. Preparation: note fluid type, clinical context (infection, malignancy, heart failure, cirrhosis). Handling: process promptly - LDH unstable at room temperature. Paired serum: essential for Light's criteria calculation. Light's criteria: pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio. Exudate: ratio >0.6. Transudate: ratio <0.6. Peritoneal fluid: LDH >250 U/L suggestive of SBP. CSF: LDH elevated in bacterial meningitis (>2x serum LDH). Synovial fluid: LDH elevated in inflammatory arthritis. Pericardial fluid: LDH elevated in malignant or inflammatory pericardial effusion. Paired fluid/serum: always measure alongside serum LDH for ratio interpretation.
ref_ranges: Light's criteria (pleural effusion): exudate = pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6 OR pleural fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of serum LDH. Transudate: pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH <0.6. Peritoneal fluid: LDH >250 U/L suggestive of SBP. CSF: bacterial meningitis CSF LDH elevated (>2x serum LDH). Synovial fluid: inflammatory arthritis LDH elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Paired fluid/serum ratio essential for interpretation. Absolute values less useful than ratios.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LDH ISOENZYMES
interpretation: Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) Isoenzymes separate and identify the tissue sources of LDH in serum. LDH exists as five isoenzymes: LDH-1 (heart, RBCs), LDH-2 (RBCs, reticuloendothelial), LDH-3 (lungs, lymphocytes), LDH-4 (liver, skeletal muscle), LDH-5 (liver, skeletal muscle). Elevated LDH-1: myocardial infarction, haemolysis. Elevated LDH-5: liver disease, skeletal muscle injury. LDH-1/LDH-2 ratio greater than 1: MI. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain, liver disease, haemolysis. Handle per standard. LDH-1: heart, RBCs. LDH-5: liver, muscle. Ratio: MI. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by isoenzyme. LDH-1/LDH-2 greater than 1: MI. LDH-5: liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA MI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LEAD - PLASMA
interpretation: Whole Blood Lead measures lead concentration in blood. Lead is a toxic heavy metal with no physiological function. Blood lead levels (BLL) are used to assess lead exposure and guide treatment. BLL less than 5 mcg/dL: normal. BLL 5-9 mcg/dL: low-level exposure. BLL 10-19 mcg/dL: moderate. BLL 20-44 mcg/dL: high. BLL greater than 45 mcg/dL: severe (chelation required). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). CRITICAL: lead-free collection. Preparation: note occupational exposure, home environment, symptoms. Handle: lead-free. Blood: recent exposure. Children: more susceptible. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 5 mcg/dL. Low-level: 5-9 mcg/dL. Moderate: 10-19 mcg/dL. High: 20-44 mcg/dL. Severe: greater than 45 mcg/dL. Chelation: greater than 45. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: CDC Lead Guidelines; ATSDR Lead Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: LEPTIN
interpretation: Leptin, the peptide hormone secreted primarily by adipocytes, serves as a key regulator of energy homeostasis and appetite suppression through its action on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus. It is primarily used in the evaluation of congenital leptin deficiency (a rare monogenic cause of severe early-onset obesity) and in the differential diagnosis of lipodystrophy syndromes (generalised and partial lipodystrophies). Leptin levels are directly proportional to fat mass and are elevated in common obesity, reflecting leptin resistance rather than deficiency. Assessment of leptin is also valuable in the evaluation of hypothalamic amenorrhea, where low leptin contributes to impaired gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion, and in the investigation of suspected leptin receptor mutations. Key limitations: the strong correlation of leptin with BMI limits diagnostic utility in common obesity; there is significant inter-assay variability; and proper interpretation requires consideration of age, sex, pubertal stage, and fasting status.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (preferred) or EDTA plasma. Collection: Morning fasting sample (08:00–10:00) after overnight fast is essential, as leptin exhibits diurnal variation with a nocturnal peak. Patient preparation: Prolonged fasting (24–72 hours) suppresses leptin, while acute overfeeding increases levels. Exercise, acute illness, and inflammation also affect circulating leptin. Avoid haemolysis. Separate serum/plasma within 2 hours. Storage: Stable 7 days at 2–8°C; longer storage at -20°C. Freeze-thaw cycles should be minimised.
ref_ranges: Reference intervals are sex- and BMI-dependent: Males 1.2–9.5 ng/mL; Females 4.1–25.5 ng/mL (assays vary). In obesity (BMI >30), leptin levels typically exceed 10–15 ng/mL and may exceed 50 ng/mL. Levels below 1.0 ng/mL in severely obese patients suggest possible congenital leptin deficiency or lipodystrophy. Reference intervals should be established by each laboratory for their specific population and assay method.
refs: Content synthesized from standard clinical biochemistry and laboratory medicine references.

name: LEUCINE QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Plasma Leucine Quantitative measures the concentration of leucine, an essential branched-chain amino acid (BCAA). Leucine is elevated in maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), an autosomal recessive disorder of BCAA metabolism. MSUD: sweet maple syrup odour in urine, encephalopathy, seizures, death if untreated. Leucine is the most toxic BCAA in MSUD. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note neonatal screening, encephalopathy, metabolic history. Handle per standard. Elevated: MSUD. Most toxic: BCAA. Sweet odour: urine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: MSUD. Leucine: most toxic BCAA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG MSUD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LEVETIRACETAM
interpretation: Serum Levetiracetam measures the concentration of levetiracetam (Keppra), a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant. Levetiracetam is used to treat focal and generalised seizures, and status epilepticus. Therapeutic range: 12 to 46 mcg/mL. Not protein-bound: no drug interactions with protein-bound drugs. Renal elimination: dose adjust in renal impairment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, renal function, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 12-46 mcg/mL. Not protein-bound: fewer interactions. Renal: dose adjust. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 12 to 46 mcg/mL. Not protein-bound: fewer interactions. Renal: dose adjust. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIPASE
interpretation: Lipase - pancreatic enzyme (triacylglycerol acylhydrolase) that hydrolyses triglycerides to free fatty acids and glycerol. More specific marker for acute pancreatitis than amylase. Elevated lipase: acute pancreatitis (most important clinical finding - lipase >3x ULN highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis; more specific than amylase), chronic pancreatitis (lipase may be normal or mildly elevated in chronic pancreatitis - exocrine insufficiency), pancreatic duct obstruction (gallstone pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer), endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) (post-procedural pancreatitis), hypertriglyceridaemia (very high triglycerides >1000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis and elevated lipase), renal failure (reduced clearance), salivary gland disease (mumps, sialadenitis), alcohol abuse, perforated peptic ulcer, bowel obstruction, diabetic ketoacidosis. Clinical use: acute pancreatitis diagnosis (lipase >3x ULN is diagnostic; more specific than amylase), monitoring acute pancreatitis (lipase peaks at 24h, normalises in 8-14 days; more prolonged than amylase), distinguishing pancreatic from non-pancreatic abdominal pain. Limitations: lipase is MORE SPECIFIC for pancreatitis than amylase but still elevated in non-pancreatic conditions. Lipase >3x ULN is diagnostic of acute pancreatitis - no imaging required for diagnosis in most cases. Lipase does NOT distinguish between aetiology (alcoholic vs gallstone vs idiopathic). Lipase normal does NOT exclude pancreatitis (early presentation <12h, very early sampling). Lipase elevated in renal failure (reduced clearance) - must interpret alongside renal function. Hypertriglyceridaemia: lipase may be falsely low if triglycerides >1000 mg/dL (interference with assay). Lipase and amylase: lipase preferred for acute pancreatitis (more specific, longer elevation). Lipase and chronic pancreatitis: lipase may be normal - exocrine insufficiency assessed by faecal elastase. Assay variability: different methods (immunoturbidimetric vs immunoseparation vs enzymatic) give different results - use laboratory-specific reference ranges.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note abdominal pain, alcohol use, gallstone history, recent ERCP, triglyceride level, renal function. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Acute pancreatitis: lipase >3x ULN (most specific marker). Amylase: lipase more specific than amylase for pancreatitis. Lipase peaks at 24h, normalises in 8-14 days. Amylase peaks at 12h, normalises in 3-5 days. Lipase elevated longer than amylase. Chronic pancreatitis: lipase may be normal - use faecal elastase for exocrine insufficiency. Gallstone pancreatitis: lipase elevated + LFTs elevated (obstructive pattern). Alcoholic pancreatitis: lipase elevated + GGT/AST elevated. Hypertriglyceridaemia: lipase may be falsely low if TG >1000 mg/dL. Renal failure: lipase elevated (reduced clearance) - interpret alongside eGFR. Monitoring: serial lipase for acute pancreatitis (declining = resolving).
ref_ranges: Normal: 0-160 U/L (method-specific). Acute pancreatitis: lipase >3x ULN (>480 U/L if ULN = 160 U/L). Mild pancreatitis: lipase 3-10x ULN. Severe pancreatitis: lipase >10x ULN. Chronic pancreatitis: lipase may be normal or mildly elevated (1-3x ULN). Renal failure: lipase elevated (reduced clearance). Hypertriglyceridaemia: lipase may be falsely low if TG >1000 mg/dL. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: lipase stable across age groups. Sex: lipase stable across sexes. Pregnancy: lipase stable.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AGA Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines; ACG Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIPID PROFILE
interpretation: Lipid Profile - comprehensive panel measuring serum lipids for cardiovascular risk assessment. Includes: total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C), LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C, calculated by Friedewald formula), and non-HDL-cholesterol. Clinical use: cardiovascular risk assessment (primary prevention - lifestyle modification and statin therapy decisions), monitoring lipid-lowering therapy (statin response, target achievement), familial hypercholesterolaemia screening, metabolic syndrome assessment (elevated TG + low HDL-C + elevated LDL-C), pancreatitis risk (very high TG >500 mg/dL). Elevated LDL-C: primary hypercholesterolaemia (familial hypercholesterolaemia - FH), diet high in saturated fat, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, medications (thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors). Low HDL-C: metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity, medications (beta-blockers, thiazides, anabolic steroids). Elevated TG: type 2 diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, alcohol excess, medications (oestrogen therapy, retinoids, protease inhibitors, thiazides), familial hypertriglyceridaemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, liver disease. Limitations: fasting required (8-12h) for accurate TG and LDL-C calculation (Friedewald formula). Friedewald formula unreliable if TG >400 mg/dL (LDL-C cannot be calculated). Non-fasting lipid profile acceptable for CV risk assessment (LDL-C less accurate but TG and HDL-C reliable). LDL-C calculation: LDL-C = TC - HDL-C - (TG/5) [Friedewald, in mg/dL]. Direct LDL-C measurement: available but not routinely used. Lipid profile affected by: acute illness (lower TC, TG, HDL-C - defer testing 6 weeks after acute event), recent lipid-lowering therapy (statin effect), pregnancy (TG elevated, TC elevated), menopause (TC rises), seasonal variation (TC higher in winter), exercise (raises HDL-C, lowers TG). Lipid profile and ASCVD risk calculator: 10-year ASCVD risk determines statin intensity (moderate vs high intensity). Familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDL-C >190 mg/dL (untreated) = FH until proven otherwise. Metabolic syndrome: elevated TG (>150 mg/dL) + low HDL-C (<40 men, <50 women) + abdominal obesity + hypertension + elevated fasting glucose.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 8-12h overnight fast required (for accurate TG and LDL-C calculation). Preparation: ensure 8-12h overnight fast. No caloric intake. Water permitted. Note lipid-lowering therapy (statins, fibrates, ezetimibe), acute illness (defer testing 6 weeks), recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, alcohol use, smoking, family history of cardiovascular disease. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting: 8-12h overnight fast required. Non-fasting: acceptable for CV risk assessment (LDL-C less accurate but TG and HDL-C reliable). Friedewald: LDL-C = TC - HDL-C - (TG/5) [mg/dL]. TG/500 [mmol/L]. Friedewald unreliable if TG >400 mg/dL. ASCVD risk: 10-year ASCVD risk calculator for statin therapy decisions. FH screening: LDL-C >190 mg/dL (untreated) = FH until proven otherwise. Monitoring: serial lipid profiles for therapy response (6-12 weeks after initiation). Acute illness: defer testing 6 weeks after acute event (lipids lower during illness). Lipid-lowering therapy: note all current medications (statin, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor, fibrates, niacin).
ref_ranges: Total cholesterol: <200 mg/dL desirable; 200-239 borderline high; >=240 high. Triglycerides: <150 mg/dL normal; 150-199 borderline high; 200-499 high; >=500 very high (pancreatitis risk). HDL-C: >=60 mg/dL optimal (cardioprotective); 40-59 acceptable; <40 low (cardiovascular risk). LDL-C: <100 mg/dL optimal; 100-129 near optimal; 130-159 borderline high; 160-189 high; >=190 very high (FH). Non-HDL-C: <130 mg/dL desirable (TC - HDL-C). ASCVD risk: 10-year risk determines statin intensity. FH: LDL-C >190 mg/dL (untreated). Metabolic syndrome: TG >150 + HDL-C <40 (M) / <50 (F). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: TC and LDL-C rise with age until menopause. Sex: men lower HDL-C than women. Ethnic variation: HDL-C higher in African Americans.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ACC/AHA Cholesterol Guidelines; ESC/EAS Dyslipidaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIPID PROFILE NON FASTING
interpretation: Lipid Profile Non Fasting - lipid panel measured without an overnight fast. Acceptable for cardiovascular risk assessment in many guidelines (ESC/EAS recommend non-fasting for population screening). Non-fasting profile includes: total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol (reliable non-fasting), triglycerides (elevated post-prandially but still useful), non-HDL-cholesterol (TC minus HDL-C - calculated without fasting). LDL-C by Friedewald formula unreliable non-fasting (TG falsely elevated by meals). Clinical use: population cardiovascular risk screening, opportunistic lipid measurement (GP visits), monitoring therapy (non-fasting acceptable for HDL-C and non-HDL-C trends). Limitations: LDL-C by Friedewald formula UNRELIABLE non-fasting (TG elevated post-prandially - LDL-C falsely low). Use non-HDL-C instead of LDL-C for non-fasting lipid assessment (non-HDL-C = TC - HDL-C, does NOT require fasting). Non-fasting TG: elevated post-prandially (20-40% higher than fasting) - still useful for cardiovascular risk assessment (non-fasting TG associated with CVD in prospective studies). Non-fasting HDL-C: reliable (does not change significantly post-prandially). Non-fasting TC: reliable (minimal post-prandial change). Non-fasting lipid profile: ESC/EAS guidelines recommend non-fasting for population screening. ACC/AHA guidelines: fasting preferred but non-fasting acceptable. If fasting required: defer to fasting lipid profile. Non-fasting and triglycerides: elevated post-prandially but still predictive of cardiovascular events.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note lipid-lowering therapy, recent meal (non-fasting), acute illness (defer 6 weeks), pregnancy status, alcohol use, smoking. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Non-fasting: no fasting required. Use non-HDL-C instead of LDL-C (Friedewald unreliable non-fasting). Non-HDL-C = TC - HDL-C (does not require fasting). Non-fasting TG: elevated post-prandially but still useful for CV risk. If LDL-C needed: request fasting lipid profile. Monitoring: non-fasting acceptable for HDL-C and non-HDL-C trends. Population screening: ESC/EAS recommends non-fasting lipid profile. If fasting required: defer to fasting lipid profile.
ref_ranges: Total cholesterol: <200 mg/dL desirable; 200-239 borderline; >=240 high. HDL-C: >=60 optimal; 40-59 acceptable; <40 low. Triglycerides: may be elevated 20-40% post-prandially. Non-HDL-C: <130 mg/dL desirable. LDL-C: unreliable non-fasting (Friedewald). Reference ranges: method-specific. Non-fasting acceptable for population screening. If LDL-C needed: fasting lipid profile required.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESC/EAS Dyslipidaemia Guidelines; ACC/AHA Cholesterol Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIPOPROTEIN - a (LP-a)
interpretation: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] - independent cardiovascular risk factor. Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle with apolipoprotein(a) covalently bound to apoB-100. Lp(a) levels are 80-90% genetically determined (LPA gene on chromosome 6). Elevated Lp(a): cardiovascular disease risk (atherosclerosis, aortic stenosis, coronary artery disease - independent of LDL-C), thrombotic risk (Lp(a) resembles plasminogen - inhibits fibrinolysis), aortic valve stenosis (calcific aortic stenosis - Lp(a) associated), familial hypercholesterolaemia (co-existent Lp(a) elevation worsens prognosis). Clinical use: cardiovascular risk assessment (Lp(a) independent of LDL-C - measure once in lifetime), aortic stenosis risk stratification, assessing residual cardiovascular risk (LDL-C at target but still high CV risk). Limitations: Lp(a) is GENETICALLY DETERMINED (80-90% heritable) - lifestyle and diet have minimal effect. Lp(a) is NOT routinely measured - only measured if: family history of premature CVD, familial hypercholesterolaemia, recurrent CVD despite optimal LDL-C, aortic stenosis. Lp(a) measurement: standardised assays available (mass-based vs particle number-based). Lp(a) mass: mg/dL. Lp(a) particles: nmol/L. Conversion varies between assays - NOT interchangeable. Lp(a) and ethnicity: levels vary significantly (South Asians and Africans have higher levels; Caucasians intermediate; East Asians lower). Lp(a) and inflammation: Lp(a) is an acute-phase reactant - may be falsely elevated during acute illness. Lp(a) and CKD: Lp(a) elevated in chronic kidney disease. Lp(a) treatment: no proven Lp(a)-lowering therapy yet (nascent antisense oligonucleotides under investigation). Statins do NOT lower Lp(a). Niacin lowers Lp(a) but does NOT reduce CV events. PCSK9 inhibitors modestly lower Lp(a) (10-20%).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred but not required (Lp(a) not significantly affected by fasting). Preparation: note cardiovascular disease history, family history of premature CVD, familial hypercholesterolaemia, aortic stenosis, ethnicity, recent acute illness (Lp(a) is acute-phase - falsely elevated during illness). Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Lp(a) measured once in lifetime (genetically determined - levels stable unless acute illness). If elevated: no specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy available. Statins do NOT lower Lp(a). Niacin lowers Lp(a) but does NOT reduce CV events. PCSK9 inhibitors modestly lower Lp(a) (10-20%). Aortic stenosis: Lp(a) elevated - monitor with echocardiography. Ethnicity: South Asians and Africans have higher Lp(a) levels. Inflammation: Lp(a) falsely elevated during acute illness - defer testing 6 weeks.
ref_ranges: Normal: <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L). Borderline: 30-50 mg/dL (75-125 nmol/L). Elevated: >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L). High: >100 mg/dL (>250 nmol/L). Cardiovascular risk: Lp(a) >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L) = increased CV risk independent of LDL-C. Aortic stenosis: Lp(a) >50 mg/dL associated with calcific aortic stenosis. Familial hypercholesterolaemia: Lp(a) elevated in many FH patients. Reference ranges: method-specific. Lp(a) mass vs particle number: NOT interchangeable between assays. Ethnic variation: South Asians/Africans higher; East Asians lower. Age: Lp(a) stable across lifetime. Pregnancy: Lp(a) may rise.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESC/EAS Lipid Guidelines; European Atherosclerosis Society Lp(a) Consensus; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIPOPROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS
interpretation: Serum Lipoprotein Electrophoresis separates and identifies lipoprotein fractions: chylomicrons, VLDL (pre-beta), LDL (beta), HDL (alpha). Lipoprotein electrophoresis is used to: classify hyperlipoproteinaemia (Fredrickson types I-V), diagnose dysbetalipoproteinaemia (broad beta disease), and assess cardiovascular risk. Elevated chylomicrons: type I, V. Elevated VLDL: type IIb, IV. Elevated LDL: type IIa. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting 12-14 hours). CRITICAL: fasting. Preparation: note lipid history, cardiovascular risk. Handle per standard. Classification: Fredrickson types. Dysbetalipoproteinaemia: broad beta. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: expected pattern. Elevated: hyperlipoproteinaemia. Fredrickson: types I-V. Broad beta: type III. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: NCEP ATP III Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LITHIUM
interpretation: Lithium - measurement of serum lithium concentration for therapeutic drug monitoring in patients receiving lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index requiring close monitoring. Therapeutic range: 0.6-1.2 mmol/L (acute mania: 0.8-1.2 mmol/L; maintenance: 0.6-0.8 mmol/L). Toxic range: >1.5 mmol/L (mild toxicity: 1.5-2.0; moderate: 2.0-2.5; severe: >2.5). Lithium toxicity symptoms: mild (tremor, nausea, diarrhoea, drowsiness), moderate (confusion, ataxia, dysarthria, blurred vision), severe (seizures, coma, cardiac arrhythmias, renal failure, death). Clinical use: therapeutic drug monitoring (maintain levels 0.6-1.2 mmol/L), toxicity detection (levels >1.5 mmol/L), compliance assessment, dose adjustment. Limitations: lithium levels affected by: renal function (reduced GFR raises levels), dehydration (reduces clearance), drugs (NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs raise lithium levels; theophylline lowers levels), sodium intake (low sodium raises lithium levels), thyroid function (lithium causes hypothyroidism in 20-30% of patients). Timing: sample collected 12h post-dose (trough level - most reproducible). Peak levels: 1-2h post-dose (not used for monitoring). Lithium and renal function: lithium is nephrotoxic - monitor renal function (eGFR, creatinine) regularly. Lithium and thyroid: lithium causes hypothyroidism in 20-30% - monitor TSH every 6 months. Lithium and parathyroid: lithium causes hyperparathyroidism (elevated calcium, PTH). Lithium and pregnancy: lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly risk) - discuss risk-benefit. Lithium and diuretics: thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels - avoid or reduce lithium dose. Lithium and NSAIDs: NSAIDs raise lithium levels - avoid or monitor closely.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: sample collected 12h post-dose (trough level). Preparation: note time of last lithium dose, renal function, thyroid function, medications (NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs), hydration status, pregnancy status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Trough level: 12h post-dose (most reproducible). Do NOT use peak levels for monitoring. Timing: if dose at 8pm, draw blood at 8am next morning. Renal function: monitor eGFR and creatinine regularly (lithium nephrotoxicity). Thyroid: monitor TSH every 6 months (lithium causes hypothyroidism). Parathyroid: monitor calcium and PTH (lithium causes hyperparathyroidism). Toxicity: if levels >1.5 mmol/L or symptoms of toxicity, consider discontinuation and supportive care. Hydration: dehydration raises lithium levels - ensure adequate hydration. Medications: NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors raise lithium levels - monitor closely.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic (acute mania): 0.8-1.2 mmol/L. Therapeutic (maintenance): 0.6-0.8 mmol/L. Toxic: >1.5 mmol/L. Mild toxicity: 1.5-2.0 mmol/L (tremor, nausea, diarrhoea). Moderate toxicity: 2.0-2.5 mmol/L (confusion, ataxia, dysarthria). Severe toxicity: >2.5 mmol/L (seizures, coma, cardiac arrhythmias). Sub-therapeutic: <0.6 mmol/L (may need dose increase). Reference ranges: method-specific. Timing: 12h post-dose (trough). Renal impairment: reduce target range. Age: elderly may need lower target (0.4-0.8 mmol/L).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; BAP Bipolar Disorder Guidelines; NICE Bipolar Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LIVER FUNCTION TEST (LFT-A)
interpretation: Liver Function Tests (LFT-A) - comprehensive panel assessing liver function, hepatocellular integrity, and biliary patency. Includes: ALT (alanine aminotransferase - hepatocellular damage marker), AST (aspartate aminotransferase - hepatocellular damage marker), ALP (alkaline phosphatase - cholestasis marker), GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase - cholestasis/alcohol marker), total bilirubin, direct (conjugated) bilirubin, albumin, total protein. Clinical use: liver disease screening, hepatitis assessment (viral, alcoholic, drug-induced), cholestasis evaluation (biliary obstruction, PBC, PSC), cirrhosis assessment (low albumin, prolonged PT), liver function monitoring (medications, toxins). Elevated ALT/AST: hepatocellular damage (viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, alcoholic hepatitis, ischaemic hepatitis, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis [NASH]). AST:ALT ratio >2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease. Elevated ALP/GGT: cholestasis (biliary obstruction, PBC, PSC, drug-induced cholestasis).
