Low albumin: chronic liver disease (reduced synthetic function), nephrotic syndrome (protein loss), malnutrition, inflammation (negative acute-phase protein). Elevated bilirubin: jaundice (pre-hepatic: haemolysis; hepatic: hepatitis; post-hepatic: biliary obstruction). Limitations: LFTs are SCREENING tests - not diagnostic alone. ALT/AST elevated in non-hepatic conditions (myocardial infarction, skeletal muscle injury, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease). ALP elevated in non-hepatic conditions (bone disease, pregnancy, intestinal ischaemia, lymphoma). GGT elevated in non-hepatic conditions (alcohol, medications, pancreatitis). Bilirubin elevated in non-hepatic conditions (haemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome). LFTs cannot determine aetiology of liver disease - additional testing required (viral serology, autoimmune markers, imaging, liver biopsy). LFTs and medications: paracetamol, statins, antibiotics, anticonvulsants can elevate ALT/AST. LFTs and pregnancy: physiological changes in ALP (placental source), elevated AST/ALT may indicate pre-eclampsia. LFTs and exercise: strenuous exercise may elevate AST (skeletal muscle source).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred for accurate triglycerides/GGT. Preparation: note alcohol use, medications (paracetamol, statins, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, viral hepatitis risk factors, autoimmune disease history. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. AST:ALT ratio: >2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease. Cholestasis: ALP/GGT elevated + conjugated bilirubin elevated. Hepatocellular: ALT/AST elevated + unconjugated bilirubin elevated. Cirrhosis: low albumin + elevated bilirubin + elevated PT. Viral hepatitis: AST/ALT elevated (ALT > AST in viral hepatitis). Drug-induced: ALT/AST elevated + temporal relationship with drug exposure. Gilbert syndrome: unconjugated bilirubin mildly elevated (1-6 mg/dL), all other LFTs normal. Alkaline phosphatase: if ALP elevated, check GGT to confirm hepatic source (bone ALP normal GGT).
ref_ranges: ALT: 7-56 U/L (men); 7-45 U/L (women). AST: 10-40 U/L (men); 9-32 U/L (women). ALP: 44-147 U/L (men); 35-105 U/L (women). GGT: 8-61 U/L (men); 5-36 U/L (women). Total bilirubin: 0.1-1.2 mg/dL. Direct bilirubin: 0-0.3 mg/dL. Albumin: 3.5-5.0 g/dL. Total protein: 6.0-8.3 g/dL. ALT/AST ratio: >2:1 alcoholic liver disease; >1 viral hepatitis (ALT > AST). Jaundice: bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL (visible scleral icterus). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: ALP higher in children (bone growth). Pregnancy: ALP elevated (placental).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD Liver Test Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LUTEINIZING HORMONE (LH)
interpretation: Luteinising Hormone (LH) - gonadotropin produced by anterior pituitary gonadotroph cells. Stimulates testosterone production in Leydig cells (men) and triggers ovulation + corpus luteum formation (women). Elevated LH: menopause (most common cause in non-pregnant women - FSH and LH elevated >25 IU/L), primary gonadal failure (Klinefelter syndrome in men, Turner syndrome in women, gonadal damage from chemotherapy/radiation), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS - LH elevated with LH:FSH ratio >2:1, though not diagnostic), testicular failure in men (cryptorchidism, orchitis, testicular tumours). Low LH: hypothalamic amenorrhoea (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea - stress, weight loss, exercise), Kallmann syndrome (congenital GnRH deficiency + anosmia), hypopituitarism (pituitary tumour, surgery, radiation, Sheehan syndrome), pregnancy (hCG suppresses LH), hormonal contraceptives (suppress LH), anabolic steroid use (suppresses LH). Clinical use: menstrual irregularity assessment (PCOS vs hypothalamic amenorrhoea), menopause confirmation (FSH + LH elevated), male hypogonadism evaluation (primary vs secondary - LH elevated in primary, low in secondary), fertility assessment (LH surge prediction for ovulation timing). Limitations: LH is PULSATILE (secreted in pulses every 1-2 hours) - random levels may not reflect average secretion. LH surge detection: urinary LH kits more reliable than serum LH for ovulation prediction (serum LH may miss surge if sampled between pulses). LH:FSH ratio: LH:FSH >2:1 suggestive of PCOS but NOT diagnostic (many normal women have ratio <2:1, and ratio varies with assay). Menopausal LH: elevated in menopause but overlap with reproductive-age women - use FSH (>25 IU/L) for more reliable menopause confirmation. LH and PCOS: LH may be normal in PCOS (only 50-70% have elevated LH). LH and pregnancy: LH suppressed (hCG cross-reacts with LH assay - measure pregnancy-specific hCG instead). Assay variability: immunoassays cross-react with hCG (TSH may also cross-react). Timing: mid-cycle LH surge prediction - sample daily from cycle day 10. Male LH: interpret alongside testosterone and FSH.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note menstrual cycle day (women), menopausal status, pregnancy status, hormonal contraceptives, recent exercise/stress, medications affecting hypothalamus/pituitary. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Menstrual cycle: LH surge prediction - sample daily from cycle day 10. LH surge: mid-cycle, 24-36h before ovulation (urinary LH kits more practical). PCOS: LH + FSH (LH:FSH ratio >2:1 suggestive but not diagnostic). Menopause: FSH + LH elevated (>25 IU/L). Male hypogonadism: LH + testosterone + FSH (primary: LH elevated + low testosterone; secondary: LH low + low testosterone). Hypothalamic amenorrhoea: LH low + FSH low + oestrogen low (functional - stress, weight loss, exercise). Kallmann: LH low + FSH low + anosmia (GnRH deficiency). Pregnancy: LH suppressed (hCG cross-reacts). Anabolic steroids: LH suppressed + low testosterone (exogenous testosterone suppresses LH).
ref_ranges: Women (follicular): 2-8 IU/L. Mid-cycle surge: 20-100 IU/L. Luteal: 1-6 IU/L. Post-menopausal: >25 IU/L (often >40). Men: 1-8 IU/L. PCOS: LH elevated (often 10-30 IU/L) with LH:FSH ratio >2:1. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea: LH low (<2 IU/L). Kallmann: LH very low (<1 IU/L). Male hypogonadism (primary): LH elevated (>8 IU/L) + low testosterone. Male hypogonadism (secondary): LH low (<1 IU/L) + low testosterone. Pregnancy: LH suppressed. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay cross-reactivity: hCG may cross-react with LH assay.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESHRE PCOS Guidelines; Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: LYSINE QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Plasma Lysine Quantitative measures the concentration of lysine, an essential amino acid. Lysine is involved in protein synthesis, carnitine production, and calcium absorption. Elevated: hyperlysinaemia (rare autosomal recessive), renal failure, maple syrup urine disease (mild). Low: malnutrition, ornithine translocase deficiency, lysinuric protein intolerance. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note metabolic disease, renal failure, nutritional status. Handle per standard. Elevated: hyperlysinaemia, renal failure. Low: OTC deficiency, LPI. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: hyperlysinaemia. Low: metabolic disorders. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MACROPROLACTIN
interpretation: Serum Macroprolactin measures the concentration of high-molecular-weight prolactin (macroprolactin, big-big prolactin). Macroprolactin is prolactin bound to IgG, which is biologically inactive but detected by immunoassays. Macroprolactinaemia: falsely elevated prolactin levels (>75% of circulating prolactin is macroprolactin). Prevalence: 10-25% of hyperprolactinaemia cases. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation: to distinguish macroprolactin from bioactive prolactin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note hyperprolactinaemia symptoms (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea). Handle per standard. Macroprolactinaemia: 10-25% of cases. PEG precipitation: to confirm. Bioactive prolactin: low in macroprolactinaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Macroprolactinaemia: falsely elevated total prolactin. PEG: to confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MAGNESIUM
interpretation: Magnesium - essential intracellular cation (2nd most abundant intracellular cation after potassium). Cofactor for >300 enzymatic reactions (ATP metabolism, protein synthesis, neuromuscular function, glucose metabolism, blood pressure regulation). ~60% body magnesium in bone, ~39% intracellular, ~1% extracellular (serum). Clinical use: hypomagnesaemia screening, hypokalaemia refractory to treatment (hypomagnesaemia causes renal potassium wasting), refractory hypocalcaemia (hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion/action), arrhythmia risk assessment (QT prolongation), critical care monitoring (ICU patients at risk), alcoholism screening (magnesium deficiency common), drug monitoring (proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, aminoglycosides). Hypomagnesaemia: PPI use (most common drug cause - reduces intestinal absorption), diuretics (loop > thiazide), alcoholism (poor intake + renal wasting), diarrhoea/vomiting (GI losses), malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, hypercalcaemia (increases renal magnesium wasting), diabetes mellitus (renal wasting), hyperaldosteronism, drugs (cisplatin, amphotericin B, aminoglycosides, ciclosporin). Symptoms: neuromuscular irritability (tremor, fasciculations, tetany, seizures), cardiac arrhythmias (torsades de pointes, VT), hypokalaemia (refractory to potassium replacement alone), hypocalcaemia (refractory to calcium replacement alone), hypertension, insulin resistance. Hypermagnesaemia: renal failure (reduced excretion - most common cause), magnesium-containing antacids/laxatives, lithium therapy, tumour lysis syndrome, adrenal insufficiency. Symptoms: nausea, flushing, hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest (>4 mg/dL). Limitations: serum magnesium represents only ~1% of total body magnesium - normal serum magnesium does NOT exclude total body magnesium depletion. Serum magnesium is a POOR indicator of total body magnesium status. Intracellular magnesium (RBC magnesium or ionised magnesium) more accurate but not routinely measured. Hypomagnesaemia may be intermittent - repeat if clinical suspicion high. Magnesium and calcium: hypomagnesaemia causes hypocalcaemia (impairs PTH secretion) - correct magnesium before calcium. Magnesium and potassium: hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypokalaemia (renal potassium wasting) - correct magnesium before potassium. Magnesium and PTH: hypomagnesaemia suppresses PTH secretion - hypocalcaemia refractory to calcium unless magnesium corrected. Magnesium and PPIs: PPIs reduce intestinal magnesium absorption - long-term PPI use associated with hypomagnesaemia.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma (heparin or EDTA). Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred (post-prandial variability). Preparation: note PPI use, diuretic use, alcohol intake, kidney function, diarrhoea/vomiting, medications (cisplatin, amphotericin B, aminoglycosides, ciclosporin), diabetes, hypercalcaemia. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Hypomagnesaemia workup: serum magnesium + calcium + potassium + PTH + vitamin D. Refractory hypokalaemia: check magnesium first (hypomagnesaemia causes renal K wasting). Refractory hypocalcaemia: check magnesium first (hypomagnesaemia suppresses PTH). PPI-induced: serum magnesium low + PPI use + symptoms (muscle cramps, arrhythmias). Critical care: serum magnesium monitored regularly (ICU patients at risk). Hypermagnesaemia: renal function essential (reduced GFR = reduced excretion). Antacid-induced: magnesium-containing antacids/laxatives. RBC magnesium: more accurate for total body status but not routinely available. Ionised magnesium: most accurate but requires specialized analyser.
ref_ranges: Adults: 1.7-2.2 mg/dL (0.70-0.95 mmol/L) - method-specific. Hypomagnesaemia: <1.7 mg/dL (<0.70 mmol/L). Mild: 1.2-1.7 mg/dL. Moderate: 0.8-1.2 mg/dL. Severe: <0.8 mg/dL (<0.33 mmol/L). Hypermagnesaemia: >2.2 mg/dL (>0.95 mmol/L). Mild: 2.5-4.0 mg/dL. Moderate: 4.0-7.0 mg/dL. Severe: >7.0 mg/dL (>2.9 mmol/L) - cardiac arrest risk. Neonates: 1.5-2.5 mg/dL (higher than adults). Elderly: may be lower (reduced absorption). PPI-induced hypomagnesaemia: often develops after >1 year of PPI use. Reference ranges: method-specific. Serum magnesium is a POOR indicator of total body status. RBC magnesium more accurate but not routinely available.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; EHJ Magnesium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MAGNESIUM SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Magnesium Spot Urine - measurement of magnesium concentration in a random (spot) urine sample. Assesses renal magnesium handling and helps differentiate causes of hypomagnesaemia. Clinical use: evaluating renal magnesium wasting (urine magnesium elevated in renal tubular defects), distinguishing GI losses from renal losses in hypomagnesaemia, monitoring magnesium supplementation therapy, assessing dietary magnesium intake. Elevated urine magnesium: renal magnesium wasting (Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, hypercalcaemia, hyperthyroidism, hyperaldosteronism, cisplatin nephrotoxicity, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus), magnesium supplementation (high intake), diuretics (loop diuretics increase renal magnesium excretion). Low urine magnesium: GI losses (diarrhoea, vomiting - kidney conserves magnesium), hypomagnesaemia with renal conservation (urine Mg <1 mmol/day suggests appropriate renal response), hypoparathyroidism, hypothyroidism. Clinical approach to hypomagnesaemia: urine magnesium >2 mmol/day (or >1 mg/day) = renal wasting (kidney is inappropriately excreting magnesium). Urine magnesium <1 mmol/day (or <1 mg/day) = appropriate renal conservation (GI losses or poor intake). Limitations: spot urine magnesium is influenced by hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low concentration; concentrated urine = falsely high). Fractional excretion of magnesium (FEMg) more accurate than spot urine: FEMg = (UMg x SCr) / (SMg x SCr) x 100. FEMg >4% = renal magnesium wasting. FEMg <2% = appropriate renal conservation. 24-hour urine magnesium more accurate than spot urine (integrates over 24h). Spot urine Mg/Cr ratio: adjusts for hydration (urine magnesium divided by urine creatinine). Reference ranges vary significantly between laboratories. Magnesium supplementation: urine magnesium rises after supplementation - not pathological. Diuretics: loop diuretics increase urine magnesium; thiazides decrease urine magnesium.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random sample). Midstream clean catch. No fasting required. Preparation: note magnesium supplementation, diuretic use, kidney function, GI losses (diarrhoea/vomiting), alcohol use, medications (cisplatin, aminoglycosides). Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Spot urine: random sample, no fasting. Hydration status: dilute urine = falsely low Mg concentration; concentrated = falsely high. Mg/Cr ratio: adjusts for hydration (urine Mg divided by urine creatinine). 24h urine: more accurate than spot (integrates over 24h). FEMg: fractional excretion of Mg (if paired serum and urine available). Renal wasting: urine Mg >2 mmol/day = kidney inappropriately excreting. GI losses: urine Mg <1 mmol/day = kidney appropriately conserving. Diuretics: loop = increased urine Mg; thiazide = decreased urine Mg. Bartter/Gitelman: urine Mg elevated (renal tubular defect). Cisplatin: renal Mg wasting (nephrotoxicity). Hypomagnesaemia workup: spot urine Mg to distinguish renal from GI losses.
ref_ranges: Random urine: 0.04-0.83 mmol/L (method-specific). 24-hour urine: 0.07-0.11 mmol/day (0.3-4.5 mmol/day). Fractional excretion of Mg: <2% = appropriate renal conservation; >4% = renal wasting. Spot urine Mg/Cr ratio: varies with hydration. Renal wasting: urine Mg >2 mmol/day (or >1 mg/day). Appropriate conservation: urine Mg <1 mmol/day (or <1 mg/day). Reference ranges: method-specific. Hydration: affects spot urine concentration significantly. Diuretics: alter urine Mg excretion. Age: varies with age. Pregnancy: urine Mg may be elevated.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; EHJ Magnesium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MANGANESE
interpretation: Whole Blood Manganese measures manganese concentration in blood. Manganese is an essential trace element required for enzyme function but is neurotoxic in excess. Elevated manganese: occupational exposure (mining, welding), liver disease (reduced biliary excretion), TPN (total parenteral nutrition). Manganese neurotoxicity: Parkinson-like syndrome (manganism). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). CRITICAL: metal-free collection. Preparation: note occupational exposure, liver disease, TPN. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Liver disease: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 4 to 15 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: occupational exposure, liver disease, TPN. Low: rarely significant. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATSDR Manganese Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: MARIJUANA (CANNABINOIDS)
interpretation: Marijuana (Cannabinoids) Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of 11-nor-delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol-9-carboxylic acid (THC-COOH) in urine, the primary metabolite of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Clinical use: drug screening (pre-employment, workplace, forensic), monitoring substance abuse treatment, detecting recent cannabis use, legal/forensic investigations, monitoring for cannabis use in patients on controlled substance agreements. Detection window: urine THC-COOH detectable for 1-7 days in occasional users, up to 30 days in chronic/heavy users (THC-COOH accumulates in fat tissue and is slowly released). Positive result: indicates cannabis use within detection window (does NOT indicate timing, dose, or impairment). Cross-reactivity: some immunoassays cross-react with other cannabinoids (synthetic cannabinoids may not be detected by standard assays). Limitations: immunoassay screening has CROSS-REACTIVITY with other cannabinoids (cannabidiol [CBD], cannabinol [CBN], synthetic cannabinoids). False positives: possible with certain medications (NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors) and foods (hemp seeds, poppy seeds - rare). Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay results. Detection window: highly variable (1-30 days depending on frequency of use, body fat, metabolism). THC-COOH is LIPID-SOLUBLE: accumulates in fat tissue - chronic users have prolonged detection. Passive inhalation: extremely unlikely to cause positive result (insufficient THC exposure). Impairment assessment: urine THC-COOH does NOT indicate current impairment (metabolite persists long after psychoactive effects resolve). Threshold: immunoassay cut-off typically 50 ng/mL (SAMHSA workplace standard). Confirmation: GC-MS/LC-MS/MS at 15 ng/mL cut-off. Cannabidiol (CBD): may cause positive result on some immunoassays (cross-reactivity) but not on confirmation testing. Synthetic cannabinoids (Spice, K2): NOT detected by standard THC immunoassays - require specific assays.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note recent cannabis use (if known), medications, dietary supplements (CBD products), body composition (obesity - prolonged detection due to fat storage). Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated, best for detection. Cut-off: immunoassay 50 ng/mL (SAMHSA workplace standard). Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS at 15 ng/mL. Detection window: occasional use 1-3 days; regular use 7-15 days; chronic heavy use up to 30 days. Passive inhalation: extremely unlikely to cause positive result. Impairment: urine THC-COOH does NOT indicate current impairment. CBD products: may cause positive immunoassay but negative confirmation. Synthetic cannabinoids: not detected by standard THC assay. False positives: NSAIDs, PPIs (rare). Chain of custody: required for legal/forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing (creatinine, pH, specific gravity) to detect dilution or adulteration.
ref_ranges: Negative: <50 ng/mL (immunoassay cut-off). Positive: >=50 ng/mL (immunoassay) - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS at 15 ng/mL. Confirmation cut-off: 15 ng/mL (SAMHSA). Detection window: 1-30 days (frequency-dependent). False positive rate: ~5-10% (cross-reactivity). Passive inhalation: extremely unlikely to cause positive result. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace testing: SAMHSA guidelines apply. Forensic: chain of custody required.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MDMA (QUALITITATIVE) ECSTASY-XTC - URINE SPOT
interpretation: Urine MDMA (Ecstasy, XTC) Qualitative detects the presence of MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) and metabolites in urine. MDMA is an empathogen-entactogen drug of abuse. Detection window: 2-5 days (urine). Active metabolites: MDA. CYP2D6 poor metabolites: prolonged detection. Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note drug use history, medications. Handle per standard. Detection: 2-5 days. CYP2D6: affects metabolism. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: MDMA use. Detection: 2-5 days. MDA: metabolite. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MERCURY
interpretation: Whole Blood Mercury measures mercury concentration in blood. Mercury is a toxic heavy metal with neurotoxic and nephrotoxic effects. Sources: dietary (fish), occupational (mining), environmental. Blood mercury: recent exposure. Hair mercury: chronic exposure. Acute toxicity: neurological symptoms. Chronic: renal, neurological. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note fish consumption, occupational exposure, symptoms. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Hair: chronic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 10 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: mercury exposure/toxicity. Hair: chronic. Blood: recent. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Mercury Guidelines; ATSDR Mercury Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: METABOLIC DISORDER PANEL-101 PARAMETER
interpretation: Metabolic Disorder Panel (101 parameters) is a comprehensive panel of biomarkers used to screen for, diagnose, and monitor a wide range of inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) and metabolic disorders. Panel includes: amino acids, organic acids, acylcarnitines, sugars, and other metabolites. Used for: newborn screening, metabolic emergencies, metabolic encephalopathy, developmental delay. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Blood (DBS) or plasma/urine. Preparation: note developmental delay, metabolic symptoms, family history. Handle per standard. Comprehensive: 101 parameters. Newborn screening: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by metabolite. Elevated: metabolic disorders. Comprehensive: 101 parameters. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Newborn Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METACHROMATIC LEUCODYSTROPHY
interpretation: Blood Metachromatic Leucodystrophy (MLD) measures arylsulphatase A activity. Arylsulphatase A deficiency causes MLD, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder characterised by demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems. MLD: progressive neurological deterioration, spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline, seizures. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note developmental regression, spasticity, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, family history. Handle per standard. Low: MLD. Arylsulphatase A: deficient. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: MLD. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG LSD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METANEPHRINE FREE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Free Metanephrines - measurement of free metanephrine (normetanephrine and metanephrine) in plasma. Metanephrines are metabolites of catecholamines (norepinephrine and epinephrine) produced by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) in adrenergic tissues. Most sensitive screening test for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma. Elevated plasma free metanephrines: phaeochromocytoma (adrenal catecholamine-secreting tumour - sensitivity >99%, specificity 85-90%), paraganglioma (extra-adrenal catecholamine-secreting tumour), medications (tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics, levodopa, caffeine, nicotine), chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance), alcohol withdrawal, anxiety/panic attacks, labile hypertension, post-surgical stress. Clinical use: phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma screening (first-line test - plasma free metanephrines or 24h urine fractionated metanephrines), monitoring post-surgical resection of phaeochromocytoma, evaluating hypertensive crisis (phaeochromocytoma as rare cause). Limitations: FALSE POSITIVES common (medications, standing position, anxiety, alcohol, foods). Specificity lower in mild/moderate elevation (1-2x ULN) - may be physiological. CRITICAL: patient must be supine for 15-30 minutes before blood draw (ambulation raises metanephrines). Medications causing false positives: tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics, levodopa, caffeine, nicotine, acetaminophen (paracetamol). Foods: bananas, avocado, caffeine, chocolate. Clinical decision: if plasma free metanephrines mildly elevated (1-2x ULN) and patient is asymptomatic, repeat with 24h urine fractionated metanephrines and/or plasma metanephrines after medication review. If >3x ULN: highly suggestive of phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma - proceed to imaging. Plasma vs urine: plasma free metanephrines more sensitive (99%) but less specific (85-90%); 24h urine fractionated metanephrines more specific but less sensitive. Supine position: CRITICAL - ambulation raises metanephrines 2-3x. False positives: 10-20% in mild elevation. Specificity improves with repeated testing and 24h urine. Phaeochromocytoma triad: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations + paroxysmal hypertension. Pregnancy: phaeochromocytoma rare but life-threatening - screen if hypertension in pregnancy.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA or heparin). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: patient must be SUPINE for 15-30 minutes before blood draw. Preparation: discontinue interfering medications if possible (tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics, levodopa, caffeine, nicotine). Avoid: strenuous exercise, alcohol, caffeine-rich foods, bananas, avocado, chocolate on day of test. Handle supine: patient supine 15-30 min before draw. Ambulation raises metanephrines 2-3x. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Phaeochromocytoma screen: plasma free metanephrines first. If normal: 24h urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines. If mildly elevated (1-2x ULN): repeat with 24h urine and medication review. If >3x ULN: proceed to imaging (CT/MRI abdomen). Supine position: essential for accurate results. Medication review: tricyclics, MAO inhibitors, sympathomimetics interfere. Foods: bananas, avocado, caffeine, chocolate interfere. Stress: anxiety raises metanephrines. CKD: reduced clearance raises metanephrines (interpret with caution). Post-surgical: metanephrines normalise after tumour resection. Hereditary syndromes: MEN2A, MEN2B, VHL, SDH mutations - screen family members.
ref_ranges: Normal: <0.50 nmol/L (normetanephrine); <0.50 nmol/L (metanephrine) - method-specific. Mildly elevated: 1-2x ULN (repeat with 24h urine). Moderately elevated: 2-3x ULN (suggestive). Markedly elevated: >3x ULN (highly suggestive of phaeochromocytoma). Phaeochromocytoma: normetanephrine elevated (most common); metanephrine elevated (epinephrine-secreting tumour). Paraganglioma: normetanephrine elevated (most common). Medications: tricyclics raise normetanephrine 2-10x. False positives: 10-20% in mild elevation. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: metanephrines increase with age. Position: supine essential. CKD: elevated (reduced clearance). Pregnancy: may be mildly elevated.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METH-HAEMOGLOBIN
interpretation: Blood Methaemoglobin (Meth-Haemoglobin) measures the percentage of haemoglobin in the oxidised (ferric) form that cannot carry oxygen. Normal methaemoglobin: less than 1%. Methaemoglobin levels greater than 10%: cyanosis. Levels greater than 50%: life-threatening. Causes: congenital (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency), acquired (dapsone, nitrites, benzocaine, local anaesthetics). Treatment: methylene blue (converts MetHb to functional Hb). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA or heparin). CRITICAL: avoid delay (MetHb can increase ex vivo). Preparation: note cyanosis, drug exposure, respiratory distress. Handle per standard. Greater than 10%: cyanosis. Greater than 50%: life-threatening. Methylene blue: treatment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1%. Cyanosis: greater than 10%. Life-threatening: greater than 50%. Treatment: methylene blue. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHADONE (MTD) - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Methadone (MTD) Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of methadone and its metabolites (EDDP - 2-ethylidene-1,5-dimethyl-3,3-diphenylpyrrolidine) in urine. Methadone is a synthetic opioid used for opioid substitution therapy (OST) and chronic pain management. Clinical use: monitoring compliance in opioid substitution therapy (OST), detecting methadone use, forensic toxicology, confirming absence of illicit opioids in patients on OST. Methadone pharmacology: long half-life (24-55 hours), accumulates with repeated dosing, achieves steady state in 5-7 days. Detection window: urine methadone detectable for 1-4 days after last dose (longer in chronic users due to accumulation). Positive result: indicates methadone use within detection window (compliance in OST patients). Limitations: immunoassay detects methadone AND metabolites (EDDP). False positives: possible with some medications (dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine - rare). False negatives: possible if urine very dilute or methadone dose very low. Methadone metabolites: EDP (2-ethylidene-1,5-dimethyl-3,3-diphenylpyrrolidine) is the primary metabolite - detected alongside methadone. Detection window: 1-4 days in acute use; up to 7-14 days in chronic users (accumulation). Compliance monitoring: positive methadone = patient taking medication; negative = non-compliance or diversion. Diversion: patients selling/distributing methadone may have negative urine (not taking their own supply). Cross-reactivity: limited with other opioids (heroin, morphine) - methadone has distinct chemical structure. Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay results. QT prolongation: methadone prolongs QT interval - baseline and periodic ECG monitoring recommended. Respiratory depression: risk in opioid-naive patients or when combined with benzodiazepines or alcohol. Neonatal withdrawal: methadone crosses placenta - neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) possible. CYP enzymes: metabolised by CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP2D6 - genetic polymorphisms affect metabolism.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note methadone dose, dosing history, concurrent medications (benzodiazepines, other opioids), QT-prolonging medications, pregnancy status, liver function (CYP metabolism). Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated, best for detection. Cut-off: immunoassay typically 300 ng/mL. Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-4 days (acute); up to 7-14 days (chronic). Compliance: positive = patient taking medication. Diversion: negative = possible non-compliance or diversion. EDDP: primary metabolite detected alongside methadone. QT monitoring: baseline and periodic ECG recommended. Neonatal: methadone crosses placenta - NAS possible. CYP metabolism: CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect metabolism. Hepatic impairment: prolonged half-life - dose adjustment may be needed. Respiratory depression: risk with concurrent benzodiazepines/alcohol.
ref_ranges: Negative: <300 ng/mL (immunoassay cut-off). Positive: >=300 ng/mL (immunoassay) - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-4 days (acute); up to 7-14 days (chronic). EDDP: primary metabolite detected. Compliance: positive = patient taking medication. Diversion: negative in setting of reported compliance. Cross-reactivity: limited with other opioids. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace/forensic: chain of custody required. QT prolongation: monitor with ECG.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHAMPHETAMINE
interpretation: Methamphetamine Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of methamphetamine and amphetamine (active metabolite) in urine. Methamphetamine is a potent central nervous system stimulant (Schedule II controlled substance). Clinical use: detecting methamphetamine use, drug screening (workplace, forensic), monitoring substance abuse treatment, evaluating patients with unexplained tachycardia/hypertension/agitation. Detection window: urine methamphetamine detectable for 1-3 days in occasional users, up to 5-7 days in chronic/heavy users. Positive result: indicates methamphetamine use within detection window. Cross-reactivity: some immunoassays cross-react with other amphetamines (amphetamine, MDMA/Ecstasy, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine). Limitations: immunoassay detects methamphetamine AND amphetamine (metabolite). Cross-reactivity: ephedrine, pseudoephedrine (decongestants), MDMA (Ecstasy), other amphetamines. False positives: possible with decongestants (ephedrine, pseudoephedrine) - though most workplace assays have cut-offs designed to minimise this. Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay results. Methamphetamine: converted to amphetamine (metabolite) - both detected. Active metabolite: amphetamine is pharmacologically active (not just a metabolite). Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment (metabolite persists). Structural isomers: levomethamphetamine (over-the-counter nasal decongestant) may cause positive on some immunoassays but NOT on confirmation testing. Dextromethamphetamine: active form (illicit drug). MDMA: cross-reacts on some immunoassays - confirmation testing distinguishes methamphetamine from MDMA. Adulteration: urine validity testing (creatinine, pH, specific gravity) required for workplace/forensic testing.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note decongestant use (ephedrine, pseudoephedrine), MDMA use, amphetamine medications (ADHD medications), dietary supplements. Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Cut-off: immunoassay typically 500 ng/mL (SAMHSA workplace standard). Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS at 250 ng/mL. Detection window: 1-3 days (occasional); up to 5-7 days (chronic). Cross-reactivity: ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, MDMA, other amphetamines. False positives: decongestants (rare at standard cut-offs). Chain of custody: required for legal/forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing required. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment. Distinguishing: GC-MS distinguishes methamphetamine from other amphetamines/MDMA. Levomethamphetamine: OTC decongestant - positive immunoassay but negative confirmation.
ref_ranges: Negative: <500 ng/mL (immunoassay cut-off). Positive: >=500 ng/mL (immunoassay) - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS at 250 ng/mL. Detection window: 1-7 days (frequency-dependent). Cross-reactivity: ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, MDMA. Confirmation: GC-MS/LC-MS/MS distinguishes methamphetamine from other amphetamines. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace testing: SAMHSA guidelines apply. Forensic: chain of custody required. Adulteration: urine validity testing required.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHAQUOLONE - URINE
interpretation: Methaqualone Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of methaqualone and its metabolites in urine. Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic (quinazolinone derivative) formerly used as a prescription sleep aid and anxiolytic (withdrawn from market in most countries due to abuse potential). Clinical use: forensic toxicology, detecting methaqualone use (illicit use), historical drug screening. Detection window: urine methaqualone detectable for up to 1-2 weeks in occasional users, up to 4-6 weeks in chronic/heavy users (long detection due to lipophilicity and accumulation). Positive result: indicates methaqualone use within detection window. Limitations: methaqualone is WITHDRAWN from market in most countries (USA, UK, Australia, EU) - positive result suggests illicit use. False positives: possible with some medications (less common than other drug immunoassays). Cross-reactivity: limited with other drugs (methaqualone has distinct chemical structure). Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay results. Detection window: unusually long (up to 4-6 weeks in chronic users) due to lipophilicity and accumulation in fat tissue. Historical context: widely abused in 1970s-1980s (Quaaludes, Mandrax). Metabolites: hydroxylated metabolites are the primary urinary metabolites. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment. Adulteration: urine validity testing required for forensic testing. Cross-reactivity with other quinazolinones: rare but possible. Assay availability: methaqualone-specific immunoassays available but not universally offered. Most standard drug panels do NOT include methaqualone (unless specifically requested).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note any prescription medications, illicit drug use, herbal supplements. Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Cut-off: immunoassay varies by manufacturer. Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-2 weeks (occasional); up to 4-6 weeks (chronic). Withdrawn drug: positive = illicit use in most countries. Lipophilic: accumulates in fat tissue - prolonged detection. Cross-reactivity: limited. Chain of custody: required for forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing required. Standard panels: methaqualone NOT routinely included (specific request required). Historical: widely abused in 1970s-1980s (Quaaludes, Mandrax). Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment.
ref_ranges: Negative: below manufacturer-specific cut-off. Positive: above cut-off - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-6 weeks (frequency-dependent, unusually long). Withdrawn drug: positive = illicit use. Lipophilic: accumulates in fat tissue. Confirmation: GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Reference ranges: method-specific. Forensic: chain of custody required. Not in standard panels: specific request needed.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHIONINE (QUANTITATIVE) - URINE SPOT
interpretation: Urine Methionine Quantitative (spot) measures the concentration of methionine, an essential sulphur-containing amino acid. Elevated urine methionine: homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), tyrosinaemia type I, liver disease. Homocystinuria: Marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation, thromboembolism, intellectual disability. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note developmental delay, thromboembolism, lens dislocation. Handle per standard. Elevated: homocystinuria, tyrosinaemia. Homocystinuria: CBS deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: homocystinuria, tyrosinaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHOTREXATE
interpretation: Serum Methotrexate measures the concentration of methotrexate, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor used in cancer chemotherapy, autoimmune diseases (RA, psoriasis), and ectopic pregnancy. Therapeutic drug monitoring: guides leucovorin rescue and assesses delayed clearance. Delayed clearance: nephrotoxicity, delayed excretion, high-dose protocols. Monitoring: serial levels until less than 0.1 mcmol/L. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: timing depends on protocol (24h, 48h, 72h post-infusion). Preparation: note cancer protocol, renal function, other medications. Handle per standard. Delayed clearance: leucovorin rescue. Less than 0.1 mcmol/L: safe. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Delayed clearance: prolonged monitoring needed. Less than 0.1 mcmol/L: safe. Leucovorin rescue: if delayed. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: NCCN Chemotherapy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: METHYL MALONIC ACID QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Serum Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) Quantitative measures MMA concentration. MMA accumulates in vitamin B12 deficiency and methylmalonic aciduria (cobalamin metabolism defects). MMA is more specific than B12 alone for functional B12 status. Elevated MMA: vitamin B12 deficiency (sensitivity 94-98%, specificity 99%), methylmalonic aciduria, renal failure (mild elevation). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note anaemia, neuropathy, B12 therapy. Handle per standard. Elevated: B12 deficiency (more specific than B12). MMA greater than 0.4 mcmol/L: suggestive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 0.4 mcmol/L. B12 deficiency: greater than 0.4. MMA: more specific than B12. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BSH B12 Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MICROALBUMIN URINE - SPOT
interpretation: Urine Microalbumin (Spot) - measurement of albumin concentration in a random (spot) urine sample. Detects early nephropathy (microalbuminuria) before clinical proteinuria becomes apparent. Most important screening test for diabetic nephropathy. Clinical use: diabetic nephropathy screening (type 1 diabetes: screen from 5 years after diagnosis; type 2 diabetes: screen at diagnosis), hypertensive nephropathy assessment, cardiovascular risk stratification (microalbuminuria is an independent CV risk factor), chronic kidney disease staging, monitoring ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy (renoprotective effect), pre-eclampsia screening (urine proteinuria). Microalbuminuria: urine albumin 30-300 mg/L (or ACR 30-300 mg/g) - indicates early glomerular damage. Macroalbuminuria: urine albumin >300 mg/L (or ACR >300 mg/g) - overt proteinuria. Normal: urine albumin <30 mg/L (or ACR <30 mg/g). Limitations: spot urine albumin influenced by: hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low), exercise (raises albumin transiently), infection (UTI raises albumin), menstruation (blood contamination), fever, heart failure (acute), uncontrolled hypertension. Confirmation: requires 2 of 3 positive samples over 3-6 months for diagnosis (single positive sample insufficient). ACR: albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) preferred over absolute albumin concentration (ACR adjusts for urine concentration). ACR 30-300 mg/g = microalbuminuria. ACR >300 mg/g = macroalbuminuria. ACR <30 mg/g = normal. First morning urine: preferred (most representative of 24h albumin excretion). Timing: morning sample avoids postural albuminuria (ambulation raises albumin). Diabetic nephropathy: microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable sign - intervene with ACE inhibitor/ARB. Cardiovascular risk: microalbuminuria independently predicts CV events (MI, stroke) - aggressive risk factor modification needed. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: ACR increases with age. Ethnicity: ACR higher in African Americans. Exercise: avoid strenuous exercise 24h before test. Infection: treat UTI before testing.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (first morning preferred). Spot urine (random) acceptable. Preparation: ensure no UTI (treat infection first), no menstruation, no strenuous exercise 24h before, no uncontrolled hypertension. CRITICAL: 2 of 3 positive samples over 3-6 months for diagnosis. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most representative. Spot urine: acceptable but ACR preferred. ACR: albumin-to-creatinine ratio (adjusts for urine concentration). ACR 30-300 mg/g: microalbuminuria. ACR >300 mg/g: macroalbuminuria. ACR <30 mg/g: normal. Diabetic screening: type 1 from 5 years; type 2 at diagnosis. Confirm: 2 of 3 positive over 3-6 months. Ambulation: postural albuminuria (ambulation raises albumin) - use first morning sample. Exercise: avoid strenuous exercise 24h before. Infection: treat UTI before testing. Menstruation: blood contamination - avoid during menses. Hypertension: uncontrolled HTN raises albumin - control BP first. ACE/ARB monitoring: microalbuminuria regression = therapeutic success. CV risk: microalbuminuria = independent CV risk factor. Reference ranges: method-specific. Ethnicity: ACR higher in African Americans.
ref_ranges: Normal: ACR <30 mg/g (<3 mg/mmol). Microalbuminuria: ACR 30-300 mg/g (3-30 mg/mmol). Macroalbuminuria: ACR >300 mg/g (>30 mg/mmol). Spot urine albumin: <30 mg/L normal; 30-300 mg/L microalbuminuria; >300 mg/L macroalbuminuria. Diabetic nephropathy: microalbuminuria = earliest sign. Cardiovascular: microalbuminuria = independent CV risk factor. Confirmation: 2 of 3 positive over 3-6 months. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: ACR increases with age. Ethnicity: ACR higher in African Americans. Exercise: transiently raises albumin. Infection: UTI raises albumin.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; KDIGO CKD Guidelines; NICE CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MORPHINE/OPIATES
interpretation: Morphine/Opiates Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of morphine and its metabolites (and other opiates) in urine. Detects natural and semi-synthetic opioids (morphine, codeine, heroin, hydrocodone, oxycodone). Clinical use: detecting opioid use, drug screening (workplace, forensic), monitoring substance abuse treatment, evaluating patients with unexplained sedation/respiratory depression, confirming absence of opioids in patients on non-opioid pain management. Opiates detected: morphine (parent compound of heroin, also found in codeine metabolism), codeine (metabolised to morphine), heroin (metabolised to morphine via 6-MAM), hydrocodone, oxycodone (some cross-reactivity). Detection window: urine opiates detectable for 1-3 days in occasional users, up to 3-4 days in regular users. Positive result: indicates opiate use within detection window (does NOT distinguish between prescription and illicit use). Limitations: immunoassay detects morphine AND cross-reacts with structurally related opioids. Cross-reactivity: codeine, heroin (metabolised to morphine), hydrocodone, oxycodone (partial cross-reactivity), poppy seeds (contain morphine/codeine). False positives: poppy seed ingestion (food contamination with morphine/codeine) - though modern cut-offs (300 ng/mL) make this less likely. Specificity: immunoassay cannot distinguish between different opioids - confirmation testing required. Heroin metabolite: 6-monoacetylmorphine (6-MAM) is unique to heroin - specific marker. Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay. Synthetic opioids: fentanyl, methadone, tramadol NOT detected by standard opiate immunoassays - require specific assays. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment. Poppy seeds: can cause positive result at lower cut-offs (modern assays use 300 ng/mL to avoid this). Prescription opioids: codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone cross-react with opiate immunoassay - prescription use possible.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note opioid medications (codeine, morphine, hydrocodone, oxycodone), poppy seed consumption, heroin use, recent dental/surgical procedures. Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Cut-off: immunoassay typically 300 ng/mL (SAMHSA workplace standard). Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-3 days (occasional); up to 3-4 days (regular). Heroin metabolite: 6-MAM unique to heroin. Codeine: metabolised to morphine (both detected). Poppy seeds: can cause positive (modern cut-offs reduce this). Cross-reactivity: codeine, heroin, hydrocodone, oxycodone. Synthetic opioids: fentanyl, methadone NOT detected by standard assay. Chain of custody: required for legal/forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing required. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment. Prescription use: possible with codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone.
ref_ranges: Negative: <300 ng/mL (immunoassay cut-off). Positive: >=300 ng/mL (immunoassay) - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-4 days (frequency-dependent). Heroin: 6-MAM unique metabolite. Codeine: metabolised to morphine. Poppy seeds: possible positive at lower cut-offs. Synthetic opioids: fentanyl, methadone require specific assays. Cross-reactivity: codeine, heroin, hydrocodone, oxycodone. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace testing: SAMHSA guidelines apply. Forensic: chain of custody required. Adulteration: urine validity testing required.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MYOGLOBIN
interpretation: Serum Myoglobin measures the concentration of myoglobin, a small heme protein found in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Myoglobin is released into blood after muscle injury and is used as an early marker of: acute myocardial infarction (MI), rhabdomyolysis, and muscle trauma. Myoglobin rises within 1-3 hours of MI (earliest marker), peaks at 6-9 hours, and returns to normal in 24-36 hours. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note chest pain, muscle trauma, crush injury. Handle per standard. Myoglobin: earliest marker of MI (1-3h). Peak: 6-9h. Return to normal: 24-36h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 85 ng/mL (method-specific). Elevated: MI, rhabdomyolysis, muscle trauma. Earliest marker: MI. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA MI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: MYOGLOBIN RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Random Urine Myoglobin measures myoglobin concentration in urine. Myoglobinuria indicates muscle injury with myoglobin filtration by the kidneys. Myoglobinuria: rhabdomyolysis, crush injury, severe exercise, muscle necrosis. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic and can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute tubular necrosis (ATN). Urine myoglobin: more specific than serum for rhabdomyolysis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note muscle pain, dark urine, crush injury, seizures. Handle per standard. Myoglobinuria: rhabdomyolysis. Nephrotoxic: AKI risk. Urine: more specific than serum. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (negative). Positive: rhabdomyolysis. Nephrotoxic: AKI. Urine: more specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA Rhabdomyolysis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: N ACETYL GLUCOSAMINE 6 SULPHATE SULPHATASE - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood N-Acetyl Glucosamine 6 Sulphate Sulphatase (GALNS) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine 6-sulphate sulphatase. GALNS deficiency causes Mucopolysaccharidosis IV A (Morquio A syndrome), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. Morquio A: skeletal dysplasia, corneal clouding, cardiac disease, normal intelligence. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note skeletal dysplasia, corneal clouding, cardiac disease, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Morquio A. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 4.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Morquio A. Carrier: variable. Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: MPS Society Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: N-TERMINAL PRO B-TYPE NATRIURETIC PEPTIDE (NT-PRO BNP)
interpretation: N-Terminal Pro B-Type Natriuretic Peptide (NT-proBNP) - prohormone of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Released from cardiac ventricles in response to volume overload and increased wall stress. More stable than BNP (longer half-life: 60-120 min vs 20 min for BNP). Most important biomarker for heart failure diagnosis and prognosis. Elevated NT-proBNP: heart failure (most important clinical finding - NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL effectively excludes heart failure; age-adjusted cut-offs: <125 pg/mL age <50; <450 pg/mL age 50-75; <900 pg/mL age >75), acute dyspnoea (differentiating cardiac from pulmonary causes of breathlessness), left ventricular dysfunction (systolic and diastolic), myocardial infarction (ventricular wall stress), atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism (right ventricular strain), chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance), sepsis, pneumonia, anaemia. Clinical use: heart failure diagnosis (age-adjusted cut-offs: <125 pg/mL age <50; <450 pg/mL age 50-75; <900 pg/mL age >75), heart failure prognosis (higher NT-proBNP = worse prognosis), monitoring heart failure therapy (serial NT-proBNP - declining levels = responding to therapy), differentiating cardiac from pulmonary dyspnoea (NT-proBNP elevated in cardiac; normal in pulmonary), risk stratification in acute coronary syndromes. Limitations: NT-proBNP is AGE-DEPENDENT (levels rise with age) - age-adjusted cut-offs essential. NT-proBNP is KIDNEY-DEPENDENT (reduced clearance in CKD) - interpret alongside eGFR (eGFR <60 may elevate NT-proBNP without heart failure). NT-proBNP is SEX-DEPENDENT (women have higher NT-proBNP than men at same age). NT-proBNP and obesity: obesity LOWERS NT-proBNP (reduced cardiac wall stress or enhanced clearance) - may mask heart failure. NT-proBNP and AF: atrial fibrillation elevates NT-proBNP (volume overload) - may mimic heart failure. NT-proBNP and CKD: reduced clearance elevates NT-proBNP - must interpret alongside eGFR. NT-proBNP and thyroid: hyperthyroidism elevates NT-proBNP. NT-proBNP and age: levels rise with age - use age-adjusted cut-offs. NT-proBNP vs BNP: NT-proBNP more stable (longer half-life); BNP affected by obestatin (recombinant BNP therapy). NT-proBNP and pregnancy: elevated (physiological). NT-proBNP and sepsis: elevated (myocardial depression + volume overload). Assay variability: different immunoassays give different results - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. Serial NT-proBNP: more useful than single measurement (trend reflects therapeutic response).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note heart failure symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling, orthopnoea), renal function (eGFR), thyroid function, recent exercise (transiently raises NT-proBNP), atrial fibrillation history, medications (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics). Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Heart failure: NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL effectively excludes HF. Age-adjusted: <125 (<50y); <450 (50-75y); <900 (>75y). Acute dyspnoea: differentiates cardiac (elevated) from pulmonary (normal) breathlessness. CKD: interpret alongside eGFR (eGFR <60 may elevate NT-proBNP). Serial monitoring: declining NT-proBNP = responding to therapy. Prognosis: higher NT-proBNP = worse prognosis. Obesity: lowers NT-proBNP (may mask HF). AF: elevates NT-proBNP (may mimic HF). Thyroid: hyperthyroidism elevates NT-proBNP. Pregnancy: elevated (physiological). Sepsis: elevated (myocardial depression). Assay variability: use laboratory-specific reference ranges.
ref_ranges: Age <50: <125 pg/mL normal; >125 = possible HF. Age 50-75: <450 pg/mL normal; >450 = possible HF. Age >75: <900 pg/mL normal; >900 = possible HF. Heart failure exclusion: <300 pg/mL effectively excludes HF (NPV >99%). Acute HF: NT-proBNP typically >1000 pg/mL. Chronic HF: NT-proBNP 400-2000 pg/mL. Severe HF: >2000 pg/mL. Prognosis: higher NT-proBNP = worse prognosis. CKD: eGFR <60 may elevate NT-proBNP. Sex: women higher than men at same age. Obesity: lowers NT-proBNP. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age-adjusted cut-offs essential. Serial: declining levels = responding to therapy.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESC Heart Failure Guidelines; ACC/AHA HF Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NAFLD (NON ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE) FIBROSIS SCORE
interpretation: NAFLD Fibrosis Score is a non-invasive calculation using routine laboratory parameters (age, glucose, platelet count, albumin, BMI) to predict advanced fibrosis in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Score less than -1.455: F0-F2 (low probability of advanced fibrosis). Score greater than 0.676: F3-F4 (high probability of advanced fibrosis). Validated against liver biopsy. Reference ranges: calculated.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum + clinical parameters. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note NAFLD, obesity, diabetes. Handle per standard. Score: calculated. Less than -1.455: F0-F2. Greater than 0.676: F3-F4. Validated: liver biopsy. Reference ranges: calculated.
ref_ranges: Less than -1.455: low probability (F0-F2). Greater than 0.676: high probability (F3-F4). Validated: liver biopsy. Reference ranges: calculated.
refs: Sources: EASL NAFLD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NEUTROPHIL GELATINASE-ASSOCIATED LIPOCALIN (NGAL) - URINE
interpretation: Urine Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL) is a biomarker of acute kidney injury (AKI). NGAL is a small protein released by renal tubular cells in response to injury. NGAL rises 2-4 hours after AKI insult (earlier than creatinine). NGAL less than 100 ng/mL: low AKI risk. NGAL greater than 100 ng/mL: high AKI risk. NGAL: predictive of AKI severity and outcomes. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note kidney injury, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs. Handle per standard. NGAL: earliest marker of AKI (2-4h). Less than 100: low risk. Greater than 100: high risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 ng/mL. Elevated: AKI risk. Earliest marker: 2-4h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO AKI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NEW BORN SCREENING(NBS)
interpretation: Newborn Screening (NBS) - comprehensive panel of tests performed on all newborns within 48-72 hours of birth to detect treatable congenital disorders. Tests vary by country/region but typically include: phenylketonuria (PKU), congenital hypothyroidism (CH), sickle cell disease (SCD), cystic fibrosis (CF), medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD), and others. Sample: heel-prick blood on special filter paper (Guthrie card). Clinical use: early detection of treatable congenital conditions before symptoms develop. PKU: elevated phenylalanine (>120 umol/L) - treat with phenylalanine-restricted diet to prevent intellectual disability. Congenital hypothyroidism: elevated TSH (>20 mIU/L) - treat with thyroxine replacement to prevent intellectual disability. Sickle cell disease: abnormal haemoglobin pattern (HbS present) - monitor for complications, prevent infections. Cystic fibrosis: elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) - confirm with sweat chloride testing. MCADD: abnormal acylcarnitine profile - avoid fasting, treat with carnitine. Limitations: NBS is a SCREENING test - positive result requires CONFIRMATORY testing (false positives occur). Timing: sample collected at 48-72 hours of life (before day 2 may miss conditions; after day 7 may have false negatives). False positives: common (especially CF screening) - confirmatory testing essential. False negatives: possible if sample collected too early (<48h), too late (>7 days), or in premature infants (immature metabolism). Premature infants: may need repeat screening at 2-4 weeks (immature metabolic pathways). Blood transfusion: recent transfusion may affect results (donor haemoglobin masks patient's). Regional variation: screening panels vary by country/region - not all conditions screened everywhere. Conditions screened: PKU, CH, SCD, CF, MCADD, galactosaemia, biotinidase deficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), homocystinuria. Confirmatory testing: required for ALL positive screening results (heel-prick is screening only). Treatment: most screened conditions are treatable if detected early (PKU, CH, SCD). Informed consent: required for newborn screening in most jurisdictions.
pre_analytical: Sample: Heel-prick blood on filter paper (Guthrie card). Collected at 48-72 hours of life. Preparation: ensure adequate feeding before sample (for PKU, galactosaemia). Note: premature infants, blood transfusion, maternal medications. Handling: air-dry at room temperature. Send to screening laboratory within 24h. Conditions screened: PKU, CH, SCD, CF, MCADD, galactosaemia, biotinidase deficiency, CAH, MSUD, homocystinuria. Timing: 48-72h (before day 2 may miss; after day 7 may have false negatives). Premature: repeat at 2-4 weeks. Blood transfusion: may affect results. False positives: common - confirmatory testing essential. False negatives: possible if timing inappropriate. Confirmation: ALL positive results require confirmatory testing. Treatment: most conditions treatable if detected early. Regional variation: screening panels vary by country.
ref_ranges: PKU: phenylalanine >120 umol/L (>2 mg/dL) - screen positive. CH: TSH >20 mIU/L - screen positive. SCD: HbS present - screen positive. CF: elevated IRT - screen positive. MCADD: abnormal acylcarnitine profile - screen positive. Galactosaemia: elevated galactose - screen positive. Biotinidase deficiency: low biotidase - screen positive. CAH: elevated 17-OHP - screen positive. Reference ranges: method-specific. Regional variation: screening panels vary by country. Timing: 48-72h of life. Premature: may need repeat.
refs: Sources: WHO Newborn Screening Guidelines; regional newborn screening programme guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NICKEL
interpretation: Whole Blood Nickel measures nickel concentration in blood. Nickel is a trace element used in industry and found in stainless steel, coins, and jewellery. Elevated nickel: occupational exposure (mining, electroplating, stainless steel), nickel allergy (contact dermatitis), renal failure. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note occupational exposure, nickel allergy, renal disease. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Allergy: contact dermatitis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: occupational exposure, renal failure. Allergy: contact dermatitis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATSDR Nickel Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: NICKEL URINE SPOT
interpretation: Nickel Urine Spot - measurement of nickel concentration in a random (spot) urine sample. Nickel is a trace metal found in many industrial processes, stainless steel alloys, and consumer products. Elevated urine nickel: occupational exposure (nickel refining, electroplating, battery manufacturing, welding), stainless steel implant corrosion, nickel-containing dental alloys, dietary exposure (chocolate, nuts, legumes), environmental contamination, kidney disease (reduced clearance). Clinical use: assessing nickel exposure (occupational, environmental), monitoring nickel workers (occupational health), evaluating implant-related nickel hypersensitivity, environmental health assessments. Nickel hypersensitivity: type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction (contact dermatitis from jewellery, belt buckles, coins). Limitations: urine nickel is a BIOMARKER OF EXPOSURE (not necessarily of toxicity). Reference ranges vary significantly between laboratories (non-standardised assay). Spot urine: influenced by hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low; concentrated = falsely high). 24-hour urine: more accurate than spot urine (integrates over 24h). Dietary nickel: foods high in nickel (chocolate, nuts, legumes, soy) can elevate urine nickel (non-toxic exposure). Implant corrosion: stainless steel implants may leach nickel (low-level chronic exposure). Occupational exposure: significant elevations in nickel workers (refining, electroplating). Nickel dermatitis: contact allergy to nickel (jewellery, coins) - but urine nickel may be normal (localized hypersensitivity). Reference ranges: non-standardised between laboratories. Ethnic variation: limited data. Age: limited data. Pre-analytical: contamination from nickel-containing equipment possible.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note occupational exposure (nickel refining, electroplating), stainless steel implants, dental alloys, dietary habits (chocolate, nuts, legumes), environmental exposure. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. 24h urine: more accurate than spot. Contamination: avoid nickel-containing equipment (use trace-metal-free containers). Occupational: significant elevations in nickel workers. Implant: stainless steel implants may leach nickel. Dietary: chocolate, nuts, legumes high in nickel. Reference ranges: non-standardised. Spot urine: influenced by hydration. 24h urine: more accurate. Nickel dermatitis: contact allergy - urine nickel may be normal (localized). Environmental: air, water, soil contamination. Implant corrosion: low-level chronic exposure. Trace-metal-free: essential for accurate results.
ref_ranges: Normal: <5 ug/L (<0.085 umol/L) - method-specific. Occupational exposure: >10 ug/L (>0.17 umol/L). Significant exposure: >20 ug/L (>0.34 umol/L). Toxicity: >50 ug/L (>0.85 umol/L) - clinical symptoms possible. Dietary: may elevate urine nickel (non-toxic). Implant corrosion: low-level elevation. Reference ranges: non-standardised between laboratories. Age: limited data. Ethnic: limited data. Gender: limited data. Method: varies significantly between laboratories. 24h urine: more accurate than spot. Contamination: trace-metal-free containers essential.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ACGIH Nickel Biological Exposure Indices; manufacturer IFU.

name: NICOTINE
interpretation: Serum Nicotine measures the concentration of nicotine, the addictive alkaloid in tobacco. Nicotine is metabolised to cotinine (primary metabolite). Serum nicotine half-life: 1-2 hours. Cotinine half-life: 16-20 hours (more stable marker of exposure). Detection window: nicotine 2-3 days, cotinine 7-10 days. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note smoking history, secondhand exposure, NRT use. Handle per standard. Nicotine half-life: 1-2h. Cotinine: more stable (16-20h). Detection: nicotine 2-3 days, cotinine 7-10 days. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (non-smoker). Positive: tobacco exposure. Cotinine: more stable marker. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: CDC Tobacco Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NICOTINE RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Nicotine Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of nicotine and its major metabolite cotinine in urine. Nicotine is the primary psychoactive component of tobacco. Cotinine is the primary metabolite of nicotine (half-life 16-20h vs nicotine half-life 2h). Clinical use: verifying tobacco/nicotine use (smoking cessation programs), detecting nicotine exposure (workplace, insurance), assessing secondhand smoke exposure (cotinine), monitoring compliance with smoking cessation. Detection window: nicotine urine detectable for 1-3 days; cotinine detectable for up to 7-10 days (longer half-life). Positive result: indicates nicotine/tobacco use within detection window. Limitations: immunoassay detects nicotine AND cotinine. Cross-reactivity: nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum, lozenges, e-cigarettes, vapes) will cause positive result (nicotine from any source detected). Passive smoke exposure: can cause positive cotinine (secondhand smoke) - though typically lower levels than active smoking. E-cigarettes/vaping: nicotine-containing e-cigarettes will cause positive result (nicotine is nicotine regardless of source). Replacement therapy: patches, gum, lozenges contain nicotine - will test positive. Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay. Cotinine: more specific marker for nicotine exposure (longer half-life, better reflects tobacco use). Secondhand smoke: passive exposure can cause positive cotinine (levels lower than active smoking). Cotine levels: active smoking cotinine >> passive exposure cotinine. Assay variability: different immunoassays have different sensitivities for nicotine vs cotinine. Adulteration: urine validity testing required for workplace/forensic testing. Tobacco products: all tobacco products (cigarettes, cigars, pipe, chewing tobacco) contain nicotine. Herbal cigarettes: may not contain nicotine (depends on product). Timing: cotinine better reflects recent tobacco use than nicotine (longer half-life).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note tobacco use (cigarettes, cigars, pipe, chewing), nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum, lozenges), e-cigarette/vaping use, secondhand smoke exposure. Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Cut-off: immunoassay varies by manufacturer. Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Detection window: nicotine 1-3 days; cotinine 7-10 days. Cotinine: better marker (longer half-life). Active smoking: cotinine >> passive exposure. Replacement therapy: positive (nicotine from any source). E-cigarettes: positive (nicotine is nicotine). Passive smoke: can cause positive cotinine (lower levels). Chain of custody: required for legal/forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing required. Tobacco products: all contain nicotine. Herbal cigarettes: may not contain nicotine.
ref_ranges: Negative: below manufacturer-specific cut-off. Positive: above cut-off - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Detection window: nicotine 1-3 days; cotinine 7-10 days. Cotinine: better marker (longer half-life). Active smoking: cotinine >> passive exposure. Replacement therapy: positive. E-cigarettes: positive. Passive smoke: lower cotinine levels. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace: chain of custody required. Forensic: chain of custody required.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NORMETANEPHRINE FREE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Free Normetanephrine measures the concentration of free normetanephrine, the O-methylated metabolite of noradrenaline. Free normetanephrine is produced in chromaffin tissue and is a highly sensitive marker for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma. Sensitivity: greater than 98%. Specificity: 80-90%. False positives: anxiety, depression, SSA inhibitors, clonidine withdrawal. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). CRITICAL: supine fasting sample (30 minutes rest). Preparation: note paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, sweating, medications. Handle per standard. Sensitivity: greater than 98%. False positives: anxiety, medications. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma. Sensitivity: greater than 98%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS PPGL Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: NORTRIPTYLINE
interpretation: Serum Nortriptyline measures the concentration of nortriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA). Nortriptyline is the active metabolite of amitriptyline. Therapeutic range: 50 to 150 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500 ng/mL. TCA toxicity: anticholinergic effects, cardiotoxicity (QRS prolongation), seizures. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note depression, suicidal ideation, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 50-150 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500 ng/mL. Active metabolite: of amitriptyline. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 50 to 150 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500 ng/mL. Cardiotoxic: QRS prolongation. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: NSE - NEURON SPECIFIC ENOLASE
interpretation: Serum Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE) is a tumour marker for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and neuroendocrine tumours. NSE is an enzyme found in neurons and neuroendocrine cells. Elevated NSE: SCLC (sensitivity 60-80%), neuroblastoma, carcinoid, medullary thyroid carcinoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note lung cancer, neuroendocrine tumours. Handle per standard. Elevated: SCLC (60-80%), neuroblastoma. Neuroendocrine: tumour marker. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 16.3 ng/mL (method-specific). Elevated: SCLC, neuroblastoma. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESMO SCLC Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OGTT–DIPSI(Single sample 2Hrs after Glucose)FOR SCREENING OF GDM
interpretation: DIPSI (Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group of India) OGTT is a simplified screening test for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) recommended by Indian guidelines. The patient does NOT fast and consumes a regular meal followed by a 75g glucose load. Blood glucose is measured at 2 hours post-load only. A single value greater than or equal to 140 mg/dL at 2 hours is diagnostic of GDM. The DIPSI method is designed for resource-limited settings where fasting OGTT is impractical. The IADPSG criteria (fasting 75g OGTT) remain the gold standard internationally. Limitations: non-fasting protocol. Less reproducible than fasting OGTT. Reference ranges: DIPSI criteria (greater than or equal to 140 mg/dL at 2 hours).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. No fasting required (non-fasting protocol). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, recent meal. Handle per standard. DIPSI: non-fasting. 75g load: 2-hour sample only. Greater than or equal to 140 mg/dL: GDM. Less reproducible: than fasting OGTT. Reference ranges: DIPSI.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL at 2 hours. GDM: greater than or equal to 140 mg/dL. Non-fasting: DIPSI protocol. Less reproducible: than fasting OGTT. Reference ranges: DIPSI.
refs: Sources: DIPSI Guidelines; IADPSG Consensus; manufacturer IFU.

name: OLIGOCLONAL BAND - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Oligoclonal Bands (OCB) detect restricted heterogeneity of intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis. OCB are present in: multiple sclerosis (MS) (sensitivity 90-95%, specificity 95%), neurosyphilis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), other CNS infections. OCB in CSF but not in serum (Type 2): intrathecal synthesis. Reference ranges: qualitative.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF and serum (paired). Preparation: note neurological symptoms, MS suspicion. Handle per standard. Type 2: CSF only (intrathecal). MS: 90-95% sensitivity, 95% specificity. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (no OCB in CSF). Positive: intrathecal Ig synthesis. MS: 90-95% sensitivity. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: McDonald MS Diagnostic Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: ORGANIC ACID (QUANTIATIVE) - FULL PANEL
interpretation: Urine Organic Acid Quantitative (Full Panel) is a comprehensive metabolic screen for inborn errors of metabolism (IEM). Panel identifies organic acidurias: methylmalonic aciduria, propionic aciduria, isovaleric aciduria, maple syrup urine disease, glutaric aciduria type I, and others. Detection: elevated organic acids and their metabolites in urine. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random or 24h). Preparation: note metabolic symptoms, developmental delay, family history. Handle: frozen. Comprehensive: panel. Organic acidurias: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by metabolite. Elevated: organic acidurias. Comprehensive: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: ORNITHINE SCREEN
interpretation: Blood Ornithine Screen measures ornithine concentration. Elevated ornithine: hyperornithinaemia-hyperammonaemia-homocitrullinuria (HHH) syndrome, gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina. Ornithine: amino acid in urea cycle. HHH syndrome: intellectual disability, seizures, liver disease. Gyrate atrophy: progressive visual loss. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Blood (DBS or plasma). Preparation: note developmental delay, visual loss, seizures. Handle per standard. Elevated: HHH syndrome, gyrate atrophy. Ornithine: urea cycle. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: HHH syndrome, gyrate atrophy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OROTIC ACID
interpretation: Urine Orotic Acid measures orotic acid concentration. Orotic acid is an intermediate in pyrimidine biosynthesis. Elevated orotic acid: orotic aciduria (uridine monophosphate synthase deficiency), ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (most common urea cycle defect). OTC deficiency: X-linked, hyperammonaemia, neurological damage. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). Preparation: note metabolic symptoms, developmental delay, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: OTC deficiency (most common urea cycle defect). Hyperammonaemia: risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: OTC deficiency, orotic aciduria. OTC: most common urea cycle defect. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OSMOLALITY
interpretation: Serum Osmolality - measurement of the concentration of solutes in serum (osmotic pressure). Reflects total solute concentration (electrolytes, glucose, urea, and other small molecules). Most important test for assessing water balance and hydration status.
