Clinical use: evaluating hydration status (hyperosmolality = dehydration; hypoosmolality = overhydration), diagnosing hyponatraemia aetiology (hypotonic, isotonic, hypertonic), assessing ADH function (central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), monitoring DKA therapy (osmolality guides fluid management), detecting toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol, ethylene glycol - osmolal gap). Elevated serum osmolality: dehydration (most common cause - water deficit), hyperglycaemia (glucose raises osmolality - DKA), hypernatraemia, methanol/ethylene glycol ingestion (osmolal gap), urea elevation (renal failure), contrast dye (post-radiological procedures), mannitol administration. Low serum osmolality: overhydration (water excess), hyponatraemia, SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion), beer potomania (low solute intake), psychogenic polydipsia (excessive water intake). Osmolal gap: measured osmolality minus calculated osmolality. Calculated osmolality = (2 x Na) + (glucose/18) + (BUN/2.8). Normal osmolal gap: <10 mOsm/kg. Elevated osmolal gap: >10 mOsm/kg suggests unmeasured solutes (methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropanol, acetone, lactic acid). Clinical use: osmolal gap >10 + high anion gap = toxic alcohol ingestion until proven otherwise. Limitations: serum osmolality affected by: glucose (hyperglycaemia raises osmolality - use corrected osmolality), urea (BUN raises osmolality but does not cause cellular dehydration), sodium (main determinant of serum osmolality), ethanol (raises osmolality). Corrected osmolality: adjust for glucose (osmolality rises 1.6 mOsm/kg per 100 mg/dL glucose). Osmolal gap: more useful than absolute osmolality for detecting toxic ingestion. Serum osmolality and sodium: sodium is main determinant - serum osmolality tracks sodium closely. Serum osmolality and ADH: ADH regulates water balance - serum osmolality is the primary stimulus for ADH release. Diabetes insipidus: central (no ADH) or nephrogenic (ADH resistance) - dilute urine + high serum osmolality. SIADH: excessive ADH - concentrated urine + low serum osmolality. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: osmolality stable across age groups. Pregnancy: osmolality mildly reduced (physiological haemodilution). Assay: freezing point depression (gold standard) or vapour pressure osmometry.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (or plasma). Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note hydration status, glucose level, renal function, recent IV fluids, mannitol use, contrast dye, alcohol use, diabetes, SIADH symptoms. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Freezing point depression: gold standard method. Vapour pressure osmometry: alternative method. Osmolal gap: measured - calculated. Calculated: (2 x Na) + (glucose/18) + (BUN/2.8). Normal gap: <10 mOsm/kg. Elevated gap: toxic alcohol ingestion. Corrected osmolality: adjust for glucose. Hyperglycaemia: osmolality rises 1.6 mOsm/kg per 100 mg/dL glucose. Diabetes insipidus: dilute urine + high serum osmolality. SIADH: concentrated urine + low serum osmolality. DKA: osmolality guides fluid management. Toxic ingestion: osmolal gap >10 + high anion gap. Sodium: main determinant of serum osmolality. ADH: regulates water balance. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 275-295 mOsm/kg. Dehydration: >295 mOsm/kg. Overhydration: <275 mOsm/kg. Hyperglycaemia: osmolality elevated (correct for glucose). SIADH: <275 mOsm/kg. Diabetes insipidus: >295 mOsm/kg. Osmolal gap: <10 mOsm/kg normal; >10 = toxic ingestion until proven otherwise. Methanol/ethylene glycol: osmolal gap >20 mOsm/kg. Mannitol: osmolality elevated. Contrast: osmolality transiently elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: stable across age groups. Pregnancy: mildly reduced. Assay: freezing point depression (gold standard).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ACEP Toxic Alcohol Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OSMOLALITY - URINE
interpretation: Urine Osmolality - measurement of the concentration of solutes in urine. Reflects the kidney's ability to concentrate or dilute urine. Used alongside serum osmolality to evaluate water balance and ADH function. Clinical use: evaluating ADH function (central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), assessing hydration status (concentrated urine = dehydrated; dilute urine = overhydrated), diagnosing SIADH (inappropriately concentrated urine), evaluating renal concentrating ability, assessing polyuria/polydipsia aetiology. Elevated urine osmolality: dehydration (kidney conserving water), SIADH (inappropriate ADH - concentrated urine despite low serum osmolality), acute kidney injury (reduced concentrating ability), heart failure (reduced renal perfusion), liver cirrhosis (sodium/water retention), adrenal insufficiency. Low urine osmolality: diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic - dilute urine despite dehydration), psychogenic polydipsia (excessive water intake - dilute urine), osmotic diuresis (glucose, urea in urine). Clinical approach: paired serum and urine osmolality interpretation: serum osmolality high + urine osmolality high = appropriate renal response (dehydration, hyperglycaemia). Serum osmolality high + urine osmolality low = diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic). Serum osmolality low + urine osmolality high = SIADH (inappropriate ADH). Serum osmolality low + urine osmolality low = psychogenic polydipsia (appropriate renal dilution). Limitations: urine osmolality is influenced by: hydration status (concentrated vs dilute), solute intake (high protein diet = higher urine osmolality), time of day (morning urine more concentrated), recent fluid intake, medications (lithium - impairs concentrating ability). Spot urine vs 24h urine: spot urine osmolality reflects current hydration state; 24h urine osmolality integrates over 24h. Reference ranges vary widely: urine osmolality ranges from 50-1200 mOsm/kg depending on hydration. Water deprivation test: gold standard for diabetes insipidus (measure urine osmolality after dehydration - DI patients cannot concentrate urine). Lithium: impairs renal concentrating ability - urine osmolality may be low. Age: elderly have reduced concentrating ability. Pregnancy: reduced concentrating ability.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note hydration status, recent fluid intake, time of day, medications (lithium, diuretics), diabetes insipidus symptoms, SIADH symptoms. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Spot urine: reflects current hydration. 24h urine: integrates over 24h. Paired serum/urine: essential for interpretation. DI: high serum osmolality + low urine osmolality. SIADH: low serum osmolality + high urine osmolality. Dehydration: high serum + high urine osmolality. Polydipsia: low serum + low urine osmolality. Water deprivation test: gold standard for DI (cannot concentrate urine). Lithium: impairs concentrating ability. Age: elderly reduced concentrating ability. Pregnancy: reduced concentrating ability. Reference ranges: 50-1200 mOsm/kg (wide range). Solute intake: affects urine osmolality. Time of day: morning more concentrated.
ref_ranges: Normal: 50-1200 mOsm/kg (wide range depending on hydration). Concentrated: >800 mOsm/kg (dehydration). Dilute: <200 mOsm/kg (overhydration). SIADH: >500 mOsm/kg despite low serum osmolality. Diabetes insipidus: <200 mOsm/kg despite high serum osmolality. Water deprivation test: DI fails to concentrate (>500 mOsm/kg excludes DI). Psychogenic polydipsia: <200 mOsm/kg. Lithium: reduced concentrating ability. Age: elderly reduced concentrating ability. Pregnancy: reduced concentrating ability. Reference ranges: wide variation. Assay: freezing point depression (gold standard). Paired serum/urine essential.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Diabetes Insipidus Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OSTEOCALCIN / BONE GLA PROTEIN (GGP)
interpretation: Serum Osteocalcin (Bone Gla Protein, BGP) is a non-collagenous protein produced by osteoblasts and used as a marker of bone formation. Osteocalcin reflects osteoblast activity and bone turnover. Elevated: Paget disease, primary hyperparathyroidism, acromegaly, bone metastases. Low: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note bone disease, parathyroid disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism. Low: hypothyroidism, GHD. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism. Low: hypothyroidism, GHD. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OVARIAN ANTIBODY AOA
interpretation: Serum Ovarian Antibody (AOA) measures autoantibodies against ovarian tissue. AOA are associated with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), autoimmune oophoritis, and Addison disease. AOA are present in approximately 60% of idiopathic POI cases. AOA combined with adrenal antibodies (21-hydroxylase) increases predictive value for autoimmune POI. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note premature menopause, amenorrhoea, Addison disease. Handle per standard. Positive: POI risk. Combined: with adrenal antibodies. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: POI risk (60% sensitivity). Combined: adrenal antibodies. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society POI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: OXCARBAZEPINE
interpretation: Serum Oxcarbazepine measures the concentration of oxcarbazepine, an anticonvulsant and prodrug of the active metabolite licarbazepine (10-monohydroxy derivative). Oxcarbazepine is used to treat focal seizures. Therapeutic range: 10 to 40 mcg/mL (licarbazepine). Hyponatraemia: risk (SIADH). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, sodium levels, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 10-40 mcg/mL (licarbazepine). Hyponatraemia: risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 10 to 40 mcg/mL (licarbazepine). Hyponatraemia: risk (SIADH). Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: P1NP(PROCOLLAGEN TYPE 1 AMINO TERMINAL PROPEPTIDE)
interpretation: Serum Procollagen Type 1 N-terminal Propeptide (P1NP) is a bone formation marker. P1NP is released during type I collagen synthesis and reflects osteoblast activity. Elevated: Paget disease, primary hyperparathyroidism, acromegaly, bone metastases, fracture healing. Low: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency. P1NP is more stable and less variable than other bone formation markers. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note bone disease, parathyroid disease. Handle per standard. Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism, mets. Low: hypothyroidism. More stable: than other bone markers. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: Paget, hyperparathyroidism, bone mets. More stable: than other bone markers. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IOF Bone Marker Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PALMITOYL PROTEIN THIOESTERASE
interpretation: Blood Palmitoyl Protein Thioesterase (PPT1) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme palmitoyl protein thioesterase 1. PPT1 deficiency causes Infantile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (CLN1, Batten disease), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. CLN1: progressive neurodegeneration, seizures, retinal degeneration, developmental regression. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note seizures, developmental regression, visual loss, family history. Handle per standard. Low: CLN1 (Batten disease). Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 1.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: CLN1 (Batten disease). Genotyping: confirm. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG LSD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PAPP-A (PREGNANCY ASSOCIATED PLASMA PROTEIN-A)-AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein-A (PAPP-A) - glycoprotein produced by the placenta (syncytiotrophoblast) during pregnancy. Levels rise throughout pregnancy, peaking at term. Used in first-trimester screening for Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and other chromosomal abnormalities. Clinical use: first-trimester screening for trisomy 21 (combined screening: PAPP-A + free beta-hCG + nuchal translucency + maternal age - detection rate 85-90%), screening for trisomy 13 and 18, screening for preeclampsia (low PAPP-A at 11-13 weeks associated with increased risk), assessing placental function. Low PAPP-A: trisomy 21 (Down syndrome - PAPP-A low in 80% of cases), trisomy 13 and 18, preeclampsia risk (low PAPP-A at 11-13 weeks), intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), miscarriage risk (very low PAPP-A). High PAPP-A: triploidy (triploid pregnancies may have very high PAPP-A), multiple pregnancy (higher PAPP-A in twins/triplets). Limitations: PAPP-A is a SCREENING test - positive result requires confirmatory testing (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, cell-free DNA). PAPP-A is PREGNANCY-SPECIFIC - not useful outside pregnancy. Gestational age: PAPP-A levels depend on accurate gestational dating (crown-rump length measurement). Multiple pregnancy: PAPP-A higher in twins/triplets - adjust for plurality. Assay variability: DELFIA assay is most common (Auto DELFIA platform). Ethnicity: PAPP-A levels vary between ethnic groups - adjusted in screening algorithms. Smoking: lowers PAPP-A (reduced placental function). IVF pregnancies: PAPP-A may be altered - adjust screening algorithms. False positives: 5% false positive rate in combined screening. Confirmatory testing: all screen-positive results require confirmatory testing (amniocentesis, CVS, cell-free DNA). Low PAPP-A in first trimester: associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes (preeclampsia, IUGR, preterm delivery, miscarriage) even with normal karyotype. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific (weeks + days). PAPP-A and free beta-hCG: combined for trisomy 21 risk calculation. PAPP-A and MoM: levels expressed as multiples of median (MoM) for gestational age.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: gestational age must be accurately determined (crown-rump length measurement). Preparation: note gestational age, number of fetuses (singleton vs multiple), IVF pregnancy, smoking status, ethnicity, previous chromosomal abnormality. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First-trimester screening: 11-13+6 weeks (CRL 45-84 mm). Combined screening: PAPP-A + free beta-hCG + nuchal translucency + maternal age. Detection rate: 85-90% for trisomy 21. False positive rate: 5%. PAPP-A low: trisomy 21 (80% of cases). PAPP-A high: triploidy, multiple pregnancy. Gestational age: accurate dating essential. Multiple pregnancy: higher PAPP-A. IVF: adjust algorithms. Smoking: lowers PAPP-A. Preeclampsia: low PAPP-A at 11-13 weeks = increased risk. Confirmatory: amniocentesis, CVS, cell-free DNA. MoM: levels expressed as multiples of median. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal first trimester (11-13+6 weeks): 0.4-2.0 MoM (multiples of median). Low: <0.4 MoM (trisomy 21 risk). Very low: <0.2 MoM (high risk chromosomal abnormality). High: >2.0 MoM (triploidy, multiple pregnancy). Trisomy 21: PAPP-A low in 80% of cases. Preeclampsia: low PAPP-A associated with increased risk. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific (weeks + days). MoM: levels expressed as multiples of median for gestational age. Multiple pregnancy: higher PAPP-A. Ethnicity: levels vary between ethnic groups. Assay: DELFIA platform most common.
refs: Sources: Fetal Medicine Foundation Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PARATHYROID HORMONE (iPTH)
interpretation: Intact Parathyroid Hormone (iPTH) - measurement of the full-length PTH molecule (1-84 amino acids) using a two-site immunoradiometric or immunoluminometric assay. PTH is secreted by parathyroid glands in response to low serum calcium. Regulates calcium homeostasis (bone, kidney, intestine). Most important test for evaluating hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism. Elevated iPTH: primary hyperparathyroidism (most common cause of hypercalcaemia in outpatients - PTH elevated despite elevated calcium), tertiary hyperparathyroidism (autonomous PTH secretion after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism), familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH - PTH may be normal or mildly elevated), lithium therapy (PTH elevated), vitamin D deficiency (PTH elevated secondary to low calcium). Low iPTH: hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical - most common cause; autoimmune; DiGeorge syndrome), hypomagnesaemia (impairs PTH secretion), autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, infiltrative diseases (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, metastases), lithium (chronic use may cause hypoparathyroidism), severe hypercalcaemia (suppresses PTH). Clinical use: hypercalcaemia evaluation (PTH elevated = primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH suppressed = non-PTH-mediated hypercalcaemia - malignancy, granulomatous disease), hypocalcaemia evaluation (PTH low = hypoparathyroidism), monitoring parathyroidectomy (PTH monitored intra-operatively), preoperative localisation of parathyroid adenoma (PTH helps distinguish adenoma from hyperplasia), renal osteodystrophy (secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD). Limitations: PTH is PULSATILE (secreted in pulses) - random levels may not reflect average secretion. PTH is CALCIUM-DEPENDENT: PTH should be interpreted alongside serum calcium (PTH elevated with low calcium = appropriate response; PTH elevated with high calcium = primary hyperparathyroidism). PTH is VITAMIN D-DEPENDENT: vitamin D deficiency raises PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) - check vitamin D before interpreting PTH. PTH and CKD: chronic kidney disease causes secondary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH) - common in dialysis patients. PTH and magnesium: hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion - check magnesium. PTH and calcium: PTH should be interpreted alongside calcium (PTH elevated with low calcium = appropriate; PTH elevated with high calcium = primary hyperparathyroidism). PTH and vitamin D: vitamin D deficiency raises PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) - correct vitamin D first. PTH assay variability: different assays detect different PTH fragments - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. PTH and FHH: calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 distinguishes FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism. PTH and malignancy: PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) causes hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH (PTHrP not detected by PTH assay).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note calcium level, vitamin D status, magnesium level, kidney function (eGFR), recent parathyroid surgery, lithium use, family history of hyperparathyroidism. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Hypercalcaemia: PTH + calcium + vitamin D + magnesium. PTH elevated + calcium elevated = primary hyperparathyroidism. PTH suppressed + calcium elevated = non-PTH-mediated (malignancy, PTHrP). PTH elevated + calcium low = secondary hyperparathyroidism (vitamin D deficiency, CKD). Hypocalcaemia: PTH + calcium + magnesium. PTH low + calcium low = hypoparathyroidism. PTH elevated + calcium low = appropriate response (vitamin D deficiency). CKD: secondary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH). Parathyroidectomy: intra-operative PTH monitoring (PTH drop >50% = successful surgery). FHH: calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01. Vitamin D: correct deficiency before interpreting PTH. Magnesium: hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion.
ref_ranges: Adults: 10-65 pg/mL (method-specific). Hyperparathyroidism: PTH elevated with elevated calcium. Hypoparathyroidism: PTH low with low calcium. Secondary hyperparathyroidism: PTH elevated with low/normal calcium (vitamin D deficiency, CKD). Tertiary: PTH elevated with elevated calcium (autonomous secretion). FHH: PTH normal/mildly elevated with elevated calcium. PTH and calcium: interpret together. PTH and vitamin D: correct deficiency first. PTH and CKD: elevated in renal failure. Reference ranges: method-specific. PTH assays detect different fragments. Age: PTH may increase with age. Pregnancy: PTH may be low (physiological).
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Hyperparathyroidism Guidelines; KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHENCYCLIDINE
interpretation: Phencyclidine (PCP) Urine Drug Test - qualitative detection of phencyclidine in urine. PCP is a dissociative anaesthetic (Schedule II controlled substance) with hallucinogenic, stimulant, and depressant effects. Clinical use: detecting PCP use, drug screening (workplace, forensic), evaluating patients with unexplained agitation/violence/psychosis, substance abuse treatment monitoring. Detection window: urine PCP detectable for 1-8 days in occasional users, up to 14-30 days in chronic/heavy users (lipophilic - accumulates in fat tissue). Positive result: indicates PCP use within detection window. Limitations: PCP is LIPID-SOLUBLE - accumulates in fat tissue, prolonged detection in chronic users. False positives: possible with some medications (dextromethorphan [DXM] at high doses, ketamine - though structurally related). Cross-reactivity: ketamine (structurally similar dissociative) may cross-react on some immunoassays. Confirmation testing: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS required to confirm positive immunoassay. PCP effects: dissociative anaesthesia, hallucinations, agitation, violence, psychosis, nystagmus, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, seizures. Clinical presentation: unexplained agitation/violence, nystagmus (horizontal/vertical), hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, blank stare, numbness. Detection window: 1-8 days (occasional); up to 14-30 days (chronic, lipophilic). Street names: angel dust, hog, wack, ozone, phencyclidine. Adulteration: urine validity testing required for workplace/forensic testing. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment (metabolite persists). Co-ingestion: PCP often combined with other drugs (marijuana, amphetamines, opioids). Assay availability: PCP-specific immunoassays available but not universally offered in standard drug panels.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note any recent drug use, psychiatric symptoms, agitation, nystagmus. Handling: 2-8C up to 72h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. Cut-off: immunoassay typically 25 ng/mL. Confirmation: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-8 days (occasional); up to 14-30 days (chronic). Lipophilic: accumulates in fat tissue. Clinical: agitation, violence, nystagmus, hypertension. Cross-reactivity: ketamine (structurally similar). False positives: dextromethorphan (high doses). Chain of custody: required for legal/forensic testing. Adulteration: urine validity testing required. Co-ingestion: often combined with other drugs. Impairment: urine positive does NOT indicate current impairment. Street names: angel dust, hog, wack, ozone.
ref_ranges: Negative: <25 ng/mL (immunoassay cut-off). Positive: >=25 ng/mL (immunoassay) - confirm with GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Detection window: 1-30 days (frequency-dependent, lipophilic). Confirmation: GC-MS/LC-MS/MS. Cross-reactivity: ketamine, dextromethorphan. Reference ranges: method-specific. Workplace testing: SAMHSA guidelines apply. Forensic: chain of custody required. Clinical: agitation, violence, nystagmus, hypertension. Lipophilic: prolonged detection in chronic users.
refs: Sources: SAMHSA Workplace Drug Testing Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHENOBARBITONE
interpretation: Serum Phenobarbitone measures the concentration of phenobarbitone, a barbiturate anticonvulsant. Phenobarbitone is used to treat generalised and focal seizures. Therapeutic range: 15 to 40 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 40 mcg/mL. Long half-life: 40-100 hours. Induction: of hepatic enzymes (CYP450). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, sedation, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 15-40 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 40. Long half-life: 40-100h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 15 to 40 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 40. Long half-life: 40-100h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHENYLALANINE (QUANTITATIVE) - RANDOM URINE
interpretation: Urine Phenylalanine Quantitative (spot) measures phenylalanine concentration. Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid. Elevated phenylalanine: phenylketonuria (PKU) (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency). PKU: intellectual disability, seizures, behavioural problems, musty odour. Screening: newborn screening (Guthrie test). Treatment: low-phenylalanine diet. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note developmental delay, seizures, musty odour, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: PKU. Intellectual disability: risk. Newborn screening: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: PKU. Newborn screening: detection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG PKU Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHENYTOIN
interpretation: Serum Phenytoin measures the concentration of phenytoin, an anticonvulsant used to treat generalised and focal seizures and status epilepticus. Therapeutic range: 10 to 20 mcg/mL (total). Phenytoin is highly protein-bound (90%) and has nonlinear (saturable) pharmacokinetics. Small dose increases can cause large level increases. Free (unbound) phenytoin: more accurate in hypoalbuminaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). CRITICAL: trough level. Preparation: note seizure control, albumin, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 10-20 mcg/mL. Nonlinear: saturation kinetics. Free: more accurate if low albumin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 10 to 20 mcg/mL (total). Nonlinear: saturable. Free: if low albumin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHOSPHORUS
interpretation: Serum Phosphorus (Phosphate) - measurement of inorganic phosphate in serum. Phosphate is essential for bone mineralisation, energy metabolism (ATP), cell membrane structure (phospholipids), and acid-base buffering. ~85% of body phosphate in bone, ~14% intracellular, ~1% extracellular. Clinical use: hypophosphataemia evaluation, hyperphosphataemia monitoring (CKD, dialysis), assessing bone metabolism, monitoring phosphate binder therapy, evaluating rickets/osteomalacia. Elevated serum phosphorus: chronic kidney disease (most common cause - reduced renal excretion), hypoparathyroidism (reduced renal excretion), hyperparathyroidism (tertiary), tumour lysis syndrome (massive cell lysis releases phosphate), phosphate-containing laxatives/enemas, Vitamin D intoxication (increased intestinal absorption), metabolic acidosis (phosphate shifts extracellularly), rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown releases phosphate), acromegaly. Low serum phosphorus: hyperparathyroidism (increased renal exposition), Vitamin D deficiency (reduced absorption), malnutrition/starvation, alcoholism (poor intake + renal wasting), diabetes mellitus (phosphate depletion), respiratory alkalosis (phosphate shifts intracellularly), phosphate-binding antacids (reduced absorption), Fanconi syndrome (renal phosphate wasting), X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets. Limitations: serum phosphorus is HIGHLY VARIABLE (circadian rhythm - lowest in morning, highest at night; post-prandial changes). Phosphorus affected by: fasting status (fasting lowers phosphorus), time of day (circadian variation), meals (post-prandial rise), glucose (glucose raises insulin - drives phosphate intracellularly), respiratory status (alkalosis lowers phosphorus; acidosis raises), PTH (PTH lowers phosphorus - renal excretion). Serum phosphorus represents only ~1% of total body phosphate - normal serum does NOT exclude total body depletion. Phosphorus and calcium: inverse relationship (PTH lowers phosphorus, raises calcium). Phosphorus and Vitamin D: Vitamin D raises phosphorus (increased intestinal absorption). Phosphorus and CKD: hyperphosphataemia in CKD - monitor with calcium and PTH (CKD-MBD). Phosphorus and rickets: hypophosphataemia + low Vitamin D = rickets/osteomalacia. Phosphorus and tumour lysis: hyperphosphataemia from massive cell lysis - emergency. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: higher in children (bone growth). Pregnancy: lower (physiological haemodilution + fetal demand).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: fasting preferred (post-prandial variability). Preparation: note renal function (eGFR), PTH level, Vitamin D status, medications (phosphate binders, diuretics), recent IV fluids, tumour lysis risk, rhabdomyolysis risk. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting: 8-12h preferred. CKD: hyperphosphataemia (monitor with calcium, PTH). Tumour lysis: hyperphosphataemia (emergency). Rhabdomyolysis: hyperphosphataemia. Rickets: hypophosphataemia + low Vitamin D. PTH: PTH lowers phosphorus. Vitamin D: raises phosphorus. Respiratory: alkalosis lowers phosphorus. Circadian: lowest morning, highest night. Phosphorus and calcium: inverse relationship. CKD-MBD: monitor phosphorus, calcium, PTH together. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: higher in children. Pregnancy: lower.
ref_ranges: Adults: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL (0.81-1.45 mmol/L) - method-specific. Children: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL (higher - bone growth). Hyperphosphataemia: >4.5 mg/dL (>1.45 mmol/L). Hypophosphataemia: <2.5 mg/dL (<0.81 mmol/L). CKD: hyperphosphataemia common (eGFR <30). Tumour lysis: hyperphosphataemia emergency. Rickets: hypophosphataemia + low Vitamin D. PTH: PTH lowers phosphorus. Vitamin D: raises phosphorus. Circadian: varies with time of day. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: higher in children. Pregnancy: lower. Method: varies between laboratories.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PHOSPHORUS SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Urine Phosphorus Spot - measurement of phosphorus (phosphate) concentration in a random (spot) urine sample. Used alongside serum phosphorus to evaluate renal phosphate handling and differentiate causes of hypophosphataemia or hyperphosphataemia. Clinical use: evaluating renal phosphate wasting (elevated urine phosphorus in hypophosphataemia), assessing phosphate reabsorption, monitoring phosphate supplementation therapy, evaluating rickets/osteomalacia aetiology, assessing tumour lysis syndrome. Elevated urine phosphorus: hyperparathyroidism (PTH increases renal phosphate excretion), phosphate supplementation (high intake), osmotic diuresis (glucose in urine), Fanconi syndrome (renal phosphate wasting), X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (renal phosphate wasting), Vitamin D deficiency (reduced intestinal absorption - kidney excretes less). Low urine phosphorus: hypoparathyroidism (reduced renal excretion), phosphate depletion (low intake), Vitamin D intoxication (increased intestinal absorption - kidney excretes more), growth hormone deficiency, acromegaly. Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO4): FEPO4 = (UPh x SCr) / (SPh x SCr) x 100. FEPO4 >5%: renal phosphate wasting (elevated urine phosphorus despite low serum). FEPO4 <5%: appropriate renal conservation. Limitations: spot urine phosphorus influenced by: dietary phosphate intake (high phosphate diet raises urine phosphorus), hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low concentration), time of day (circadian variation), recent meals (post-prandial rise). 24-hour urine phosphorus: more accurate than spot urine (integrates over 24h). Spot urine phosphorus/creatinine ratio: adjusts for hydration (phosphorus divided by creatinine). Reference ranges vary between laboratories. Dietary influence: high phosphate diet (dairy, meat, cola) raises urine phosphorus. Phosphorus and PTH: PTH increases urine phosphorus (renal excretion). Phosphorus and Vitamin D: Vitamin D decreases urine phosphorus (increased intestinal absorption). Rickets: hypophosphataemia + elevated urine phosphorus = renal phosphate wasting (Fanconi, XLH). Tumour lysis: hyperphosphataemia + elevated urine phosphorus (massive cell lysis). CKD: hyperphosphataemia + low urine phosphorus (reduced GFR - kidney cannot excrete phosphorus).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note dietary phosphate intake, PTH level, Vitamin D status, renal function (eGFR), phosphate supplementation, rickets/osteomalacia history. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. 24h urine: more accurate than spot. Phosphorus/Cr ratio: adjusts for hydration. FEPO4: fractional excretion of phosphate (if paired serum available). Hyperparathyroidism: elevated urine phosphorus. Fanconi syndrome: elevated urine phosphorus + hypophosphataemia. XLH: elevated urine phosphorus + hypophosphataemia. CKD: low urine phosphorus + hyperphosphataemia. Rickets: hypophosphataemia + elevated urine phosphorus = renal wasting. Tumour lysis: hyperphosphataemia + elevated urine phosphorus. Dietary: high phosphate diet raises urine phosphorus. Circadian: varies with time of day.
ref_ranges: Random urine: 13-47 mg/dL (4.2-15.2 mmol/L) - method-specific. 24-hour urine: 400-1300 mg/day (13-42 mmol/day). FEPO4: <5% = appropriate renal conservation; >5% = renal phosphate wasting. Spot urine phosphorus/Cr ratio: varies with dietary intake. Renal wasting: FEPO4 >5% (hypophosphataemia + elevated urine phosphorus). Appropriate conservation: FEPO4 <5%. Reference ranges: method-specific. Dietary intake: affects urine phosphorus significantly. Circadian: varies with time of day. Age: varies with age. Pregnancy: urine phosphorus may be elevated.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD-MBD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PIIINP (PROCOLLAGEN TYPE III AMINO TERMINAL PROPEPTIDE)
interpretation: Serum Procollagen Type III N-terminal Propeptide (PIIINP) is a marker of type III collagen synthesis and fibrosis. PIIINP is used to assess liver fibrosis (as an alternative to liver biopsy), cardiac fibrosis, and pulmonary fibrosis. Elevated: hepatic fibrosis, cardiac fibrosis, interstitial lung disease, wound healing. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver disease, cardiac disease, pulmonary fibrosis. Handle per standard. Elevated: fibrosis (liver, cardiac, pulmonary). Non-invasive: alternative to biopsy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: fibrosis. Non-invasive: alternative to biopsy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: EASL Liver Fibrosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PLAC TEST (LIPOPROTEIN-ASSOCIATED PHOSPHOLIPASE A2) - LP - PLA2 ACTIVITY
interpretation: Serum Lipoprotein-Associated Phospholipase A2 (Lp-PLA2, PLAC test) is a vascular-specific inflammatory marker. Lp-PLA2 is produced by inflammatory cells and is associated with atherosclerosis and cardiovascular risk. Elevated Lp-PLA2: increased cardiovascular risk (stroke, MI). Lp-PLA2 activity: more reliable than mass. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note cardiovascular risk factors. Handle per standard. Elevated: cardiovascular risk. Activity: more reliable than mass. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 200 nmol/min/mL (activity). Elevated: cardiovascular risk. Activity: more reliable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AHA CV Risk Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PLATELET ANTIBODIES BY IFA
interpretation: Serum Platelet Antibodies by Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA) detect autoantibodies against platelet surface glycoproteins. Platelet antibodies are used in the diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT), and post-transfusion purpura (PTP). Sensitivity: 60-80% for ITP. Specificity: greater than 95%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thrombocytopenia, bleeding, transfusion history. Handle per standard. Positive: ITP, NAIT, PTP. Sensitivity: 60-80%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: ITP, NAIT, PTP. Sensitivity: 60-80%. Specificity: greater than 95%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ASH ITP Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PLGF (PLACENTAL GROWTH FACTOR)-AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Placental Growth Factor (PlGF) - angiogenic protein belonging to the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) family. Produced primarily by the placenta (syncytiotrophoblast) during pregnancy. Levels rise during first trimester, peak at 28-32 weeks, then decline. Low PlGF is associated with impaired placental function and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Clinical use: preeclampsia screening (low PlGF at 11-13 weeks or 20-24 weeks predicts preeclampsia), assessing fetal growth restriction (FGR - low PlGF suggests impaired placental perfusion), differentiating preeclampsia from other causes of hypertension in pregnancy, predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm delivery, stillbirth). Low PlGF: preeclampsia (most important clinical finding - PlGF <5th centile for gestational age), severe preeclampsia (PlGF very low), fetal growth restriction (impaired placental perfusion), preterm delivery, stillbirth, placental insufficiency. High PlGF: normal pregnancy (PlGF rises in first trimester), multiple pregnancy (higher PlGF in twins/triplets). Limitations: PlGF is PREGNANCY-SPECIFIC - not useful outside pregnancy. PlGF is GESTATIONAL AGE-DEPENDENT - levels vary significantly with gestational age. PlGF levels vary between assays - use laboratory-specific reference ranges. PlGF alone has limited predictive value for preeclampsia - combined screening (PlGF + maternal factors + blood pressure + uterine artery Doppler) more predictive. PlGF and PAPP-A: combined first-trimester screening for preeclampsia (low PlGF + low PAPP-A = high risk). PlGF and sFlt-1: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio is more predictive than either alone (ratio >38 associated with preeclampsia). False positives: PlGF may be low in other conditions (FGR, preterm birth without preeclampsia). False negatives: PlGF may be normal in early preeclampsia (before 20 weeks). Timing: screening at 11-13 weeks (first trimester) and/or 20-24 weeks (second trimester). PlGF and Doppler: combined with uterine artery Doppler for improved prediction. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific. Ethnicity: limited data. IVF pregnancies: may need adjustment. Multiple pregnancy: higher PlGF.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note gestational age, number of fetuses (singleton vs multiple), IVF pregnancy, previous preeclampsia, hypertension history, FGR history. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Gestational age: accurate dating essential. First trimester: 11-13+6 weeks. Second trimester: 20-24 weeks. Preeclampsia: low PlGF (<5th centile). Combined screening: PlGF + maternal factors + BP + Doppler. sFlt-1/PlGF ratio: >38 associated with preeclampsia. FGR: low PlGF suggests impaired placental perfusion. Preterm delivery: low PlGF predicts risk. Stillbirth: low PlGF associated. Multiple pregnancy: higher PlGF. IVF: may need adjustment. Assay variability: use laboratory-specific reference ranges. Ethnicity: limited data. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal first trimester (11-13+6 weeks): >5th centile for gestational age. Low: <5th centile (preeclampsia risk). Very low: <1st centile (high risk preeclampsia). Preeclampsia: PlGF typically <5th centile. sFlt-1/PlGF ratio: >38 associated with preeclampsia. FGR: low PlGF. Multiple pregnancy: higher PlGF. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific. Assay: method-specific. Ethnicity: limited data. Timing: 11-13+6 weeks or 20-24 weeks.
refs: Sources: Fetal Medicine Foundation Preeclampsia Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POMPE DISEASE (DEFICIENCY OF NZYME ALPHA GLUCOSIDASE)
interpretation: Blood Acid Alpha-Glucosidase (GAA) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase. GAA deficiency causes Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. Infantile-onset: cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, death by age 1 if untreated. Late-onset: progressive proximal myopathy. Treatment: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT, alglucosidase alfa). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Dried blood spot (DBS) or leucocytes. Preparation: note hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, family history. Handle per standard. Low: Pompe disease. Infantile: cardiomyopathy. Late-onset: myopathy. ERT: treatment. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 3.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: Pompe disease. Infantile: cardiomyopathy. Late-onset: myopathy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Pompe Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PORPHYRIA PROFILE - URINE SPOT
interpretation: Urine Porphyria Profile is a comprehensive screen for porphyrin metabolism disorders. Profile includes: porphobilinogen (PBG), delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), uroporphyrin, coproporphyrin, protoporphyrin. Acute porphyrias: AIP, HCP, VP (elevated PBG, ALA). Cutaneous porphyrias: PCT, EPP (elevated porphyrins, normal PBG). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). Preparation: note abdominal pain, neuropathy, skin blistering, medications, family history. Handle: light-protected. PBG: acute porphyrias. Porphyrins: cutaneous. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable by metabolite. Acute: elevated PBG, ALA. Cutaneous: elevated porphyrins. Light-protected: required. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AIP Clinical Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POST BREAKFAST GLUCOSE
interpretation: Post Breakfast Plasma Glucose measures blood glucose concentration approximately 2 hours after a meal (typically breakfast). Used to monitor glycaemic control in diabetic patients. Target postprandial glucose is less than 180 mg/dL (ADA) or less than 160 mg/dL (some guidelines). Postprandial hyperglycaemia is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease and microvascular complications. The post-breakfast glucose is particularly important as morning cortisol (dawn phenomenon) and overnight insulin resistance can cause higher post-breakfast excursions compared to other meals. Limitations: timing is critical (approximately 2 hours after first bite). Pre-meal glucose affects postprandial result. Insulin timing and dose affect result. Reference ranges: ADA/IDF guidelines.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Timing: approximately 2 hours after breakfast. Preparation: note diabetes medications, insulin dose, pre-meal glucose, meal composition. Handle per standard. Target: less than 180 mg/dL (ADA). Dawn phenomenon: may elevate. Timing: critical (2 hours). Reference ranges: ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Target: less than 180 mg/dL (diabetic). Elevated: greater than 180 mg/dL. Dawn phenomenon: morning elevation. Timing: 2 hours post-meal. Reference ranges: ADA/IDF.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; IDF Postprandial Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POST DINNER GLUCOSE
interpretation: Post Dinner Plasma Glucose measures blood glucose concentration approximately 2 hours after evening meal. Used to monitor glycaemic control in diabetic patients. Post-dinner glucose is often lower than post-breakfast due to absence of dawn phenomenon and better insulin sensitivity later in the day. Target postprandial glucose is less than 180 mg/dL (ADA). Evening hyperglycaemia may indicate need for basal insulin adjustment or dietary modification. Limitations: timing is critical (approximately 2 hours after first bite). Pre-meal glucose affects result. Reference ranges: ADA guidelines.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Timing: approximately 2 hours after dinner. Preparation: note diabetes medications, insulin dose, pre-meal glucose, meal composition. Handle per standard. Target: less than 180 mg/dL. Evening: lower than morning (no dawn phenomenon). Reference ranges: ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Target: less than 180 mg/dL (diabetic). Evening: typically lower than morning. Timing: 2 hours post-meal. Reference ranges: ADA.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POST GLUCOSE PLASMA GLUCOSE 100 GRAMS (PGPG)
interpretation: Post Glucose Plasma Glucose (PGPG) 100 grams measures blood glucose at specific time points after a 100g oral glucose load. This test is used as part of the diagnostic OGTT for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Blood glucose is measured at 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours post-load. The results are interpreted using Carpenter-Coustan or NDDG criteria. Multiple time points allow assessment of glucose disposal rate and insulin response. Limitations: requires fasting beforehand. Inconvenient for patients (multiple blood draws). Stress and illness affect results. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan criteria.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, medications. Handle per standard. 100g load: 3 samples (1h, 2h, 3h). Carpenter-Coustan: 1h less than 180, 2h less than 155, 3h less than 140 mg/dL. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
ref_ranges: Normal: all values below cutoffs. 1 hour: less than 180 mg/dL. 2 hours: less than 155 mg/dL. 3 hours: less than 140 mg/dL. GDM: 2 or more abnormal. Reference ranges: Carpenter-Coustan.
refs: Sources: ACOG GDM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POST GLUCOSE PLASMA GLUCOSE 75 GRAMS (PGPG)
interpretation: Post Glucose Plasma Glucose (PGPG) 75 grams measures blood glucose at specific time points after a 75g oral glucose load. This test is used as part of the diagnostic OGTT for GDM (IADPSG criteria) or diabetes mellitus. Blood glucose is measured at 1 hour and 2 hours post-load. The results are interpreted using IADPSG criteria for GDM or WHO criteria for diabetes. The 75g load is simpler than the 100g load (fewer samples). Limitations: requires fasting beforehand. Reference ranges: IADPSG for GDM, WHO for diabetes.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting (8-14 hours). Preparation: note gestational age, risk factors, medications. Handle per standard. 75g load: 2 samples (1h, 2h). IADPSG: fasting less than 92, 1h less than 180, 2h less than 153 mg/dL. Reference ranges: IADPSG/WHO.
ref_ranges: Normal: all values below cutoffs. 1 hour: less than 180 mg/dL. 2 hours: less than 153 mg/dL (IADPSG) or less than 140 mg/dL (WHO). GDM: 1 or more abnormal (IADPSG). Reference ranges: IADPSG/WHO.
refs: Sources: IADPSG Consensus; WHO Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POST LUNCH GLUCOSE
interpretation: Post Lunch Plasma Glucose measures blood glucose concentration approximately 2 hours after midday meal. Used to monitor glycaemic control in diabetic patients. Target postprandial glucose is less than 180 mg/dL (ADA). Post-lunch glucose is influenced by morning medications, insulin dosing, and meal carbohydrate content. Post-lunch testing is useful for assessing the effectiveness of bolus insulin or oral medications taken before lunch. Limitations: timing is critical (approximately 2 hours after first bite). Pre-meal glucose affects result. Reference ranges: ADA guidelines.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Timing: approximately 2 hours after lunch. Preparation: note diabetes medications, insulin dose, pre-meal glucose, meal composition. Handle per standard. Target: less than 180 mg/dL. Timing: critical (2 hours). Reference ranges: ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Target: less than 180 mg/dL (diabetic). Timing: 2 hours post-meal. Reference ranges: ADA.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POTASSIUM
interpretation: Serum Potassium (K+) - measurement of potassium concentration in serum. Potassium is the major intracellular cation (98% intracellular, 2% extracellular). Critical for maintaining resting membrane potential, cardiac conduction, neuromuscular function, and acid-base balance. Clinical use: evaluating cardiac arrhythmias, assessing neuromuscular weakness, monitoring diuretic therapy, evaluating metabolic acidosis/alkalosis, monitoring renal function, emergency assessment (hyperkalaemia). Elevated serum potassium (hyperkalaemia): renal failure (most common cause - reduced excretion), medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim), acidosis (potassium shifts extracellularly), cell lysis (haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis), adrenal insufficiency (reduced aldosterone), pseudohyperkalaemia (haemolysed sample, prolonged tourniquet, fist clenching), hypothermia (potassium shifts extracellularly), digoxin toxicity. Low serum potassium (hypokalaemia): diuretics (loop and thiazide - most common cause), vomiting/diarrhoea (GI losses), alkalosis (potassium shifts intracellularly), insulin therapy (drives potassium intracellularly), beta-agonists (salbutamol), hyperaldosteronism, renal tubular acidosis, magnesium deficiency (renal potassium wasting). Limitations: potassium is HIGHLY SENSITIVE to pre-analytical errors. Pseudohyperkalaemia: haemolysed sample (RBC lysis releases potassium), prolonged tourniquet, fist clenching, delayed separation, thrombocytosis, leucocytosis. Potassium shifts: acidosis raises potassium (H+ shifts intracellular, K+ shifts extracellular); alkalosis lowers potassium. Insulin: drives potassium intracellularly (used to treat hyperkalaemia). Glucose: hyperglycaemia + insulin = potassium shifts intracellularly (transfusion-related hyperkalaemia). Sample handling: process within 30 min - delay causes potassium leakage from cells. Venous vs arterial: arterial may be 0.1-0.2 mmol/L higher than venous. Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: higher than adults. Age: stable across age groups. Hemolysis: even mild haemolysis falsely elevates potassium - reject haemolysed samples.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (or plasma). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: process within 30 min - delay causes potassium leakage from cells. Preparation: note medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, heparin), recent IV fluids, renal function (eGFR), acid-base status, tissue injury, fasting status. Handling: CRITICAL - separate within 30 min. Do NOT leave whole blood at room temperature. Haemolysis: reject haemolysed samples (RBC lysis releases potassium). Pseudohyperkalaemia: haemolysis, prolonged tourniquet, fist clenching, delayed separation, thrombocytosis, leucocytosis. Acidosis: raises potassium. Alkalosis: lowers potassium. Insulin: drives potassium intracellularly. Hyperglycaemia: potassium shifts intracellularly. Venous vs arterial: arterial ~0.1-0.2 mmol/L higher. Emergency: hyperkalaemia requires immediate treatment (calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose, salbutamol, bicarbonate, kayexalate, dialysis). Monitoring: serial potassium for diuretic therapy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Adults: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L. Neonates: 3.5-5.5 mmol/L (higher). Children: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L. Hyperkalaemia: >5.0 mmol/L (mild: 5.0-5.5; moderate: 5.5-6.5; severe: >6.5 - ECG changes, cardiac arrest risk). Hypokalaemia: <3.5 mmol/L (mild: 3.0-3.5; moderate: 2.5-3.0; severe: <2.5 - paralysis, arrhythmias). Emergency: hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L requires immediate treatment. ECG changes: peaked T waves (mild), widened QRS (moderate), sine wave (severe). Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: higher. Age: stable. Hemolysis: falsely elevates potassium. Sample handling: process within 30 min.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ACLS Hyperkalaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: POTASSIUM - URINE
interpretation: Urine Potassium - measurement of potassium concentration in a random (spot) or 24-hour urine sample. Used alongside serum potassium to evaluate renal potassium handling and differentiate causes of hypokalaemia or hyperkalaemia. Clinical use: evaluating renal potassium wasting (elevated urine potassium in hypokalaemia), assessing aldosterone excess (Conn syndrome), monitoring potassium supplementation therapy, evaluating metabolic alkalosis aetiology, assessing diarrhoea vs vomiting (urine potassium helps distinguish). Elevated urine potassium: hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome - renal potassium wasting), diuretic therapy (loop and thiazide), renal tubular acidosis, hypomagnesaemia (renal potassium wasting), Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, vomiting (metabolic alkalosis - kidney excretes potassium), alkalosis. Low urine potassium: diarrhoea (GI losses - kidney conserves potassium), hypokalaemia with appropriate renal conservation (urine K <20 mmol/L = extrarenal losses), hyperkalaemia with appropriate renal excretion, hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 RTA). Clinical approach to hypokalaemia: urine potassium >20 mmol/L (or >15 mmol/L) = renal potassium wasting (inappropriate renal excretion). Urine potassium <20 mmol/L = appropriate renal conservation (GI losses or poor intake). Limitations: spot urine potassium is influenced by: hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low concentration), dietary intake (high potassium diet raises urine potassium), time of day (circadian variation). 24-hour urine potassium: more accurate than spot urine (integrates over 24h). Spot urine K/Cr ratio: adjusts for hydration (potassium divided by creatinine). Fractional excretion of potassium (FEK): FEK = (UK x SCr) / (SK x SCr) x 100. FEK >20%: renal potassium wasting. FEK <20%: appropriate renal conservation. Diarrhoea vs vomiting: diarrhoea = low urine K (GI losses, kidney conserves); vomiting = high urine K (metabolic alkalosis, kidney excretes). Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia: correct magnesium first (hypomagnesaemia causes renal potassium wasting). Reference ranges: method-specific. Dietary intake: affects urine potassium. Age: varies with age. Pregnancy: may be elevated.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (random/midstream clean catch or 24-hour collection). First morning urine preferred (most concentrated). Preparation: note potassium supplementation, diuretic use, aldosterone status, renal function (eGFR), GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea), medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs). Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most concentrated. 24h urine: more accurate than spot. K/Cr ratio: adjusts for hydration. FEK: fractional excretion of K (if paired serum available). Hyperaldosteronism: elevated urine K + hypokalaemia. Diuretics: elevated urine K. Vomiting: elevated urine K (metabolic alkalosis). Diarrhoea: low urine K (GI losses, kidney conserves). Hypomagnesaemia: correct Mg first (renal K wasting). Hypokalaemia workup: serum K + urine K to distinguish renal from GI losses. Renal wasting: urine K >20 mmol/L = kidney inappropriately excreting. GI losses: urine K <20 mmol/L = kidney appropriately conserving. Metabolic alkalosis: urine K elevated (vomiting). Reference ranges: method-specific. Dietary intake: affects urine potassium. Age: varies with age.
ref_ranges: Random urine: 25-125 mmol/L (method-specific). 24-hour urine: 25-125 mmol/day. Renal wasting: urine K >20 mmol/L (or >15 mmol/L) = inappropriate renal excretion. Appropriate conservation: urine K <20 mmol/L = GI losses. Diarrhoea: low urine K. Vomiting: high urine K (metabolic alkalosis). Hyperaldosteronism: elevated urine K. FEK: >20% = renal wasting; <20% = appropriate conservation. Reference ranges: method-specific. Dietary intake: affects urine potassium. Diuretics: increase urine K. Age: varies with age. Pregnancy: may be elevated.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU.

name: PRE DINNER GLUCOSE
interpretation: Pre Dinner Plasma Glucose measures blood glucose concentration before the evening meal (typically 4 to 5 PM). Used to assess basal glucose control and guide pre-dinner insulin or oral medication dosing. Pre-dinner glucose target is typically 80 to 130 mg/dL (ADA) or less than 110 mg/dL (some guidelines). Pre-dinner hyperglycaemia indicates inadequate basal insulin coverage or post-lunch glucose excursion that has not resolved. Limitations: timing varies (4 to 5 PM typically). Reference ranges: ADA guidelines.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Timing: before dinner (typically 4 to 5 PM). Preparation: note diabetes medications, basal insulin dose, post-lunch glucose. Handle per standard. Target: 80 to 130 mg/dL. Elevated: basal insulin insufficient. Reference ranges: ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Target: 80 to 130 mg/dL (diabetic). Elevated: basal insulin inadequate. Timing: before dinner. Reference ranges: ADA.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PRE LUNCH GLUCOSE
interpretation: Pre Lunch Plasma Glucose measures blood glucose concentration before the midday meal (typically 11 AM to 12 PM). Used to assess basal glucose control and guide pre-lunch insulin or oral medication dosing. Pre-lunch glucose target is typically 80 to 130 mg/dL (ADA). Pre-lunch hyperglycaemia indicates inadequate basal insulin coverage or fasting hyperglycaemia that has not resolved. This test helps assess the effectiveness of morning medications and basal insulin. Limitations: timing varies (11 AM to 12 PM typically). Reference ranges: ADA guidelines.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Timing: before lunch (typically 11 AM to 12 PM). Preparation: note diabetes medications, basal insulin dose, fasting glucose. Handle per standard. Target: 80 to 130 mg/dL. Elevated: basal insulin insufficient. Reference ranges: ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 100 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Target: 80 to 130 mg/dL (diabetic). Elevated: basal insulin inadequate. Timing: before lunch. Reference ranges: ADA.
refs: Sources: ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PRE-ECLAMPSIA SCREENING-GESTATIONAL WEEKS(19 TO 37)
interpretation: Pre-eclampsia Screening (Gestational Weeks 19-37) - combined screening test for preeclampsia using maternal factors, blood pressure, uterine artery Doppler, and serum biomarkers (PlGF, PAPP-A). Predicts risk of developing preeclampsia in the second half of pregnancy. Preeclampsia: new-onset hypertension (BP >=140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks gestation with proteinuria or end-organ damage. Affects 2-8% of pregnancies. Major cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity/mortality worldwide. Clinical use: early identification of high-risk pregnancies, guiding aspirin prophylaxis (high-risk women benefit from low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks), planning surveillance (increased antenatal monitoring for high-risk women), reducing adverse outcomes (preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, stillbirth). Screening approach (FMF algorithm): maternal factors (age, weight, ethnicity, medical history, obstetric history), mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (UtA-PI), serum PlGF or PAPP-A. Risk calculation: combined algorithm produces individual risk estimate (risk of preeclampsia before 34 weeks, before 37 weeks, or at any gestational age). High risk: >=1 in 50 (1 in 50 or higher) - recommend low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks. Intermediate risk: 1 in 50 to 1 in 500 - consider aspirin. Low risk: <1 in 500 - no intervention needed. Limitations: screening is performed at TWO TIME POINTS: first trimester (11-13+6 weeks) and second trimester (19-24 weeks). First-trimester screening: PlGF + PAPP-A + MAP + UtA-PI + maternal factors. Second-trimester screening: PlGF + MAP + UtA-PI + maternal factors. PlGF alone has limited predictive value - must be combined with other markers. Aspirin prophylaxis: only effective if started BEFORE 16 weeks (ideally from 12 weeks). Late screening (>16 weeks): limited value for preventing early-onset preeclampsia. False positives: 5-10% false positive rate (unnecessary aspirin, increased surveillance). False negatives: not all preeclampsia cases are detectable (some develop despite normal screening). Multiple pregnancy: screening algorithms differ for twins/triplets. IVF pregnancies: may need adjustment. Ethnicity: risk varies between ethnic groups (higher in African descent). Previous preeclampsia: highest risk group - still needs screening. Reference ranges: risk-based (not absolute values). Aspirin: low-dose (150 mg/day) from 12 weeks until 36 weeks.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum + blood pressure + ultrasound (uterine artery Doppler). CRITICAL: combined screening requires maternal factors + BP + Doppler + serum biomarkers. Preparation: note gestational age, weight, ethnicity, medical history (chronic hypertension, diabetes, autoimmune disease), obstetric history (previous preeclampsia, FGR, preterm birth), number of fetuses, IVF pregnancy. Handling: serum processing within 30 min. Gestational age: accurate dating essential. First trimester: 11-13+6 weeks. Second trimester: 19-24 weeks. Risk calculation: individual risk estimate. Aspirin: high-risk >=1 in 50 (150 mg/day from 12 weeks). Intermediate: 1 in 50-1 in 500 (consider aspirin). Low: <1 in 500 (no intervention). Aspirin: only effective before 16 weeks. Late screening: limited value for prevention. Multiple pregnancy: different algorithms. IVF: may need adjustment. Ethnicity: risk varies. Previous preeclampsia: highest risk group.
ref_ranges: Risk-based: >=1 in 50 (high risk) - aspirin recommended. 1 in 50 to 1 in 500 (intermediate) - consider aspirin. <1 in 500 (low risk) - no intervention. Preeclampsia incidence: 2-8% of pregnancies. Early-onset: before 34 weeks (most severe). Late-onset: after 34 weeks (milder). Screening: combined algorithm (maternal factors + MAP + UtA-PI + PlGF/PAPP-A). Aspirin: 150 mg/day from 12 weeks to 36 weeks. Prevention: aspirin reduces preeclampsia risk by 60%. Reference ranges: risk-based. Method: FMF algorithm. Ethnicity: risk varies. Gestational age: screening at two time points.
refs: Sources: Fetal Medicine Foundation Preeclampsia Screening Guidelines; NICE Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PREGNENOLONE
interpretation: Serum Pregnenolone measures the concentration of pregnenolone, the precursor to all steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone). Pregnenolone is produced in the adrenal glands, gonads, and brain. Elevated: congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), adrenocortical tumour. Low: adrenal insufficiency, CYP17A1 deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note adrenal disease, hormonal symptoms. Handle per standard. Elevated: CAH, adrenocortical tumour. Low: adrenal insufficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: CAH, adrenocortical tumour. Low: adrenal insufficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society CAH Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROCALCITONIN (PCT)
interpretation: Procalcitonin (PCT) - precursor of calcitonin. Produced by C-cells of the thyroid gland in normal physiology, but during bacterial infection, PCT is produced by virtually all tissues (liver, lung, kidney, adipose tissue). Most important biomarker for differentiating bacterial from viral infection and guiding antibiotic therapy. PCT is NOT elevated in viral infections (viral infections stimulate interferon-gamma, which inhibits PCT production). Clinical use: guiding antibiotic therapy in respiratory infections (PCT <0.25 = no antibiotics; PCT 0.25-0.5 = consider antibiotics; PCT >0.5 = antibiotics indicated), diagnosing sepsis (PCT >0.5 strongly suggests bacterial sepsis), monitoring sepsis therapy (serial PCT - declining levels = responding to therapy), differentiating bacterial from viral infection (PCT elevated in bacterial; normal in viral), assessing surgical site infections (PCT rises 6-12h after surgery - peak at 24h), predicting outcome in critically ill patients (higher PCT = worse prognosis). Elevated PCT: bacterial sepsis (PCT >0.5 - strongest clinical use), severe bacterial infection (PCT >2.0), pneumonia (bacterial > viral), surgical site infection (PCT >0.5 after 24h), pancreatitis (necrotising - bacterial infection), meningitis (bacterial > viral), endocarditis (bacterial), intra-abdominal infection (bacterial), burns (extensive - PCT correlates with burn surface area). Low PCT: viral infection (PCT <0.25 - viral infections do NOT elevate PCT), post-viral inflammation, autoimmune disease, localised infection (may be normal). Limitations: PCT is ELEVATED IN NON-INFECTIOUS CONDITIONS: major surgery (peaks at 24h, normalises by day 3-5), trauma (correlates with injury severity), burns (correlates with burn surface area), pancreatitis (sterile inflammation initially), cardiogenic shock, severe heart failure, renal failure (reduced clearance), certain medications (antithymocyte globulin, OKT3). PCT is NOT USEFUL IN: viral infections, localised infections (may be normal), immunocompromised patients (may not mount PCT response), haematological malignancies (may elevate PCT). PCT and antibiotic stewardship: PCT-guided therapy reduces antibiotic use by 30-40% without increasing adverse outcomes. Serial PCT: more useful than single measurement (trend reflects therapeutic response - declining = responding). PCT half-life: 24-30 hours (rapid clearance after infection resolution). PCT and renal failure: reduced clearance - elevated PCT in CKD/dialysis patients (interpret with caution). PCT and liver failure: reduced clearance - elevated PCT in cirrhosis. PCT and surgery: normal elevation peaks at 24h - rising PCT after day 3 suggests infection. PCT and burns: PCT correlates with burn surface area (not necessarily infection). Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: higher PCT (physiological elevation in first 24-48h of life). Age: PCT may be higher in elderly.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum or plasma. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note symptoms (fever, chills, rigors), recent surgery, trauma, burns, renal function (eGFR), liver function, medications (antithymocyte globulin, OKT3), suspected infection site. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Bacterial sepsis: PCT >0.5 (strongly suggests bacterial). Viral infection: PCT <0.25 (viral does NOT elevate PCT). Antibiotic guidance: <0.25 = no antibiotics; 0.25-0.5 = consider; >0.5 = indicated. Serial PCT: declining = responding to therapy. Surgery: peaks at 24h, normalises by day 3-5. Trauma: elevated (correlates with injury severity). Burns: elevated (correlates with burn surface area). Pancreatitis: elevated (sterile inflammation initially). CKD: reduced clearance - interpret with caution. Liver failure: reduced clearance. Neonates: physiological elevation first 24-48h. Half-life: 24-30 hours. Stewardship: PCT-guided therapy reduces antibiotics 30-40%. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly.
ref_ranges: Normal: <0.05 ng/mL. Sepsis: >0.5 ng/mL (strongly suggests bacterial). Severe sepsis: >2.0 ng/mL. Septic shock: >10.0 ng/mL. Bacterial infection: >0.5 ng/mL. Viral infection: <0.25 ng/mL (does NOT elevate PCT). Antibiotic guidance: <0.25 = no antibiotics; 0.25-0.5 = consider; >0.5 = indicated. Post-surgery: peaks at 24h, normalises by day 3-5. Trauma: elevated (correlates with injury severity). Burns: elevated (correlates with burn surface area). CKD: may be elevated (reduced clearance). Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: physiological elevation first 24-48h. Serial: declining = responding to therapy.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines; ProHOSP/SAPS Trial; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROGESTERONE
interpretation: Serum Progesterone - steroid hormone produced by the corpus luteum (ovary) after ovulation, and by the placenta during pregnancy. Prepares endometrium for implantation, maintains early pregnancy, regulates menstrual cycle. Levels rise after ovulation (luteal phase), peak at day 21-22 of a 28-day cycle, and fall if pregnancy does not occur. Clinical use: confirming ovulation (progesterone >3 ng/mL in mid-luteal phase confirms ovulation), assessing luteal phase deficiency (low progesterone in luteal phase), monitoring early pregnancy (progesterone >25 ng/mL strongly suggests viable intrauterine pregnancy), evaluating ectopic pregnancy (progesterone <5 ng/mL strongly suggests non-viable pregnancy), monitoring progesterone therapy, evaluating hirsutism/virilisation (progesterone elevated in 21-hydroxylase deficiency, adrenal tumours). Progesterone levels by cycle phase: follicular: <1 ng/mL (0.2-1.5 ng/mL), ovulation: 1-3 ng/mL, luteal: 3-25 ng/mL (peak day 21-22), pregnancy (first trimester): 10-44 ng/mL, pregnancy (second trimester): 65-290 ng/mL, pregnancy (third trimester): 65-290 ng/mL. Elevated progesterone: pregnancy (most common cause), ovarian cysts (corpus luteum cyst), adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency), adrenal tumours, molar pregnancy, multiple pregnancy (twins/triplets). Low progesterone: anovulation (no ovulation - no corpus luteum), luteal phase deficiency (short/insufficient luteal phase), ectopic pregnancy (low progesterone), threatened abortion, menopause. Limitations: progesterone is PULSATILE (secreted in pulses) - random levels may not reflect average. Progesterone varies with MENSTRUAL CYCLE PHASE - must know cycle day. Timing: mid-luteal phase (day 21-22 of 28-day cycle) for ovulation assessment. Progesterone and oestrogen: progesterone should be interpreted alongside oestrogen (progesterone/oestrogen ratio). Progesterone and LH: LH surge triggers ovulation - progesterone rises after ovulation. Progesterone and pregnancy: progesterone >25 ng/mL strongly suggests viable intrauterine pregnancy; <5 ng/mL strongly suggests non-viable (ectopic, miscarriage). Progesterone therapy: exogenous progesterone (oral, vaginal, IM) will elevate serum progesterone - interpret carefully. Progesterone and 17-OHP: 17-OHP elevated in 21-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) - progesterone may be elevated. Assay variability: different immunoassays give different results. Reference ranges: method-specific. Menopause: low progesterone. Pregnancy: high progesterone (placental production).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. CRITICAL: note menstrual cycle day (day 21-22 for luteal assessment), pregnancy status, exogenous progesterone use, hormonal contraceptive use. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Ovulation confirmation: progesterone >3 ng/mL mid-luteal phase (day 21-22). Luteal phase: 3-25 ng/mL. Ectopic: <5 ng/mL (strongly suggests non-viable). Viable IUP: >25 ng/mL. Pregnancy: 10-44 ng/mL (1st trimester); 65-290 ng/mL (2nd-3rd trimester). Cycle day: must know for interpretation. Mid-luteal: day 21-22. Exogenous progesterone: will elevate serum levels. Hormonal contraceptives: may alter levels. Assay variability: method-specific. Menopause: low. Anovulation: low.
ref_ranges: Follicular (<1 ng/mL): <1.5 ng/mL. Luteal phase: 3-25 ng/mL. Mid-luteal (day 21-22): >3 ng/mL = ovulation confirmed. Pregnancy 1st trimester: 10-44 ng/mL. Pregnancy 2nd/3rd trimester: 65-290 ng/mL. Ectopic: <5 ng/mL. Viable IUP: >25 ng/mL. Luteal phase deficiency: low progesterone in luteal phase. Anovulation: <1 ng/mL throughout cycle. Reference ranges: method-specific. Cycle day: must be known. Menopause: low. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; ESHRE Early Pregnancy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROLACTIN(PRL)
interpretation: Serum Prolactin (PRL) - peptide hormone produced by lactotroph cells of the anterior pituitary gland. Primary physiological role is stimulation of lactation (milk production) after childbirth. Prolactin secretion is inhibited by dopamine (tuberoinfundibular pathway) and stimulated by oestrogen, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), and suckling reflex. Most important test for evaluating galactorrhoea (abnormal milk production), amenorrhoea, and infertility. Elevated prolactin (hyperprolactinaemia): prolactinoma (most common pituitary adenoma - microprolactinoma: <10 mm; macroprolactinoma: >=10 mm), medications (antipsychotics/risperidone - most common drug cause; metoclopramide, domperidone, SSRIs, methyldopa, verapamil, H2 blockers), hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates prolactin), stalk effect (pituitary stalk compression from any mass - reduces dopamine inhibition), renal failure (reduced clearance), liver cirrhosis (reduced clearance), pregnancy (physiological elevation), lactation (physiological), chest wall lesions (herpes zoster, trauma - reflex), idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia. Low prolactin: hypopituitarism (pituitary insufficiency), dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine - treat prolactinomas), ergot derivatives. Clinical use: evaluating galactorrhoea (abnormal milk production), amenorrhoea (absent periods), infertility, erectile dysfunction, hypogonadism, pituitary mass (stalk effect vs prolactinoma), monitoring prolactinoma therapy. Limitations: prolactin is PHYSIOLOGICALLY ELEVATED: pregnancy (10-fold elevation), lactation, nipple stimulation, sleep, stress, exercise, food intake. Prolactin is PHYSIOLOGICALLY ELEVATED in pregnancy: prolactin rises throughout pregnancy - interpret carefully. Medications: many drugs elevate prolactin (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs, methyldopa, verapamil, H2 blockers) - ALWAYS check medication list. Hook effect: very large prolactinomas may give falsely LOW prolactin (dilute sample to detect true level). Macroprolactin: big prolactin (IgG-bound prolactin) - biologically inactive but detected by immunoassay - causes false elevation. Hypothyroidism: untreated hypothyroidism elevates prolactin - check TSH. Prolactin and dopamine: dopamine inhibits prolactin - dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) lower prolactin. Prolactin and oestrogen: oestrogen stimulates prolactin - pregnancy and OCP elevate prolactin. Prolactin and TRH: TRH stimulates prolactin - hypothyroidism (elevated TRH) elevates prolactin. Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: prolactin may decrease with age.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. CRITICAL: note medications (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs), pregnancy status, menstrual history, lactation, nipple stimulation, recent exercise, sleep status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Stress/exercise: avoid strenuous exercise before test. Medications: ALWAYS check medication list (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs, methyldopa, verapamil, H2 blockers). Hypothyroidism: check TSH (TRH stimulates prolactin). Macroprolactin: biologically inactive but detected by immunoassay (false elevation). Hook effect: very large prolactinomas may give falsely LOW prolactin (dilute sample). Prolactinoma: micro (<10 mm) vs macro (>=10 mm). Galactorrhoea: abnormal milk production. Amenorrhoea: absent periods. Stalk effect: pituitary stalk compression reduces dopamine. Pregnancy: physiological elevation (10-fold). Lactation: physiological elevation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Non-pregnant women: 4-23 ng/mL. Men: 4-15 ng/mL. Pregnancy: 10-fold elevation (physiological). Lactation: elevated (physiological). Hyperprolactinaemia: >25 ng/mL (women); >20 ng/mL (men). Prolactinoma: typically >100 ng/mL (macroprolactinoma often >200 ng/mL). Microprolactinoma: 25-100 ng/mL. Macroprolactinoma: >100 ng/mL (often >200 ng/mL). Medications: variable elevation (antipsychotics >25 ng/mL). Hook effect: falsely LOW prolactin in very large tumours. Macroprolactin: biologically inactive (false elevation). Reference ranges: method-specific. Hypothyroidism: elevated prolactin. Age: may decrease with age.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROPOXYPHENE
interpretation: Serum Propoxyphene measures the concentration of propoxyphene (Darvon), a synthetic opioid analgesic. Propoxyphene has been withdrawn from many markets due to cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes). Metabolite: norpropoxyphene. Toxic: greater than 1 mcg/mL. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note drug use, cardiac history. Handle per standard. Toxic: greater than 1 mcg/mL. Withdrawn: many markets. Cardiotoxic: QT prolongation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: absent (not prescribed). Toxic: greater than 1 mcg/mL. Withdrawn: many markets. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: FDA Propoxyphene Withdrawal Notice; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROSTATE SPECIFIC ANTIGEN (PSA) - FREE PSA
interpretation: Free Prostate-Specific Antigen (Free PSA) - unbound form of PSA in serum. PSA exists as free PSA and complexed PSA (bound to protease inhibitors). The free/total PSA ratio is more clinically useful than free PSA alone for differentiating BPH from prostate cancer in the 4-10 ng/mL grey zone. Clinical use: improving specificity of prostate cancer screening, reducing unnecessary biopsies, distinguishing BPH from cancer. Free/total ratio: <10% = prostate cancer likely (biopsy recommended); 10-25% = grey zone (clinical context); >25% = BPH likely (biopsy may not be needed). Elevated free PSA: BPH (produces more free PSA), prostatitis, recent biopsy, urinary retention. Low free PSA: prostate cancer (produces more complexed PSA). Limitations: free PSA alone has limited utility - the RATIO is more important. Best in the grey zone (total PSA 4-10 ng/mL). Total PSA <4 ng/mL: ratio not clinically useful. Total PSA >10 ng/mL: cancer likely regardless. Age-specific: PSA rises with age. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: lower PSA by 50%. Assay variability: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note recent prostate biopsy (wait 6-8 weeks), DRE, sexual activity, medications (5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA 50%). Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Free/total ratio: free PSA / total PSA x 100. <10%: cancer likely. 10-25%: grey zone. >25%: BPH likely. Biopsy: wait 6-8 weeks. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: lower PSA 50%. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Free/total ratio: <10% = cancer likely; 10-25% = grey zone; >25% = BPH likely. Total PSA 4-10 ng/mL: ratio most useful. Total PSA <4 ng/mL: ratio not useful.
