Total PSA >10 ng/mL: cancer likely. BPH: higher ratio. Cancer: lower ratio. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AUA/EAU Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROSTATE SPECIFIC ANTIGEN (PSA) - TOTAL
interpretation: Total Prostate-Specific Antigen (Total PSA) - measurement of total PSA (free + complexed) in serum. PSA is produced by prostate epithelial cells. Most important biomarker for prostate cancer screening and monitoring. Clinical use: prostate cancer screening (men >50, or >40 with risk factors), monitoring recurrence post-treatment, guiding biopsy decisions, monitoring BPH therapy. Elevated PSA: prostate cancer, BPH, prostatitis, recent biopsy (wait 6-8 weeks), urinary retention, recent DRE, advanced age, recent sexual activity. PSA levels: normal <4 ng/mL; grey zone 4-10 ng/mL; elevated >10 ng/mL; markedly elevated >50 ng/mL (advanced/metastatic). Age-specific: <2.5 (<50y); <3.5 (50-59y); <4.5 (60-69y); <6.5 (>70y). Limitations: PSA is NOT cancer-specific - many false positives (BPH, prostatitis). Specificity poor: 70-80% with elevated PSA do NOT have cancer. False negatives: some cancers produce normal PSA; 5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA 50%; obesity lowers PSA. Free/total ratio: helps in grey zone (4-10 ng/mL). PSA velocity: >0.75 ng/mL/year suggestive of cancer. PSA density: PSA/prostate volume (>0.15 suggestive). Assay variability: method-specific. Ethnicity: African American men higher risk - lower threshold for biopsy.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note recent prostate biopsy (wait 6-8 weeks), DRE, sexual activity, urinary retention, BPH history, medications (5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA 50%), family history, ethnicity. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Age-specific: <2.5 (<50y); <3.5 (50-59y); <4.5 (60-69y); <6.5 (>70y). Grey zone: 4-10 ng/mL. Biopsy: wait 6-8 weeks. DRE: transient elevation. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: lower PSA 50%. PSA velocity: >0.75 ng/mL/year. PSA density: PSA/prostate volume. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: <4 ng/mL. Age-specific: <2.5 (<50y); <3.5 (50-59y); <4.5 (60-69y); <6.5 (>70y). Grey zone: 4-10 ng/mL. Elevated: >10 ng/mL. Markedly elevated: >50 ng/mL. Prostate cancer: elevated PSA. BPH: elevated PSA. Prostatitis: elevated PSA. PSA velocity: >0.75 ng/mL/year. PSA density: >0.15 ng/mL/cc. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: PSA rises with age. Ethnicity: African American higher risk.
refs: Sources: AUA/EAU Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines; NCCN Prostate Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROTEIN A/G RATIO
interpretation: Protein A/G Ratio - ratio of albumin to globulin in serum. Total serum protein consists of albumin (60% of total) and globulins (40% - alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, gamma). The A/G ratio reflects the balance between albumin (synthesised by liver) and globulins (synthesised by liver, immune cells, and other tissues). Clinical use: assessing liver synthetic function (low albumin = liver failure), evaluating chronic inflammation (elevated globulins), screening for multiple myeloma (elevated globulins), monitoring nephrotic syndrome (low albumin + high globulins), assessing nutritional status. Low A/G ratio (<1.0): chronic liver disease (cirrhosis - reduced albumin, elevated globulins), nephrotic syndrome (low albumin in urine + elevated globulins), multiple myeloma (elevated paraprotein), chronic inflammation/infection (elevated gamma globulins), autoimmune disease (elevated immunoglobulins), malnutrition (reduced albumin synthesis). High A/G ratio (>2.0): dehydration (hemoconcentration - elevated albumin), overproduction of albumin (rare). Low albumin: liver failure (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss), malnutrition (reduced intake), chronic inflammation (negative acute phase reactant), burns (losses), protein-losing enteropathy. Elevated globulins: chronic infection/inflammation (elevated gamma globulins), multiple myeloma (monoclonal paraprotein), autoimmune disease (elevated immunoglobulins), chronic liver disease (elevated immunoglobulins from gut antigens). Limitations: A/G ratio is a SURROGATE marker - more useful than either albumin or globulin alone. A/G ratio affected by: hydration status (dehydration raises albumin), liver function (low albumin = liver failure), kidney function (nephrotic syndrome - low albumin), immune activation (elevated globulins). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: albumin may decrease with age. Ethnicity: albumin may differ between ethnic groups.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver function (AST, ALT, bilirubin), kidney function (eGFR, urine protein), nutritional status, chronic disease, medications. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Albumin: liver synthetic function. Globulins: immune function, inflammation. A/G ratio: albumin / globulins. <1.0: liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, myeloma, chronic inflammation. >2.0: dehydration. Low albumin: liver failure, nephrotic, malnutrition, inflammation. High globulins: infection, myeloma, autoimmune. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: albumin decreases with age.
ref_ranges: Normal A/G ratio: 1.0-2.0 (varies by laboratory). Low A/G: <1.0 (chronic liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, myeloma). High A/G: >2.0 (dehydration). Albumin: 3.5-5.0 g/dL. Globulins: 2.0-3.5 g/dL. Total protein: 6.0-8.3 g/dL. Cirrhosis: low albumin + high globulins = low A/G. Nephrotic syndrome: low albumin + high globulins. Myeloma: elevated globulins (paraprotein). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: albumin decreases with age. Dehydration: elevated albumin.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS
interpretation: Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) - laboratory technique that separates serum proteins based on their electrical charge and size. Produces characteristic pattern with 5 bands: albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, and gamma globulins. Most important test for detecting monoclonal gammopathies (multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia, MGUS). Clinical use: screening for multiple myeloma (monoclonal band in gamma region), detecting MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance), evaluating chronic inflammation (polyclonal gamma elevation), assessing liver disease (reduced albumin, elevated gamma globulins), evaluating nephrotic syndrome (low albumin, elevated alpha-2). Protein electrophoresis bands: albumin (largest band - liver synthetic function), alpha-1 (alpha-1 antitrypsin, alpha-1 acid glycoprotein), alpha-2 (alpha-2 macroglobulin, haptoglobin), beta (transferrin, complement C3), gamma (immunoglobulins - IgG, IgA, IgM). Monoclonal gammopathy: sharp, narrow band (M-spike) in gamma region - suggests monoclonal proliferation (myeloma, MGUS, Waldenstrom). Polyclonal gammopathy: broad-based elevation in gamma region - suggests polyclonal immune activation (chronic infection, autoimmune disease, liver disease). Clinical patterns: multiple myeloma: M-spike in gamma region + low other immunoglobulins + lytic bone lesions, MGUS: M-spike without end-organ damage (follow for life), Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia: IgM M-spike + hyperviscosity, chronic liver disease: reduced albumin + broad gamma elevation, nephrotic syndrome: low albumin + elevated alpha-2, acute inflammation: elevated alpha-1 and alpha-2. Limitations: SPEP is a SCREENING test - positive result requires IMMUNOFIXATION (IFE) to identify the monoclonal protein. SPEP may MISS small monoclonal proteins (low sensitivity for small M-spikes). SPEP may MISS light chain only myeloma (no intact immunoglobulin - requires urine protein electrophoresis [UPEP] or free light chains). SPEP is NOT a diagnostic test for myeloma - requires clinical correlation (bone marrow biopsy, imaging, calcium, renal function). SPEP and immunofixation: IFE is more sensitive than SPEP for detecting monoclonal proteins. SPEP and free light chains: serum free light chains (kappa/lambda ratio) more sensitive for light chain myeloma. SPEP and UPEP: urine SPEP detects Bence Jones proteinuria (light chains in urine). Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note symptoms (bone pain, anaemia, renal failure, recurrent infections), family history, medications. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. M-spike: sharp band in gamma region = monoclonal protein. Polyclonal: broad gamma elevation = immune activation. Albumin: liver synthetic function. Alpha-1: acute phase reactant. Alpha-2: inflammation. Beta: transferrin, complement. Gamma: immunoglobulins. IFE: confirm monoclonal protein. UPEP: detect light chains. Free light chains: kappa/lambda ratio. Myeloma: M-spike + end-organ damage. MGUS: M-spike without damage. Waldenstrom: IgM M-spike + hyperviscosity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: no M-spike; albumin 3.5-5.0 g/dL; gamma region polyclonal. M-spike: monoclonal band (myeloma, MGUS, Waldenstrom). MGUS: M-spike <3 g/dL, <10% plasma cells, no end-organ damage. Multiple myeloma: M-spike + lytic lesions + anaemia + renal failure. Waldenstrom: IgM M-spike + hyperviscosity. Polyclonal: chronic infection, autoimmune, liver disease. Nephrotic: low albumin + elevated alpha-2. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific. IFE: confirm monoclonal protein.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; IMWG Myeloma Diagnostic Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Protein Electrophoresis separates CSF proteins into fractions: albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, gamma globulins. Used to detect: intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis (oligoclonal bands), CNS infections, CNS malignancies. Elevated gamma: multiple sclerosis (MS), neurosyphilis, CNS infections. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: CSF. Preparation: note neurological symptoms, MS suspicion, infections. Handle per standard. Gamma elevation: intrathecal synthesis. Oligoclonal bands: MS (90-95% sensitivity). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: expected CSF pattern. Elevated gamma: intrathecal synthesis. Oligoclonal bands: MS. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: McDonald MS Diagnostic Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROTEIN SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Urine Protein Spot - measurement of total protein concentration in a random (spot) urine sample. Used for detecting proteinuria (protein in urine), which is an early marker of kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy, and pre-eclampsia. Clinical use: screening for proteinuria (kidney disease), monitoring diabetic nephropathy, evaluating pre-eclampsia (proteinuria + hypertension), assessing glomerular disease, monitoring nephrotic syndrome. Normal urine protein: <150 mg/day (or <30 mg/L in spot urine). Microalbuminuria: 30-300 mg/L (or ACR 30-300 mg/g) - early diabetic nephropathy. Proteinuria: >300 mg/L (or >300 mg/g ACR) - overt kidney disease. Nephrotic range: >3500 mg/day (>3.5 g/day) - heavy proteinuria. Clinical use: diabetic nephropathy screening (type 1: from 5 years; type 2: at diagnosis), pre-eclampsia evaluation (proteinuria + hypertension), CKD staging (proteinuria level), monitoring nephrotic syndrome (protein loss), assessing glomerular disease (proteinuria type). Elevated urine protein: diabetic nephropathy (most common cause in developed countries), pre-eclampsia (proteinuria + hypertension after 20 weeks), glomerulonephritis (glomerular damage), nephrotic syndrome (>3.5 g/day), tubulointerstitial disease (tubular proteinuria), orthostatic proteinuria (proteinuria when upright - benign), exercise-induced proteinuria (transient). Limitations: spot urine protein is INFLUENCED BY: hydration status (dilute urine = falsely low), exercise (raises protein transiently), infection (UTI raises protein), menstruation (blood contamination), fever, heart failure (acute), uncontrolled hypertension. Spot urine vs 24h urine: spot urine is convenient but less accurate; 24h urine is gold standard but impractical. Albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) preferred over total protein for diabetic nephropathy screening. Protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR) used for total proteinuria assessment. Confirmation: requires 2 of 3 positive samples over 3-6 months for diagnosis. First morning urine: preferred (most representative). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (first morning preferred). Spot urine acceptable. Preparation: ensure no UTI, no menstruation, no strenuous exercise 24h before. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. First morning urine: most representative. 24h urine: gold standard but impractical. ACR: preferred for diabetic nephropathy. PCR: for total proteinuria. Microalbuminuria: 30-300 mg/L. Proteinuria: >300 mg/L. Nephrotic range: >3500 mg/day. Diabetic screening: type 1 from 5y; type 2 at diagnosis. Confirm: 2 of 3 positive over 3-6 months. Exercise: transiently raises protein. Infection: UTI raises protein. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: <150 mg/day (<30 mg/L spot). Microalbuminuria: 30-300 mg/L (ACR 30-300 mg/g). Proteinuria: >300 mg/L (>300 mg/g ACR). Nephrotic: >3500 mg/day (>3.5 g/day). Diabetic nephropathy: microalbuminuria earliest sign. Pre-eclampsia: proteinuria + hypertension. Reference ranges: method-specific. ACR preferred for diabetic screening. PCR for total proteinuria.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; KDIGO CKD Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PROTEINS - CSF
interpretation: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Proteins - measurement of total protein concentration in cerebrospinal fluid. CSF protein reflects blood-CSF barrier integrity and intrathecal immunoglobulin production. Elevated CSF protein is a non-specific marker of CNS inflammation, infection, or malignancy. Clinical use: evaluating CNS infection (bacterial meningitis - very high protein), assessing subarachnoid haemorrhage (xanthochromia/elevated protein), diagnosing Guillain-Barre syndrome (elevated protein with albuminocytological dissociation), evaluating CNS malignancy (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis), assessing multiple sclerosis (oligoclonal bands), monitoring shunt function. Normal CSF protein: 15-45 mg/dL (0.15-0.45 g/L). Elevated CSF protein: bacterial meningitis (markedly elevated - >100 mg/dL), viral meningitis (mildly elevated - 50-100 mg/dL), subarachnoid haemorrhage (elevated from blood), Guillain-Barre syndrome (elevated with normal cell count - albuminocytological dissociation), CNS malignancy (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis), multiple sclerosis (oligoclonal bands), multiple sclerosis (normal or mildly elevated), normal pressure hydrocephalus (elevated), spinal cord compression (elevated), chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). Albuminocytological dissociation: elevated CSF protein with NORMAL cell count - characteristic of Guillain-Barre syndrome. CSF/serum albumin ratio: more accurate than total protein for assessing blood-CSF barrier disruption. Oligoclonal bands: intrathecal immunoglobulin production - suggestive of multiple sclerosis. Limitations: CSF protein is NON-SPECIFIC - elevated in many conditions. CSF protein affected by: traumatic tap (blood contamination raises protein), collection technique (manipulation), standing time (protein increases over time), patient position. Traumatic tap: blood in CSF falsely elevates protein - use CSF/serum albumin ratio. Opening pressure: should be measured during lumbar puncture. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: CSF protein may be higher in elderly and neonates.
pre_analytical: Sample: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via lumbar puncture. CRITICAL: aseptic technique. Preparation: note symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, neurological deficits), recent procedures (CT/MRI), anticoagulant use, platelet count. Handling: process immediately; 2-8C up to 24h (protein degrades). Opening pressure: measure during LP. Collect: 1-2 mL in sterile tube. Aseptic: strict sterile technique. Traumatic tap: blood contamination raises protein - use CSF/serum albumin ratio. Bacterial meningitis: markedly elevated protein (>100 mg/dL). Viral meningitis: mildly elevated (50-100 mg/dL). Guillain-Barre: elevated protein + normal cells (albuminocytological dissociation). Oligoclonal bands: MS (intrathecal Ig production). Leptomeningeal: CNS malignancy. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: higher in elderly and neonates.
ref_ranges: Normal: 15-45 mg/dL (0.15-0.45 g/L). Bacterial meningitis: >100 mg/dL. Viral meningitis: 50-100 mg/dL. Guillain-Barre: elevated + normal cells (albuminocytological dissociation). Subarachnoid haemorrhage: elevated (xanthochromia). MS: oligoclonal bands (normal or mildly elevated total protein). CNS malignancy: elevated. Traumatic tap: falsely elevated (blood contamination). CSF/serum albumin ratio: >0.7 suggests blood-CSF barrier disruption. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: higher in elderly and neonates.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AAN MS Diagnostic Criteria; IDSA Meningitis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PSA WITH FREE PSA RATIO
interpretation: PSA with Free PSA Ratio - combined measurement of total PSA, free PSA, and calculation of free/total PSA ratio in a single test. Provides more comprehensive assessment of prostate cancer risk than total PSA alone. The free/total ratio improves specificity of prostate cancer screening, particularly in the 4-10 ng/mL grey zone. Clinical use: prostate cancer screening with improved specificity, reducing unnecessary biopsies in the grey zone, distinguishing BPH from prostate cancer. Free/total ratio interpretation: <10%: prostate cancer likely (biopsy recommended). 10-25%: grey zone (clinical context determines biopsy). >25%: BPH likely (biopsy may not be needed). Total PSA <4 ng/mL: ratio not clinically useful. Total PSA >10 ng/mL: cancer likely regardless of ratio. Clinical approach: total PSA <4 ng/mL: generally no further testing needed. Total PSA 4-10 ng/mL: free/total ratio helps distinguish BPH from cancer. Total PSA >10 ng/mL: prostate cancer likely - biopsy usually recommended. Limitations: free/total ratio is most useful in the 4-10 ng/mL range. Below 4 ng/mL: low pre-test probability - ratio not helpful. Above 10 ng/mL: high pre-test probability - ratio not needed. Free PSA affected by: BPH (elevated free PSA, higher ratio), prostatitis, recent biopsy (wait 6-8 weeks), 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (lower PSA by 50%). Age-specific: PSA rises with age. Assay variability: method-specific. Ethnicity: African American men higher risk - lower threshold for biopsy.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note recent prostate biopsy (wait 6-8 weeks), DRE, sexual activity, medications (5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA 50%), family history, ethnicity. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Free/total ratio: free PSA / total PSA x 100. <10%: cancer likely. 10-25%: grey zone. >25%: BPH likely. PSA <4 ng/mL: ratio not useful. PSA >10 ng/mL: cancer likely regardless. Age-specific: PSA rises with age. Assay: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Free/total ratio: <10% = cancer likely; 10-25% = grey zone; >25% = BPH likely. Total PSA <4 ng/mL: ratio not useful. Total PSA 4-10 ng/mL: ratio most useful. Total PSA >10 ng/mL: cancer likely. Age-specific: <2.5 (<50y); <3.5 (50-59y); <4.5 (60-69y); <6.5 (>70y). BPH: higher ratio. Cancer: lower ratio. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AUA/EAU Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PSEUDO CHOLINESTERASE OPC POISONING
interpretation: Serum Pseudocholinesterase (Butyrylcholinesterase, BChE) measures the activity of the enzyme that metabolises succinylcholine and other choline esters. Low pseudocholinesterase: prolonged apnoea after succinylcholine, organophosphate/nerve agent poisoning, liver disease. Pseudocholinesterase activity: inversely proportional to duration of apnoea. Genotyping: for atypical variants. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note anaesthesia history, organophosphate exposure, liver disease. Handle per standard. Low: prolonged apnoea. Organophosphate: poisoning. Genotyping: atypical variants. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 4000 to 12000 IU/L (method-specific). Low: prolonged apnoea, liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ASA Anaesthesia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: PTHrP PARATHYROID HORMONE RELATED PEPTIDE
interpretation: Serum Parathyroid Hormone-Related Peptide (PTHrP) is a parathyroid hormone-like peptide that causes hypercalcaemia of malignancy. PTHrP is secreted by squamous cell carcinomas (lung, oesophageal), renal cell carcinoma, breast cancer, and lymphomas. PTHrP: inhibits bone resorption, increases renal calcium reabsorption. Elevated: malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note hypercalcaemia, malignancy. Handle per standard. Elevated: hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Squamous cell: lung, oesophageal. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1.5 pmol/L (method-specific). Elevated: malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Hypercalcaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: QUADRUPLE MARKER SCREENING - AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Quadruple Marker Screening (Quad Screen) - second-trimester maternal serum screening test combining four biomarkers to assess risk of chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 21, trisomy 18) and neural tube defects (NTD). Markers: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), unconjugated oestriol (uE3), and inhibin A. Performed at 15-20 weeks gestation (most accurate at 16-18 weeks). Clinical use: second-trimester screening for Down syndrome (trisomy 21), screening for trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), detecting neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly via elevated AFP), identifying high-risk pregnancies requiring further testing (amniocentesis, CVS). Marker patterns in trisomy 21: AFP: low, hCG: high, uE3: low, inhibin A: high. Marker patterns in trisomy 18: AFP: low, hCG: low, uE3: low, inhibin A: low. Elevated AFP: neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly - AFP elevated due to fetal CSF leak), multiple pregnancy (higher AFP in twins), incorrect gestational dating, abdominal wall defects, renal anomalies (fetal proteinuria). Limitations: quad screen is a SCREENING test - positive result requires confirmatory testing (amniocentesis, CVS). False positives: 5% false positive rate (unnecessary amniocentesis). False negatives: not all cases detectable. Gestational age: accurate dating essential (incorrect dating causes false results). Multiple pregnancy: AFP higher in twins - adjust for plurality. IVF pregnancies: may need adjustment. Ethnicity: AFP levels vary between ethnic groups - adjusted in screening algorithms. Smoking: lowers AFP (reduced placental function). Weight: maternal weight affects marker levels - adjusted in algorithms. Previous trisomy: higher risk - may need different screening approach. AFP and NTD: elevated AFP suggests neural tube defect - confirm with ultrasound (anatomy scan at 18-20 weeks). Confirmatory testing: all screen-positive results require confirmatory testing (amniocentesis, CVS, cell-free DNA). Combined with first-trimester screening: integrated screening (first trimester + second trimester) more accurate than either alone.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: gestational age must be accurately determined (15-20 weeks). Preparation: note gestational age, number of fetuses, IVF pregnancy, weight, ethnicity, smoking status, diabetes, previous chromosomal abnormality. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Gestational age: 15-20 weeks (most accurate 16-18 weeks). Trisomy 21: low AFP + high hCG + low uE3 + high inhibin A. Trisomy 18: low AFP + low hCG + low uE3 + low inhibin A. NTD: elevated AFP (confirm with anatomy scan). Multiple pregnancy: higher AFP. IVF: may need adjustment. Ethnicity: AFP varies. Smoking: lowers AFP. Weight: affects marker levels. Confirmatory: amniocentesis, CVS, cell-free DNA. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific.
ref_ranges: Risk-based: screen positive vs screen negative. Trisomy 21: low AFP + high hCG + low uE3 + high inhibin A. Trisomy 18: low AFP + low hCG + low uE3 + low inhibin A. NTD: elevated AFP (>2.0-2.5 MoM). AFP: 0.1-1.0 MoM (normal). hCG: 0.2-2.5 MoM (normal). uE3: 0.2-1.0 MoM (normal). Inhibin A: <1.0 MoM (normal). False positive rate: ~5%. Detection rate: ~80% for trisomy 21. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific. MoM: multiples of median for gestational age.
refs: Sources: ACOG Second-Trimester Screening Guidelines; Fetal Medicine Foundation; manufacturer IFU.

name: RANDOM PLASMA GLUCOSE
interpretation: Random Plasma Glucose (RPG) measures blood glucose concentration at any time of day without regard to meals or fasting. RPG is used as a screening test for diabetes mellitus. An RPG greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) is diagnostic of diabetes without the need for confirmatory testing. RPG is convenient and does not require fasting, making it useful for opportunistic screening. However, RPG alone cannot diagnose prediabetes or impaired fasting glucose as these require fasting measurements. Limitations: does not distinguish between fasting, postprandial, and random states. Cannot diagnose prediabetes. Stress, illness, and medications affect results. Reference ranges: WHO/ADA criteria.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. No fasting required. Preparation: note symptoms of hyperglycaemia (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss), medications, recent meal. Handle per standard. Greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL plus symptoms: diabetes. Cannot diagnose: prediabetes. Convenient: no fasting. Reference ranges: WHO/ADA.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 140 mg/dL (non-diabetic). Diabetes: greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL plus symptoms. Prediabetes: cannot be diagnosed. Stress: falsely elevates. Reference ranges: WHO/ADA.
refs: Sources: WHO Diabetes Guidelines; ADA Diagnosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RBC FOLATE
interpretation: Red Blood Cell (RBC) Folate measures folate concentration within red blood cells, reflecting long-term folate stores (2-3 months). RBC folate: more reliable than serum folate for assessing folate status. Low RBC folate: megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects (pregnancy), malabsorption. Serum folate: recent intake. RBC folate: stores. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note anaemia, pregnancy, malabsorption, medications. Handle per standard. Low: megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects. More reliable: than serum folate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 400 ng/mL (method-specific). Low: megaloblastic anaemia, NTD risk. More reliable: than serum. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: BSH Folate Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RENIN ACTIVITY
interpretation: Plasma Renin Activity (PRA) - measurement of the rate of angiotensin I generation in plasma, reflecting renin secretion from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney. Renin is released in response to: decreased renal perfusion (hypotension, renal artery stenosis), decreased sodium delivery to macula densa, sympathetic nervous system activation (beta-1 adrenergic), and decreased angiotensin II (feedback loop). Most important test for evaluating secondary hypertension (renovascular disease, primary hyperaldosteronism). Clinical use: diagnosing primary hyperaldosteronism (renin suppressed, aldosterone elevated), evaluating renovascular hypertension (renin elevated), assessing renal artery stenosis (renin elevated), differentiating causes of secondary hypertension. Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome): suppressed renin (<0.5 ng/mL/h) + elevated aldosterone (>15 ng/dL). Renovascular hypertension: elevated renin (>3.5 ng/mL/h) + elevated aldosterone. Essential hypertension: normal renin + normal aldosterone. Renin and aldosterone: aldosterone/renin ratio (ARR) >30 with aldosterone >15 ng/dL = primary hyperaldosteronism. Limitations: renin is INFLUENCED BY: posture (supine lowers renin; upright raises renin - standard: 2h supine), sodium intake (high sodium suppresses renin), medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, diuretics elevate renin; NSAIDs, mineralocorticoids suppress renin), time of day (circadian variation), pregnancy (renin elevated physiologically), oral contraceptives (renin elevated). Medications: ALWAYS withhold interfering medications before testing (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, NSAIDs, mineralocorticoids). Posture: 2 hours supine before blood draw (standard). Sodium: high sodium diet suppresses renin; low sodium diet elevates renin. Sample handling: process within 30 min - renin is temperature-sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: direct renin concentration (DRC) or plasma renin activity (PRA).
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (EDTA). Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: 2h supine before blood draw. Preparation: withhold interfering medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, NSAIDs, mineralocorticoids) for 2-4 weeks if possible. Note: sodium intake, posture, medications, pregnancy. Handling: process within 30 min; 2-8C up to 24h or -20C. Supine: 2h before blood draw. Primary hyperaldosteronism: suppressed renin + elevated aldosterone. Renovascular: elevated renin + elevated aldosterone. Essential: normal renin + normal aldosterone. ARR: aldosterone/renin ratio >30 + aldosterone >15 ng/dL = primary hyperaldosteronism. Medications: withhold ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, NSAIDs. Sodium: high sodium suppresses renin. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: PRA or DRC.
ref_ranges: Supine (2h): 0.5-3.5 ng/mL/h. Upright: 1.0-5.0 ng/mL/h. Primary hyperaldosteronism: <0.5 ng/mL/h (suppressed). Renovascular hypertension: >3.5 ng/mL/h (elevated). Essential hypertension: 0.5-3.5 ng/mL/h (normal). ARR: aldosterone/renin ratio >30 + aldosterone >15 ng/dL = primary hyperaldosteronism. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: PRA or DRC. Age: may vary. Pregnancy: renin elevated physiologically.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS IgG (RSV) ANTIBODY
interpretation: Serum Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) IgG Antibody measures anti-RSV IgG levels. RSV IgG: indicates past infection or immunity. RSV: common respiratory virus, especially in infants and elderly. IgG: seroconversion (4-fold rise) confirms recent infection. IgG: does not distinguish active from past infection. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note respiratory symptoms, age, immunocompromised status. Handle per standard. IgG: past infection or immunity. Seroconversion: 4-fold rise. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative or low titre. Positive: past infection. Seroconversion: 4-fold rise. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: CDC RSV Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS IgM (RSV) ANTIBODY
interpretation: Serum Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) IgM Antibody measures anti-RSV IgM levels. RSV IgM: indicates acute or recent infection. IgM: positive within 1 week of infection, persists 1-3 months. IgM: more useful than IgG for acute infection diagnosis. False positives: rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note respiratory symptoms, age, immunocompromised status. Handle per standard. IgM: acute infection. False positives: RF, hypergammaglobulinaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: acute infection. False positives: RF. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: CDC RSV Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION PROFILE IgG
interpretation: Serum Respiratory Tract Infection (RTI) Profile IgG measures IgG antibodies against multiple respiratory pathogens simultaneously. Profile typically includes: influenza A/B, parainfluenza, adenovirus, RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae. IgG: indicates past infection or immunity. Seroconversion: 4-fold rise confirms recent infection. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note respiratory symptoms, immunocompromised status. Handle per standard. IgG: past infection. Seroconversion: 4-fold rise. Multiple pathogens: simultaneous. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative or low titre. Positive: past infection. Seroconversion: 4-fold rise. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
refs: Sources: IDSA RTI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION PROFILE IgM
interpretation: Serum Respiratory Tract Infection (RTI) Profile IgM measures IgM antibodies against multiple respiratory pathogens simultaneously. Profile typically includes: influenza A/B, parainfluenza, adenovirus, RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae. IgM: indicates acute or recent infection. IgM: positive within 1 week of infection. False positives: RF, hypergammaglobulinaemia. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note respiratory symptoms, immunocompromised status. Handle per standard. IgM: acute infection. False positives: RF. Multiple pathogens: simultaneous. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative. Positive: acute infection. False positives: RF. Reference ranges: pathogen-specific.
refs: Sources: IDSA RTI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: RHEUMATOID FACTOR (RA FACTOR)
interpretation: Rheumatoid Factor (RF) - autoantibody (typically IgM) directed against the Fc portion of IgG. Found in 70-80% of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. Non-specific - also elevated in other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections, and elderly. Clinical use: diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis (part of ACR/EULAR classification criteria), evaluating inflammatory arthritis, assessing disease activity, monitoring treatment response, evaluating other autoimmune diseases. Elevated RF: rheumatoid arthritis (70-80% of RA patients - RF positive), Sjogren syndrome (elevated in 60-70%), systemic lupus erythematosus (30-40%), mixed connective tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia (essential mixed cryoglobulinaemia - type II/III), chronic infections (hepatitis C, TB, endocarditis, HIV), cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, elderly (5-10% of healthy elderly have low-titre RF). RF and RA: RF positive RA: more aggressive disease, higher risk of extra-articular manifestations (nodules, vasculitis, lung disease), higher mortality. RF negative RA: less aggressive, better prognosis. Anti-CCP antibodies: more specific for RA than RF (95% specificity vs 80% for RF). Combined RF + anti-CCP: highest sensitivity and specificity for RA. Limitations: RF is NON-SPECIFIC - elevated in many conditions besides RA. RF can be elevated in: other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections, cirrhosis, elderly (age-related). RF false positives: 5-10% of healthy elderly have low-titre RF. RF false negatives: 20-30% of RA patients are RF-negative (seronegative RA). RF titre: high titre (>40 IU/mL) more suggestive of RA than low titre. RF and anti-CCP: anti-CCP more specific for RA (use both). RF and disease activity: RF titre correlates with disease activity in some patients. RF and treatment: RF titre may decrease with effective treatment. Assay variability: method-specific (latex agglutination, nephelometry, ELISA). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: RF increases with age.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note symptoms (joint pain, swelling, stiffness, fatigue), family history, other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. RA: RF positive in 70-80%. RF positive RA: more aggressive disease. Anti-CCP: more specific for RA than RF. Combined RF + anti-CCP: highest sensitivity. High titre (>40 IU/mL): more suggestive of RA. False positives: elderly, infections, autoimmune. False negatives: 20-30% of RA (seronegative RA). Sjogren: RF elevated 60-70%. Cryoglobulinaemia: RF elevated. Hepatitis C: RF elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: RF increases with age.
ref_ranges: Normal: <14 IU/mL (method-specific). Low positive: 14-40 IU/mL. High positive: >40 IU/mL (more suggestive of RA). RA: positive in 70-80% of patients. RF positive RA: more aggressive disease. RF negative RA: 20-30% of patients. Sjogren: 60-70% positive. Cryoglobulinaemia: positive. Hepatitis C: may be elevated. Elderly: 5-10% have low-titre RF. Reference ranges: method-specific. Anti-CCP: more specific for RA. Age: RF increases with age.
refs: Sources: ACR/EULAR RA Classification Criteria; manufacturer IFU.

name: ROMA (RISK FOR OVARIAN MALIGNANCY ALGORITHM)
interpretation: Serum Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) is a mathematical formula that combines HE4 and CA-125 with menopausal status to predict the likelihood of ovarian cancer. ROMA: greater than 12.5% in premenopausal, greater than 14.4% in postmenopausal = high risk. Sensitivity: 85-94%. Specificity: 75-92%. Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note ovarian mass, menopausal status. Handle per standard. ROMA: combines HE4 + CA-125. High risk: greater than 12.5% (pre), greater than 14.4% (post). Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
ref_ranges: Low risk: less than 12.5% (pre), less than 14.4% (post). High risk: greater than 12.5% (pre), greater than 14.4% (post). Reference ranges: menopause-dependent.
refs: Sources: NCCN Ovarian Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SARS – CoV – 2 IgG (Neutralizing Antibodies)-Quantitative
interpretation: SARS-CoV-2 IgG (Neutralising Antibodies) Quantitative - measurement of IgG antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, including functional neutralising antibodies that prevent viral entry into cells. Quantitative assay measures antibody concentration (BAU/mL - Binding Antibody Units). More informative than qualitative IgG (provides actual antibody level). Clinical use: assessing immune status after COVID-19 infection (natural immunity), evaluating vaccine response (post-vaccination antibody levels), monitoring antibody waning over time, determining need for booster vaccination, evaluating immunocompromised patients (poor vaccine response). Positive IgG (>1.0 BAU/mL): previous SARS-CoV-2 infection, successful vaccination response, hybrid immunity (infection + vaccination - highest antibody levels). Neutralising antibodies: functional antibodies that block viral spike protein from binding ACE2 receptor - correlate with protective immunity. Limitations: IgG antibodies do NOT indicate current infection (IgM or PCR needed for acute diagnosis). Antibody levels WANE over time after both infection and vaccination. Neutralising antibodies do NOT guarantee protection against reinfection (variants may escape immunity). Assay variability: different assays give different results - use same assay for serial monitoring. Cross-reactivity: SARS-CoV-1, common cold coronaviruses may cause low-level cross-reactivity (modern assays reduced this). Immunocompromised: may not mount adequate antibody response after infection or vaccination. Variants: antibody levels may differ between variants (Delta, Omicron). Timing: IgG detectable 2-4 weeks after infection; peak at 4-6 weeks; wanes over months. Reference ranges: assay-specific. BAU/mL: Binding Antibody Units per mL (WHO standard).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note COVID-19 infection history, vaccination status (number of doses, type of vaccine, timing), immunosuppressive medications, immunocompromised status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Positive: >1.0 BAU/mL. Neutralising: functional antibodies that block viral entry. Waning: antibodies decline over months. Vaccination: antibodies detectable 2-4 weeks post-vaccination. Infection: antibodies detectable 2-4 weeks post-infection. Hybrid immunity: highest antibody levels. Variants: antibody levels may differ. Assay: use same assay for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: assay-specific.
ref_ranges: Negative: <1.0 BAU/mL. Positive: >1.0 BAU/mL. Low positive: 1.0-10 BAU/mL (waning immunity). High positive: >10 BAU/mL (recent infection/vaccination). Neutralising: protective immunity correlate. Waning: antibodies decline over months. Variants: may differ. Immunocompromised: may have poor response. Reference ranges: assay-specific. BAU/mL: WHO standard. Timing: IgG 2-4 weeks post-infection/vaccination.
refs: Sources: WHO SARS-CoV-2 Antibody Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SELENIUM
interpretation: Serum Selenium measures selenium concentration. Selenium is an essential trace element required for glutathione peroxidase function and thyroid hormone metabolism. Deficiency: Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy), Kashin-Beck disease (osteoarthropathy), thyroid dysfunction. Excess: selenosis (hair loss, garlic breath, nail changes). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid disease, cardiomyopathy, nutritional status. Handle per standard. Deficiency: Keshan, Kashin-Beck. Excess: selenosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 70 to 150 mcg/L (method-specific). Deficiency: Keshan, Kashin-Beck. Excess: selenosis. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Selenium Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SERINE QUANTITATIVE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Serine Quantitative measures the concentration of serine, a non-essential amino acid involved in phospholipid synthesis, one-carbon metabolism, and glutathione production. Elevated serine: serine deficiency disorders, hyperhomocysteinaemia, maternal serine synthesis defect. Low serine: 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency (PHGDH). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note developmental delay, seizures, growth restriction. Handle per standard. Elevated: serine deficiency, hyperhomocysteinaemia. Low: PHGDH deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (age and method specific). Elevated: serine deficiency. Low: PHGDH deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SERUM ASCITIC ALBUMIN GRADIENT (SAAG)
interpretation: Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) - calculated parameter: SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin. Used to classify ascites into portal hypertensive (SAAG >=1.1 g/dL) and non-portal hypertensive (SAAG <1.1 g/dL). Most important test for evaluating the aetiology of ascites. Clinical use: differentiating portal hypertensive from non-portal hypertensive ascites, evaluating cirrhotic ascites (SAAG >=1.1), diagnosing cardiac ascites (SAAG >=1.1), identifying peritoneal carcinomatosis (SAAG <1.1), guiding diagnostic approach and treatment. SAAG >=1.1 g/dL (portal hypertensive): cirrhosis (most common cause - SAAG >=1.1), alcoholic hepatitis, cardiac ascites (right heart failure - SAAG >=1.1), constrictive pericarditis, portal vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, hepatic vein thrombosis, massive hepatic metastases. SAAG <1.1 g/dL (non-portal hypertensive): peritoneal carcinomatosis (most common cause of low SAAG), tuberculosis (peritoneal TB), nephrotic syndrome (protein loss), pancreatitis (pancreatic ascites), biliary ascites. SAAG accuracy: SAAG >=1.1 correctly classifies portal hypertension in 90-97% of cases. Limitations: SAAG requires SIMULTANEOUS serum and ascitic fluid albumin measurement (within hours of each other). SAAG affected by: hypoalbuminaemia (serum albumin <2.8 g/dL reduces SAAG accuracy), mixed ascites (portal hypertension + peritoneal disease - may have intermediate SAAG), timing (serum and ascites must be collected simultaneously). Mixed ascites: SAAG may be intermediate (0.9-1.1 g/dL) - portal hypertension coexists with peritoneal disease. Hypoalbuminaemia: serum albumin <2.8 g/dL reduces SAAG accuracy - use total protein gradient instead. Peritoneal dialysis: SAAG not applicable (dialysate affects results). Sample handling: process ascitic fluid promptly - cell count and protein degrade. Reference ranges: SAAG >=1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension. SAAG <1.1 g/dL = non-portal hypertension.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum + ascitic fluid (via paracentesis). CRITICAL: serum and ascitic fluid must be collected SIMULTANEOUSLY (within hours). Preparation: note cirrhosis history, heart failure, renal function, recent paracentesis. Handling: process both samples within 30 min. Serum albumin: standard venipuncture. Ascitic fluid: paracentesis (sterile technique). SAAG: serum albumin - ascitic fluid albumin. >=1.1 g/dL: portal hypertension. <1.1 g/dL: non-portal hypertension. Simultaneous: essential (serum and ascites within hours). Mixed ascites: intermediate SAAG (0.9-1.1). Hypoalbuminaemia: serum <2.8 g/dL reduces accuracy. Peritoneal dialysis: not applicable. Reference ranges: SAAG >=1.1 = portal hypertension.
ref_ranges: SAAG >=1.1 g/dL: portal hypertensive (cirrhosis, cardiac, Budd-Chiari). SAAG <1.1 g/dL: non-portal hypertensive (carcinomatosis, TB, nephrotic). Accuracy: 90-97% for classifying portal hypertension. Mixed ascites: intermediate (0.9-1.1). Hypoalbuminaemia: serum <2.8 g/dL reduces accuracy. Reference ranges: SAAG is a calculated gradient. Method: serum albumin - ascitic fluid albumin. Simultaneous collection: essential.
refs: Sources: AASLD Paracentesis Guidelines; EASL Ascites Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SEX HORMONE BINDING GLOBULIN (SHBG)
interpretation: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin (SHBG) - glycoprotein produced by the liver that binds sex hormones (testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, oestradiol) with high affinity. SHBG regulates the bioavailability of sex hormones - only unbound (free) hormones are biologically active. Clinical use: evaluating hyperandrogenism (PCOS - SHBG low, testosterone elevated), assessing hypogonadism (SHBG helps interpret total testosterone), evaluating gynaecomastia, monitoring anti-androgen therapy (SHBG rises with treatment), assessing liver disease (SHBG is liver-produced). Low SHBG: polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS - SHBG low, free testosterone elevated), obesity (SHBG decreases with increasing BMI), insulin resistance/metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, androgens/testosterone therapy, glucocorticoids, progesterone (synthetic), acromegaly, Cushing syndrome. High SHBG: hyperthyroidism, oestrogen therapy (OCP, HRT), liver cirrhosis (paradoxically elevated in some cases), anorexia nervosa, ageing (SHBG increases with age), anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone), phenytoin,valproate. Clinical approach to testosterone interpretation: total testosterone + SHBG + calculated free testosterone (or directly measured free testosterone). If SHBG is abnormal: free testosterone is more accurate than total testosterone. Low total testosterone + low SHBG = free testosterone may be normal (obesity). Low total testosterone + high SHBG = free testosterone even lower (hypogonadism). Limitations: SHBG is INFLUENCED BY: oestrogen (raises SHBG - OCP, pregnancy), androgens (lower SHBG - testosterone therapy, anabolic steroids), obesity (lowers SHBG), insulin resistance (lowers SHBG), liver disease (variable), thyroid function (hyperthyroidism raises, hypothyroidism lowers), age (increases with age), medications (many drugs affect SHBG). SHBG and testosterone: must interpret total testosterone alongside SHBG to calculate free testosterone. SHBG and PCOS: low SHBG + high free testosterone = PCOS. SHBG and hypothyroidism: hypothyroidism lowers SHBG - correct thyroid function first. Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: SHBG increases with age. Gender: women have higher SHBG than men.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note testosterone level, thyroid function, liver function, medications (OCP, HRT, androgens, anti-androgens), BMI, menstrual history, symptoms of hyperandrogenism or hypogonadism. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. SHBG + total testosterone + free testosterone: complete picture. Low SHBG: PCOS, obesity, insulin resistance. High SHBG: hyperthyroidism, oestrogen therapy, ageing. Free testosterone: more accurate when SHBG abnormal. PCOS: low SHBG + high free testosterone. Hypothyroidism: lowers SHBG - correct first. Obesity: lowers SHBG. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: SHBG increases with age.
ref_ranges: Men: 10-57 nmol/L. Women (premenopausal): 18-144 nmol/L. Women (postmenopausal): 14-68 nmol/L. Low SHBG: <10 nmol/L (men); <18 nmol/L (women). High SHBG: >57 nmol/L (men); >144 nmol/L (women). PCOS: low SHBG + high free testosterone. Obesity: low SHBG. Hyperthyroidism: high SHBG. Hypothyroidism: low SHBG. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: SHBG increases with age. Gender: women higher than men.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Testosterone Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SGOT/AST (ASPARTATE TRANSAMINASE)
interpretation: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST/SGOT) - intracellular enzyme found in many tissues (liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, brain, red blood cells). Catalyses the transfer of amino groups from aspartate to alpha-ketoglutarate. Elevated AST indicates cell damage/lysis in any tissue containing AST. Clinical use: assessing liver injury (AST elevated in hepatocellular damage), evaluating myocardial infarction (AST elevated - though largely replaced by troponin), assessing muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis, myositis), evaluating alcohol-related liver disease (AST:ALT ratio >2:1), monitoring drug-induced liver injury. Elevated AST: liver disease (most common cause - AST elevated in hepatocellular damage), myocardial infarction (AST elevated - largely replaced by troponin), skeletal muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis, myositis, trauma), alcohol-related liver disease (AST:ALT ratio >2:1), pancreatitis, haemolysis (RBC AST), medications (statins, paracetamol, isoniazid), renal infarction. AST:ALT ratio: >2:1: strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease. >1:1: liver fibrosis/cirrhosis. <1:1: non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). <1:1: viral hepatitis. Limitations: AST is NON-SPECIFIC - elevated in many tissues (liver, heart, muscle, RBC). AST is NOT liver-specific (unlike ALT). AST and ALT: ALT is more liver-specific than AST. AST:ALT ratio: more useful than either alone for aetiology. Haemolysis: AST elevated by RBC lysis (haemolysed sample falsely elevated). Muscle injury: AST elevated in rhabdomyolysis, myositis, MI. AST half-life: ~17 hours (rises faster than ALT in acute injury). AST and alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1 strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease. AST and paracetamol: AST markedly elevated in paracetamol hepatotoxicity. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: AST may be higher in elderly. Gender: men may have slightly higher AST.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note alcohol use, medications (statins, paracetamol, isoniazid), muscle symptoms, recent exercise, recent procedure. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Haemolysis: reject haemolysed samples (RBC AST falsely elevated). AST:ALT ratio: >2:1 = alcoholic liver disease. >1:1 = fibrosis/cirrhosis. <1:1 = NAFLD, viral hepatitis. Alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1 strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease. Paracetamol: AST markedly elevated in hepatotoxicity. Muscle: AST elevated in rhabdomyolysis, myositis. Half-life: ~17 hours. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly.
ref_ranges: Normal: 5-40 U/L (method-specific). Liver disease: elevated AST. Alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1. MI: elevated AST (largely replaced by troponin). Muscle injury: elevated AST. Haemolysis: falsely elevated. Paracetamol: markedly elevated in hepatotoxicity. AST:ALT ratio: >2:1 = alcoholic; <1:1 = NAFLD/viral. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD Liver Injury Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SGPT/ALT (ALANINE TRANSAMINASE)
interpretation: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT/SGPT) - intracellular enzyme found predominantly in the LIVER (more liver-specific than AST). Catalyses the transfer of amino groups from alanine to alpha-ketoglutarate. Most important liver-specific enzyme for detecting hepatocellular damage. Clinical use: detecting liver injury (ALT most sensitive marker of hepatocellular damage), evaluating viral hepatitis (ALT markedly elevated), monitoring drug-induced liver injury, assessing NAFLD/NASH (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease), evaluating alcoholic liver disease (AST:ALT ratio), monitoring cholestatic liver disease (ALT less elevated than ALP/GGT). Elevated ALT: viral hepatitis (ALT markedly elevated - 10-100x ULN in acute hepatitis), drug-induced liver injury (many drugs elevate ALT), NAFLD/NASH (mild-moderate elevation), alcoholic liver disease (AST:ALT >2:1 - ALT less elevated), ischaemic hepatitis (ALT very high - shock liver), autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, coeliac disease, muscle injury (ALT from muscle less than AST). AST:ALT ratio: <1:1: NAFLD/NASH, viral hepatitis. >1:1: alcoholic liver disease, cirrhosis. >2:1: strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease. Limitations: ALT is LIVER-SPECIFIC but NOT liver-exclusive (small amounts in kidney, heart, skeletal muscle). ALT and AST: ALT is more liver-specific than AST; AST is elevated in more tissues. ALT and muscle: ALT from muscle injury is less than AST (AST:ALT >2:1 in rhabdomyolysis). ALT half-life: ~47 hours (longer than AST - rises later, falls later). ALT normal does NOT exclude liver disease (early or mild disease). ALT and alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease (ALT less elevated due to pyridoxal phosphate deficiency). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: ALT may be higher in elderly. Gender: men may have slightly higher ALT.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note alcohol use, medications (statins, paracetamol, isoniazid, oral contraceptives), recent exercise, muscle symptoms, jaundice, hepatitis risk factors. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. ALT: most liver-specific enzyme. Viral hepatitis: ALT markedly elevated (10-100x ULN). NAFLD: mild-moderate elevation. Alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1. Drug-induced: many drugs elevate ALT. Ischaemic: ALT very high (shock liver). Half-life: ~47 hours (longer than AST). AST:ALT ratio: <1:1 = NAFLD/viral; >2:1 = alcoholic. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly.
ref_ranges: Normal: 7-56 U/L (method-specific). Viral hepatitis: ALT markedly elevated (10-100x ULN). NAFLD: mild-moderate elevation (1.5-3x ULN). Alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1 (ALT less elevated). Drug-induced: variable elevation. Ischaemic: ALT very high (100-1000x ULN). Muscle injury: ALT mildly elevated (less than AST). AST:ALT ratio: <1:1 = NAFLD/viral; >2:1 = alcoholic. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; AASLD Liver Injury Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SIROLIMUS (RAPAMYCIN)
interpretation: Serum Sirolimus (Rapamycin) measures the concentration of sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor immunosuppressant used in organ transplantation (kidney, liver), tuberous sclerosis complex, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Therapeutic range: 4 to 12 ng/mL (trough). Sirolimus: inhibits T-cell activation via mTOR. Synergistic: with ciclosporin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). CRITICAL: trough level (12-24h post-dose). Preparation: note transplant status, rejection risk, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 4-12 ng/mL. mTOR inhibitor: immunosuppressant. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 4 to 12 ng/mL (trough). mTOR inhibitor: immunosuppressant. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Transplant Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SODIUM
interpretation: Serum Sodium (Na+) - measurement of sodium concentration in serum. Sodium is the major extracellular cation and the primary determinant of serum osmolality. Regulates water balance, acid-base status, and cellular function. Most important electrolyte for assessing hydration status. Clinical use: evaluating dehydration (hypernatraemia), assessing overhydration (hyponatraemia), guiding fluid resuscitation, monitoring IV fluid therapy, evaluating endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency, SIADH, diabetes insipidus). Elevated sodium (hypernatraemia): dehydration (most common cause - free water deficit), diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic - dilute urine), excessive sodium intake (salt poisoning), aldosterone excess (Conn syndrome), hypodilutional (burns, diarrhoea), hyperventilation (water loss). Low sodium (hyponatraemia): SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH - most common cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia), water excess (psychogenic polydipsia, beer potomania), diuretics (thiazides - dilutional), heart failure (dilutional), liver cirrhosis (dilutional), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol), renal failure, medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide). Hyponatraemia evaluation: euvolaemic: SIADH (most common), hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency, psychogenic polydipsia. Hypovolaemic: dehydration (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns), Addison disease. Hypervolaemic: heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Limitations: sodium is HIGHLY SENSITIVE to pre-analytical errors. Pseudohyponatraemia: hyperlipidaemia (elevated triglycerides - dilutional effect), hyperproteinaemia (multiple myeloma - dilutional effect). Pseudohypernatraemia: haemolysed sample (RBC sodium falsely elevates serum sodium). Hyponatraemia correction: DO NOT correct too rapidly (risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome - central pontine myelinolysis). Correction rate: <10-12 mmol/L per 24h. Sodium and osmolality: sodium is main determinant of serum osmolality. Sodium and glucose: hyperglycaemia causes dilutional hyponatraemia (correct sodium for glucose). Corrected sodium: measured Na + 1.6 x (glucose - 100) / 100. Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: lower than adults. Age: stable across age groups.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (or plasma). Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note fluid intake, diuretic use, recent IV fluids, renal function, endocrine status (thyroid, adrenal), glucose level, triglycerides, protein level. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Haemolysis: falsely elevates sodium (RBC sodium). Pseudohyponatraemia: hyperlipidaemia, hyperproteinaemia. Corrected sodium: adjust for glucose. SIADH: low Na + concentrated urine. Diabetes insipidus: high Na + dilute urine. Correction rate: <10-12 mmol/L per 24h (avoid ODS). Hyponatraemia: evaluate volume status (hypo, eu, hypervolaemic). Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: lower.
ref_ranges: Adults: 136-145 mmol/L. Neonates: 135-145 mmol/L. Hypernatraemia: >145 mmol/L (dehydration, DI). Hyponatraemia: <136 mmol/L (SIADH, diuretics, HF, cirrhosis). Mild hyponatraemia: 130-135 mmol/L. Moderate: 125-129 mmol/L. Severe: <125 mmol/L (symptomatic). Correction rate: <10-12 mmol/L per 24h. Pseudohyponatraemia: hyperlipidaemia, hyperproteinaemia. Corrected Na: adjust for glucose. Reference ranges: method-specific. Neonates: lower. Age: stable.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Hyponatraemia Treatment Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SODIUM - URINE
interpretation: Urine Sodium - measurement of sodium concentration in urine. Used to evaluate the kidney's ability to excrete sodium and to differentiate causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) and hyponatraemia. Clinical use: differentiating prerenal from intrinsic AKI (urine Na <20 mmol/L = prerenal; >40 mmol/L = intrinsic), evaluating hyponatraemia (SIADH vs dehydration), assessing diuretic efficacy, evaluating sodium wasting syndromes. Urine sodium <20 mmol/L: prerenal AKI (kidney is appropriately retaining sodium), dehydration, heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Urine sodium >40 mmol/L: intrinsic AKI (acute tubular necrosis - kidney cannot retain sodium), SIADH (kidney excreting sodium inappropriately), diuretic use, salt-wasting nephropathy, adrenal insufficiency. Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa): FENa = (urine Na x serum Cr) / (serum Na x urine Cr) x 100. FENa <1%: prerenal AKI (kidney retaining sodium). FENa >2%: intrinsic AKI (ATN). FENa 1-2%: grey zone (diuretics, early ATN, sepsis). Limitations: urine sodium is INFLUENCED BY: diuretic use (raises urine Na - interpret with caution), recent sodium intake, renal function, hydration status. Diuretics: invalidate FENa in AKI assessment (use fractional excretion of urea instead - FEUrea >50% suggests intrinsic AKI). Sodium intake: high sodium diet raises urine Na. Sample timing: spot urine acceptable; 24h urine more accurate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot or 24h). Preparation: note diuretic use (invalidates FENa), recent sodium intake, renal function, fluid status. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h. Spot urine: acceptable for FENa. 24h urine: more accurate. FENa: (urine Na x serum Cr) / (serum Na x urine Cr) x 100. <1%: prerenal AKI. >2%: intrinsic AKI (ATN). Diuretics: invalidate FENa - use FENa <50% instead. Sodium intake: high Na raises urine Na. Prerenal: low urine Na (<20 mmol/L). Intrinsic: high urine Na (>40 mmol/L). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Prerenal AKI: <20 mmol/L. Intrinsic AKI (ATN): >40 mmol/L. FENa <1%: prerenal. FENa >2%: intrinsic AKI. SIADH: >40 mmol/L (inappropriate excretion). Diuretics: variable (invalidate FENa). Normal: 40-220 mmol/L/24h. Reference ranges: method-specific. Spot urine: acceptable. 24h: more accurate.
refs: Sources: KDIGO AKI Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: SOLUBLE TRANSFERRIN RECEPTOR BIOCHEMICAL
interpretation: Serum Soluble Transferrin Receptor (sTfR) measures the concentration of the circulating form of the transferrin receptor. sTfR reflects erythropoietic activity and iron demand. Elevated sTfR: iron deficiency anaemia, ineffective erythropoiesis (thalassaemia, sideroblastic anaemia). sTfR/log ferritin index: more sensitive than ferritin alone for iron deficiency. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note anaemia, iron status. Handle per standard. Elevated: iron deficiency, ineffective erythropoiesis. Index: sTfR/log ferritin. More sensitive: than ferritin alone. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: iron deficiency, ineffective erythropoiesis. Index: more sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: SUCCINYLACETONE - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Succinylacetone measures the concentration of succinylacetone, a metabolite that accumulates in tyrosinaemia type 1 (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency). Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: SUCROSE LYSIS TEST
interpretation: Blood Sucrose Lysis Test measures complement-mediated lysis of red blood cells in isotonic sucrose solution. Sucrose lysis test: screening test for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH). PNH: acquired clonal disorder characterised by absence of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59) on blood cells. Positive: complement-mediated lysis. Reference ranges: qualitative.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (heparin). Preparation: note haemolysis, dark urine, anaemia. Handle per standard. Positive: PNH. Complement: lysis. Screening: not confirmatory. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Normal: negative (less than 10%). Positive: PNH (greater than 10%). Screening: not confirmatory. Reference ranges: qualitative.
refs: Sources: British Committee for Standards in Haematology; manufacturer IFU.

name: T3 TOTAL
interpretation: Total Triiodothyronine (T3 Total) - measurement of total T3 (bound + free) in serum. T3 is the biologically active thyroid hormone, produced by peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 (80%) and direct thyroid secretion (20%). Total T3 includes protein-bound T3 (99.7%) and free T3 (0.3%). Less commonly measured than TSH and free T4. Clinical use: evaluating hyperthyroidism (T3 toxicosis - T3 elevated, T4 may be normal), confirming thyroid dysfunction, evaluating Graves disease (T3 elevated), assessing T3 thyrotoxicosis (elevated T3, normal T4). Elevated T3: hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre), T3 toxicosis (T3 elevated, T4 normal - early or mild hyperthyroidism), thyroiditis (subacute, painless), TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous T3 intake), struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid tissue). T3 toxicosis: T3 elevated with normal T4 - occurs in early hyperthyroidism, T3-predominant Graves disease, and iodine deficiency. Low T3: hypothyroidism (T3 low, T4 low, TSH high), non-thyroidal illness (low T3 syndrome - sick euthyroid), severe illness (low T3 due to reduced peripheral conversion). Limitations: total T3 is INFLUENCED BY: thyroid binding globulin (TBG) levels, protein levels, pregnancy (TBG elevated - total T3 elevated), oral contraceptives (TBG elevated), androgens (TBG reduced), oestrogen therapy (TBG elevated), medications. Total T3 vs free T3: free T3 is more clinically useful (not affected by TBG). Total T3 is largely replaced by free T3 in modern practice. Free T3: more accurate for assessing thyroid status. Total T3 affected by: TBG abnormalities (pregnancy, OCP, androgens), protein abnormalities (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis). Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: T3 may be lower in elderly. Gender: no significant gender difference.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid symptoms (weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance, fatigue), medications (amiodarone, beta-blockers, thyroid hormones, oestrogen), pregnancy, TBG abnormalities. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Total T3: bound + free T3. T3 toxicosis: T3 elevated, T4 normal. TBG: affects total T3 (pregnancy, OCP). Free T3: more clinically useful. Total T3: largely replaced by free T3. Hypothyroidism: T3 low, T4 low, TSH high. Hyperthyroidism: T3 high, T4 high, TSH low. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: T3 may be lower in elderly.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.8-2.0 ng/mL (method-specific). Hyperthyroidism: >2.0 ng/mL. T3 toxicosis: T3 elevated, T4 normal. Hypothyroidism: <0.8 ng/mL. Non-thyroidal illness: low T3 (low T3 syndrome). Pregnancy: total T3 elevated (TBG increase). Oral contraceptives: total T3 elevated (TBG increase). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be lower in elderly. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: T4 TOTAL
interpretation: Total Thyroxine (T4 Total) - measurement of total T4 (bound + free) in serum. T4 is the major secretory product of the thyroid gland (90% of thyroid output). Total T4 includes protein-bound T4 (99.97%) and free T4 (0.03%). Less commonly measured than TSH and free T4. Clinical use: evaluating hypothyroidism (T4 low, TSH high), confirming hyperthyroidism (T4 high, TSH low), assessing thyroid function in patients with abnormal thyroid binding globulin (TBG), monitoring thyroid hormone replacement. Elevated T4: hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre), thyroiditis (subacute, painless), TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous T4 intake), struma ovarii. Low T4: hypothyroidism (primary - T4 low, TSH high; secondary - T4 low, TSH low/normal), non-thyroidal illness (low T3/T4 syndrome), severe illness, medications (amiodarone, iodine). Limitations: total T4 is INFLUENCED BY: thyroid binding globulin (TBG) levels - pregnancy, OCP, oestrogen raise TBG and total T4; androgens reduce TBG and total T4. Total T4 vs free T4: free T4 is more clinically useful (not affected by TBG). Total T4 is largely replaced by free T4 in modern practice. Total T4 affected by: TBG abnormalities, protein abnormalities (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis). Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: T4 stable across age groups. Gender: no significant gender difference.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid symptoms, medications (amiodarone, thyroid hormones, oestrogen), pregnancy, TBG abnormalities. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Total T4: bound + free T4. TBG: affects total T4 (pregnancy, OCP). Free T4: more clinically useful. Total T4: largely replaced by free T4. Hypothyroidism: T4 low, TSH high. Hyperthyroidism: T4 high, TSH low. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 5.0-12.0 ug/dL (method-specific). Hyperthyroidism: >12.0 ug/dL. Hypothyroidism: <5.0 ug/dL. Pregnancy: total T4 elevated (TBG increase). Oral contraceptives: total T4 elevated (TBG increase). Non-thyroidal illness: low T4 (low T4 syndrome). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: stable. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TACROLIMUS
interpretation: Serum Tacrolimus measures the concentration of tacrolimus (FK506), a calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant used in organ transplantation (kidney, liver, heart, lung), autoimmune diseases, and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Therapeutic range: 5 to 15 ng/mL (trough, kidney). Tacrolimus: inhibits T-cell activation via calcineurin. Narrow therapeutic index: drug monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). CRITICAL: trough level (12h post-dose). Preparation: note transplant status, rejection risk, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 5-15 ng/mL. Narrow index: monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 5 to 15 ng/mL (trough). Narrow index: monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO Transplant Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TEAR FLUID FOR CALCIUM
interpretation: Tear Fluid Calcium - measurement of calcium concentration in tear fluid (lacrimal fluid). Specialised test used to evaluate calcium metabolism in patients with chronic dry eye (Sjogren syndrome), and to assess systemic calcium status in certain populations. Tear calcium reflects local lacrimal gland function and systemic calcium homeostasis. Clinical use: evaluating Sjogren syndrome (tear calcium elevated in some studies), assessing lacrimal gland function, monitoring calcium metabolism in patients with chronic dry eye, research tool for evaluating ocular surface disease. Elevated tear calcium: Sjogren syndrome (lacrimal gland dysfunction may alter calcium secretion), hypercalcaemia (systemic elevation may raise tear calcium), chronic kidney disease (calcium-phosphate imbalance), aging. Low tear calcium: hypocalcaemia (systemic), lacrimal gland dysfunction (reduced secretion), dry eye syndrome (reduced tear volume). Limitations: tear fluid calcium is a SPECIALISED test - not routinely available in most laboratories. Tear calcium is INFLUENCED BY: tear flow rate (fast tears dilute calcium), sample collection method (reflex tears vs stimulated tears), time of day, ocular surface disease, medications. Tear flow rate: fast tears dilute calcium concentration. Sample collection: reflex tears (crying) vs stimulated tears (onion) vs basal tears (medically collected). Reference ranges: limited data - method-specific. Clinical utility: limited - research tool rather than clinical diagnostic test. Standardisation: no standardised reference ranges available. Collection technique: affects results significantly.
pre_analytical: Sample: Tear fluid. CRITICAL: specialised collection method required. Preparation: note dry eye symptoms, autoimmune disease history, medications, ocular surface disease. Handling: process immediately (tear fluid degrades rapidly). Reflex tears (crying) vs stimulated tears vs basal tears: different collection methods affect results. Sjogren: tear calcium may be elevated. Hypercalcaemia: tear calcium may be elevated. Tear flow rate: fast tears dilute calcium. Standardisation: no standardised reference ranges. Clinical utility: limited - research tool. Collection technique: significantly affects results.
ref_ranges: Limited reference data - method-specific. Tear calcium: varies with collection method and tear flow rate. Sjogren syndrome: tear calcium may be elevated (limited data). Hypercalcaemia: tear calcium may be elevated. Standardisation: no standardised ranges. Clinical utility: limited. Research tool: more than clinical diagnostic test. Collection method: affects results significantly.
refs: Sources: Limited literature; manufacturer IFU.

name: TESTOSTERONE TOTAL
interpretation: Total Testosterone - measurement of total testosterone (bound + free) in serum. Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone produced by Leydig cells of the testes (men) and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands (women). 98% bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin; only 2% free and biologically active. Clinical use: diagnosing male hypogonadism, evaluating female hyperandrogenism (PCOS), assessing delayed/precocious puberty, monitoring testosterone replacement therapy, evaluating gynaecomastia, assessing infertility. Low testosterone (male hypogonadism): primary hypogonadism (testicular failure - low testosterone, high LH/FSH), secondary hypogonadism (pituitary/hypothalamic - low testosterone, low/normal LH/FSH), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), orchitis, testicular trauma, mumps, chemotherapy, obesity, chronic illness, medications (opioids, glucocorticoids, spironolactone), aging. Elevated testosterone (women): PCOS (most common cause - elevated free testosterone, low SHBG), ovarian tumour (androgen-secreting), adrenal tumour, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, exogenous androgens (anabolic steroids). Limitations: total testosterone is INFLUENCED BY: SHBG levels (high SHBG = low free testosterone even if total normal), diurnal variation (highest 6-10 AM - always sample in morning), pulsatile secretion (single value unreliable - multiple samples needed), age (testosterone declines with age), body mass (obesity lowers testosterone), medications. Morning sample: ESSENTIAL (testosterone peaks 6-10 AM). SHBG: must interpret alongside total testosterone. Free testosterone: more accurate when SHBG abnormal. Multiple samples: testosterone is pulsatile - single value may be unreliable. Assay variability: method-specific. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: testosterone declines with age. Ethnicity: may differ between ethnic groups.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: morning sample (6-10 AM). Preparation: note symptoms (fatigue, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, hot flushes), medications (opioids, glucocorticoids, spironolactone, testosterone), BMI, recent illness. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Morning: sample 6-10 AM (diurnal variation). SHBG: must interpret alongside total testosterone. Free testosterone: more accurate when SHBG abnormal. PCOS: elevated free testosterone, low SHBG. Hypogonadism: low testosterone, assess LH/FSH. Multiple samples: testosterone pulsatile. Age: declines with age. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Men: 300-1000 ng/dL (varies by age). Women: 15-70 ng/dL. Hypogonadism (men): <300 ng/dL. PCOS (women): elevated free testosterone. Morning: highest 6-10 AM. Assay: method-specific. Age: declines with age. Ethnicity: may differ. SHBG: must interpret with total testosterone. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Endocrine Society Testosterone Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: THALLIUM
interpretation: Whole Blood Thallium measures thallium concentration in blood. Thallium is a toxic heavy metal historically used as a rodenticide and in industrial processes. Thallium toxicity: alopecia, peripheral neuropathy, gastrointestinal symptoms, encephalopathy. Blood thallium: recent exposure. Urine: cumulative. Chelation: if toxic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (metal-free collection). CRITICAL: metal-free tubes. Preparation: note alopecia, neuropathy, GI symptoms, exposure history. Handle: metal-free. Blood: recent exposure. Urine: cumulative. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 1 mcg/L (method-specific). Elevated: thallium toxicity. Chelation: if toxic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATSDR Thallium Profile; manufacturer IFU.

name: THEOPHYLLINE
interpretation: Serum Theophylline measures the concentration of theophylline, a methylxanthine bronchodilator used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Therapeutic range: 10 to 20 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 20 mcg/mL. Narrow therapeutic index: drug monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note respiratory disease, other medications, caffeine intake. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 10-20 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 20. Narrow index: monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 10 to 20 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 20. Narrow index: monitoring essential. Reference ranges: method-specific.

interpretation: Urine Threonine Quantitative measures threonine concentration. Threonine is an essential amino acid. Elevated urine threonine: hyperthreoninaemia (threoninase deficiency), nonketotic hyperglycinaemia (NKH). Threonine: one of the branched-chain amino acids. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note developmental delay, seizures, metabolic history. Handle per standard. Elevated: hyperthreoninaemia, NKH. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: hyperthreoninaemia, NKH. Reference ranges: method-specific.

name: THYROGLOBULIN
interpretation: Thyroglobulin (Tg) - large glycoprotein produced by thyroid follicular cells. Serves as the storage form of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) within the thyroid gland. Released into the blood during thyroid hormone synthesis and thyroid gland destruction. Most important tumour marker for differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) after thyroidectomy.
