Clinical use: monitoring differentiated thyroid cancer (post-thyroidectomy - Tg should be undetectable), assessing thyroid cancer recurrence (rising Tg after treatment), evaluating congenital hypothyroidism, diagnosing subacute thyroiditis (Tg elevated from gland destruction), monitoring thyroid hormone therapy. Elevated thyroglobulin: differentiated thyroid cancer (post-thyroidectomy - rising Tg suggests recurrence), thyroiditis (subacute, painless - Tg elevated from gland destruction), Graves disease (Tg elevated), goitre (multinodular goitre), ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis (Tg low in exogenous thyroid hormone intake). Low/undetectable thyroglobulin: after total thyroidectomy (should be undetectable if complete), hypopituitarism (reduced TSH stimulation), factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses Tg). Tg and thyroid cancer monitoring: post-thyroidectomy: Tg should be undetectable (<0.2 ng/mL). Rising Tg: suggests recurrence or metastatic disease. Tg and thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb): MUST check TgAb - TgAb can interfere with Tg assay (false low Tg). If TgAb positive: Tg measurement unreliable - use TgAb trend instead. Limitations: thyroglobulin is a TUMOUR MARKER for differentiated thyroid cancer - but ONLY useful AFTER total thyroidectomy (normal thyroid produces Tg). TgAb interference: TgAb can cause falsely LOW Tg (most common assay interference). MUST measure TgAb alongside Tg. TgAb trend: if TgAb positive, use TgAb trend (falling = good; rising = concern). Assay variability: Tg assays vary significantly between manufacturers - use same assay for serial monitoring. Heterophilic antibodies: can cause falsely elevated Tg (rare). Reference ranges: method-specific. TgAb: must be measured alongside Tg.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid cancer history (type, stage, treatment), thyroidectomy status, TSH suppression therapy, TgAb status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. TgAb: MUST check alongside Tg (TgAb interferes with Tg assay). Post-thyroidectomy: Tg should be undetectable (<0.2 ng/mL). Rising Tg: suggests recurrence. TgAb trend: falling = good; rising = concern. Assay: use same assay for serial monitoring. Hypothyroidism: Tg elevated. Thyroiditis: Tg elevated. Graves: Tg elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Post-thyroidectomy: <0.2 ng/mL (undetectable). Thyroid cancer: rising Tg suggests recurrence. Thyroiditis: Tg elevated (gland destruction). Graves: Tg elevated. Goitre: Tg elevated. TgAb: must check alongside Tg. TgAb interference: falsely low Tg. Assay: use same assay for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Cancer Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: THYROID PROFILE
interpretation: Thyroid Profile (Complete Panel) - combined measurement of TSH, free T4, and free T3 in a single panel. The most comprehensive assessment of thyroid function. TSH is the most sensitive marker (reflects pituitary-thyroid feedback), free T4 reflects thyroid hormone production, free T3 reflects peripheral conversion and biological activity. Clinical use: comprehensive thyroid assessment, evaluating hypothyroidism (TSH high, FT4 low), diagnosing hyperthyroidism (TSH low, FT4 high, FT3 high), subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH high, FT4 normal), subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH low, FT4 normal), monitoring thyroid hormone replacement therapy, evaluating non-thyroidal illness. Thyroid profile interpretation: Primary hypothyroidism: TSH high + FT4 low (most common - autoimmune thyroiditis). Secondary hypothyroidism: TSH low/normal + FT4 low (pituitary disease). Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH high + FT4 normal (early/mild disease). Primary hyperthyroidism: TSH low + FT4 high + FT3 high (Graves disease, toxic goitre). T3 toxicosis: TSH low + FT4 normal + FT3 high (early/mild hyperthyroidism). Subclinical hyperthyroidism: TSH low + FT4 normal + FT3 normal (early/mild disease). Non-thyroidal illness: TSH normal/low + FT4 low/normal + FT3 low (sick euthyroid syndrome). Limitations: thyroid profile is the COMPREHENSIVE assessment - but TSH alone is often sufficient for initial screening. TSH and FT4: discordant results (TSH high, FT4 normal) may indicate subclinical hypothyroidism, assay interference (heterophilic antibodies), or TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (rare). FT3: may be normal in hypothyroidism (reduced conversion); elevated in T3 toxicosis. Assay variability: method-specific (different assays for FT4 and FT3). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: TSH may be higher in elderly. Pregnancy: TSH lower in first trimester.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid symptoms, medications (thyroid hormones, amiodarone, biotin), pregnancy, family history of thyroid disease. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. TSH: most sensitive marker. FT4: reflects thyroid hormone production. FT3: reflects peripheral conversion. Hypothyroidism: TSH high, FT4 low. Hyperthyroidism: TSH low, FT4 high, FT3 high. T3 toxicosis: TSH low, FT4 normal, FT3 high. Subclinical: TSH abnormal, FT4 normal. Biotin: interferes with assays (stop biotin 48h before). Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: TSH: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L. FT4: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL. FT3: 2.3-4.2 pg/mL. Hypothyroidism: TSH >4.0, FT4 <0.8. Hyperthyroidism: TSH <0.4, FT4 >1.8, FT3 >4.2. Subclinical hypo: TSH high, FT4 normal. Subclinical hyper: TSH low, FT4 normal. Non-thyroidal: TSH normal, FT3 low. Reference ranges: method-specific. Pregnancy: TSH lower first trimester. Age: TSH may be higher in elderly.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Disease Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: THYROID STIMULATING HORMONE (TSH)- Ultrasensitive
interpretation: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) Ultrasensitive - measurement of TSH using an ultrasensitive immunometric assay (detection limit <0.01 mIU/L). TSH is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and regulates thyroid hormone production via negative feedback. Most sensitive single test for screening thyroid dysfunction. Clinical use: initial screening for thyroid disease (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism), monitoring thyroid hormone replacement therapy, evaluating subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH elevated, FT4 normal), diagnosing hyperthyroidism (TSH suppressed), assessing pituitary-thyroid axis. Elevated TSH: primary hypothyroidism (most common cause - TSH elevated, FT4 low), subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH elevated, FT4 normal), Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune - most common cause in iodine-sufficient areas), iodine deficiency (endemic goitre), post-thyroidectomy (inadequate replacement), medications (lithium, amiodarone, interferon-alpha), central hypothyroidism (TSH may be normal/high with low FT4 - rare), TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (very rare). Suppressed TSH: primary hyperthyroidism (TSH suppressed, FT4 elevated), subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH suppressed, FT4 normal), Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre, thyroiditis, exogenous thyroid hormone intake, non-thyroidal illness (low T3 syndrome). Normal TSH with abnormal FT4: assay interference (heterophilic antibodies), TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (rare), central hypothyroidism (pituitary disease). Limitations: TSH is the MOST SENSITIVE screening test for thyroid dysfunction - but has limitations. TSH and FT4: discordant results require further investigation. Biotin interference: HIGH-DOSE BIOTIN (>5 mg/day) interferes with immunoassays - falsely LOW TSH in hyperthyroidism, falsely HIGH TSH in hypothyroidism. Stop biotin 48h before testing. TSH and non-thyroidal illness: TSH may be transiently abnormal in acute illness (euthyroid sick syndrome). Wait 6-8 weeks after acute illness before testing. TSH and medications: many drugs affect TSH (lithium, amiodarone, corticosteroids, dopamine). TSH pulsatility: TSH is secreted in pulses - single measurement generally reliable. Assay variability: method-specific (ultrasensitive assays detect <0.01 mIU/L). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: TSH may be slightly higher in elderly. Pregnancy: TSH lower in first trimester.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid symptoms (fatigue, weight changes, heat/cold intolerance, palpitations), medications (biotin, thyroid hormones, amiodarone, lithium), pregnancy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Biotin: stop 48h before testing (interferes with assays). Non-thyroidal illness: wait 6-8 weeks after acute illness. Hypothyroidism: TSH elevated (>4.0 mIU/L). Hyperthyroidism: TSH suppressed (<0.4 mIU/L). Subclinical: TSH abnormal, FT4 normal. Assay: ultrasensitive (<0.01 mIU/L detection). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: TSH may be higher in elderly.
ref_ranges: Normal: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L (method-specific). Hypothyroidism: >4.0 mIU/L. Hyperthyroidism: <0.4 mIU/L. Subclinical hypo: 4.0-10.0 mIU/L + FT4 normal. Subclinical hyper: <0.1 mIU/L + FT4 normal. Biotin interference: falsely low TSH (hyperthyroidism pattern) or falsely high TSH (hypothyroidism pattern). Non-thyroidal illness: TSH may be transiently abnormal. Pregnancy: lower in first trimester. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: ultrasensitive. Age: may be higher in elderly.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Disease Guidelines; Biotin Interference Alert (FDA); manufacturer IFU.

name: THYROXINE BINDING GLOBULIN (TBG)
interpretation: Serum Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG) measures the concentration of thyroxine-binding globulin, the main transport protein for thyroid hormones (T3, T4). TBG: binds 75% of circulating T4. Elevated TBG: pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, liver disease, genetic TBG excess. Low TBG: nephrotic syndrome, androgens, genetic TBG deficiency. Total T4: affected by TBG. Free T4: not affected. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid disease, pregnancy, medications. Handle per standard. TBG: transport protein. Elevated: pregnancy, oestrogen. Free T4: not affected. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 12 to 30 mcg/mL (method-specific). Elevated: pregnancy, oestrogen. Low: nephrotic syndrome, androgens. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATA Thyroid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TOPIRAMATE
interpretation: Serum Topiramate measures the concentration of topiramate, an anticonvulsant used to treat focal seizures, generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and migraine prophylaxis. Therapeutic range: 1 to 15 mcg/mL. Topiramate: carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Metabolic acidosis: risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, kidney stones, metabolic acidosis. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 1-15 mcg/mL. Carbonic anhydrase: inhibitor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 1 to 15 mcg/mL. Carbonic anhydrase: inhibitor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TOTAL BILE ACIDS
interpretation: Total Bile Acids (TBA) - measurement of total bile acid concentration in serum. Bile acids are synthesised from cholesterol in the liver (primary bile acids: cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid), conjugated with glycine or taurine, secreted into bile, and recycled via enterohepatic circulation. Elevated serum bile acids indicate hepatobiliary disease or impaired bile acid metabolism. Clinical use: detecting cholestasis (elevated bile acids), diagnosing intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP - bile acids elevated), evaluating liver disease (more sensitive than bilirubin for early hepatocellular injury), screening for bile acid malabsorption (terminal ileum disease), monitoring liver transplant rejection. Elevated bile acids: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP - bile acids elevated, pruritus in pregnancy), primary biliary cholangitis (PBC - cholestasis), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), drug-induced cholestasis, viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, cirrhosis, bile duct obstruction (extrahepatic cholestasis), sepsis, total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP): bile acids >10 umol/L (fasting), pruritus in pregnancy (usually 3rd trimester), elevated risk of fetal distress, preterm birth, stillbirth. Bile acids and liver function: bile acids more sensitive than bilirubin for detecting early hepatocellular injury. Bile acids and pruritus: elevated bile acids cause pruritus (cholestatic pruritus). Limitations: bile acids are SENSITIVE but NOT SPECIFIC for hepatobiliary disease. Bile acids are INFLUENCED BY: fasting status (fasting bile acids more reliable - postprandial elevation is physiological), time of day (circadian variation), meal composition (fatty meals raise bile acids), hepatic blood flow, kidney function. Fasting sample: ESSENTIAL (postprandial bile acids falsely elevated). Postprandial elevation: physiological - not pathological. Time of day: morning fasting sample most reliable. Sample timing: fasting (8-12h) preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may be higher in elderly. Gender: women may have slightly higher bile acids.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting sample (8-12h). Preparation: note pregnancy status (ICP), pruritus, liver disease history, medications, recent meals. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting: essential (postprandial elevation is physiological). ICP: bile acids >10 umol/L (fasting). Pruritus: bile acids cause cholestatic pruritus. Liver function: more sensitive than bilirubin. PBC: elevated bile acids. PSC: elevated bile acids. Drug-induced: cholestasis. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Fasting: <10 umol/L (method-specific). ICP (pregnancy): >10 umol/L (fasting). Cholestasis: elevated bile acids. PBC: elevated. PSC: elevated. Viral hepatitis: elevated. Cirrhosis: elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Fasting: essential. Postprandial: physiological elevation. Age: may be higher in elderly.
refs: Sources: AASLD Cholestasis Guidelines; RCOG ICP Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TOTAL IRON BINDING CAPACITY(TIBC)
interpretation: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) - measurement of the total capacity of transferrin to bind iron. Reflects transferrin concentration (TIBC is directly proportional to transferrin). TIBC is calculated from serum iron and transferrin saturation (TIBC = serum iron / transferrin saturation x 100). Clinical use: evaluating iron deficiency (TIBC elevated), assessing iron overload (TIBC low), differentiating causes of anaemia (iron deficiency vs chronic disease vs thalassaemia), monitoring iron supplementation therapy. Elevated TIBC: iron deficiency anaemia (most common cause - TIBC elevated as body tries to capture more iron), pregnancy (increased transferrin synthesis), oral contraceptive use (oestrogen raises transferrin), acute hepatitis (transient elevation), iron-deficient erythropoiesis. Low TIBC: iron overload (haemochromatosis - TIBC low as body reduces iron binding capacity), chronic disease/inflammation (low TIBC from inflammation), malnutrition (reduced protein synthesis), liver cirrhosis (reduced transferrin synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss of transferrin), chronic kidney disease, thalassaemia. TIBC and iron deficiency: TIBC elevated + serum iron low + ferritin low + transferrin saturation low = iron deficiency anaemia. TIBC and chronic disease: TIBC low + serum iron low + ferritin normal/elevated + transferrin saturation low = anaemia of chronic disease. Limitations: TIBC is INFLUENCED BY: liver function (transferrin is liver-produced - cirrhosis lowers TIBC), nutritional status (malnutrition lowers TIBC), inflammation (acute phase - lowers TIBC), pregnancy (raises TIBC), oral contraceptives (raise TIBC), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss). TIBC vs transferrin: TIBC is more commonly measured than transferrin directly. TIBC and transferrin saturation: transferrin saturation = serum iron / TIBC x 100. Low saturation (<16%): iron deficiency. High saturation (>45%): iron overload. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary. Gender: women may have slightly higher TIBC.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note anaemia symptoms, iron supplementation, recent transfusions, inflammation, liver function, menstrual history, pregnancy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. TIBC: total iron binding capacity. Directly proportional to transferrin. Iron deficiency: TIBC elevated. Iron overload: TIBC low. Chronic disease: TIBC low. Transferrin saturation: serum iron / TIBC x 100. <16%: iron deficiency. >45%: iron overload. Liver function: cirrhosis lowers TIBC. Inflammation: lowers TIBC. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary.
ref_ranges: Normal: 250-370 ug/dL (method-specific). Iron deficiency: >370 ug/dL (elevated). Iron overload: <250 ug/dL (low). Chronic disease: low TIBC. Pregnancy: elevated TIBC. Oral contraceptives: elevated TIBC. Liver cirrhosis: low TIBC. Nephrotic syndrome: low TIBC. Transferrin saturation: <16% = iron deficiency; >45% = iron overload. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary.
refs: Sources: WHO Iron Deficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TOTAL PROTEIN
interpretation: Total Serum Protein - measurement of total protein concentration in serum, comprising albumin (60% of total) and globulins (40% - alpha-1, alpha-2, beta, gamma). Reflects the balance between protein synthesis (liver, immune cells) and protein loss (renal, gastrointestinal, burns). Clinical use: evaluating liver function (low albumin = liver failure), assessing nutritional status (low protein = malnutrition), screening for multiple myeloma (elevated globulins), evaluating nephrotic syndrome (low albumin + high globulins), monitoring chronic inflammation. Elevated total protein: dehydration (hemoconcentration - falsely elevated), multiple myeloma (monoclonal paraprotein), chronic inflammation/infection (elevated gamma globulins), autoimmune disease (elevated immunoglobulins), chronic liver disease (elevated immunoglobulins from gut antigens), sarcoidosis. Low total protein: malnutrition (reduced intake), liver failure (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary protein loss), protein-losing enteropathy, burns (protein losses), chronic illness (negative acute phase response), haemodilution (overhydration). Protein fractions: albumin (liver synthetic function - low in liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition), alpha-1 (acute phase reactant - elevated in inflammation), alpha-2 (haptoglobin, alpha-2 macroglobulin - elevated in inflammation), beta (transferrin, complement C3), gamma (immunoglobulins - elevated in chronic infection, autoimmune disease, multiple myeloma). Limitations: total protein is NON-SPECIFIC - elevated or low in many conditions. Dehydration: falsely elevates total protein (hemoconcentration). Haemodilution: falsely lowers total protein. Total protein alone: less useful than protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for evaluating myeloma. Age: albumin may decrease with age. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note liver function, kidney function, nutritional status, chronic disease, medications, hydration status. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Albumin: liver synthetic function. Globulins: immune function, inflammation. Dehydration: falsely elevates total protein. Haemodilution: falsely lowers total protein. SPEP: more informative than total protein alone. Myeloma: elevated globulins (M-spike). Nephrotic: low albumin + elevated globulins. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: albumin decreases with age.
ref_ranges: Normal: 6.0-8.3 g/dL (method-specific). Dehydration: >8.3 g/dL (falsely elevated). Malnutrition: <6.0 g/dL. Liver failure: low total protein. Nephrotic syndrome: low albumin + elevated globulins. Myeloma: elevated globulins. Chronic inflammation: elevated gamma globulins. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: albumin decreases with age. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRANSFERRIN
interpretation: Serum Transferrin - glycoprotein produced by the liver that binds and transports iron from the gut (absorption) and stores (reticuloendothelial system) to the bone marrow (erythropoiesis). Transferrin is the major iron transport protein in blood. Transferrin saturation (TSAT) = serum iron / TIBC x 100 reflects iron availability for erythropoiesis. Clinical use: evaluating iron deficiency (transferrin elevated), assessing iron overload (transferrin low), differentiating causes of anaemia (iron deficiency vs chronic disease), monitoring iron supplementation therapy, evaluating hereditary haemochromatosis. Elevated transferrin: iron deficiency anaemia (most common cause - body produces more transferrin to capture iron), pregnancy (increased transferrin synthesis), oral contraceptive use (oestrogen raises transferrin), iron-deficient erythropoiesis. Low transferrin: iron overload (haemochromatosis - body reduces transferrin), chronic disease/inflammation (acute phase - lowers transferrin), malnutrition (reduced protein synthesis), liver cirrhosis (reduced transferrin synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss of transferrin), chronic kidney disease, thalassaemia. Transferrin saturation (TSAT): TSAT = serum iron / TIBC x 100 (TIBC is directly proportional to transferrin). Low TSAT (<16%): iron deficiency (insufficient iron for erythropoiesis). High TSAT (>45%): iron overload (haemochromatosis - iron toxicity). Normal TSAT (16-45%): adequate iron availability. Clinical approach: iron deficiency anaemia: TSAT <16% + ferritin <30 ng/mL + TIBC elevated. Anaemia of chronic disease: TSAT low + ferritin normal/elevated + TIBC low. Haemochromatosis: TSAT >45% + ferritin elevated + HFE genotype. Limitations: transferrin is INFLUENCED BY: liver function (transferrin is liver-produced - cirrhosis lowers transferrin), nutritional status (malnutrition lowers transferrin), inflammation (acute phase - lowers transferrin), pregnancy (raises transferrin), oral contraceptives (raise transferrin), nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss). Transferrin vs TIBC: TIBC is more commonly measured than transferrin directly (TIBC directly proportional to transferrin). Transferrin and iron: transferrin transports iron - TSAT reflects iron availability. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary. Gender: women may have slightly higher transferrin.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note anaemia symptoms, iron supplementation, recent transfusions, inflammation, liver function, menstrual history, pregnancy. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Transferrin: iron transport protein. TIBC: directly proportional to transferrin. TSAT: serum iron / TIBC x 100. <16%: iron deficiency. >45%: iron overload. Liver function: cirrhosis lowers transferrin. Inflammation: lowers transferrin. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary.
ref_ranges: Normal: 200-360 mg/dL (method-specific). Iron deficiency: >360 mg/dL (elevated). Iron overload: <200 mg/dL (low). Chronic disease: low transferrin. Pregnancy: elevated. Oral contraceptives: elevated. Liver cirrhosis: low. Nephrotic syndrome: low (urinary loss). TSAT: <16% = iron deficiency; >45% = iron overload. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Iron Deficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRANSFERRIN SATURATION
interpretation: Transferrin Saturation (TSAT) - calculated parameter: TSAT = (serum iron / TIBC) x 100. Reflects the percentage of transferrin that is saturated with iron. Directly indicates iron availability for erythropoiesis. More clinically useful than serum iron alone for assessing iron status. Clinical use: evaluating iron deficiency (TSAT low), assessing iron overload/haemochromatosis (TSAT high), differentiating causes of anaemia, guiding iron supplementation therapy, screening for hereditary haemochromatosis. Low TSAT (<16%): iron deficiency anaemia (most common cause - insufficient iron for erythropoiesis), anaemia of chronic disease (iron sequestered in macrophages), chronic kidney disease (functional iron deficiency), recent blood loss, malabsorption (coeliac disease, gastric bypass), dietary insufficiency. High TSAT (>45%): hereditary haemochromatosis (HFE gene mutations - iron overload), secondary iron overload (thalassaemia major - transfusional), sideroblastic anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis), acute hepatic necrosis (iron release from damaged hepatocytes), lead poisoning (sideroblastic changes). Normal TSAT (16-45%): adequate iron availability, excludes significant iron deficiency or overload. Clinical approach: iron deficiency anaemia: TSAT <16% + ferritin <30 ng/mL + TIBC elevated + serum iron low. Anaemia of chronic disease: TSAT low + ferritin normal/elevated + TIBC low/normal + serum iron low. Haemochromatosis: TSAT >45% + ferritin elevated + HFE genotype positive. Limitations: TSAT is INFLUENCED BY: serum iron (diurnal variation - highest morning), inflammation (acute phase - lowers TSAT), liver function (transferrin synthesis), recent iron intake (meal affects serum iron), menstrual cycle (blood loss lowers TSAT). Serum iron diurnal variation: highest in morning (fasting morning sample recommended). Inflammation: lowers TSAT (acute phase response - iron sequestered). Postprandial: serum iron rises after meals (affects TSAT calculation). TSAT and ferritin: TSAT + ferritin together more informative than either alone. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: TSAT may vary. Gender: women may have lower TSAT (menstrual blood loss).
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred (8-12h). Preparation: note anaemia symptoms, iron supplementation, recent transfusions, inflammation, liver function, menstrual history, family history of haemochromatosis. Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting: preferred (serum iron diurnal variation). TSAT: (serum iron / TIBC) x 100. <16%: iron deficiency. >45%: iron overload. Ferritin: must interpret with TSAT. Haemochromatosis: TSAT >45% + ferritin elevated + HFE genotype. Anaemia of chronic disease: TSAT low + ferritin normal/elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: may vary.
ref_ranges: Normal: 16-45% (method-specific). Iron deficiency: <16%. Iron overload: >45%. Haemochromatosis: >45% + elevated ferritin. Anaemia of chronic disease: low TSAT + normal/elevated ferritin. Reference ranges: method-specific. Fasting: preferred. Age: may vary. Gender: women may have lower TSAT.
refs: Sources: WHO Iron Deficiency Guidelines; AASLD Haemochromatosis Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRICYCLIC ANTIDEPRESSANT DRUG (QUALITATIVE)
interpretation: Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Drug Screen (Qualitative) - immunoassay screening test for tricyclic antidepressant drugs and their metabolites in urine. TCAs are commonly used antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine, doxepin) that inhibit serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake. Qualitative test: detects presence or absence of TCA drugs/metabolites above a threshold concentration. Clinical use: evaluating suspected TCA overdose, confirming TCA ingestion, monitoring compliance (therapeutic drug monitoring), assessing toxicity in unconscious patients, forensic toxicology. Positive TCA screen: recent TCA ingestion (therapeutic or overdose), active metabolites (nortriptyline, desmethyldoxepin), previous TCA use (metabolites may persist 3-7 days), false positives (structurally similar drugs). Negative TCA screen: no recent TCA ingestion (within detection window), very old ingestion (metabolites cleared), sub-therapeutic levels. Limitations: qualitative test gives POSITIVE/NEGATIVE result only - does NOT quantify drug level. For therapeutic drug monitoring or overdose assessment: use quantitative TCA level. Cross-reactivity: structurally similar drugs may cause false positives (phenothiazines, antihistamines, carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine). Detection window: urine TCA metabolites detectable for 3-7 days after last dose (longer in chronic use). Metabolites: active metabolites (nortriptyline, desmethyldoxepin) may cause effects even after parent drug is cleared. False negatives: very old ingestion, low-dose ingestion, renal impairment (delayed excretion). Quantitative levels: for therapeutic monitoring, use serum quantitative TCA level. Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative). Detection threshold: assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note TCA use history, overdose suspicion, symptoms (cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, anticholinergic effects). Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Positive: TCA ingestion detected (within 3-7 days). Negative: no TCA detected. Cross-reactivity: phenothiazines, antihistamines, carbamazepine. Detection window: 3-7 days. False positives: structurally similar drugs. Quantitative: use serum level for therapeutic monitoring. Overdose: cardiac monitoring essential (QRS widening). Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative).
ref_ranges: Positive: TCA ingestion detected (qualitative). Negative: no TCA detected. Detection window: 3-7 days (urine metabolites). Cross-reactivity: phenothiazines, antihistamines, carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine. False positives: structurally similar drugs. False negatives: old ingestion, low dose. Quantitative: use serum level for monitoring. Overdose: cardiac monitoring (QRS >100ms = severe). Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative). Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU; TOXBASE (UK Poisons Information Service).

name: TRIGLYCERIDES
interpretation: Serum Triglycerides - measurement of triglyceride concentration in serum. Triglycerides are the main form of dietary fat transported in the blood as lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL). Elevated triglycerides are an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease and a major cause of acute pancreatitis. Clinical use: assessing cardiovascular risk (part of lipid profile), evaluating hypertriglyceridaemia (risk of pancreatitis), monitoring lipid-lowering therapy, assessing metabolic syndrome (triglycerides >150 mg/dL), evaluating familial hyperlipidaemia. Elevated triglycerides: obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled), alcohol excess (major cause), hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, medications (oestrogen therapy, retinoids, protease inhibitors, thiazides, beta-blockers), familial hypertriglyceridaemia, chylomicronaemia syndrome (TG >1000 mg/dL - pancreatitis risk). Triglyceride categories: normal <150 mg/dL, borderline high 150-199 mg/dL, high 200-499 mg/dL, very high >=500 mg/dL (pancreatitis risk), extremely high >1000 mg/dL (chylomicronaemia syndrome). Triglycerides and metabolic syndrome: >150 mg/dL is one of 5 criteria. Limitations: HIGHLY SENSITIVE to fasting status. MUST be measured fasting (8-12h) - non-fasting triglycerides unreliable. Alcohol: major elevating factor - abstain 72h before testing. Medications: many drugs elevate triglycerides (oestrogen, retinoids, protease inhibitors, thiazides, beta-blockers). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: triglycerides increase with age. Gender: men higher than women until menopause.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: fasting sample (8-12h). Preparation: note diabetes control, alcohol use, medications (oestrogen, retinoids, protease inhibitors, thiazides, beta-blockers). Handling: separate within 30 min; 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Fasting: essential. Pancreatitis risk: >500 mg/dL. Chylomicronaemia: >1000 mg/dL. Metabolic syndrome: TG >150 mg/dL. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: <150 mg/dL. Borderline high: 150-199. High: 200-499. Very high: >=500 (pancreatitis risk). Extremely high: >1000 (chylomicronaemia). Fasting: essential. Age: increases with age.
refs: Sources: ACC/AHA Cholesterol Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRIGLYCERIDES - FLUID
interpretation: Triglycerides in Body Fluids - measurement of triglyceride concentration in pleural, ascitic, or CSF. Diagnoses chylothorax (pleural TG above 110 mg/dL) and chylous ascites (ascitic TG above 200 mg/dL). Pseudochylothorax: cholesterol above 200 plus TG below 110. Clinical utility for differentiating chylous from non-chylous effusions. Limitations: fasting preferred. Process promptly. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Pleural fluid via thoracentesis, ascitic fluid via paracentesis, or CSF via lumbar puncture. Note fasting status and fluid appearance. Handle promptly. Chylothorax: pleural fluid TG above 110 mg/dL. Chylous ascites: ascitic fluid TG above 200 mg/dL. Fasting preferred.
ref_ranges: Pleural fluid: below 110 non-chylous; above 110 chylothorax. Ascitic fluid: below 200 non-chylous; above 200 chylous. Pseudochylothorax: cholesterol above 200 plus TG below 110. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Pleural Effusion Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRIMIPRAMINE
interpretation: Serum Trimipramine measures the concentration of trimipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) with sedative properties. Trimipramine is unique among TCAs as it is not a serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. Therapeutic range: 100 to 300 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500 ng/mL. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note depression, sedation, other medications. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 100-300 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500. Sedative: TCA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 100 to 300 ng/mL. Toxic: greater than 500. Sedative: TCA. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: APA Depression Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRIPEPTIDYL PEPTIDASE 1 - BLOOD
interpretation: Blood Tripeptidyl Peptidase 1 (TPP1) measures the activity of the lysosomal enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1. TPP1 deficiency causes Late Infantile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (CLN2, Batten disease), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder. CLN2: seizures, developmental regression, visual loss, death by age 10. Treatment: cerliponase alfa (enzyme replacement). Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Leucocytes (EDTA blood) or dried blood spot. Preparation: note seizures, developmental regression, visual loss, family history. Handle per standard. Low: CLN2 (Batten disease). ERT: cerliponase alfa. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: greater than 2.0 nmol/h/mg protein (method-specific). Low: CLN2 (Batten disease). ERT: cerliponase alfa. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG LSD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRIPLE MARKER SCREENING - AUTO DELFIA
interpretation: Triple Marker Screening (Triple Screen) is a second-trimester maternal serum screening test combining three biomarkers to assess risk of chromosomal abnormalities and neural tube defects. Markers include alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and unconjugated oestriol (uE3), performed at 15 to 20 weeks gestation. Trisomy 21 pattern: AFP low, hCG high, uE3 low. Trisomy 18 pattern: all three markers low. Elevated AFP suggests neural tube defects such as spina bifida or anencephaly, but also multiple pregnancy or incorrect gestational dating. Detection rate for trisomy 21 is approximately 80 percent with a false positive rate of 5 percent. Screening positive result requires confirmatory testing via amniocentesis or CVS. Limitations: screening test only. Gestational age must be accurately determined. Multiple pregnancy requires adjustment. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific MoM values.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum via standard venipuncture. CRITICAL: gestational age must be accurately determined at 15 to 20 weeks. Preparation: note gestational age, number of fetuses, IVF pregnancy, maternal weight, ethnicity, smoking status. Handle per standard. Trisomy 21: low AFP, high hCG, low uE3. Trisomy 18: low AFP, low hCG, low uE3. NTD: elevated AFP above 2.0 to 2.5 MoM. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific MoM values.
ref_ranges: Risk-based: screen positive versus screen negative. Trisomy 21: low AFP, high hCG, low uE3. Trisomy 18: low AFP, low hCG, low uE3. NTD: elevated AFP above 2.0 to 2.5 MoM. False positive rate: approximately 5 percent. Detection rate: approximately 80 percent for trisomy 21. MoM: multiples of median. Reference ranges: gestational age-specific.
refs: Sources: ACOG Second-Trimester Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TROPONIN I - QUALITATIVE
interpretation: Troponin I Qualitative is a rapid immunoassay screening test for cardiac troponin I (cTnI) in serum. Provides positive or negative result for myocardial injury. Used as point-of-care test for rapid assessment of acute myocardial infarction in emergency settings. Positive result indicates myocardial injury, which includes acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and renal failure. The test is not specific for acute MI alone. Negative result means myocardial injury is unlikely at time of testing, but does not exclude early MI as troponin may not yet be elevated. Troponin elevates 3 to 6 hours after myocardial injury. Limitations: qualitative test gives positive or negative only, not quantitative. For quantitative assessment and serial monitoring use high-sensitivity troponin. False positives occur with myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure, and sepsis. Reference ranges: qualitative result, detection threshold is assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum via standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain timing, ECG findings, cardiac risk factors, renal function. Handle per standard. Positive: myocardial injury detected. Negative: myocardial injury unlikely at time of testing. Timing: troponin may not be elevated in very early MI. Repeat: if clinical suspicion high despite negative result. False positives: myocarditis, heart failure, PE, renal failure. Quantitative: use high-sensitivity troponin for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Positive: myocardial injury detected. Negative: myocardial injury unlikely at time of testing. Timing: troponin elevates 3 to 6 hours after injury. False positives: myocarditis, heart failure, PE, renal failure. Quantitative: use hs-troponin for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: qualitative. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESC ACS Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TROPONIN I HIGH SENSITIVITY (TNIH) - QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: High-sensitivity Troponin I (TNIH) Quantitative is an ultrasensitive immunoassay measuring cardiac troponin I concentrations at levels far below conventional assays. Enables detection of myocardial injury within 1 to 3 hours of symptom onset, compared to 3 to 6 hours with conventional assays. The 0 hour and 1 hour algorithm using high-sensitivity troponin has revolutionised rapid rule-in and rule-out of acute myocardial infarction in emergency departments. Serial measurements at 0 and 1 hour with delta change provide near-instant diagnostic certainty. Elevated TNIH indicates myocardial injury, which encompasses acute coronary syndromes, myocarditis, takotsubo cardiomyopathy, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, renal failure, sepsis, and strenuous exercise. A rising and/or falling pattern with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit confirms acute myocardial injury. Limitations: elevated in chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance plus subclinical myocardial injury), making interpretation in renal patients complex. Sex-specific cutoffs improve accuracy: women have lower baseline troponin. Biotin supplementation at high doses may cause false low results on some immunoassay platforms. Assay harmonisation remains incomplete across manufacturers. Reference ranges: 99th percentile URL is assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain timing (0 hour sample essential), ECG findings, cardiac risk factors, renal function (eGFR, creatinine), medications, strenuous exercise in past 24 hours. Handling: separate within 30 min. 0-hour and 1-hour algorithm for AMI rule-in/rule-out. Rising and falling pattern essential. Sex-specific cutoffs recommended. 99th percentile URL: assay-specific. Renal impairment: elevated baseline. Biotin: false low on some platforms.
ref_ranges: Normal: below 99th percentile URL (sex-specific). Acute MI: above 99th percentile with rise and/or fall pattern. 0-hour and 1-hour algorithm: rule-out if below LOD at 0h and below URL at 1h. Rule-in if above URL at 0h with delta above minimum delta. Renal failure: chronically elevated. Exercise: transient elevation. 99th percentile URL: assay-specific. Sex-specific: women lower than men.
refs: Sources: ESC 0h/1h Algorithm Guidelines; manufacturer IFU; 4th Universal Definition of MI.

name: TROPONIN T - QUALITATIVE
interpretation: Troponin T Qualitative is a rapid immunoassay screening test for cardiac troponin T (cTnT) in serum. Provides positive or negative result for myocardial injury. Similar in principle to Troponin I Qualitative but targets the troponin T subunit. Used as point-of-care test for rapid triage in emergency settings. Positive result indicates myocardial injury, which includes acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and renal failure. The test is not specific for acute MI alone. Negative result means myocardial injury is unlikely at time of testing but does not exclude early MI as troponin may not yet be elevated. Troponin T elevates 3 to 6 hours after myocardial injury. Limitations: qualitative test gives positive or negative only, not quantitative. For quantitative assessment and serial monitoring use quantitative or high-sensitivity troponin T. False positives occur with myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure, and sepsis. Reference ranges: qualitative result, detection threshold is assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum via standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain timing, ECG findings, cardiac risk factors, renal function. Handle per standard. Positive: myocardial injury detected. Negative: myocardial injury unlikely at time of testing. Timing: troponin may not be elevated in very early MI. Repeat: if clinical suspicion high despite negative result. False positives: myocarditis, heart failure, PE, renal failure. Quantitative: use quantitative or hs-troponin T for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Positive: myocardial injury detected. Negative: myocardial injury unlikely at time of testing. Timing: troponin elevates 3 to 6 hours after injury. False positives: myocarditis, heart failure, PE, renal failure. Quantitative: use quantitative or hs-troponin T for serial monitoring. Reference ranges: qualitative. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ESC ACS Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TROPONIN T - QUANTITATIVE
interpretation: Quantitative Troponin T measures the exact concentration of cardiac troponin T in serum using a conventional immunoassay. Unlike the qualitative version, this provides a numerical value enabling serial monitoring and risk stratification. Troponin T is released from damaged cardiomyocytes and elevated levels indicate myocardial injury. Serial measurements at 0 and 3 to 6 hours allow assessment of the rise and/or fall pattern essential for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction per the Universal Definition of MI. A rising and/or falling pattern with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit confirms acute myocardial injury. Chronically elevated troponin T (without dynamic change) is common in chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and stable coronary artery disease, reflecting chronic subclinical myocardial injury rather than acute events. Limitations: elevated in chronic kidney disease due to reduced clearance plus subclinical myocardial injury. Biotin supplementation at high doses may interfere on some platforms. Assay harmonisation is incomplete across manufacturers. Exercise can cause transient elevation. Reference ranges: 99th percentile URL is assay-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note chest pain timing, ECG findings, cardiac risk factors, renal function (eGFR, creatinine), medications, strenuous exercise in past 24 hours. Handling: separate within 30 min. Serial measurements essential for acute MI diagnosis. 0 and 3 to 6 hour algorithm. Rise and/or fall pattern required. 99th percentile URL: assay-specific. Renal impairment: chronically elevated baseline. Biotin: interference on some platforms.
ref_ranges: Normal: below 99th percentile URL. Acute MI: above 99th percentile with rise and/or fall pattern. Serial: 0h and 3 to 6h. Chronic elevation: CKD, heart failure, stable CAD. 99th percentile URL: assay-specific. Exercise: transient elevation.
refs: Sources: 4th Universal Definition of MI; ESC ACS Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TRYPTOPHAN QUANTITATIVE - PLASMA
interpretation: Plasma Tryptophan Quantitative measures the concentration of tryptophan, an essential aromatic amino acid and precursor to serotonin and niacin. Elevated tryptophan: Hartnup disease (impaired intestinal absorption), carcinoid syndrome (increased serotonin synthesis). Low tryptophan: malabsorption, kwashiorkor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Plasma (fasting preferred). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note diarrhoea, dermatitis, neurological symptoms. Handle per standard. Elevated: Hartnup disease, carcinoid. Low: malabsorption, kwashiorkor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: Hartnup, carcinoid. Low: malabsorption, kwashiorkor. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG IEM Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TSH RECEPTOR ANTIBODY
interpretation: TSH Receptor Antibody (TRAb) measures autoantibodies directed against the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells. TRAb are the pathognomonic autoantibodies of Graves disease, present in greater than 95 percent of untreated Graves patients. The test distinguishes autoimmune hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) from other causes of thyrotoxicosis such as toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, or subacute thyroiditis, where TRAb are typically negative. TRAb can be stimulating (TSI, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) or blocking (TBI, TSH-binding inhibitory immunoglobulins). Stimulating antibodies cause unregulated thyroid hormone production, while blocking antibodies cause hypothyroidism. In pregnancy, maternal TRAb cross the placenta and can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis if present at high titres in the third trimester. Serial monitoring during pregnancy guides decisions about antithyroid therapy in the neonate. Limitations: TRAb may be positive in other autoimmune thyroid conditions (Hashimoto thyroiditis) at lower titres. Early or mild Graves may show false negative results. Assay methodology varies (competitive binding versus cell-based bioassays) with different sensitivities. Reference ranges: method-specific. A negative TRAb does not exclude Graves disease if clinical suspicion is high.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note thyroid symptoms (weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance), pregnancy status, family history of thyroid disease, prior thyroid treatment. Handling: separate within 30 min. Graves disease: TRAb positive in greater than 95 percent. Toxic MNG: TRAb typically negative. Subacute thyroiditis: TRAb negative. Pregnancy: maternal TRAb crosses placenta. Neonatal: assess for thyrotoxicosis risk. Blocking antibodies: cause hypothyroidism. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Positive: Graves disease (greater than 95 percent of untreated patients). Negative: toxic MNG, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis. Low positive: Hashimoto thyroiditis, early Graves. Pregnancy: maternal TRAb crosses placenta. Neonatal risk: high titre in third trimester. Blocking antibodies: hypothyroidism. Stimulating antibodies: hyperthyroidism. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ATA Graves Disease Guidelines; Endocrine Society Thyroid Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TUMOUR NECROSIS FACTOR (TNF) ALPHA
interpretation: Serum Tumour Necrosis Factor Alpha (TNF-alpha) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in immune regulation, inflammation, and apoptosis. Elevated TNF-alpha: autoimmune diseases (RA, Crohn disease), infections (sepsis), malignancy (lymphoma). Anti-TNF therapy: infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. No fasting required. Preparation: note autoimmune disease, infection, malignancy. Handle per standard. Elevated: RA, Crohn, sepsis. Anti-TNF: therapy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: RA, Crohn, sepsis. Anti-TNF: therapy. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR RA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: TYROSINE QUANTITATIVE - URINE
interpretation: Urine Tyrosine Quantitative measures tyrosine concentration. Tyrosine is a non-essential amino acid derived from phenylalanine. Elevated tyrosine: tyrosinaemia types I, II, III (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate oxidase deficiency), liver disease, hypothyroidism. Neonatal screening: detects tyrosinaemia. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note hepatorenal failure, liver tumour, developmental delay. Handle per standard. Elevated: tyrosinaemia types I-III. Liver disease: elevates. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: tyrosinaemia, liver disease. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG Tyrosinaemia Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: UNSATURATED IRON BINDING CAPACITY (UIBC)
interpretation: Unsaturated Iron Binding Capacity (UIBC) measures the amount of transferrin that is NOT currently bound to iron. UIBC is calculated as TIBC minus serum iron, or measured directly. UIBC reflects the reserve capacity of transferrin to bind additional iron. UIBC is elevated when iron stores are depleted (iron deficiency anaemia) because the body produces more transferrin with fewer iron molecules attached. UIBC is reduced when iron stores are increased (haemochromatosis) or when transferrin synthesis is impaired (chronic disease, liver cirrhosis). UIBC provides complementary information to TIBC and serum iron for assessing iron status. Limitations: UIBC is influenced by the same factors as TIBC including liver function, nutritional status, inflammation, pregnancy, and oral contraceptive use. UIBC is rarely measured directly in routine practice as TIBC is more commonly available. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age and gender: may vary.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred. Preparation: note anaemia symptoms, iron supplementation, recent transfusions, inflammation, liver function, menstrual history. Handling: separate within 30 min. UIBC: TIBC minus serum iron. Elevated: iron deficiency. Low: iron overload, chronic disease. TIBC: directly proportional to transferrin. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 40 to 150 ug/dL (method-specific). Iron deficiency: elevated UIBC. Iron overload: low UIBC. Chronic disease: low UIBC. Liver cirrhosis: low UIBC. Pregnancy: variable. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Iron Deficiency Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: UREA
interpretation: Serum Urea (Blood Urea Nitrogen, BUN) measures the concentration of urea in serum. Urea is the primary end-product of protein metabolism, synthesised in the liver from ammonia via the urea cycle and excreted by the kidneys. Serum urea is influenced by protein intake, catabolism, hydration status, and renal function. Elevated serum urea (azotaemia) occurs in prerenal causes (dehydration, high protein diet, upper GI bleeding, heart failure), intrinsic renal causes (acute or chronic kidney disease), and postrenal causes (urinary obstruction). Low serum urea is seen in liver failure (reduced urea synthesis), severe malnutrition (low protein intake), pregnancy (expanded plasma volume), and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Urea is less specific than creatinine for assessing renal function as it is influenced by non-renal factors. The urea-to-creatinine ratio helps differentiate prerenal from intrinsic renal causes: ratio greater than 20 to 1 suggests prerenal azotaemia. Limitations: influenced by protein intake, catabolic state, hydration, liver function, and medications (corticosteroids, tetracyclines). Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: increases with age. Gender: men typically higher than women. Diet: high protein diet elevates urea.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred but not essential. Preparation: note protein intake, hydration status, kidney function, liver function, medications (corticosteroids, tetracyclines, nephrotoxic drugs). Handling: separate within 30 min. Prerenal: urea/creatinine ratio greater than 20. Intrinsic renal: ratio normal or low. Liver failure: low urea. Malnutrition: low urea. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 15 to 40 mg/dL (2.5 to 7.1 mmol/L). Azotaemia: greater than 40 mg/dL. Prerenal: urea/creatinine ratio greater than 20. Intrinsic renal: ratio normal or low. Liver failure: low urea. Malnutrition: low urea. Pregnancy: low urea. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: increases with age.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: UREA URINE (SPOT)
interpretation: Spot Urine Urea measures urea concentration in a random urine sample. Unlike 24-hour urine urea which provides total daily excretion, spot urine urea reflects current renal handling of urea and is influenced by hydration status, protein intake, and time of day. Spot urine urea is primarily used in the calculation of estimated protein intake (from urea nitrogen excretion) and in the assessment of renal tubular function. Urine urea nitrogen (UUN) from a 24-hour collection is used to estimate dietary protein intake: protein intake (g/day) equals UUN (g/day) times 6.25. Spot urine urea is less clinically useful than 24-hour urea for these calculations. Limitations: spot urine urea is highly variable depending on hydration status and recent protein intake. 24-hour urine collection is preferred for protein intake estimation. Reference ranges: method-specific. Fasting status affects results.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note protein intake, hydration status, kidney function. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Spot urine: less useful than 24h for protein intake estimation. 24h urine: preferred for UUN. Protein intake: UUN x 6.25. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (diet and hydration dependent). Protein intake estimation: UUN x 6.25 g/day. Spot urine: variable. 24h urine: preferred. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDOQI Nutrition Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URIC ACID
interpretation: Serum Uric Acid measures the concentration of uric acid in serum. Uric acid is the final metabolic product of purine metabolism in humans, produced by the enzyme xanthine oxidase. Uric acid is freely filtered by the glomerulus, then partially reabsorbed and secreted by the renal tubules. Elevated serum uric acid (hyperuricaemia) is the major risk factor for gout, uric acid nephrolithiasis, and urate nephropathy. Hyperuricaemia is also associated with cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, and hypertension, though causality remains debated. Primary hyperuricaemia results from inborn errors of purine metabolism (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, HGPRT deficiency). Secondary hyperuricaemia is caused by increased purine production (myeloproliferative disorders, tumour lysis syndrome, psoriasis), decreased renal excretion (chronic kidney disease, medications such as thiazides, loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporine), or increased dietary purine intake. Low serum uric acid is rare and may indicate severe liver disease, SIADH, Fanconi syndrome, or X-linked hypophosphataemia. Limitations: serum uric acid has significant diurnal variation (higher in morning). Affected by diet (purine-rich foods), alcohol, fructose, and medications. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: increases with age. Gender: men typically higher than women until menopause.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. Standard venipuncture. Fasting preferred. Preparation: note gout symptoms, kidney function, medications (thiazides, loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporine), diet (purine-rich foods, alcohol, fructose). Handling: separate within 30 min. Hyperuricaemia: greater than 7.0 mg/dL (men), greater than 6.0 mg/dL (women). Gout risk: greater than 6.8 mg/dL (saturation point). Tumour lysis: markedly elevated. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 2.5 to 7.0 mg/dL (men), 1.5 to 6.0 mg/dL (women). Hyperuricaemia: greater than 7.0 mg/dL (men), greater than 6.0 mg/dL (women). Gout threshold: greater than 6.8 mg/dL (urate saturation). Low: severe liver disease, SIADH, Fanconi syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age: increases with age.
refs: Sources: ACR Gout Guidelines; EULAR Gout Recommendations; manufacturer IFU.

name: URIC ACID SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Spot Urine Uric Acid measures uric acid concentration in a random urine sample. Used alongside serum uric acid to assess renal uric acid handling and to evaluate the cause of hyperuricaemia. The fractional excretion of uric acid (FEUA) can be calculated from spot urine uric acid, serum uric acid, and urine creatinine to differentiate renal underexcretion from overproduction of uric acid. FEUA less than 5 percent suggests renal underexcretion (most common cause of hyperuricaemia, associated with chronic kidney disease, medications such as thiazides and loop diuretics). FEUA greater than 12 percent suggests overproduction (myeloproliferative disorders, tumour lysis syndrome) or Fanconi syndrome. Urine uric acid greater than 800 mg/day (or greater than 600 mg per gram creatinine on spot) in a patient on a standard diet suggests overproduction. Limitations: spot urine uric acid is influenced by hydration status, diet, and time of day. 24-hour urine collection is preferred for quantitative assessment. Urine pH affects uric acid solubility: acidic urine promotes uric acid crystallisation and stone formation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note serum uric acid, kidney function, diet (purine intake), medications. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. FEUA: less than 5 percent = underexcretion; greater than 12 percent = overproduction. Spot urine: variable. 24h urine: preferred for quantification. pH: acidic promotes crystallisation. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (diet and hydration dependent). FEUA less than 5 percent: renal underexcretion. FEUA greater than 12 percent: overproduction or Fanconi. Spot urine greater than 600 mg/g creatinine: overproduction. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACR Gout Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINARY CALCIUM SPOT
interpretation: Spot Urine Calcium measures calcium concentration in a random urine sample. Used as a screening test for hypercalciuria, a major risk factor for calcium-containing kidney stone formation. Spot urine calcium to creatinine ratio (Ca/Cr) is more reliable than random urine calcium concentration alone as it corrects for urine concentration. Ca/Cr ratio greater than 0.14 mg/mg (or greater than 0.20 mg/mg in some references) suggests hypercalciuria. Spot urine calcium is a reasonable alternative to 24-hour urine calcium for initial screening, though 24-hour collection remains the gold standard for quantification. Elevated spot urine calcium is seen in primary hyperparathyroidism, distal renal tubular acidosis, sarcoidosis, idiopathic hypercalciuria, and vitamin D intoxication. Low spot urine calcium may indicate hypoparathyroidism, severe vitamin D deficiency, or malabsorption. Limitations: spot urine calcium is influenced by recent dietary calcium intake and time of collection. 24-hour urine collection is preferred for definitive assessment. Ca/Cr ratio corrects for hydration status. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note serum calcium, PTH, vitamin D, kidney stone history, diet (calcium intake). Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Ca/Cr ratio: greater than 0.14 mg/mg suggests hypercalciuria. Spot urine: screening only. 24h urine: gold standard. Dietary: affects results. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: Ca/Cr ratio less than 0.14 mg/mg. Hypercalciuria: Ca/Cr ratio greater than 0.14 mg/mg. Low: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency. Spot urine: screening. 24h urine: definitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: European Association of Urology Stone Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINE FOR DNPH TEST
interpretation: Urine DNPH (2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine) Test is a qualitative screening test that detects ketone bodies (acetone and acetoacetic acid) in urine. The DNPH reagent reacts with the carbonyl group of ketone bodies to form a yellow-orange precipitate. This test is used to screen for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), starvation ketosis, and alcoholic ketoacidosis. Positive DNPH test indicates the presence of ketone bodies in urine, which occurs when脂肪酸 (fatty acid) oxidation exceeds the capacity of the citric acid cycle, leading to ketogenesis in the liver. Causes of positive DNPH: diabetic ketoacidosis (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus), starvation ketosis (prolonged fasting, severe calorie restriction), alcoholic ketoacidosis (heavy alcohol use with poor nutrition), high-fat low-carbohydrate diets (ketogenic diet), pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum). The DNPH test detects acetone and acetoacetic acid but NOT beta-hydroxybutyrate, which is the predominant ketone body in DKA. Limitations: semi-quantitative at best (colour intensity correlates roughly with concentration). Does not detect beta-hydroxybutyrate. False positives: levodopa metabolites, phenylketonuria, melanogenuria. False negatives: old urine samples (acetoacetic acid degrades). Reference ranges: qualitative (positive/negative).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (spot). Preparation: note diabetes control, fasting status, alcohol use, diet, pregnancy. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Positive: ketone bodies present. Negative: no ketone bodies detected. DNPH: detects acetone and acetoacetic acid only. NOT beta-hydroxybutyrate. DKA: positive. Starvation: positive. Alcoholic: positive. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Positive: ketone bodies present (acetone, acetoacetic acid). Negative: no ketone bodies. DKA: positive. Starvation: positive. Alcoholic ketoacidosis: positive. Beta-hydroxybutyrate: NOT detected. False positives: levodopa, PKU. False negatives: old urine. Reference ranges: qualitative. Assay: qualitative.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINE FOR FERRIC CHLORIDE TEST
interpretation: Urine Ferric Chloride Test is a qualitative chemical screening test that detects abnormal metabolites in urine. Ferric chloride (FeCl3) reacts with phenolic compounds, keto acids, and certain drug metabolites to produce characteristic colour changes. Historically used as a broad screening test for inborn errors of metabolism (phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, tyrosinaemia) and for detecting salicylate poisoning. Green colour: phenylketonuria (phenylpyruvic acid). Purple-violet: maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain keto acids). Brown-green: salicylate (aspirin) poisoning. Red-brown: tyrosinaemia (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid). Yellow-orange: normal urine (no abnormal metabolites). Limitations: non-specific and largely superseded by more specific assays (amino acid chromatography, tandem mass spectrometry, drug-specific immunoassays). Many medications produce colour reactions (phenothiazines, isoniazid, para-aminosalicylic acid). Semi-quantitative only. Must be performed on fresh urine as abnormal metabolites degrade. Reference ranges: qualitative (colour-based interpretation).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (fresh spot). Preparation: note medications, diet, family history of metabolic disease, suspected poisoning. Handle fresh. Green: PKU. Purple: MSUD. Brown-green: salicylate. Red-brown: tyrosinaemia. Yellow-orange: normal. Non-specific: many medications interfere. Superseded by: specific assays. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Green: PKU (phenylpyruvic acid). Purple-violet: MSUD (branched-chain keto acids). Brown-green: salicylate poisoning. Red-brown: tyrosinaemia. Yellow-orange: normal. Non-specific: many drugs interfere. Superseded by: specific assays. Reference ranges: qualitative. Assay: qualitative chemical test.
refs: Sources: Tietz Clinical Guide; Inborn Errors of Metabolism Screening Guidelines.

name: URINE FOR MUCOPOLYSACHHARIDES
interpretation: Urine Mucopolysaccharides (MPS) test detects and semi-quantifies glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in urine. GAGs are long-chain complex carbohydrates that are components of connective tissue. Elevated urine GAGs are the hallmark of mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS), a group of inherited lysosomal storage diseases caused by deficiency of specific enzymes required for GAG degradation. The test screens for conditions including Hurler syndrome (MPS I), Hunter syndrome (MPS II), Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS III), Morquio syndrome (MPS IV), and Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome (MPS VI). Elevated urine GAGs are also seen in other connective tissue disorders and may be non-specifically elevated in infants (normal in first year of life). The test uses dye-binding methods (Alcian blue, toluidine blue) or electrophoresis to detect GAGs. Limitations: semi-quantitative screening test only. False positives in neonates (physiologically elevated GAGs in first year). Non-specific: elevated GAGs may occur in non-MPS connective tissue disorders. Must be followed by specific enzyme assays and GAG profiling for definitive diagnosis. Reference ranges: age-specific. Assay: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note family history of metabolic disease, developmental delay, skeletal abnormalities, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Elevated: mucopolysaccharidosis. Neonates: physiologically elevated (first year). Semi-quantitative: screening only. Confirm with: specific enzyme assays. Reference ranges: age-specific.
ref_ranges: Elevated: mucopolysaccharidosis (Hurler, Hunter, Sanfilippo, Morquio, Maroteaux-Lamy). Neonates: physiologically elevated (first year). Non-specific: connective tissue disorders. Semi-quantitative: screening only. Confirm with: enzyme assays. Reference ranges: age-specific. Assay: dye-binding or electrophoresis.
refs: Sources: ACMG MPS Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINE FOR NITROSO-NAPHTHOL TEST
interpretation: Urine Nitroso-Naphthol Test is a qualitative screening test for tyrosine metabolites, specifically detecting homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria) and p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (tyrosinaemia). The test is used in the screening of inborn errors of tyrosine metabolism. Alkaptonuria (homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency) produces a characteristic red or orange colour when nitroso-naphthol reagent is added to urine. Tyrosinaemia type I (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency) may produce a positive reaction with p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid. The test has been largely superseded by more specific methods (tandem mass spectrometry, quantitative homogentisic acid, specific enzyme assays). Limitations: non-specific and semi-quantitative. Many substances can produce colour reactions (aspirin metabolites, salicylates, phenothiazines, melanogen). Must be performed on fresh urine as metabolites degrade. Reference ranges: qualitative (colour-based interpretation).
pre_analytical: Sample: Urine (fresh spot). Preparation: note darkening of urine on standing (alkaptonuria), joint problems, family history of metabolic disease. Handle fresh. Positive (red-orange): homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria). Positive (colour): p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (tyrosinaemia). Non-specific: many drugs interfere. Superseded by: MS/MS. Reference ranges: qualitative.
ref_ranges: Positive red-orange: homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria). Positive colour change: p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (tyrosinaemia). Non-specific: many drugs interfere. Superseded by: tandem mass spectrometry. Reference ranges: qualitative. Assay: qualitative chemical test.
refs: Sources: Inborn Errors of Metabolism Screening Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINE FOR PORPHOBILINOGEN
interpretation: Urine Porphobilinogen (PBG) measures the concentration of delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) deficiency precursor in urine. PBG is an intermediate in the haem biosynthesis pathway. Elevated urine PBG is the hallmark biochemical finding in acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), the most common acute porphyria caused by deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS). An acute porphyria attack presents with severe abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark (port-wine) urine. Other causes of elevated urine PBG include hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria. Urine PBG is normal in cutaneous porphyrias (porphyria cutanea tarda) where uroporphyrinogen is elevated instead. Limitations: urine PBG must be measured during an acute attack for reliable results. PBG is light-sensitive and degrades rapidly in urine left at room temperature. False negatives: urine collected between attacks, old urine samples, PBG degradation. False positives: certain medications (sulphonamides, barbiturates, ergot alkaloids) can precipitate acute attacks in genetically susceptible individuals. Reference ranges: method-specific. Screening: qualitative (Watson-Schwartz test) or quantitative.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (fresh). CRITICAL: must be collected during acute attack. Preparation: note symptoms (abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric, dark urine), medications, family history of porphyria. Handle: protect from light, process immediately or freeze. Positive: acute porphyria (AIP, HCP, VP). Negative: cutaneous porphyrias. PBG: light-sensitive. Attack-dependent: between attacks may be normal. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 4 mg/day (or less than 1 mg/L qualitative). Elevated: AIP, HCP, VP. Normal: between attacks, cutaneous porphyrias. PBG: light-sensitive. Attack-dependent: must be acute phase. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: quantitative or qualitative.
refs: Sources: European Porphyria Network Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: URINE PROTEIN CREATININE RATIO SPOT
interpretation: Spot Urine Protein Creatinine Ratio (PCR) estimates 24-hour urine protein excretion from a single spot urine sample. The ratio of urine protein to urine creatinine corrects for urine concentration and provides a reasonable approximation of daily protein excretion. Normal PCR is less than 0.15 mg/mg (or less than 150 mg/g creatinine). PCR greater than 0.15 mg/mg indicates proteinuria. PCR greater than 0.5 mg/mg suggests significant proteinuria (nephrotic-range when greater than 3.5 mg/mg). PCR is primarily used for screening and monitoring of proteinuria in chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. PCR greater than 3.5 mg/mg in the context of nephrotic syndrome indicates severe glomerular proteinuria. Limitations: PCR provides an approximation of 24-hour protein excretion and is influenced by postural proteinuria (orthostatic proteinuria is benign and may cause false positive spot PCR). Exercise, fever, and heart failure can cause transient proteinuria. PCR is less accurate than 24-hour urine protein for quantification. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note kidney function, diabetes control, blood pressure, medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs), exercise, fever. Handling: 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. PCR: less than 0.15 mg/mg normal. Greater than 0.15 mg/mg: proteinuria. Greater than 3.5 mg/mg: nephrotic range. Spot urine: less accurate than 24h. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: PCR less than 0.15 mg/mg. Proteinuria: PCR greater than 0.15 mg/mg. Significant: PCR greater than 0.5 mg/mg. Nephrotic: PCR greater than 3.5 mg/mg. Orthostatic: benign false positive. Exercise: transient. 24h urine: more accurate. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: KDIGO CKD Guidelines; ADA Diabetes Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VALPROIC ACID (VALPROATE)
interpretation: Serum Valproic Acid (Valproate) measures the concentration of valproic acid, a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser. Therapeutic range: 50 to 100 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 100 mcg/mL. Highly protein-bound (90%). Teratogenic: neural tube defects. Hepatotoxic: risk in children less than 2 years. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough level). Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note seizure control, liver function, pregnancy. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: 50-100 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 100. Teratogenic: NTDs. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: 50 to 100 mcg/mL. Toxic: greater than 100. Teratogenic: NTDs. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: AAN Epilepsy Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VANCOMYCIN
interpretation: Serum Vancomycin measures the concentration of vancomycin, a glycopeptide antibiotic used to treat methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Clostridioides difficile infection. Therapeutic: AUC/MIC-guided dosing. Traditional trough: 10 to 15 mcg/mL. Nephrotoxic: risk. Ototoxic: risk at high levels. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (trough or AUC-guided). CRITICAL: timing depends on protocol. Preparation: note MRSA, C. difficile, renal function. Handle per standard. Therapeutic: AUC-guided. Trough: 10-15 mcg/mL. Nephrotoxic: risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Therapeutic: AUC-guided. Trough: 10 to 15 mcg/mL. Nephrotoxic: risk. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: IDSA MRSA Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VANILLYL MANDLIC ACID (VMA) SPOT - URINE
interpretation: Urine Vanillyl Mandelic Acid (VMA) Spot measures the concentration of VMA, the final metabolic product of catecholamine (adrenaline and noradrenaline) metabolism, in a random urine sample. VMA is used as a screening test for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Elevated urine VMA is found in approximately 90 percent of phaeochromocytomas. However, urine metanephrines (normetanephrine and metanephrine) are now preferred as the first-line screening test due to superior sensitivity (97 to 99 percent versus 90 percent for VMA). VMA is less sensitive than metanephrines because it represents a smaller proportion of catecholamine metabolism. Spot urine VMA is less reliable than 24-hour urine VMA as VMA excretion varies throughout the day. Limitations: less sensitive than urine metanephrines for PPGL screening. Spot urine less reliable than 24-hour collection. False positives: certain foods (vanilla, bananas, caffeine, chocolate), medications (catecholamines, salicylates, levodopa), stress, and strenuous exercise. Reference ranges: method-specific. Age and gender: may vary.
pre_analytical: Sample: Spot urine (random). Preparation: note symptoms (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, palpitations, diaphoresis), medications (catecholamines, salicylates, levodopa), diet (vanilla, bananas, caffeine). Handle: protect from light, 2-8C up to 48h or -20C. Elevated: phaeochromocytoma (approximately 90 percent). Less sensitive than: metanephrines. Spot urine: less reliable than 24h. False positives: foods, medications. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 6.5 mg/day (or less than 3.5 mg/g creatinine). Elevated: phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma. Less sensitive: than metanephrines. False positives: foods, medications, stress. Reference ranges: method-specific. Assay: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VASOACTIVE INTESTINAL POLYPEPTIDE (VIP)
interpretation: Serum Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) measures the concentration of VIP, a 28-amino acid neuropeptide. Elevated VIP: VIPoma (Verner-Morrison syndrome, WDHA syndrome - watery diarrhoea, hypoklaemia, achlorhydria). VIPoma: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. VIP: stimulates intestinal secretion. Greater than 75 pg/mL: diagnostic. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum. CRITICAL: on ice. Preparation: note secretory diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria. Handle per standard. VIPoma: pancreatic NET. Greater than 75 pg/mL: diagnostic. WDHA: syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: less than 75 pg/mL (method-specific). Greater than 75: VIPoma. WDHA: syndrome. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ENETS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VERY LONG CHAIN FATTY ACID
interpretation: Plasma Very Long Chain Fatty Acid (VLCFA) measures concentrations of C22:0, C24:0, C26:0 and ratios (C24/C22, C26/C22). VLCFA elevations: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD), which is a peroxisomal beta-oxidation defect. X-ALD: cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency, axonal neuropathy. Males: screening test. Females: less sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Whole blood (EDTA). Preparation: note adrenal insufficiency, neurological symptoms, family history. Handle per standard. Elevated: X-ALD. Males: screening. Females: less sensitive. Peroxisomal: defect. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: variable (method-specific). Elevated: X-ALD. Males: screening. Females: less sensitive. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: ACMG X-ALD Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.

name: VITAMIN A (RETINOL)
interpretation: Serum Vitamin A (Retinol) measures retinol concentration. Retinol is essential for vision, immune function, epithelial differentiation, and reproduction. Deficiency: xerophthalmia, night blindness, immune dysfunction, keratomalacia. Excess: hepatotoxicity, pseudotumour cerebri, teratogenicity. Beta-carotene: pro-vitamin A; does not cause toxicity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
pre_analytical: Sample: Serum (fasting preferred). CRITICAL: light-protected tube. Standard venipuncture. Preparation: note vision problems, immune dysfunction, liver disease. Handle: light-protected. Deficiency: xerophthalmia. Excess: hepatotoxicity. Reference ranges: method-specific.
ref_ranges: Normal: 20 to 60 mcg/dL (method-specific). Deficiency: less than 20. Excess: greater than 80. Reference ranges: method-specific.
refs: Sources: WHO Vitamin A Guidelines; manufacturer IFU.
